# Alcinous the Platonist’s Introduction to the Dialogues of Plato
<note>original: "Alcini platonis Introductio i dialogos platonis"</note>

A 2

A dialogue is a form of discourse composed of questions and answers regarding some political or philosophical matter, combined with the appropriate <term>characterization</term> <note>original: "ethopoieia," the art of crafting a speech that fits the specific character and personality of the speaker</note> of the persons involved and the arrangement of the wording. There are two primary characters of the dialogue: the <term>instructional</term> <note>original: "hyphegetikos"</note> and the <term>inquiry-based</term> <note>original: "zetetikos"</note>. The instructional type is directed toward teaching, action, and the demonstration of the truth. The inquiry-based type is directed toward mental exercise, debate, and the refutation of falsehood. Furthermore, the instructional type aims at the subject matter itself, while the inquiry-based type focuses on the persons involved. 

The dialogues of Plato are classified as follows: to the **natural** <note>original: "physikos," concerning the physical world and nature</note> and the **ethical** belong the *Timaeus* and the *Apology*; to the **logical** belong the *Theaetetus*, *Cratylus*, *Lysis*, *Sophist*, *Laches*, and *Statesman*; to the **refutative** belong the *Parmenides* and *Protagoras*; to the **political** belong the *Crito*, *Republic*, *Phaedo*, *Minos*, *Symposium*, *Laws*, *Epistles*, *Epinomis*, *Menexenus*, *Cleitophon*, and *Philebus*; to the **testing** <note>original: "peirastikos"</note> belong the *Euthyphro*, *Meno*, *Ion*, and *Charmides*; to the **midwifery** <note>original: "maieutikos," referring to Socrates’ method of helping others "give birth" to their own ideas</note> belongs the *Alcibiades*; and to the **subversive** belong the *Hippias*, *Euthydemus*, and *Gorgias*.

Since we have observed their differences as they naturally occur, let us also discuss their characters, and from which dialogues one ought to begin when encountering the works of Plato. Different opinions have arisen: some begin with the *Epistles*, others with the *Theaetetus*. Still others, dividing them into <term>tetralogies</term> <note>original: "tetralogian," groups of four, modeled after the sets of four plays performed at Athenian drama festivals</note>, place as the first tetralogy the one containing the *Euthyphro*, the *Apology*, the *Crito*, and the *Phaedo*. They choose the *Euthyphro* because the legal charge against Socrates is announced in it; the *Apology* because it is then necessary for him to defend himself; after these, the *Crito* because of his time spent in prison; and then the *Phaedo*, since in it Socrates reaches the end of his life. Dercyllides and Thrasyllus <note>Thrasyllus (died 36 AD) was a scholar and astrologer who is credited with the standard arrangement of Plato's works into nine tetralogies.</note> are of this opinion. It seems to me, however, that they wished to impose an order based on persons and life circumstances, which is not useful for the goal we now desire: to find the beginning and arrangement for the teaching of wisdom.

Some say, therefore, that there is no single, fixed beginning to Plato’s work. For it resembles a perfect shape, like a **circle**. Just as in a circle there is no one primary beginning, so it is with his discourse. For this reason, we may touch upon it wherever we happen to start. Just as one does not write a circle by beginning at any specific point, so one may attempt the dialogues starting from wherever each of us finds a particular <term>disposition</term> <note>original: "schesis," a state of mind or personal connection</note> toward the discourse. There are many and varied dispositions among us toward...

<summary>This page introduces the definition and classification of Plato's dialogues, distinguishing between instructional and inquiry-based styles. It also debates the proper order for reading the dialogues, contrasting a biographical/chronological approach with a more flexible, circular pedagogical model.</summary>
<keywords>Alcinous, Plato, Dialogues, Socrates, Tetralogies, Thrasyllus, Dercyllides, classification of dialogues, pedagogy, Maieutics</keywords>

--- Page 8 ---
<meta>This page continues a discussion on the curriculum and pedagogical order of Plato's dialogues, likely from a Neoplatonic commentary or introduction to philosophy.</meta>

...the discourse. For one [disposition] is according to nature, such as being naturally gifted or ungifted; another is according to age, such as being in the prime for practicing philosophy <note>original: "φιλοσοφεῖν"</note> or being past one's prime; another is according to purpose, such as for the sake of philosophy or history; another is according to linguistic skill, such as being previously initiated or unlearned; and another is according to the subject matter, such as having fallen in love with philosophy or being drawn toward practical affairs. 

Now, the student who is naturally gifted, in the prime of age for philosophy, and who approaches the discourse with the purpose of practicing virtue and beauty—having been previously initiated in the preparatory sciences <note>The "mathematics" or liberal arts</note> and released from political affairs—begins with the *Alcibiades*. For it is inscribed for this purpose, and in reality, he will not cease his care, as if looking toward a beautiful model of who the philosopher is, what his pursuit entails, and upon what premise the present discourse announces itself. 

Second, he encounters the *Phaedo* in due order. For in it, [Plato] says who the philosopher is and what the pursuit is, and on the premise that the soul is immortal, he directs the preceding discourse. After this, he may encounter the *Republic* <unclear>divinely</unclear>; for beginning from the first birth, [Plato] sketches the entire system of education <term>Paideia: the holistic upbringing and cultural education of a Greek citizen</term>, by using which one might arrive at the land of eternal motion. 

Since it is also necessary to come near to the gods, so as to be able to liken one's virtue to them by becoming like them, we shall encounter the *Timaeus*. For in it, by inquiring into the things concerning nature and the so-called theology <note>In this context, "theology" refers to the study of divine causes and the cosmos</note> and the arrangement of the whole, we clearly grasp the more divine matters. 

There is also a way to beautifully summarize the proper order of the dialogues for one beginning the teachings according to Plato. For since it is necessary to become spectators of one's own soul, of the gods, of divine things themselves, and of the beauty of the soul, one must first clear away the false opinions of one's assumptions. For even physicians <unclear>do not consider</unclear> that the body can enjoy the nourishment offered to it before one casts out the internal obstacles. After this cleansing, it is necessary to awaken and call forth our innate ideas...

<summary>This text outlines the ideal student's disposition and the specific pedagogical sequence of Plato's dialogues—starting with the Alcibiades for self-knowledge and moving through the Phaedo, Republic, and Timaeus to reach divine understanding.</summary>
<keywords>Plato, Alcibiades, Phaedo, Republic, Timaeus, philosophy, education, theology, soul, virtue</keywords>

--- Page 9 ---
<meta>This page concludes the introductory discussion on the curriculum of Plato's dialogues. It transitions from the purpose of the preparatory dialogues to a classification of the dialogues by their "character" (characteros) or pedagogical function, focusing on how different types of dialogues prepare the soul for the ultimate goal of "becoming like God."</meta>

...which cleanses all things and reveals those [faculties of the soul] as first principles. Upon these, once the soul has been prepared, he instills the right doctrines <note>original: "δόγματα" (dogmata)</note> through the soul itself, according to its ultimate end. These doctrines are physical and theological, as well as ethical and political. By reshaping the parts of the soul with these doctrines, it becomes necessary to drive away error through the reasoning of cause <note>Using "cause" (aitia) to anchor the mind in true origins rather than mere opinion</note>, so that the proposed goal may remain secure.

In addition to these things, one must establish an "incapability of being deceived" so that we are not led astray by some sophist <note>The Sophists were professional teachers in Ancient Greece often accused of using clever but fallacious arguments</note> and turn our own disposition <term>Hexis: a stable state of character or mind</term> toward the worse. To cast out false opinions, it is necessary to study Plato’s dialogues of the **testing** character <note>original: "πειραστικός" (peirastic). These are dialogues where Socrates tests his interlocutor’s beliefs to reveal their ignorance.</note>; these possess a refutative and what is called a **cleansing** power. 

If one wishes to call forth the natural workings of the mind as a light, it is necessary to study the dialogues of the **midwifery** character <note>original: "μαιευτικός" (maieutic). Referring to the Socratic method of "giving birth" to knowledge already latent within the soul.</note>; for this is their specific trait. 

To receive the appropriate doctrines, one must study the dialogues of the **instructional** character <note>original: "ὑφηγητικός" (hyphegetic). These are dialogues that provide direct teaching rather than just asking questions.</note>; for this is their specific trait. In these, the physical doctrines are demonstrated, as well as the ethical, political, and **economic** <note>original: "οἰκονομικά" (oikonomika). In the classical sense, this refers to the management of the household or private estate.</note> ones. Some of these refer to contemplation and the **contemplative life**, while others refer to action and the **practical life**. Both of these aim toward the goal of **becoming like God** <note>original: "ὁμοιωθῆναι θεῶ" (homoiosis theo). This is the central aim of Neoplatonic philosophy: to restore the soul to its divine likeness through virtue and knowledge.</note>.

So that the teachings given to us remain inescapable, it is necessary to study dialogues of the **logical** character, as they were established. For they contain the methods of **division** and **definition**, as well as those of **analysis** and **syllogism**, through which truths are demonstrated and falsehoods are refuted. 

Furthermore, since we may be deceived by sophists, we shall study dialogues of the **demonstrative** and **subversive** character. In these, we can learn how to understand the sophists, how to deal with them, and in what way they act maliciously against the truth of discourse.

-> . The End . <-

<summary>This page concludes a pedagogical introduction to Plato, classifying his dialogues into functional categories (testing, midwifery, instructional, and logical) designed to cleanse the soul, instill doctrine, and protect the student from sophistic deception. The ultimate aim of this curriculum is stated as "becoming like God" through both contemplation and action.</summary>

## <unclear>Porphyry’s *On the Life of Plotinus and the Order of His Writings*</unclear>

Plotinus, the philosopher who lived in our time, seemed like a man who was ashamed of being in a body. Because of this disposition, he could not bear to talk about his ancestry, his parents, or his native land. <gloss>to himself</gloss> <gloss>to endure</gloss> <gloss>but</gloss> He held such a strong aversion to these matters that when Amelius <note>Amelius Gentilianus was Plotinus's student and primary assistant for eighteen years.</note> asked him to allow a portrait of himself to be made, he replied: “Is it not enough to carry this image which nature has wrapped us in? Must you also ask me to consent to leave behind a longer-lasting image of an image <note>original: "εἴδωλον εἰδώλου". This reflects the Platonic idea that the physical body is already a mere copy of the true soul; a painting would be a copy of a copy, further removed from reality.</note>, as if it were something worth looking at?” 

Because he refused and would not agree to sit for a portrait, Amelius brought in his friend Carterius—the best painter of that era—and allowed him to attend the lectures. Anyone who wished was allowed to attend. Carterius accustomed himself to the sight of Plotinus by paying close attention during these sessions. Then, he secretly drew a sketch from the memory of what he had seen. With Amelius directing the corrections to ensure it matched the man's likeness, the skill of Carterius produced a portrait of Plotinus without Plotinus ever knowing it. 

The portrait was a striking likeness. <gloss>and indeed the body</gloss> Yet, his body was often in distress; however, he would not endure the use of an enema <term>enema: a liquid medical treatment injected into the lower bowel, common in ancient medicine</term>.

He said that for a man of his age <margin>elderly</margin>, it was not fitting to undergo such treatments. Nor would he agree to take "theriac" <term>theriac: a famous ancient medicinal concoction used as a universal antidote, often containing many herbal and animal ingredients</term>; instead, he accepted only simple food from domestic animals. He avoided public baths, but he made use of daily massages at home. 

However, when those who used to perform these massages died during a plague, he neglected the treatment. Consequently, his condition grew worse and turned into a violent ailment. While I was away <note>Porphyry is referring to himself here; he had traveled to Sicily on Plotinus's advice to recover from depression.</note>, no such symptom had appeared.

He received these supplies from the property of Castricius <note>Castricius Firmus was a wealthy friend and student of Plotinus who supported the philosopher and his circle.</note>. Castricius held his possessions in those parts. Porphyry <note>The author of this biography.</note>, who had hoped to be with him and stay with him, arrived to see him only slowly, as he was staying elsewhere. At that place, Plotinus sought to spend his remaining time in peace, trying to achieve what the myth calls "the good leader" <note>This likely refers to the "daimon" or guiding spirit, or the pursuit of the "Good" in Neoplatonic philosophy.</note>. During this time, a divine serpent <unclear>crawled</unclear> under the bed where he lay and disappeared into a hole in the wall, indicating his passing. For he had reached the end of his strength. He died at the completion of the second year of the reign of the Emperor Claudius <note>Claudius II Gothicus, placing the death in 270 CE.</note>, as reported to him. Porphyry was not present, but Hellenus and the students of Amelius or Aspasius of Syria were. Castricius was in Rome. Plotinus himself told us that from the second year of the reign of Claudius, counting back sixty-six years, the time of his birth falls in the thirteenth year of the reign of Severus <note>Septimius Severus, placing his birth around 204 or 205 CE.</note>. He treated the details of his birth with a sort of amusement, and would never reveal his birthday or celebrate it with a feast. However, on the traditional birthdays of Plato and Socrates, he would offer sacrifices and host a feast for his companions, where those who were able were expected to deliver a discourse before the gathered friends.

<meta>This page continues the biography of the philosopher Plotinus by his student Porphyry. The previous page detailed Plotinus’s final days in Campania and his death during the second year of the Emperor Claudius II’s reign. The narrative now shifts back in time to recount Plotinus’s early education in Alexandria, his meeting with his master Ammonius Saccas, and his journey to the East.</meta>

Therefore, when he was twenty-eight years old <note>The OCR transcription reads "eight," but historically Plotinus began his studies in his twenty-eighth year.</note> he was impelled <gloss>to set out for philosophy</gloss> and this <margin>according to common report</margin> led him to be introduced to the most respected teachers in Alexandria. He went there to hear their lectures, but he would come away feeling <gloss>full</gloss> <note>original: "plērē." Likely meaning "heavy-hearted" or "burdened" by the lack of depth in their teaching.</note> of distress, as if the benefit was worth nothing and he was wasting his time. He told his plan and his honors to a friend of his, who suggested he try Ammonius <note>Ammonius Saccas (c. 175–242 AD), the influential and largely self-taught philosopher of Alexandria who is considered the founder of Neoplatonism.</note>. Plotinus had not yet tried him, but upon entering and hearing him, he said to his companion, "This is the man I was looking for!" And <gloss>from that day</gloss> forward, staying continuously with Ammonius, he acquired such a high capacity in philosophy that he was even entrusted with <unclear>spirits</unclear> <note>original: "daimones." In this context, it refers to higher spiritual intelligences or the guiding genius of a person.</note> to receive wisdom from him. Having been trained in this education and character for <unclear>eleven years</unclear>, he wished to observe the philosophy practiced by the Persians and the most excellent traditions among the Indians.

He joined the expedition of the Emperor <unclear>Gordian</unclear> <note>Gordian III, who led an ill-fated campaign against the Sassanid Persian Empire in 243 AD.</note>. But when Gordian was murdered in Mesopotamia, Plotinus barely escaped and was saved upon reaching Antioch. When Philip <note>Philip the Arab, who succeeded Gordian as Emperor.</note> took over the empire, Plotinus, having reached forty years of age, went up to Rome. <gloss>Explaining</gloss> both Origen <note>This refers to Origen the Pagan, a fellow student of Ammonius, not the famous Christian theologian Origen.</note> and Plotinus, they held to the <gloss>doctrines of Ammonius in common</gloss>, which they had brought forth from their private declarations.

Plotinus remained there, keeping silent for a time while others who approached him brought up these doctrines of Ammonius. But <gloss>he was annoyed</gloss> when the first one broke the agreement, for it had been determined that they should follow what had been previously established. He wrote nothing at first. Plotinus did not write a treatise before his studies on spirits. <margin>Origen on demons</margin> And during the time of Gallienus <note>Roman Emperor from 253 to 268 AD, who was a friend and patron to Plotinus.</note>, it is agreed by all that the <unclear>Emperor</unclear> favored him. He did not immediately begin writing a great deal, but continued his lectures as if they were <unclear>scattered unorganized gatherings</unclear>. And in this way, he spent a total of ten years. He wrote nothing; he was only in discourse, as if he were being urged on by those who were with him. He spoke of the <gloss>Christian nonsense</gloss> <note>original: "christianikēs phluarias." And from the third year of the Emperor Philip's reign, until the first year of the reign of Claudius, he remained there for the whole duration.

<meta>This page continues Porphyry’s account of Plotinus’s circle in Rome. Having discussed the senators and politicians who admired him, the text now turns to specific scholars and a detailed description of Plotinus’s unique, almost meditative method of writing, as well as the women who formed part of his inner philosophical circle.</meta>

Serapion of Nicaea, an Alexandrian who was at first a teacher of rhetoric but later associated with philosophers, was also among them; however, he struggled to tear himself away from his preoccupation with money and lending. He also held us—Porphyry—in the highest honor and was one of our closest companions; he even requested that I correct his writings. For once Plotinus had written something, he could never bear to go over the text a second time; 
<margin>note</margin> 
indeed, he did not even read it through once, because his eyesight did not serve him well enough for reading. He wrote without forming the letters beautifully, without separating the syllables clearly, and without caring for <term>orthography</term> <note>The set of conventions for writing a language, including spelling, hyphenation, and capitalization.</note>; he focused only on the thought. 

And what we all marveled at was the manner in which he worked until the end: having completed the entire "struggle" <note>original: "skamma"; literally the dug-up ground of a wrestling pit, here metaphorically referring to the mental exertion of completing a complex philosophical argument from start to finish.</note> in his own mind from beginning to end, he would then commit his thoughts to writing, pouring them out continuously as if he were transcribing them from a book. Even when he was conversing with someone and maintaining a dialogue, he remained focused on his mental inquiry without interruption. He would attend to the necessity of the conversation and the matter at hand while keeping his intellect undivided. 

<margin>Plotinus was constant in mind.</margin> 

When the visitor left, he would not even re-read what he had written—because, as we mentioned, his vision was insufficient for reading—but he would pick up the next part of the text as if no time had passed since he had been interrupted by the conversation. 
<margin>note</margin> 
He was thus able to be present to himself and to others at the same time, and he never relaxed this inward attention to himself except during sleep (which he fought off) or due to his meager diet; for he did not eat much. His turning toward the intellect was constant.

<margin>note / 12 / already</margin>

<margin>The sanctity of Plotinus</margin> 
...bringing their own children, both boys and girls, they would entrust them to him along with their property, as if to a certain holy and divine guardian. For this reason, his house was filled with young boys and maidens; among them was Potamon, whose education Plotinus took great care to oversee. 

<margin>ffᵃ 12</margin> 

He would often listen to those presenting the accounts of the children’s <term>estates</term> <note>original: "klemata"; literally "branches," but here referring to the divided portions of an inheritance or family tree.</note> and would personally involve himself in the details. He used to say that as long as they were not yet living as philosophers, they ought to have their possessions and incomes kept intact and preserved for them. 

And yet, despite providing so much care and attention to the practical needs of life for so many people, he never relaxed his mental concentration during the day. He remained present to himself and to others simultaneously, even during his activities and in all the various and sometimes difficult circumstances he encountered. Because of this, though he spent twenty-six whole years in Rome and acted as an arbitrator for a great many people in their disputes with one another, he never made an enemy of any public official. 

<margin>The envious spirit [attacking] Plotinus</margin> 

However, a man named Olympius of Alexandria, who had been a student of Ammonius for a short time, developed a contemptuous attitude toward the philosopher because of his own desire to be first. Olympius attacked him so relentlessly that he even attempted to strike Plotinus with magical spells. But when Olympius saw the attempt turning back upon himself, he told his close companions that the power of Plotinus’s soul was so great that it could repel the "discharges" of evil and turn them back upon those who sent them. 

Plotinus himself said that while Olympius was attempting these things, he felt his body being pulled together like a <term>drawstring purse</term> <note>original: "syspasta balantia"; a common ancient purse or bag that closes by pulling strings, causing it to contract and wrinkle.</note>, with his limbs being pressed tightly against each other. After Olympius found himself frequently in danger of suffering the very things he intended for Plotinus, he finally stopped. 

Indeed, there was an extraordinary quality to Plotinus’s nature from birth. <insert>For</insert> a certain Egyptian priest who had come up to Rome and was introduced to him through a friend, wanting to give a demonstration of his own wisdom, asked Plotinus to come and witness the manifestation of his "companion spirit" <term>daemon</term> <note>original: "oikeios daimon"; in ancient Greek thought, this was a personal guardian spirit or guiding divinity that accompanied a person throughout life.</note>. 

<margin>Plotinus's guardian spirit</margin> 

Plotinus readily agreed, and the invocation took place in the Iseum;

for the priest said that this was the only pure spot...

He promised to retire there himself with his companions. This wish would have been very easily fulfilled for the philosopher, had it not been for certain courtiers of the Emperor who, out of envy, spite, or some other malicious reason, prevented it.

In his gatherings, he was remarkably capable of expression, and most adept at discovering and perceiving the truth of a matter. However, he would occasionally make mistakes in certain words; for he did not care for the precision of his **stylus** <term>stylus</term> <note>original: "stylou"; here referring to his literary style and the technical manner of his writing.</note>, but looked only to the meaning. He was lovely to behold, but he appeared at his most beautiful at those moments. A faint dew of sweat would stand out on him, and his gentleness shone through; he showed a gracious and vigorous spirit in responding to questions.

Indeed, when I, Porphyry, questioned him for three days on how the soul is joined to the body, he continued his demonstration for all those days. He thought that he should expect nothing newer from me, nor anything at all of the old works which you say you have lost. <meta>This page continues the long quotation from Cassius Longinus, a prominent third-century scholar and critic. In the previous section, Longinus began his survey of contemporary philosophers, distinguishing between those who left behind written works and those who did not. He now turns to specific authors and their scholarly contributions, eventually leading to his assessment of Plotinus and Amelius.</meta>

After having dealt with the *Philebus* and the *Gorgias* <note>Two famous dialogues by Plato concerning pleasure and rhetoric, respectively.</note> and the works of **Aristotle**, which were interpreted less thoroughly, I did not proceed to be numbered among the teachers of his doctrines; for this would have required the same level of intense study. Turning then to those who were already inclined toward writing, I consider **Callimachus** among the Stoics <note>A follower of the Stoic school, which emphasized virtue and logic.</note>, and those who lived to an old age, **Athenaeus** and **Musonius**, as well as **Ammonius** and **Ptolemy** regarding the *Topics* <note>Referring to Aristotle’s *Topics*, a treatise on logical argumentation.</note>. 

These were the most <term>philological</term> <note>In this context, "philological" refers to scholars who were extremely learned in existing texts and commentaries, rather than purely original "speculative" philosophers.</note> of the men flourishing in their time, especially **Ammonius**, for there is no one who was more practiced in study than him. Similarly, even after the formal arts, there were no remains of their works that were not examples of their demonstrative skill, though they sometimes employed a lack of refinement. 

There are others who, I believe, did not receive these teachings directly from him, but later attempted to publish them through their own books, and those who stored their own knowledge in more serious compositions. As for what should be written, some know nothing more than what they find in scripts, and they simply reproduced the works composed by the elders, such as **Euclides**, **Democritus**, and **Proclinus**. Others, having memorized small portions of the histories of the ancients, attempted to compose books on the same subjects as those men, such as **Agnoites**, **Madios**, and **Phaidon**. The latter, because of his <margin>Of Plotinus</margin> success, might be considered worthy of recognition more for his own unique arrangement than for his familiarity with the subject.

And who would not also bring up **Heliodorus** and those who composed works after him? One might refute those who are brought into accusations regarding the elders, specifically those who skip over the internal structure of the discourse. <meta>This page continues the conclusion of Porphyry's "Life of Plotinus." The previous page presented the beginning of the Oracle of Apollo, which praised Plotinus's soul. Here, Porphyry provides his own commentary on the Oracle and explains how he organized Plotinus's writings into the "Enneads." The catchword "hypostatically" suggests the transition to a discussion on the levels of divine reality.</meta>

<margin>Plotinus was often seized by the divine.</margin>

For him, the goal and purpose was to draw near to and be joined with the God who is over all things. While I was with him, he achieved this goal four times, through an ineffable activity <term>energeia: actualized divine presence or activity</term> and not merely through potential. And because he was often carried along crooked paths, the gods frequently set him straight, radiating frequent beams of light, so that his writings might be seen as images and letters sent from them. From his sleepless vision, both within and without, he claimed to see many manifestations and beautiful signs. This man was among those who applied themselves to philosophy before all else; from whom this same contemplation <term>theoria: the act of seeing or contemplating divine truth</term> might arise in human peak. As for divine knowledge, these visions are beautiful, so that they might grasp the depths that are smoothed over when the senses are stripped away. The oracle said these things concerning Plotinus. He passed through the gates after this, having ceased from the body. He entered into the peak of his own nature, whatever it might be. Many such things happened because of his long ambition for the holy love of God, which was kindled within him. He has been ranked with those called the judges of souls, the children of God: Minos, Rhadamanthys, and Aeacus <note>In Greek mythology, these three were the judges of the Underworld who decided the fate of the deceased.</note>. He does not even stand trial before them, but goes to dwell with them, alongside whom these best eternal gods also dwell: Plato, Pythagoras, and as many others who established the choir of immortal love. There, he attains the most noble birth among the good spirits <term>daimons: divine beings or guardian spirits</term>, finding delight in festivities and joys. He continues to live this way, blessed by the gods. Such, then, was the life of Plotinus according to history. Since he himself entrusted the arrangement and the correction of his books to me—not having permitted this beauty to us, as I promised in a certain place and announced to the other companions that I would do—first, I did not leave the books published in a confused, chronological order. Instead, I imitated Apollodorus the Athenian <note>An important scholar and grammarian from the 2nd century BCE.</note> and Andronicus the Peripatetic <note>The scholar credited with organizing Aristotle’s works into the system we use today.</note>. The former collected the works of the comic writer Epicharmus into ten volumes, while the latter divided the works of Aristotle and Theophrastus into treatises, grouping them by their proper subjects.

<meta>This page transitions from the divine accolades of the Oracle of Apollo to Porphyry’s practical editorial work. Having established Plotinus’s spiritual authority, Porphyry now explains how he organized the philosopher’s chaotic collection of writings into the structured format known today as the "Enneads."</meta>

Having brought together these fifty-four books of Plotinus, I have divided them into six <term>Enneads: From the Greek "ennea" (nine); a collection of nine books or treatises</term>. I was pleased to find this arrangement by utilizing the perfection of the number six <note>In ancient Pythagorean numerology, 6 was considered a "perfect number" because it is the sum of its divisors (1+2+3).</note> and by assigning nine books to each Ennead. It also seemed appropriate to arrange them in a sequence beginning with the easier problems.

The first Ennead contains the more ethical subjects, as follows: 
*   "What is the Living Being and What is Man?"
*   Next, "On Virtues"
*   Then, "On Dialectic"
*   Then, "On Happiness"
*   Then, "On Whether Happiness Increases with Time"
*   Then, "On Beauty"
*   Then, "On the First Good and Other Goods"
*   Then, "Whether Some Other Good Exists for Each Being"
*   "Whence Come Evils"
*   And finally, "On the Well-Reasoned Departure" <note>This refers to the philosophical discussion on the conditions under which a person might rationally choose to leave life (suicide).</note>. 

The first Ennead, therefore, encompasses these works, covering ethical themes. 

The second Ennead contains a collection of physical <term>physics: in the ancient sense, the study of "physis" or nature and the material world</term> matters, including those concerning the cosmos and the things belonging to the cosmos. These are: 
*   "On the World"
*   Then, "On the Circular Motion"
*   Then, "On the Planets"
*   Then, "That the Stars Do Not Cause Events" <note>original: "οὐκ ἔστιν ἐκ τῶν ἄστρων τὰ σημαίνοντα" — Plotinus argued that stars are signs of the future rather than the literal causes of human fate.</note>
*   "On the Second Essence"
*   "On Actuality and Potentiality"
*   "On Quality and Form"
*   "On Matter"
*   "On Total Blending"
*   Then, "On the Whole Essence"
*   Then, "On How the Stars Act"
*   Then, "On Evil and the Creator of the World"
*   And "Against Those Who Say the Creator of the World is Evil" <note>This refers to Plotinus's famous polemic against the Gnostics, who believed the material world was created by a flawed or malicious deity.</note>. 

Such is the content of the second Ennead. The third Ennead, also containing matters of physics, encompasses theories regarding the world.

Yet it is also private, because each individual possesses it as a whole in their primary part. We therefore possess the Forms <term>Forms (Eide): The eternal, perfect patterns of all things in the intelligible world.</term> in two ways: in the soul, they are unfolded and, as it were, separated; but [in the Intellect] they are all united. And what of God? How do we have Him? Perhaps as one riding upon the intelligible nature and upon True Being. We are "third" from God. One might say we come from the indivisible part above and from the part that is divided among bodies. It is necessary to say it is "divided" among bodies because the soul gives itself to the physical dimensions of the bodies, according to how large each living creature may be. Because of this, the soul is imagined to be present throughout the bodies. But while it illuminates them and gives them life, it does not do so by merging itself with the body. Instead, it remains itself, while providing images <term>Eidola: Reflections or "shadows" of the soul's true power that interact with matter.</term> of itself, just as a face might appear in many mirrors. The first image is the sensory faculty, which exists in the "common" <note>The "common" (koinon) refers to the union of body and soul.</note>. After this, there is another "light" of the soul, which consists of the virtues and the rest of the <unclear>faculty of judgment</unclear> and perception. This is generally the cause of "making" and of other finished results produced by the active parts of the soul. If the active parts are directed toward the things above <unclear>ordered</unclear>, then the lower part follows the movements of the soul. This lower part is the cause of evils—of all that it does and suffers. These things happen regarding the "living being" (the common union). A difficult question is asked: how can the opinions and the ignorance of the soul be "sinless"? Perhaps opinions and the schemes of the wicked belong to the part that touches evil; for we are often moved by desire, or anger, or a "bad image." Even what is called "ignorance"—being a product of the imagination—does not allow the judgment of the thinking faculty to come through. Instead, we act because we are persuaded by the worse parts, just as with sensation, before the thinking faculty can judge. It is not just that we perceive evils, but we are touched by them. We should not demand that they be entirely the same, but rather different, if indeed it is made like in a different way. What, then, are the virtues, either as a whole or individually? The reasoning will be clearer regarding each one; for in this way the common element, according to which all virtues are what they are, will easily become clear.

Moving forward, he is led by certain "erotic" or "love-driven" impulses <note>referring to the *erotikos*, the "Lover" type</note>, through which everything is sought. He must be taught, therefore, not to fall for physical bodies, but to look beyond them. For this [physicality] is the very nature of the body. Living is necessary for all, yet we must explain that this beauty—which seems so strong in physical bodies—actually comes from elsewhere.

It must be shown that beauty exists even more in other things: for instance, in character, in the brightness of beautiful deeds, in laws, and in the sciences. For immediately after the beauty of bodies, one encounters the incorporeal <note>non-physical realities</note>. This beauty is found in the arts, the sciences, and the virtues. Then, one must bring these together into a unity and teach the true source from which they arise. From the virtues, the seeker is already ascending toward the **Intellect** <note>original Greek: *nous*</note> and toward **Being**. And there, one must walk the "upward path."

**The philosopher**, by nature, is ready and "winged," so to speak <note>A reference to Plato’s *Phaedrus*, where the soul grows wings to fly back to the divine realm</note>. He does not require the same kind of "separation" from the world as the others. He has already been moved toward the heights, yet he remains in a state of doubt; he only needs someone to show him the way—one who is willing and holy by nature.

As for the remaining steps, he must be given mathematical studies <note>arithmetic, geometry, etc.</note> solely to habituate him to the understanding of and belief in the incorporeal. Because he is a "lover of learning" <note>original Greek: *philomathes*</note>, he will accept these easily. Since he is virtuous by nature, he must be led to the perfection of the virtues. After the mathematical studies, he must be given "dialectical discourses," and he must be made entirely a **Dialectician**.

<insert> What is **Dialectic**? </insert>

Which must also be handed down to the previous types [the musician and the lover]? It is the state of mind <note>original Greek: *hexis*</note> regarding each thing, being able to say in speech what each thing is, how it differs from others, and what they have in common. It identifies where each thing exists, and whether it truly is what it is; it accounts for how many beings there are, and likewise for "non-beings," which are different from beings.

This science of **Dialectic** also discourses about the **Good**, and about what is not good; it examines everything that falls under the Good and everything under its opposite. It clarifies what is eternal and what is not. Having settled its mind on all things, it will not cease its journey until it stops the "wandering" concerning the Intelligible realm. It sees everything within **Being**, and there it occupies itself, leaving falsehood behind and nourishing the soul in what is called the "**Plain of Truth**." It uses the **Platonic Division** <note>A method of logical classification and definition used by Plato</note> to distinguish the **Forms** <note>original Greek: *eide*; the eternal archetypes of things</note> and to define the essence of what a thing is.

We posit that **happiness** <term>eudaimonia</term> <note>True flourishing or "the good life," more robust than simple "feeling happy."</note> is a constitutive **activity** <term>energeia</term> <note>In Greek philosophy, this is "being-at-work" or actualized existence.</note> of these things which we produce. And the participation of these things, which possess this difference, is by a <unclear>logical</unclear> analogy; and likewise for the more irrational thing, which is <unclear>logical</unclear> and like an **image** <note>original: "eidolon."</note> of the higher life. <summary>Plotinus argues that happiness (eudaimonia) is not merely the act of being alive, but is specifically a "constitutive activity" (energeia) of the rational soul, distinguishing it from the biological life shared with plants and animals.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the examination of Plotinus’s treatise on happiness. While the previous page questioned if life itself is the "good," this section refines the definition, arguing that only a specific, "perfect" kind of life—the intellectual life—can truly be called happiness. It includes significant Latin marginalia attempting to reconcile Plotinus's Neoplatonism with Christian Trinitarian theology.</meta>

<margin>
The highest of all things is life itself, which is the same as the Trinity itself. <note>original: "Summūꝫ omniūꝫ ꝫ ip̄a vita. ꝙ idē est ꝙ ip̄a trinitas."</note> And since it is one essence, I do not change all life from a certain order toward this same thing. Which is one and is called the Good.
</margin>

<margin>
The Highest Good is called the first life, that is, the Trinity, that is, the first life without addition, but life itself, the first Good. <note>original: "Summū bō̄ dicit huic nōneq̄ ē p̄ma vita .i. trinitas .i. p̄ma nōnē ē vita cū additamētō."</note> I change what is most human and the order. Why? Because man is the image of the Trinity; man is a part, man is a quality.
</margin>

By this reasoning, **happiness** <term>eudaimonia</term> <note>The state of flourishing or living well.</note> would belong to man alone among all other living things. For this [intellectual life] is the best, if indeed the best among these is the "truly living" being. And it follows: for the Good would not belong even to dogs, nor would it be a law <note>original: "nomimon"</note> existing elsewhere behind the subject; they will not be permitted to exist within any [true] good. For what could be added to the perfect beings to make them the best? If there is some irrational nature, it will dwell [in life], but not in the Good itself, and it is certainly not the same thing. To those things which are in no way perfect, or true, or "really" beings, there is not even a purely intellectual essence. And that which is entirely incomplete [cannot be happy]. And the other animals are just as they appear. Even if they are called "living" completely or purely, they are not "mostly" living; for as one might say, the term is often used loosely. But now it shall be stated concisely: that as long as all living things depend on that first principle, the others never diminish the principle of the first life. This perfection and the whole of all life exists as if in its own life. And those in whom these lives exist find happiness. This same happiness is even attributed to the gods.

<margin>
True **Intellect** <term>intellectus</term> is perfect life, and it is alive in the Good. <note>original: "Intellectꝫ veruꝫ ē̄ vita p̄fecta viva est in bono."</note> But the Good is not called this or that by act or by power. If life were the same as the Good for this purpose, then the rest would follow so that it could not be opposed. Let it appear to none... do this to me through him, so that I can return to life, and the will, and the order, just as man. Or the "capons" <note>likely a scribal error or obscure reference to "heads/chapters" or perhaps a metaphor for the flightless/irrational.</note> which pertain to life.
</margin>

If, then, life is set apart for these [rational] beings alone, and if we say that this being happy exists also in us, we must consider how this might be. For if this man possesses perfect life, he possesses not only every good, but also what remains; and at least it is true, as if derived from causes <insert>he takes it away as being the cause</insert>, and not from some other thing, and he is not himself entirely [happy] unless he has this. Just as if he were in **activity** <term>energeia</term> <note>The state of being "in work" or fully realized.</note>; we say the other things are common <insert>but these are like parts of him, possessing the form of life</insert>. This is what it means to be perfect. Another man has this only in potential, but the happy man is already this, and has transitioned into being this very thing. All other things are wrapped around him. One would not place those things as "parts" of him, as they hang around him against his will. They are joined to him according to his will; for this man, his own Good is what he has. But that which is "Beyond" is the cause of the Good within him. And so it is otherwise.

---

Everything, therefore, exists. But it is known to happen differently in this way; for it is the **substance** <term>hypostasis</term> <note>The underlying reality or fundamental essence.</note> of all things that are created by God. For how does everyone know, if they are not even brothers? For if they are not even brothers, as everyone knows.

When the mirror is present, it produces the image of the activity. In this way, the immaterial intellectual thought works within the soul. It brings those things within us into a state where the images of **discursive thought** and the **Mind** are reflected. When these things are known, they are like sensations, according to our prior knowledge: that the Mind and discursive thought are active. But if this [mirror] is shattered because the **harmony of the body** is disturbed, the **Mind** and **discursive thought** still think, but they do so without an image; then the act of thinking occurs **without imagination**. <note>Plotinus is explaining how a sage can be "thinking" or "happy" even while unconscious or in deep sleep; the "mirror" of consciousness is broken, but the "light" of the mind still shines.</note> 

Thus, thinking can be seen as a movement accompanied by imagination. For it is not necessary for one who is **reading** to be consciously aware that he is reading, especially when he reads with intense focus. Nor does the **brave man**, in the moment he acts with bravery, realize "I am acting bravely." He simply acts according to his courage, and there are a thousand other examples. Consequently, conscious apprehensions <note>the "accompaniments" or "monitoring" of our own thoughts</note> actually make the actions themselves dimmer...

<summary>Plotinus explains that intellectual activity (thinking) occurs constantly in the higher soul, but we only become "conscious" of it when it is reflected in the "mirror" of the imagination. <meta>This page continues Plotinus’s investigation in Enneads I.4 into the nature of true happiness (eudaimonia). The previous page discussed the "Noble Man" in the Bull of Phalaris, establishing that internal virtue is the only source of well-being, independent of physical circumstances.</meta>

<margin>//</margin>
And by providing a mixture of good and evil, one would not be the cause of good and evil in the way that such a mixture implies; and it is not easy to find someone who, though possessing this, would not be called **happy** <note>original: "eudaimōn" — referring to a state of flourishing or well-being</note> or worthy. He does not possess "greatness" or things worthy of **Wisdom** <note>original: "sophia"</note>, nor does his essence consist of some pure good in a common or public sense, but rather he lives alone in himself. For correctly **Plato** removes the Good from external things and deems it right to receive it from above. And he who intends to be wise and happy must look toward that reality, and be made like unto it, and live according to it.
<insert>This, then, is the only thing one must hold toward the **End** <note>original: "telos" — the ultimate purpose of human life</note>. And again, even these circumstances might change.</insert>
He does not possess happiness through the additions of chance, but by aiming for it entirely. Even when other things are poured around him, he remains as he is, as long as he remains in this state. These external things are up to me, as it were, regarding life and its power; but the man himself is the cause of his own state, and is not hindered. He will let go of the body and depart when nature’s timing is right, being himself the master of his own counsel. Regarding this, some of his works will tend toward **happiness** <note>original: "eudaimonia"</note> and others will not; nor will they be for the sake of what remains, and in general they are not "his," but belong to the service he provides. He will not worry, and he will keep himself away as much as possible.

Consider how a musician treats a **lyre**: he uses it as long as he can; if he cannot, he will exchange it, or he will abandon the use of the lyre and cease his activity upon it. He has another task to perform without the lyre; he will look with indifference upon the instrument lying nearby, as he now sings without instruments. Yet it was not in vain that the instrument was given to him from the beginning, for he has already used it many times.

<margin>5.</margin> Does happiness increase with the passage of time, because it is being experienced continuously? For neither does the length of time create the quality of happiness, nor does it make it "complete." Rather, let happiness be a standing still, a disposition in the present, and the **activity** <note>original: "energeia"</note> of life. If someone should say—just as with living or finding health—that he who has more of such a thing is "more happy," we must first ask if this makes it "more" of a happiness. If so, then a subsequent moment would be better than the one before it, and happiness would no longer be measured by the ancient standard—

<summary>Plotinus uses the metaphor of a musician and his lyre to explain that the soul (the musician) uses the body (the instrument) but can flourish and "sing" without it. He concludes by arguing that true happiness is a present state of being that does not increase simply because more time passes.</summary>

Beauty is mostly found in the sense of sight. It is also found in hearing, through the composition of words. It is also present in all music, for melodies and rhythms are beautiful. What likeness, then, exists between the beauties of this world and those of the higher realm? If there is a likeness, in what way are both "there" and "here" beautiful? We say these things are beautiful by their **participation in Form.** 

For anything that lacks shape—even though it is naturally meant to receive shape and form—remains ugly and outside the <term>Divine Reason</term> <note>original: "theiou logou"; the rational principle that gives order to the universe</note> so long as it has no share in that Reason or <term>Form</term> <note>original: "eidos"; the ideal blueprint of a thing</note>. This is ugliness in its absolute state. A thing is also ugly if it has not been fully mastered by shape and reason, because its <term>Matter</term> <note>original: "hyle"; the raw, chaotic "stuff" of the universe</note> has refused to be completely molded according to the Form. 

When Form approaches, it takes that which is destined to be made of many parts and organizes them; it brings them into a single arrangement and forces them to exist in harmony. Since the object was not a unity by itself, the Form makes it a single shaped entity as far as it is possible for something made of many parts to be one. 

Form establishes beauty upon the object by harmonizing it into a unity. It gives of itself to both the parts and the whole. When it finds something that is already a single, uniform substance, it gives that same beauty to the entire thing at once—for example, sometimes to an entire house with all its components, and sometimes to a single stone. 

Nature provides beauty in the first case, while Art <note>Plotinus is likely referring to the architect or the sculptor who imposes an idea upon stone.</note> provides it in the second. Thus a beautiful body comes into being through a Reason-Principle descending from the gods. The power within the soul recognizes this beauty; it is the most authoritative judge of its own concerns, especially when the rest of the soul's perceptive faculty joins in. 

Perhaps the soul itself speaks, harmonizing the object with the Form within itself, using that Form as a rule for judgment, just as a carpenter uses a ruler to test what is straight. Thus, the beauty found in a body is that which is in harmony with the beauty that existed *prior* to the body. 

How does the soul, by harmonizing the external architecture of a house with the internal standards within you, declare the house to be beautiful? Is it not because the external house—if you were to strip away the stones—is really an internal, indivisible Idea manifested in a divisible, material form, appearing in many...

Once the soul takes up the **Form** within a body, binding it and mastering the opposing nature—which is shapeless—it grants it shape and rides extensively upon other shapes. Coming together into a single unity, which is Beauty itself, the soul still lacks full knowledge and continues to seek, but it refers everything back to what is within itself. From where, then, does the beauty of color come? How does its shape master this darkness through the presence of something that is lightless, incorporeal, a <term>Reason</term> <note>original: "logos"; here meaning the rational structure or "formula" of a thing</note>, and a <term>Form</term>? 

This is why **fire** itself is beautiful compared to all other bodies; it holds the rank of Form in relation to the other elements. It is lowly in its position on earth, yet it is the most subtle of all bodies, being nearly incorporeal. It alone does not receive other things into itself, while other things receive it. For they are heated by it, but it is not cooled by them. It is the first thing to be colored, and others receive the "form of color" from it. It is, therefore, bright and shining, as if it were Form itself. That which does not master the light becomes faded and is no longer beautiful, as if it no longer participates in the form of color.

There are also **harmonies** in sounds; the invisible harmonies create the manifest ones, and in this way, they cause the soul to grasp a sense of beauty by showing the same principle in another medium. This beauty follows the senses, being measured by numbers in every <term>Proportion</term> <note>original: "logo"; referring to mathematical or rational ratio</note>; but it would not exist unless these proportions held sway in the creation of the Form. 

Concerning these beauties in the senses—which are like images and shadows that have run out into <term>Matter</term> <note>original: "hyle"</note> and, by appearing there, have organized and decorated it—one must look beyond them toward the higher beauties. These are beauties that the sense-perception is not permitted to see, but which the soul sees and speaks of without the use of physical organs. One must ascend to behold these, leaving sense-perception behind to look elsewhere.

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s "On Beauty" (Ennead I.6). Having previously described the soul’s "ugliness" as a result of it being covered in the "mud" of material concerns, Plotinus now explains how the soul recovers its natural beauty through purification (katharsis) and its ascent back to the divine Intellect.</meta>

...as they truly say. If we were to say that the soul’s danger lies in its involvement with the body and the material world in general, we would be speaking correctly.

And this state is what is ugly for a soul: to be neither pure nor unmixed—just as if someone were to sprinkle earthy matter over gold. If someone were to strip this away, what remains is gold, and it is beautiful; set apart from other things, it is left <unclear>perhaps</unclear> to be with itself alone. In the same way, the soul also: when it is set apart from the desires it holds because of the body—with which it associated too closely—and when it is delivered from the other passions and purified of what it acquired while becoming "embodied," it recovers its nature. It is not that the passions themselves are the soul; rather, its ugliness comes from the removal of its [true] nature by the presence of an alien one.

<margin>Every virtue is a purification</margin> For indeed, as the ancient saying goes, self-control, courage, and every virtue are a purification of the soul; and so too is wisdom itself. Therefore, it is well said by those who speak in riddles <note>Plotinus refers here to the Orphic mysteries or Plato's *Phaedo*, which suggest that the "uninitiated" or "unpurified" wallow in mud in the afterlife</note> that the unpurified person will lie in mud in the underworld. For that which is impure is a "friend to mud" because of its vice—just as pigs, whose bodies are unclean, delight in such things. 

For what would true self-control <term>temperance</term> <note>original: "sōphrosynē", the virtue of moderation and self-mastery</note> be, except to not associate with the pleasures of the body, but to flee from them as being neither pure nor belonging to a pure being? And courage is the lack of fear regarding death; and death is simply the soul being apart from the body. One does not fear this if they love to be alone. And greatness of soul <term>magnanimity</term> <note>original: "megalopsychia", literally "having a large soul," implying a disdain for petty, worldly matters</note> is the looking down upon things here [in the material world]. And wisdom <term>prudence</term> <note>original: "phronēsis"</note> is a type of thinking that turns away from things below and leads the soul toward things above. 

Thus the soul, once purified, becomes both a Form and a Reason-Principle <note>original: "eidos te kai logos"; technical terms meaning the soul takes on its true, intelligible structure</note>; it is entirely incorporeal and intellectual. It belongs wholly to the divine, which is the source of beauty and all things related to it. Therefore, when the soul is led up to the Intellect, it becomes even more beautiful. For Intellect and the things that come from Intellect are the soul's own beauty, not something foreign to it; because this alone is what the soul truly is. 

This is why it is rightly said that for the soul to become good and beautiful is to be made like unto God <note>original: "homoiōtheisan tō theō", a central Platonic goal of "likeness to God"</note>, for beauty comes from that source. And reality—or rather, the things that truly exist—to the degree they exist more fully, they are more beautiful. But the "other nature" is the ugly, and this is the same as the Primary Evil. Thus, that which is the same as the Good is also the Beautiful, or rather, the Good and Beauty are one. Therefore, in the same way, we must seek...

<summary>Plotinus argues that the soul’s beauty is its natural state, which is obscured by the "mud" of the body; through the purification of the virtues, the soul returns to its divine, intellectual source. He identifies the soul's ultimate beauty with its likeness to God and its unity with the Good.</summary>

# Page 16

...there are things which even that [the soul] sees. If, then, one says he could not see it by himself, nor could he see into it in this way, remaining here in the midst of this world’s wealth and enjoying it, while making himself like it—what then would this Beauty still be? For this itself is the highest Beauty, being the <term>First Principle</term> <note>original: "τὸ πρῶτον" (to proton); the source from which all existence flows.</note>, and it makes its lovers beautiful and lovely. 

And so, the greatest and ultimate contest lies before souls, for which all our labor is spent: not to be without a share in this most excellent of visions. He who achieves it is blessed, having beheld a blessed sight; but he is unfortunate who fails to achieve it. For the unfortunate man is not he who fails to attain beautiful colors or bodies, nor power, nor high office, nor even he who fails to attain kingship; rather, it is he who fails to attain this and this alone. For the sake of this vision, one should cast away kingships and commands over the whole earth and sea and sky, if by leaving these behind and looking beyond them, one might turn toward That and see it.

<margin>Note.</margin>

What then is the way? What is the means? How shall one behold this unimaginable beauty, which stays within the holy sanctuaries and does not come forth where the <term>uninitiated</term> <note>original: "βέβηλος" (bebelos); those who are profane or have not been purified through philosophy.</note> might see it? Let him who can, go and follow into the inner place, leaving behind the sight of the eyes, and let him not turn back toward the former splendors of bodies. 

For when one sees the beauties in bodies, one must not run after them, but recognizing that they are only images and traces and shadows, one must flee toward that of which these are images. For if one should rush to grasp it as though it were true—like a beautiful phantom riding upon the water—in wanting to catch it (as a certain myth, I believe, enigmatically suggests), he sinks down into the depths of the stream and vanishes. <note>Plotinus is referring to the myth of Narcissus, who fell in love with his own reflection in a pool and drowned while trying to embrace it. For Plotinus, this is a metaphor for the soul becoming lost in the material world.</note> In the same way, the one who clings to beautiful bodies and does not let go will sink—not in body, but in soul—into the dark and joyless depths of the mind. There, remaining blind in <term>Hades</term> <note>The Greek underworld; here used metaphorically for a state of spiritual ignorance.</note>, both here and in the life to come, he will consort only with shadows. 

"Let us flee then to our beloved fatherland," <note>Quoting a famous line from Homer's *Iliad* (2.140). Plotinus reinterprets the "fatherland" as the divine realm where the soul originated.</note> this is a more truthful exhortation. What then is the flight? And how shall we set sail? Just as, he says, one escapes from the sorceress <term>Circe</term> <note>The enchantress from the *Odyssey* who turned Odysseus's men into swine; she represents the seductive power of the physical senses.</note> or...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the soul's ascent toward the "First Beauty." # 1

...and by rejecting it with the eyes, so it seems to me. <note>original: "μῆνας οὐ καρδι-" – this line in the transcription appears to be a fragmented or corrupted rendering of the Greek text which usually warns against chasing physical shadows.</note> And by giving names to these places. And again, concerning the most beautiful of **sensible bodies** <note>original: "αἰσθητῶν σωμάτων" (aisthēton sōmatōn); things that can be perceived by the physical senses rather than the mind.</note>, let us pass over that from which we came. And our fatherland is where we came from. And our Father is there. 

But how shall we travel? Not by feet, for feet only carry us from one land to another here on earth. Nor do you need to prepare a carriage of horses or a sea vessel; rather, you must let all these things go <insert>must</insert> and not look. Instead, as if closing your eyes, you must exchange your vision for another <gloss>ai</gloss> and awaken <gloss>ai</gloss> another way of seeing, which everyone possesses, but few actually use.

What then does this inner vision see? When newly awakened, it is not at all able to look upon brilliant things. Therefore, the soul itself must be trained: first, to look at beautiful ways of life; then, at beautiful works—not those produced by the technical crafts, but those performed by men who are called "good." Then, look at the soul of those who have performed these beautiful works. 

<insert>How</insert> then might you see a good soul? Observe what beauty a good soul has within yourself. And if you do not yet see yourself as beautiful, act like the creator of a **statue** <note>This is Plotinus’s famous "sculpture metaphor" for the moral life; the philosopher is both the artist and the marble.</note> which is to become beautiful: he removes one part, scrapes another away, makes one area smooth and another clean, until he reveals the beautiful face of the statue. 

In the same way, you too must remove everything that is superfluous, and straighten whatever is crooked. Whatever is shadowed, work to make it bright. Do not cease "building" your own statue until the divine splendor of **virtue** <note>original: "ἀρετῆς" (aretēs); excellence or moral power.</note> shines out upon you—until you see **Self-Mastery** <term>Temperance</term> <note>original: "σωφροσύνην" (sōphrosunēn); a core Greek virtue involving moderation and healthy-mindedness.</note> standing upon its holy pedestal. 

And if you have seen this, and you are pure within yourself, having no obstacle to becoming **One** in this way, nor having anything else mixed within you, but being entirely yourself: a light that is true and alone. A light not measured by symmetry, nor restricted by a shape that diminishes it, nor expanded into infinity by a lack of size, but unmeasured everywhere, as something greater than every measure and superior to every quantity. If you find yourself becoming this...

And with its inner sight it gazes, and through it, it sees; and this is a god for that soul. This is the blessed life; and evil is nowhere to be found here. If one were to stand in this place, they would not see evil at all. Instead, there are the first, second, and third goods; all things are around the King. <note>Plotinus is quoting the Pseudo-Platonic *Second Letter*, which was used by Neoplatonists to explain the hierarchy of the One (the King), the Intellect, and the Soul.</note> And that King is the cause of all beautiful things, and all things belong to him. And the second things are around the second, and the third things are around the third.

If, then, these are the real beings, and there is also that which is beyond being, evil cannot exist within these; nor can it exist in that which is beyond being, for these are the Good. It remains, therefore—if it exists at all—that evil must be found among "non-beings," as a kind of form of non-being, or something associated with things that are non-beings or things that participate in and communicate with non-being. 

By "non-being," we do not mean that which is absolutely nothing, but only that which is "other" than Being. This is not non-being in the sense of motion or rest <note>Terms from Plato's *Sophist* used to describe the "Great Kinds" of Being.</note> which surround Being, but rather like an image of Being, or even more truly, non-being. This is the entire sensible world and all the passions associated with it, or perhaps something that comes after these, like an accident to them, or a principle of them, or one of the elements that completes them. It is such that it is a reflection of itself and its own nature: it is unmeasuredness in relation to <term>measure</term> <note>Measure represents the order and limit imposed by the Divine Intellect.</note>, the infinite in relation to limit, the undefined in relation to the defining, the always-needing in relation to the self-sufficient; always indeterminate, never standing still, all-receiving, never satisfied, a total poverty. <note>Plotinus identifies Evil/Matter with "Poverty" (Penia), the mother of Love in Plato's *Symposium*.</note>

And these are not merely accidents of it, but constitute its very substance. Whatever part of it you look at, it is all of these things. Other things that participate in it and are made like it become evil, though they are not truly evil in themselves. What then is the underlying nature of this? It is not truly different from that substance [of non-being]; for by being "other" than being, evil results. 

If we must say what it is in itself: it is not a substance. For just as the Good is that which is "in itself," so too is Evil. One is Evil in itself, while another is evil because it happens to participate in that primary Evil. For what is unmeasuredness, if not in that which is unmeasured? And what is measure, if not in that which has been measured?

<meta>catchword: λείπετ (it remains)</meta>

<summary>Plotinus defines Evil not as a positive force, but as "Non-being"—a state of total privation, lack of measure, and "poverty" that exists at the furthest possible point from the Good. He distinguishes between the primary Evil (Matter) and things that become evil through association with it.</summary>

He used this argument: just as privation does not have some "presence" of the Good, so too the good person possesses the Good no less, while the evil person who is present is not evil simply by being present. Privation itself is not an evil accident. For he who receives—

<margin>Chapter 27</margin>

—that which is beside the Good (to be equally a non-perceived privation) calls it "good." He speaks of vice and the evil in the soul as an infinite privation of the Good. But in this state, possessing one thing while being deprived of the other, they have a mixed perception. And Evil is not unmixed, nor is the "other" primary; yet there is also "unmixed" evil. 

<margin>Chapter 28</margin>

And the non-perceiving part happens to be, existing out of itself, while Evil is an accident; unless it is a perceived evil; a hindering thing. For example, in the eye, [evil is a hindrance] in relation to the act of seeing.

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the physical composition of the heavens, specifically addressing whether the celestial bodies are subject to the same "flow" or decay as earthly elements. Therefore, to what extent must it be divided in its shape? This is so that there might be two motions in accordance with nature. Since each thing is essentially the whole earth, why are some parts outside while others originate from it? But how could we hold this view? For how are the things derived from them also the same, since we would accept that as they move, they return into themselves?

We say that for us, the things proceeding from them are as much a whole as the parts themselves. For how could bodies that move without variation possess something in the same way? And under the pretext of endurance, because it is not even in harmony with the things in which it was composed, it carries an unharmed movement according to nature. The matter is appropriate for the existence of the body's result. (For these things—the matter and the body—of those among whom they exist, would at least contribute to the immortality of the <term>Cosmos</term> <note>original: "kosmos"; the ordered, harmonious universe.</note>, while air and dust, we say, are not outside themselves.)

Fire is neither of these two forms itself, but rather something else. One type is sharper and more refined than a flame, and is called "hot" in name only. This light is a body, or rather, that which is sent out from itself; but the light that comes after it is what we more commonly call a "burning." This burning quality is also provided by that primary light, for it shines out from it, just as it glitters among those things belonging to it. For this reason, in the body that is truly white, it especially takes on the brightness that surrounds it. Adopting the solemnity of the **Platonists** <note>followers of Plato who, in late antiquity, developed complex theories about the "luminous body" of the soul and the heavens.</note> regarding earthly things—from which it happens that different states of "becoming" arise—they also categorize that light. This earthly flame does not remain among the things that endure there <note>i.e., in the celestial spheres</note>, but it vanishes after a certain point. It is extinguished when it encounters the dense air; even when it rises as far as possible, it is cast back down, unable to transcend the region above. It remains below the **lunar sphere** <note>original: "seleniake"; the moon was considered the boundary between the changing, decaying earth and the eternal, unchanging heavens.</note>, so that it makes the air even thinner; for it is lighter as it withers away from being "strained" out. This is manifested in various ways throughout all the stars, just as in the branches of learning, so too is it given form in the differences of colors. Another part is **radiant** <note>original: "augoeides"; often used to describe the "luminous vehicle" or "aura" of the soul in Neoplatonism.</note>, and instead of being that same light, it is not seen when the body and its transparency are absent. These do <gloss>not</gloss> fall away, just as you might observe the pure air and that which is far off. <gloss>This is</gloss> the greatest struggle of such light: in <gloss>the</gloss> things where it is ordered purely within the purest medium, who could reach it from so far away? For the curved nature of the heavens is not naturally disposed to flow downward, nor again can those things that are forced bring it toward the bottom. Every body, along with its own motion, is like this alone. It is not like a mere part. But when do these things happen? Either when they are throughout the years, or when the things required for the universe suffer from a lack of harmony.

<margin>
To prove that the motion of the spirit of the mind is its eye <note>original: *oculus*; likely a metaphor for intellectual perception</note>. It would certainly not exist without some soul, for since it is bodily, the life of a body is motion. The whole universe, too, must move in its entirety. It does not move simply, but as a living body—just as a small living thing <note>A reference to the "microcosm," the idea that a human being mirrors the structure of the "macrocosm" or universe</note> is composed of both a bodily and a soulful element. The body is naturally perceived by the senses, while the soul holds it together through a radiating presence.
It moves while also remaining stable. If one speaks of the body moving in a circle, it is always looking back; and this is, in turn, its upright path. Each thing is arranged within the whole. For just as things are there <note>referring to the intelligible or divine realm</note>, so too are things here, naturally carried toward that which they possess, into which nothing else enters. The nature of fire is thin, and if it does not move in a circle, it will be scattered. Therefore, everything moves in a circle. This is a work of providence. It is the cause of providence for itself, so that one might say it moves in a circle out of its own nature. As the ether <term>aither: the "fifth element" which makes up the heavens; unlike earthly fire which rises, ether moves naturally in circles</term> desires [the center], but has nothing else to do, it turns back like one slipping; you could say it moves as it is able. The center stays still according to nature. If one places the movement outside, then the center itself—or rather, the movement around the center—is held naturally by the body. For in this way, they move safely toward the center.
Perhaps, then, it leaves the circle. But its power is capable of this. Through this whirling, it barely fulfills its desire; if it is led around, it does not bend, for nothing pulls it, nor is it against nature.
What is natural? That which has shared in all that is ordained. Again, the soul is whole and not fragmented, but it reaches through every part of the whole. It is everywhere as the whole, as much as it is able. The causes remain, even as they attempt to reach out. For the soul is gathered in each part, having come as a whole; it is more truly its whole self in its desiring. When does it stop? If it happens to be thus. Beauty for the soul consists in looking toward itself; for that which is, is motionless and...

### On whether the stars are causes. Book III.

That the circuit of the stars signifies the things that are to happen to each person, but does not itself cause everything—as has become the common opinion—has been stated before in other works. And let it provide the causes for a moment. But now we must speak more accurately as we examine the matter. For it is no small thing to give credence to this argument <gloss>to those things carried in revolutions</gloss>. They say the stars cause not only other things, such as poverty and wealth, and health and disease, but even things that are shameful and beautiful. And most importantly, they even cause vices and virtues, and indeed the individual actions resulting from these. Each of these does not happen without reason, as if each were destined...
