<meta>This page transitions from the physical mechanics of the heavens (discussed on the previous page) to the ethical and psychological consequences of those influences. It examines how the soul’s expression is mediated by the "instrument" of the physical body and external circumstances like wealth or social status, heavily drawing on Platonic metaphors.</meta>

<margin><unclear>...</unclear> some slaves, as if in the [circumstances]</margin>

To be deceived by a deceptive argument. One should never judge changes in value simply based on what is most visible or what appears "better," or ask whether beautiful things can fail to arise from the same internal nature. It is always said regarding the **body** that when it is sympathetic to what is base, as was given in the teachings of <term>Plato</term> <note>Plato often used the "analogy of the lyre" to describe the soul's relationship to the body</note>, a certain baseness may occur by accident. This happens when a body is poorly "tuned" or constructed, creating obstacles to the soul’s ability to act through it. 

Consider the example of the strings of a tuned **lyre**: if they possess a precise **harmony**, they are able to produce musical notes according to the art of music. The same applies to poverty and wealth, to fame and authority, and all such things in order. For where men are prosperous, they regard wealth as "good order" <note>original: "eunomia" — a state of being well-governed or law-abiding</note>. Just as in the past, those who possessed status found it fitting to have a private identity. 

But if the body of enslaved people is not made equal, it follows that the body's strength is one clear thing, while to grumble is considered base. Whether the heavenly bodies hold the same influence for them—even if one takes away the physical body—it is necessary that they possess nothing further. And as many as refer to the power of good things, they contribute in this way: if they are good, they lead to the acquisition of **virtue**. And so, first, if they are base, it will rightly seem that a "better" nature is implanted within them. 

**Wealth**, however, comes by birth (or) from parents; some prefer the "poverty of the blind" over wealth. Having established the order of wealth, one must also assume it will be the same for the incorporeal <note>referring to things without physical bodies, like the soul or mathematical truths</note>. But if it is wicked, as if from mere theory, one must again consider the contribution—just as that which surrounds us from the heavens, or even a treasure from above that falls to someone from the universe. 

All these things follow one another, which is why if wealth happens to all, it will fail if taken away, and that man is stripped of all authority. But if these things are base, they will fall upon the famous man, and rightly so. But if they are unjust, they will seem better even if they are more obvious. Or rather, they are rightly directed toward some who possess injustice or sin. Thus is the end: for the "better" is attached to one side of the desires. Or it is carried along by itself, while the composition and substance of other things are formed differently.

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s investigation into the governance of the world. Moving from the "tuning" of the individual soul and body discussed on the previous page, it now addresses the "Universal Reason-Principle" (Logos) and how it accounts for the seemingly chaotic or "base" aspects of nature, such as animals preying on one another and the limitations imposed by physical matter.</meta>

...taking another beginning later on. For we must investigate this well, since it was necessary to speak of **souls**—insofar as we discuss this matter, even if only through our hopes—and say how they are governed according to the <term>Reason-Principle</term> <note>original: "logos" — the formative, rational force that translates the divine Intellect into the physical world</note> that administers the whole. 

For we must see whether each soul, as an active force, might err in some way or another. Indeed, we should also look at the **wild beasts**, and whether it is the case that everything happens as a result of them seeing and destroying one another and being of no use to the whole. For those things that perish together in their kind, we see only that. And it is likely that the things that happen to the soul later follow in a logical sequence. But if the soul only produces the things from the beginning by itself, and joins them with its passive powers, then as some say, it is the cause. 

<margin>
And receiving that which comes from chance
</margin>

Because these things happen by the soul's own doing, the subsequent events are drawn along with them. And the <term>Logos</term> <note>Reason-Principle</note> makes this point somewhat clear: it is no longer a matter of scientific knowledge <note>original: "episteme"</note> regarding none of the things that are coming to be. Rather, they occur all at once in this way, just as with those who produce things despite not knowing what they do. Or rather, we should say that the **Reason-Principles** possess the "divisions" of those things that are known. It is a completion for the things that follow from the starting principles. For when the same things happen and are beneficial, the same and the immediate consequences are granted. 

And having received and foreseen <unclear>chance</unclear> <unclear>events</unclear>, it brings these subsequent things to a conclusion. And thus—at least primarily and for all that follows—each of these things is a predecessor to what follows, just as present things are perhaps inseparable from the sequence. For instance, if there were no other things, there would be others among the intermediate and necessary things. 

The **Reason-Principles**, yielding to the "affections" <note>original: "pathemasi" — the passive experiences or sufferings of the physical world</note> of **matter**, do not always observe the initial impulse, but rather the causes. And by following the affections of its own [material] parts, the soul possesses such a life. This is not contradicted by the care for things outside itself. The end result is a "good state" <note>original: "euthesia"</note> for the creation. Having engineered everything beautifully and clearly, the soul acts like a **farmer** who has sown or planted; he does not merely leave it, but corrects the conditions of his own crops and [the environment]...

<summary>Plotinus explores how the universal Reason-Principle (Logos) manages the physical world, explaining that even the "affections of matter" and the destruction found in nature are integrated into a larger, purposeful sequence. He uses the analogy of a farmer tending his crops to describe how Providence corrects and manages the messy reality of material existence.</summary>

In this way, it is volume; and it is so twice over, because it is under the influence of volume. It is seen **contracting** from the great to the small and expanding from the small to the great; it runs through volume, as it were. By itself and from itself, such volume is a receptacle <note>original: "hypodochē"</note> for my own imagination <note>original: "phantasia"</note>, and it is wearying. It remains distinct, and all the things that come from it are in the middle, carried through the whole by its projection. All things, and in every way, can become many; it is all things to all, and to all things it provides their coming-to-be <note>original: "genesis" — the process of birth or generation</note>.

Or perhaps neither is a quality, since one is different from the other, so that it is not even a quality; rather, it is only "other" than the qualified things, not a quality itself. 

But since "the other" is something, and "the same" is the same, then the qualities found in privation are not even "qualified things," but rather a destitution of quality. It is better to call it a lack of property, or of whatever else. For privation exists in relation to these things. 

The "qualified thing" has an appearance <insert>which is</insert> of matter, not of form <note>original: "morphe"</note>. Because of its failure to be "qualified" or to possess any form, it is called "qualified" in a sense by having fallen away from those states. Just as with magnitude, it is said to be "of a certain size" by the very fact of being deprived of magnitude. If this [privation] belongs to matter itself, is "privation" not a better term? And yet, quality is not simply privation, but rather the relationship it has to other things: the fact that it is "other" than them. 

While other things are not only "other" but also "what each is" as a specific form, matter might properly be called "the other" alone. Or perhaps "others" <note>in the plural</note>, so that you do not define "the other" in the singular, but let the plural "others" indicate its indeterminate nature—if indeed it is also "the different."

<meta>This page transitions from the discussion of the "infinite" as an accidental property to a more specific ontological investigation: how matter (hyle) relates to potentiality (dynamis) and actuality (energeia). It continues the previous inquiry into whether matter has a distinct existence of its own or only exists in relation to the forms it receives.</meta>

<margin>Whether matter is in itself something in actuality <term>energeia | a state of being fully realized, active, or "at work"</term></margin>

How can something be bronze <note>original: "chalkos"</note> and fire at the same time? Since potentiality is of such a nature, can we speak of it as being "in potential" relative to what it will become? For instance, we say bronze is the potentiality of a statue. If potentiality were understood only through the act of making, it would by no means exist as its own distinct thing at the same time. Potentiality is not only spoken of in relation to the finished activity, but also toward an activity that might be <unclear>better</unclear> and clearer. On one hand, there is "being in potential"; on the other, there is "actuality." Again, potentiality is defined in relation to actuality; that which is "according to potential" is like a subject lying ready for experiences and forms. 

And yet, if matter receives nothing—which is clear—it is as if the Forms <note>the ideal patterns or essences of things</note> exist there in a "better" way. But there are also things tending toward the worse and the destructive. These follow along, and actuality is something else entirely. We must consider whether the matter is something different from the "falling together" in potentiality toward the things being formed. They are not even divided. Generally, other things we call "potential," once they receive the form and remain themselves, become "actual." For example, the "statue-like" quality will be spoken of in opposition to the statue; specifically, the "actual statue" is contrasted with the "potential statue." It is not that the actuality and the thing conceived are the same, insofar as the potential is less than the abundant. If this is so, the "potential" does not strictly *become* the "actual," but rather the actual arises as something else *out of* that which was potential. The actual comes later. For in the division of parts, the composite whole is not the matter; the form is what is imposed upon it. This composite is a different thing, a substance <note>original: "ousia"</note> like the bronze statue; but the substance as a whole is the statue. <unclear>Nor</unclear> is it at all something that simply remains.

It is clear then that the same applies to other cases. If a person who is a "potential grammarian" <term>grammatikos | someone capable of reading and writing or a scholar of literature</term> becomes actual, the potentiality remains there; for the subject remains the same. The "potential Socrates" is the same as the "actual Socrates." When the unlearned man becomes learned, he "is" the knowledge. Each of these is an accidental property <term>symbebekos | a feature that is not essential to a thing's nature, like a person's height or their current knowledge</term> placed upon us. For it is not the "ignorant" that is the "potential scholar"; rather, it happens to him to be ignorant, and knowledge is a power that happens to come to him. That which is the starting point and the knowledge is already that by which we define the potential: the potential grammarian and the actual grammarian.

<meta>catchword: grammat- [grammarian]</meta>

What is corporeity? 
Generally speaking

Concerning the intermediate state of **corporeity** <note>the quality of being a physical body</note>, we must investigate whether it belongs to bodies, or if it is merely a reflection or a form of bodies. Thus, while the body exists, having both matter and a rational principle, the principle itself is by nature indivisible. This is one path of description; the other appears much smaller.

*Inclination*, at least according to the composition of the world surrounding it and what we see from there toward this world; not [inclining] toward others, but as is beneficial to themselves. # That the Father is not by Fault the Creator of the Intelligible World and those things within it

<margin>How great a multitude of incorporeal substances! And their creation alone among <unclear>many</unclear> <unclear>angels</unclear></margin>
And there is a contradiction. For if someone is made into the likeness [of a divine pattern], it is because that pattern governs in number. And how will all these human affairs be demonstrated? Then there is the third <insert>differences of souls in passions</insert> which are traces in nature. And what they themselves call—misinterpreting as they do—

<margin>Love is a wound according to the ancient theologian <note>original: "παλαιὸν θεολόγον" — likely referring to Plato</note></margin>
immortality and the cosmos, the first God, and the manifest communion of those things toward the Intellect <term>Nous: the divine Mind or second hypostasis in Neoplatonism</term>, and the separation from the body. And yet, if they are to be of the gods,

looking toward the truth, they would not so unthinkingly and in a merely human way judge men who have been distinguished from of old. They do not refuse to admit that these men were good, yet they end by saying that they themselves are the only ones worthy of those things. <insert>And the writings of the ancients concerning the intelligibles</insert> <term>noetōn: things grasped by the mind rather than the senses</term> are lovable only to them and to those who have been "initiated." They blame the soul for its communion with the body, and they speak against the one who governs this universe, saying that the Creator <term>Demiurge: the "Craftsman" or maker of the physical world</term> is the cause of evils. And they say the same things again: that for the parts [of the world], we believe it neither began nor will it cease.

<meta>Continuing from the previous page, Plotinus further critiques the Gnostic view that devalues the material world. He argues that true divinity is not found by rejecting the cosmos, but by recognizing the hierarchy of being and the "Great King" who governs all. This page specifically addresses the arrogance of those who claim to be superior to the celestial gods (the stars and planets) while neglecting the cultivation of true virtue and likeness to the Divine.</meta>

<margin>
Concerning the leaders: every king according to Plato in the *Letters* and in the *Phaedrus* <note>Plotinus often cites Plato’s Letters and the Phaedrus to support his hierarchy of the One, Intellect, and Soul.</note>.
</margin>

<margin>
Every multitude of the gods' offspring; it is not necessary <unclear>etc.</unclear> of Plato; let the power of the Idea be thus <unclear>etc.</unclear> Every multitude is necessary for them.

<margin>
Against the arrogance and rashness of the Christians, the mystics, and the <insert>Catholics</insert> <note>original: "catholicorum" — this marginal note reflects a later reader's interpretation identifying Plotinus's Gnostic opponents with the broader Christian Church.</note>.
</margin>

<margin>
An error of this kind! We say God is good(?) to those who are seen, not just to themselves.
</margin>

It is best for one to strive to become excellent oneself. One should not think that they alone are able to achieve virtue <note>original: "αρετη"</note> through a referral to the best. Rather, one must be restored to this state: it is necessary to be good, but much more to be a god <note>original: "θεον"</note>. This consists in being made like <term>homoiosis: the Platonic ideal of becoming like God as far as possible</term> the divine. One should look again at the beauty and the image of the One of the All. The most blessed state is to know the source itself and to participate with the common gods. Above all, one must honor the Great King <note>A famous Neoplatonic reference to the First Principle or the Good, derived from Plato’s Second Letter.</note> and place him foremost in the universe. For the universe does not contract into the One, but the One expands into all the gods, as much as was necessary for him. 

He saw this most clearly: for when many things are made by position, he himself provides them. Through judgment, those who provide and those who are in the middle are just, both looking and seeing. And each of the gods acts according to his own choice <note>original: "προαιρεσιν"</note>. One should use things dear to the gods. If someone does not consider himself to be these things, but rather possesses a nature that is added so as to glorify himself—as if he were a part standing directly at the head—he should not disregard the principles and the sacred things in his daring. This state of "undisturbedness" <note>original: "ατορακιας" (ataraxia)</note> is deifying. Nature is able to be stronger than others, and not merely what others imagine it to be. 

If someone says he is another name, let it be as was said before: he has hidden himself and as much as he is able, he conquers his own. He can enter into the world and even those things beyond; but he stands upon that which he knows. God educates such people who speak in this way, even if they claim to be better than all things—not only better than men <note>original: "ανων" (abbreviation for ανθρωπων)</note> but also of the gods. They speak of the sphere and the sea, and the primary sources, measures, and harbors <unclear>etc.</unclear>, and they compose these with eternal and wondrous substances. One should not blame all things, taking each part separately. Rather, one becomes better by becoming [like] him. Others enter into knowledge <note>original: "γνωσιν"</note> involuntarily; as many as are numbered, numbers are not everything. One hears of thousands, or ten-thousand parts; it happens to others around him, but they only hear that the thousands are numbers. He follows these things only into labor, for all things of the just will disturb him, unless we ourselves...

<summary>Plotinus argues that true divinity requires honoring the hierarchical order of the universe and its "Great King" rather than claiming a private, arrogant superiority over the stars and celestial gods. He emphasizes that being "made like God" is a process of virtue and recognition of the beauty of the whole, directed against the Gnostic rejection of the material world.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s sustained polemic against Gnostic cosmology (specifically Ennead II.9). The incomplete knowledge below, according to the watery [realm] <unclear>under</unclear>. Nothing to them <note>original: "nihil ad illos"</note>.

Wisdom <note>The Gnostic "Sophia," a divine figure who, in their myths, falls from the higher realm or mistakenly creates a lower reality.</note> is called the cause, whenever they wish both to exist. They say that some [souls or beings] have descended together with her. And they claim that these companions of Wisdom are certainly not bodies, like those <gloss>and</gloss> for the sake of guidance. They say these very souls descended, while others merely passed through. They ask if she was perhaps with this [soul] and not in the darkness. 

If, on the one hand, the Father gave Wisdom permission to proceed from that place, and she then formed an image <term>Eidolon: a reflection, phantom, or inferior copy of a true reality</term>, how can they not immediately call this "acting a part"? While saying this and that, and introducing many many other names, they do not realize if they are in darkness or not; or they say a Craftsman <term>Demiurge: the "artisan" or creator of the material world, whom Gnostics often viewed as an ignorant or secondary god</term> was born among them. First, you say the cause is not so bright—how could that be stated correctly? For either no "head" or guiding principle was present for her in the shaping—something like a light—so that he is said to have approached even there (a thing we say involves moving from a place in the region below) and that he approached there spatially. For he came into being from where she was shining. But if she shone while remaining [above], and did not even reach into the region below, why did she alone shine? Instead, they look at what is among them <insert>they say it is an image</insert> and say it has not yet received its form, and then the intellect shone. And why did this one not shine at the same time? 

And did he make the world? But is the foundation of all things found in knowing what an "image" is? And the reasoning of the world, so that in them what is to be has come to be; but because they claim he is greater, he is not the cause of its existence. They had arrangements of it <margin>They say an image, a beloved one.</margin> <insert>for the whole was illuminated by her</insert>, they happen to be an image. But as much as pertains to nature—and the outcomes are an image—it is "not even in my houses," as he says to you <note>This likely refers to a poetic or tragic fragment used to mock the Gnostic idea that the Divine could be contained in or produce such flawed "houses" or material bodies.</note>, having come to be (if it did) to follow from those who made it. And it could never have happened all at once; they say it flowed toward him from some proper essence of the work. If it is indeed essence, what is the difference for each thing from which she gave an image? For being consists of "colored" things, the ambiguous and aged things themselves upon him; how could one say a thing is full? And is this part bright and something bold? In general, the shining there became indivisible in such a way. What then does he demonstrate by Wisdom?

He questions how a divine being could produce a "dark" world or a secondary creator without being diminished or acting hypocritically.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s critique of Gnostic views on the physical world. While the previous page focused on the mythical "fall" of Wisdom (Sophia) and the creation of the Demiurge, this section addresses the Gnostic claim that the physical universe is inherently deficient or "dark." Plotinus argues that what they call "evil" or "unnatural" is actually a necessary part of a harmonious, ordered system.</meta>

They blame the world; for they say it declines, and then again that it grows. And if there is indeed <gloss>from</gloss> a state contrary to nature an increase and a decrease, it is not "nature" <note>original: "kata-physis," meaning according to the laws of nature</note> that is the cause—for nature is truly the cause of its being, not of its deviation. They blame the "unnatural" and the evils that have approached this world, yet the world itself is not the cause of these evils; rather, they come from the outside—from the primary things and from other things derived from nature herself. For instance, things here, and the way things moving together through one another cause the world to decline, as they say. But one must also consider the "matter" from which they say it comes—not as something that has dissolved, but as they say, as if <gloss>from</gloss> darkness. Yet the things within matter, if indeed matter is the cause of this, and if the whole is illuminated by light, how can it not all be light? Darkness <gloss>darkness</gloss> itself cannot be the cause of the disease; rather, it is the nature that arises from it. But how so? This argument is altogether weak. They blame the cause of the cause of <gloss>weakness</gloss>; and their accusation is a blasphemy.

<margin>
One must not blame the cosmic order on account of fate; rather, it should be gently accepted by good men.
</margin>

They speak against the world, not because of what it is, nor even if it were somehow "bold" <note>Plotinus uses "boldness" (tolma) to describe the soul’s desire for independence, a term the Gnostics also used to explain the fall of Sophia.</note>. Aside from this, they do not understand the order of sequence—the first, second, and third ranks of being. They do not realize that the things coming from those third-rank beings are not worthy of being compared to the first-rank beings. Rather, one must gently allow for things "contrary to nature" <note>original: "paraphyses"</note>, as the world is better understood in relation to the primary things. They say they complain when they see the terrifying phantoms <term>Eidolon: reflections, images, or "idols" that Gnostics believed were deceptive masks of the material world</term> by which the spheres of the cosmic heavens were introduced. But these are merely thoughts, and they shame those who hold them; for if they are "terrifying," it is only because of the power attributed to them. They fear the "ethereal words," and being destructively heretical, they are maddened by "knowledge" <term>Gnosis: the "secret knowledge" that Gnostics claimed gave them superiority over the material world and its creator</term>. For the evil is not in their body; rather, they should fear in a way that is proportional to the whole. They are harmed by the very harms they perceive, which those who offer them counsel insist they must obey. And yet, their own bodies are parts of the world, and it is not impossible that their proportions—

<margin>
The celestial bodies are fiery and proportionally warm.
</margin>

—and those things that are shared with things happening according to nature, would allow this to be so. But as things stand, the whole is filled up, including the parts of the whole. If they should suffer something contrary to nature, even more so, it is not for the sake of a tyranny of those who arrange things, but rather—

<margin>
From where comes the difference in characters and fortunes among men?
</margin>

—they provide an order. It is also said that things come from them <note>The celestial bodies or stars</note>, signifying what is to come. For while some things happen differently and by chance, it is not for the same reasons that these things happen to them. They do not blame the positions of the stars <gloss>on</gloss> for being pure of "becoming" <note>The realm of change and birth</note> or for being far removed from them, nor for the positions of honors.

<summary>Plotinus defends the physical world against Gnostic claims that it is a dark, accidental, or "unnatural" creation. He argues that what they perceive as evil or terrifying is actually part of a complex, hierarchical order that must be understood in relation to its divine source.</summary>

<margin>Epicurus</margin>

<unclear>...</unclear> handing over the <term>divine spirit</term> <note>original: "daimon"; here referring to a guiding spirit or higher soul-power rather than a malevolent entity</note> to such things, she established no chosen cause, but saw that one must listen to everything with endurance, as to why the spirit must command such things. ...whatever they themselves do, into the extreme necessities of the world and the <term>downward-rushes</term> <note>original: "kataphoras," likely referring to the downward motion of elements or souls</note> of the things within it. <insert>For there are two schools</insert> regarding these outcomes: one placing the <term>goal</term> <note>original: "telos," the ultimate end or purpose of life</note> in bodily <term>pleasure</term> <note>original: "hedone"</note>, the other choosing the "Beautiful" <note>original: "to kalon," which also means the Noble or the Good</note> and its own nature, which is always suspended from God and directed toward God as a longing, as must be viewed through friends. And the virtue arising from this, defending itself against time, places the goal in this end, so that the "Beautiful" might be corrected in this, while the other school commands <term>temperance</term> <note>original: "sophrosyne," or moderation</note>. <summary>This page contrasts the Platonic pursuit of the "Beautiful" (the divine and noble) with the Epicurean focus on pleasure (hedone) and utility. Plotinus argues that true virtue and justice are rooted in reason and a connection to the divine, rather than the mere satisfaction of physical needs or the avoidance of pain.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the defense of the physical world (the cosmos) against the Gnostic view that the material realm is inherently evil or a mistake. Plotinus argues for divine omnipresence and the role of beauty as a ladder to the divine.</meta>

<margin>
That God is everywhere and present to all
</margin>
<margin>
That God provides for the whole world
</margin>
<margin>
That the world is ensouled <note>original: "empsychos"; meaning the world possesses a living soul that directs it</note>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s polemic against the Gnostic view of the universe. Having established divine presence in the previous section, he now addresses the relationship between the beauty of the physical world and the inner state of the soul, emphasizing that our own souls are "sisters" to the soul that animates the universe.</meta>

<margin>
Everything beautiful is good.

Every holy one is beautiful by nature, and is either good or wise.

The Soul of the World is the sister of our own soul.
</margin>

One should not revile these things; and since they are beautiful within, he <note>Likely referring to the "skilful maker" or the Divine Mind</note> says it is harmonious to feel affection for them. But if some things are base, it is not strange that they are surpassed by the better; just as in a house, where things may appear shameful on the outside, but within they reveal what is beautiful. When the better form prevails, it makes other things like itself; and in this way, they possess an outward beauty as well. But if someone appears beautiful by nature but is base within, then even saying they are beautiful is a lie <gloss>to be</gloss>. Nevertheless, one must consider them as <term>images</term> <note>original: "eidola"; reflections or shadows of a higher reality</note> <gloss>images</gloss> for all on the stage of being, rather than of true nature. For to behold the things of that higher realm and to reach them is the ultimate goal. But how could one choose according to the <term>Intellect</term> <note>original: "nous"; the realm of pure thought and divine forms</note> <gloss>intellect</gloss> and what follows it? Then they would be said to have the least of their original nature. For if they do not reach the end, they fail to reach the omnipresent; thus, it is possible for things to become base when they cease their movement and begin to add to the body. How so? For these things belong to another and to those that follow. He might grant <gloss>images</gloss> to these things themselves, but they would not know it themselves. Those listening to the arguments might say the body suffers because it is hated by Him; yet sometimes He holds His rank toward it. For beautiful things are indeed divine, and it is right to credit their beauty. This place is what is possessed. And it is not that other nature of the body that acts here, but the one who made it skillfully. Closing off the things toward him in the beginning of time—perhaps the <term>Soul</term> <note>original: "psyche"</note> <gloss>soul</gloss> would rather do this, dwelling not far away, if it were necessary for it to be wiser. Whether from there, because these things happened to be loosened stones, or because some who shared in improvement chose a sturdy dwelling instead of an elegant one, it makes a difference. Even if he does not make it smooth, just as what happens to the stones there, in houses and the parts that compose them all. For being brothers, they fulfill the power of many. Since it would be madness to look at the relation of <gloss>brothers</gloss> even to the base, and to call those in the world brothers and sisters, yet to claim that the souls in the world are <gloss>base</gloss> merely because of the body.

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s argument against the Gnostic dismissal of the material world. Here, he explores the necessary harmony between internal goodness and external beauty, asserting that the physical universe (the Cosmos) is not a mistake but a reflection of divine artistry. He specifically uses the analogy of a "sister soul" to show that our own souls and the Soul of the World come from the same divine source.</meta>

<margin>
Everything Beautiful <note>original: "Kalon"; in Greek philosophy, this word implies both aesthetic beauty and moral excellence</note> is good.
</margin>

<margin>
Every human who is beautiful is by nature either good or wise.
</margin>

We should not revile these things. Because the things within are Beautiful, it is beneficial to say they are in harmony. But if the things within are base, they are all the more diminished by comparison to the better; yet perhaps this is not even reasonable, for it would be shameful for the internal reality to be ugly when the external is Beautiful. Indeed, not everything that is Beautiful would be seen to have mastery over the internal state. But if the internal things are Beautiful while the external are shameful, then certainly even the external must possess some beauty. If the prime of nature belongs to a being that is Beautiful in its entirety, it would be shameful for any part of it to be ugly; at the same time, such a being would not be truly blessed.

But how must we think of these Beautiful things? If, then, we are to bring this to all things, what is it to be among the Beautiful? Among those things that exist by nature, some exist here and some in the primary sense; the former are already moving toward their completion. Since all these things are Beautiful, what were they intended to be? Both the internal things and those that are not—did nature not give the most perfect <term>Nature</term> <note>original: "physis"</note> <gloss>nature</gloss> from the beginning? In that case, it might perhaps not reach this completion. Thus, the body might receive it poorly; but it is not so. Whenever there are deficiencies in the return, his own works remain untouched; and to this, the body is added. For how could it be otherwise? For it must be so in every way, and not as if it were a mere molded thing of itself. If indeed it should ever grant a favor to these same things, but perhaps they say this is not their own doing. They might say that the body is just "situated" there; but the spirit <note>original: "pneuma"</note> is hated. Yet the <term>Soul</term> <note>original: "psyche"</note> <gloss>soul</gloss> is very well attached to it and holds it together. 

These things pertain to the beauty of a man; as if one were present in a Beautiful house or were the builder himself. Certainly, the act of constructing it and the works of one who labors would not be his own... no, by these gods! Rather, he himself made the things pertaining to the body, and though they may be inferior to the builder's own dignity, they are not a cause for misery. The building is not the man himself; it requires him to be wiser. And while some things are external, such as stones or whatever may happen to be there, they belong to such people and to the arts of adornment.

<margin>
The art of the Universe <note>original: "Kosmos"</note> is the sister of our own art.
</margin>

When the dwelling is moved, they blame the habitation; yet they are all carried along together because the <term>Cosmos</term> <note>original: "Kosmos"; the ordered universe</note> <gloss>cosmos</gloss> carries all things. It makes a difference, even if they do not act. And a man, in whom order <gloss>cosmos</gloss> is present—but let there be a madness of stones! Within each person, having a body, they are to be prepared. This is because they are brothers to one another, and there is great power even from what is pure—the human being. To the extent that they are brothers even to the base, his own things are present with dignity and goodness, even to those brothers who think themselves unworthy. Nor is it the case that the things of the world happen upon a body and forms that are base, even if the whole...

<meta>This page continues the transition from general causality to the specific physical makeup of the universe. While the previous page discussed the "why" of events (causes and choice), this page delves into the "what"—moving into the mechanical realm of atoms and the void, characteristic of Epicurean physics.</meta>

For some thinkers depend upon a single source for all things; but others say that they arise from infinites <note>original: "ex apeirōn"; referring to an infinite number of building blocks or an infinite universe</note>. This was also pointed out in the first principles. Since we must also investigate other types of bodies, we must look at all those things that are known in this way, which he will classify as so-called elements. And what the motion is from these very things, then the account and the leading origin—both perspectives for all things. And yet, more simply, whatever he may say, this is composed of atoms. And concerning these, one must inquire, and examine the rest; according to those very principles one might call them, and no others. Their state is a series of negations <note>original: "aphaseōn"; a philosophical term for the absence of specific qualities</note>, nor are they like things made of different parts.

For they say it follows that the atoms are first; these themselves move downward—those that are below—and I cast them back up; others move sideways in whatever way and according to another [force]. Nor do they move in this way quickly or with <term>equal speed</term> <note>original: "isotachōs"; the Epicurean theory that all atoms move at the same speed through the void regardless of weight, unless they collide</note>. Both together, whenever it might happen, these are somehow neither predictions nor testimonies for the present, as these individual things are.
<margin>still in <term>conception</term> <note>original: "epinoias"; a mental grasping or the way the mind forms an idea of something not immediately present</note></margin>
For all art is restricted among disordered things, preserving that which is according to conception. For in this way, it is safely divided, to be both a being and a body; yet it is certainly not something other than the atoms themselves. Again, they bring denials of every limit; and the arrangement of atoms is as it should be. For what else is there besides the downward motion, and then again they strike against each other with such collisions, which always maintain a sequence? This occurs by impulses and necessary motions, until they become a multitude of bodies; perhaps the strength of the body lies in the specific differences of the atoms. These will be squeezed out among rough surfaces; others in turn are hollowed out by moving parts, and their own nature is not softened by any easy cause. And the state of being here is released, for the bodies to be carried along, as if closer through the density of <unclear>gaps</unclear> among all things, and there to be placed again among their own firm structures. And what of the hotter portion and the motion? It is carried toward the other parts; for these reasons, whatever has a flow falls into the thin spaces. At the same time, and in this way, the entries are rather frequent; perhaps again by passing through. Each of these is completed while moving in parts, or according to a rational principle; being carried over a greater distance.

It explores the different types of atomic motion—downward, sideways, and through collisions—and how these movements form the physical bodies we perceive.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s discourse on Providence from the previous section. Having established that the universe is like a grand stage play, he now addresses the "cruelty" of nature—animals eating one another and human warfare—explaining these as necessary parts of a larger, harmonious movement where nothing truly perishes.</meta>

<margin>60</margin>
There are <unclear>embassies</unclear> laid out, lying for <unclear>everyone</unclear>, and again things being raised up from themselves in this way. The interconnection of these occurrences, and of each individual part, might cause one to pause and feel at a loss. This applies to the mutual devouring <note>original: "allelophagia," the act of animals eating one another</note> of animals and their attacks upon each other. One might wonder why wars and battles then take no rest or truce. Why would a creator have made things so? It is said that this state of affairs is "well," but not because it is a moral virtue. Rather, it helps only in this sense: that even evil here has a cause from "there" <note>meaning from the higher, divine realm</note>. There is a suspicion that if the governing principle were diminished, then these evils would not be able to be removed. For if it were

<margin>61</margin>
indeed so, it would be well thus. It is not that matter <note>the physical substance of the world</note> has bypassed and conquered the governing principle, but rather that from the beginning, it was necessary for it to be this way, rather than another. These things happen according to that principle from every side. And thus the whole, divided into parts, is set in motion.

<margin>62</margin>
This whole has been made. Wars and battles are not products of wisdom, yet battles are a necessity. Mutual devouring must be a part of it, for these things happen while life is present. They could not even happen if things remained equal and static. <unclear>Treasuries</unclear> of wealth are disregarded; it was necessary to depart in such a way so that there might be a need for them again later. Or elements last for a short time and then rest. Instead, there is a kind of "acting" by the actors.

<margin>
Nothing is destroyed, but changing forms, they come into being again.
</margin>
Just as someone who has changed his costume, taking on another mask <note>original: "prosōpon," which means both "face" and the theatrical "mask" used by actors</note>, might enter the stage again; yet that inner person who thinks has not died. This refers to death and the subsequent <unclear>return</unclear> to a body. One should view the casting off of the body as if it were a costume, or an exit from the stage, as if one were just playing a part on the scene for a time. Later, there is another entrance. Regarding the killing of animals: they are merely transformed into one another, so that their original nature remains. Those killed in wars do not find a final end, but rather a "rest," much like the play of gymnasts and children.

<margin>
The armed and rhythmic dance called after Pyrrhus, or the Pyrrhic dance.
</margin>
They are like children playing as we live. Providence does not tolerate doing nothing; it is always creating something. And again, these "games" of theirs do not cease to exist, with ranks and formations of those fighting, such as those they call "at play" in the <term>Pyrrhic dances: an ancient Greek war-dance performed in armor, mimicking combat moves</term>. All human seriousness is called "child’s play" because people learn that in dying, they have lost nothing of their true being. Those dying in wars and battles have simply taken a small head start on what is inevitable for everyone; for death is always near to them...

<summary>Plotinus argues that natural predation and human conflict are part of a divine "drama" where the soul is an actor. He explains that death is merely a change of "costume" or "mask," and that the underlying soul remains unharmed by the physical world's struggles.</summary>
<keywords>Plotinus, Enneads, Providence, Logos, animal predation, theater metaphor, Pyrrhic dance, immortality of the soul, reincarnation</keywords>

And as if appearing from a flash of light and from art. And from pure intellect. For those exercising this reason <term>Logos: The rational, formative principle that Plotinus believes shapes the material world according to a divine plan.</term>, which is a certain living reason or one not intertwined, it acts intensely and poorly—not in the way that fire acts, but from within itself. Just as with those things concerning the shaping of animals, it is necessary that it shapes. For even on the stage <note>original: "skenes," referring to the theatrical backdrop or the world-as-stage</note> the one acting does not immediately become the thing shaped, nor do its artistic elements. So that even when moving through hardship; for the director <note>original: "choregos," the producer or leader of a chorus who organizes the performance</note> moves this skillfully, vitally, and by art itself. And thus he moves, and makes these lives as they are; let them be divided in this way. For example, as if there were a life of the just and in this, a life of the noble.

Therefore, this reason <note>the Logos</note>, being the son of the One <note>The "One" is the ultimate, simple source of all existence in Plotinus's philosophy</note> and of a single life, is not simply one thing in the way that things below are. It contributes to its own fulfillment, not as a division of the whole, but as if the parts themselves were brought into one. And to those who are in the composition of war and battle, bringing forth to each what is necessary, the whole would be a single unity. If then, with the parts being in such a state, there is also something friendly, just as the single reason of a drama <note>meaning the script or the logic of the play</note>, though it contains many battles and many fighting parts, creates a total harmony. It is like the symphonies created by voices in songs, part by part.

It is said that all things come to be from a single reason. So it is more likely that the fighting parts within it are meant to be there. And then, why are there fighting parts within it? For again, it contains within itself reasons and compositions, as if nothing were outside of reason. Harmony comes from itself, and is not a failure of reason, nor are those things lying separate from it. We see evidence of this within it, such as white and black, or hot and cold. These orders are made by the underlying reason; they are a certain whole. This is just like a part of the universe. And the whole, which composes music within itself, contains a catalog of many fighting things out of necessity. And they had this reason for being, and they come to be by antithesis <note>original: "antithesis," the juxtaposition of opposites</note>. They bring about such compositions, like an essence. And if the parts were not many, they would be nothing. Nor would they exist without more differences among them. And the greatest differences are found in the opposites.

<summary>Plotinus argues that the conflicts of the world, such as war and natural opposition, are necessary components of a "cosmic drama" where opposites like hot and cold or white and black create a higher harmony.</summary>

Another person performs divination; he himself transfers the qualities of the doctor to his actions.

<vocab>
**Providence** (Pronoia): The divine ordering principle.
**Fortune/Luck** (Tyche): Seemingly random events that Providence nevertheless incorporates.
**Failure/Sin** (Ptaisma): Literally a "stumble" or error in conduct.
**Oracles** (Chresmodoi): Those who deliver divine messages.
**Astronomers**: Here meaning astrologers who read the cosmic signs.
**Sympathy** (Sympatheia): The "co-suffering" or interconnectedness of all things in the universe.
**Formations** (Morphomata): The shapes or patterns that appear in the material world.
**Ether** (Aither): The celestial substance.
**Reason-Principle** (Logos): The rational structure of the universe.

<meta>This page continues from the previous discussion on the governance of Providence, transitioning into a specific analysis of the Soul's relationship with the body and the physical world. ...stones in them; as if we should wish [to see] small trees. And because of this, it is prior; older than the sun; not otherwise; as if the branches were stretching out from a root. And it appears to be foreign to them—those [parts] from which even the very tips of the branches [arise]; as if the whole would ascend from the mud. For even if something happens through their starting principle, one part suffers while another acts, and it is not the case that [the Soul] itself changes along with them at a distance, but such things originate from those from the beginning from the same source; as if they were two brothers, or rivals of equal honor, starting from the same impulses; those of the most diverse kind. —
...the body of that third [principle]... concerning which not least even there is the role of a tutelary spirit <note>original: "daimonos." In Neoplatonic thought, a 'daimon' is a guiding spirit or a level of soul that mediates between the divine and the human.</note>: —

Concerning the underlying reality <term>hypostasis (substantial existence)</term>, there is a middle state of those things. And now also concerning the [body], and from where and how and why it receives its reality and to what extent. For either it is this very thing, being the strongest part in all of it. But when it is born, it is self-governing; as if alone within. It does not even have empty space on either side of it; for it is not according to this [void]. But how should it move; how, ceasing, did it come to be before this, being still formless in form? From every side, it is shaped by impressions to what is nearest; like [drawing] from nourishment. What kind of thing is that which is near and the hope; not a release but a ray <note>original: "aktina"</note> from itself. For she [the Soul] sits even with the prior things, seeing for herself; for not everything is indefinite; but as toward what they call this very thing. Being perfected, it becomes a body; having been shaped as if to show the fruit-bearing power of that which generated and nourished it. And it seems to me that even there the body itself is everything; it was composed of it and as [the Soul]... it will share in this; since it is especially of this. It perceives while observing; and concerning many things because of the body, there is a world; but perception is in the soul itself; as if there; in it is the vegetative power; and the strongest of its parts makes it suitable. The others it carries; for let it be, even if it is eternal, it holds power over this; but below; nor is the better part of it [there]; for these also exist, characteristic and sensory; for there is also that which is the soul of sensation; and many tribes [of living things]; for there is the body of [something] growing. And cranes [move] as toward their parts; if the better part returns again; having gone out because it was <unclear>prior</unclear> to the body.

Nor will it always give the parts to the lowest [realm]; for it neither held them nor did it leave them behind; rather they remain. But the body is attached, and it is, so to speak, illuminated. In this Neoplatonic context, referring to Plotinus’s "On Our Allotted Guardian Spirit," the daimon is a higher level of the soul that guides the individual.</note>, which is specifically its own, becoming the leader of its affairs. Nor is it base; but the evils are those things which do not please [it]. Nor is the soul of each one [base] if the body is of a base sort, as if it were of a god-star; nor would it be a greater hindrance. And in the whole, there are souls of both [kinds], even though the bodies are provided; for the sake of the heap and being pushed out, the whole by choice and not by gift. But whenever he says that it is first inhabited, then the whole has passed into the living for these souls. And as if [choosing] lives from present circumstances, and to breathe again, or rather the souls are disposed within bodies, and the best things from them [go] to the outside—for it would not have been hidden, not because of the senses, but so that it might be seen as clearly as possible. Nor is it a matter of speaking; for the one is from the things of the soul where she is within herself. Not only the divine things there; as for instance they are educated or they cease not having [them], but it is witnessed by the precious things received in the sight. Nor [can one] have even one [part] of her that is in harmony; but if in such things it might be received. But to answer if anything is, and this itself is beneficial to the [soul]; for by much labor it was taken for the worse. Concerning the universals, to which [the soul] inclines...

Not being satisfied with myths alone, they did not dishonor this subject as if there were evils among the gods; for they were not mere men, and where there are gods, there is not only beauty and ugliness together. Nor do they speak of ugliness when they say that the **Beautiful** <note>original: "kalon." Often used interchangeably with the "Good" in Neoplatonic thought.</note> and the **Good** are in nature, discovering a certain attraction in all souls. Let us speak of the first things: one would rightly call her a god, and not only that. For she remains as a whole, inseparable and pure, living from that source, being pure and unforced in her nature. As the saying goes, she "holds herself apart." And who would not hear them even now speaking of the **Sun** in this way? That one is beautiful and all-conquering so that he may serve the light within her, or rather, his circle would have its light from itself, as much as he might shine forth the light that each part contributes. Her form, they say, is carried along. Her path is one of those coming from Cronus; there is a natural union with him, as she is from there and remains there, holding close to him and looking toward him, so that she might be present to all. There is a certain form and a birth for both of them.

<meta>This page continues the exploration of Plotinus’s "Ennead on Love." Having established that every soul has an accompanying Intellect, the text now descends into the specific relationship between the soul and its presiding "spirit" (daimon) and how "Love" (Eros) acts as the driving force behind the soul's desires and its connection to the physical world.</meta>

<margin>Who is the **spirit** <note>original: "daimon." In Greek philosophy, a *daimon* is not a "demon" but a guardian spirit or a guiding power that bridges the human and divine.</note> accompanying each one?</margin>

...moving the souls of living beings. And how is it possible for those who turn away from beauty; whether indeed it is also of that nature; for all the nature of beings contains a certain portion; and it exists in that which has come to be in it, and in the subsequent image; for indeed, a presiding power of this kind stands over each soul. For substance has a portion for everyone and for myself; and this among living beings is **Love** <note>original: "eros."</note>, or the cause for each, and nothing further; and this is so in all other living beings. And then it is not light, nor even the **Intellect** <note>original: "nous."</note> which they say follows each person; it is the Love of each for themselves, for this is the **spirit** <note>original: "daimon."</note> who activates the desires, the natural impulses of the soul, acting as rational drivers toward their own nature. And Love is also the driver of **generation** <note>original: "geneseos." The process of birth or becoming.</note>. For whether it is in someone, or against whom it fights because of errors; for it is entirely a sense of shame, or a part of each soul's own self, and as much as it possesses, it possesses through its "mask" <note>original: "prosopon." Likely a metaphor for the persona or the outward manifestation of the soul in the physical world.</note>; it joins itself to that which it has passed through, so that all souls are, in a sense, one. And it is not possible for each soul to be with the same soul according to that principle; for that which is "there" <note>A common Neoplatonic shorthand for the higher, intelligible realm.</note> is in the whole, and does not transition, and it is not found in the things of this world but is everywhere present. And many things are placed together within it. And when everything is woven together, this would create the straight lines in a certain configuration toward its own nature. And we imagine if something is lacking; so indeed is the **Aphrodite** <note>In this context, Aphrodite represents the soul's capacity for beauty and its role in animating the world.</note> who is in the whole entirely. And we call the spirit a "sacred lover," being born from a certain Aphrodite; and it happens that her attributes are again a part according to the **Reason-principle** <note>original: "logos." The structuring logic that flows from the divine.</note> of those participating from that realm. We say that Aphrodite belongs to the soul, and her powers are in that higher realm, as if by a choice toward her own nature. But these are the powers of each individual soul. Therefore, that great spirit is called the spirit; and generally, it is not in the nature of spirits for evil to coincide; rather, it is in evil, and again in one's own nature, as if in a shadow. And having become an example of the father, just as with the various "Aphrodites," there are afflictions toward her own world. It shines through, just as the things among us are situated; but the world appears in itself and often clearly concerning the soul. Of the world as a part of which the spirit-god himself is called; that one is acknowledged to be true to this, and he fails neither in divinity nor in self-sufficiency, having promised himself. Since the world is made of the "strokes" or movements of the soul, and it was situated within the world, and Aphrodite is in it, a primary part of its power.

<margin>
**Two spirits in each soul**
Two loves: as in the soul, one who will honor [the good] in growth. One is a **god**, while the other is only a **spirit**. One is of the passions, and the other is because it draws toward **matter** <note>original: "hyle."</note> for the sake of **generation** <note>original: "gonen." Procreation or the birthing of physical forms.</note>.
</margin>

<margin>
The **first love** is of those who desire the body because of the first beauty. The **second love** is of those who desire to generate a second beauty. Or indeed, there are two spirits—one that seizes and one that pulls away—within all souls. And **Love the third** is a passion of the soul toward the beautiful, a visible love that generates the beauty that comes from the first, then the second and third.
</margin>

<meta>This page continues the investigation into Neoplatonic theology, transitioning from the nature of spirits (daimones) discussed on the previous page to the specific divine power of Aphrodite. It explores her role as both a "male" principle within the Intellect and a "female" principle within the Soul, responsible for the beauty and procreation of the universe. The text appears to be a commentary or synthesis of Proclus’s teachings on the celestial hierarchy.</meta>

<margin>
One might call [the divinity] male according to the **Intellect** <note>original: "noun." The higher realm of pure thought in Neoplatonic philosophy.</note>, but female according to the **Souls** <note>original: "psychas." The level of reality that mediates between the Intellect and the physical world.</note> that follow after it.
</margin>

<margin>
Aphrodite is properly the **mother of all things** <note>original: "pantogenetis." Literally "the one who generates all."</note>.
</margin>

<margin>
47
</margin>

...to have been arranged in a specific order throughout the cosmos and the whole universe. And for such great cosmic **splendors** <note>original: "habra." Referring to the delicate or luxurious beauty of the heavens.</note>, he assigned Aphrodite. For indeed, the particular parts of the Intellect are the "males" who are entirely devoted to God, but according to their divine souls, he speaks of them as "females." For the saving powers of each soul also belong to these things, among which Aphrodite is counted with the gods. Again, these words bear witness that even divine beings and the gods possess both Intellect and Aphrodite. 

And the cause of Aphrodite is the cause of **Loves** <note>original: "eroton." Not merely romantic love, but the cosmic force of attraction.</note>. And since she brings forth **Offspring** <note>original: "Gonon." Referring to the generation of life and form.</note>, it is said that there is a season of the right moments. And even more so and surpassingly, having been shaped around life and art, she might come to be. For this act of loving is a blessed thing. And she does not create this for herself from any other source; rather, having produced a fountain from herself, she often does so for the sake of the whole and for all beings. Her **Glory** <note>original: "doxa."</note> itself understands the beginning and all things. 

It is a holy thing for the soul to hear of the whole from her, which is said concerning Aphrodite; and those who belong to Aphrodite are those who are "in love." And all the **radiance** <note>original: "aglaiai." A term used for the Graces, meaning brilliance or festive splendor.</note> and the plants of the universe and the body are made radiant by the things of the [Intellect]; and its ornaments are those things which stand beside the beauty of the soul. The splendors of the virgins and the loves and his splendors and the ornaments that lead one astray are her splendors. Both the ornaments and the shameful things are brought to completion through her. 

Therefore, the **Reason-Principle** <note>original: "logos." The rational structure or "blueprint" of the world.</note> that addresses them at the right time is that which calls upon all the air; and so, among these things, is the learned quality of the radiant ones. For what is not mortal, the divine carries and receives—it is received by reverence alone. Again, I pray for myself and not for one who is merely a student. For it is not for me to speak of the "prize-gatherers," the **offspring** <note>original: "gennema."</note> and the **hypostasis** <note>original: "hypostasis." The fundamental underlying reality or "personhood" of a divine being.</note> that exists with him. And because she is the cause, she is said to possess love through the purity of the gods, whenever Aphrodite is established among beings.

Those who say many things and wish to possess knowledge should understand that these things [the passions] only happen around it, without touching its essence.

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the nature of Matter (Hyle), specifically focusing on Plotinus's argument that Matter remains "impassible"—meaning it is never truly changed or "hurt" by the forms of fire, water, or air that appear to inhabit it. This follows the previous page’s discussion on the permanence of essence.</meta>

First, let us demonstrate its <term>impassibility</term><note>original: "apatheian." In Neoplatonism, this refers to the quality of being "unaffectable" or incapable of suffering change from external forces.</note>. Concerning the images and certain shadows that appear, and those things present in it which give a certain account of its impassibility, those who teach do so as if using the common habits of names, saying that the "suffering" itself belongs to them. For example, they say that fire burns; yet all things that are set on fire possess only the "fiery" quality and its arrangement. 

They also speak of the forms of air and water in various places; for while they receive the forms of air and water, the underlying things remain as they were even while these forms are present. Just as a body might be engineered, the <term>matter</term><note>original: "hyle." The underlying "stuff" of the universe that lacks its own form.</note> itself has not "suffered" or been changed by them. If they were to receive only the forms of things being burned, one would not say that the matter itself is changed; rather, they become fiery in the way that fire itself comes to be and is ignited. This is even more the case if we consider that in the "Whole," something is at one time fire, and at another time water and air.

<u>This is just like the products of the mechanical arts, such as things appearing in a mirror, or what I might call the image in a signet ring, which exists without the physical body of the ring.</u>

And concerning the act of igniting, they will speak even of oil—how could it ignite a body without the body itself being set on fire? Then, how could it be so if both were in motion? Or even within a human and within fire? When elements move from one place to another, both are changed at once, and one thing stands in place of another, not by its own nature, but by <term>accident</term><note>original: "symbebekos." A philosophical term for a property that a thing possesses but which is not essential to its nature (e.g., a person being "clothed" or "seated").</note>. 

When one is deprived of those parts, how—after "suffering" something in this same state—could it still exist by that same logic while these things are perishing? How is it that when the body has perished, the greater part has not also perished? For it must be so great as to not succumb, because it is <term>indestructible</term><note>original: "aphtharton."</note>. Neither do magnitudes become "affections" within the matter of bodies, nor are the bodies themselves "passive" so as to be a mere composition of affections. 

Body does not penetrate body, yet everything must resist it and be set on fire—how can they say this instead of "the body"? For the things surrounding it involve one another. Regarding stones, for they are not made of parts, yet they say many parts exist by nature from them, so that it is possible for the <term>intellect</term><note>original: "dianoias." Refers to discursive reasoning or the mind's ability to process information.</note> to grasp them. It never happens that when fire is given off, it shines entirely as an irrational matter for each thing, while living within a body.

<summary>Plotinus argues that magnitude (physical extension) is not an inherent quality of Matter, but a "phantom" or "image" that appears within it, much like a reflection in a mirror. <meta>This page continues Plotinus’s investigation into the nature of Matter (hyle). <margin>

...not only if it is that itself, but also as if coming near to this, it appeared better to have taken on a nature; at any rate, if it stood toward it, it would not proceed in it, for these things were again meant to be together with her <note>In Plotinian philosophy, Matter is often treated as a feminine principle that "receives" the "seeds" of the forms.</note> alone. She will do these things no less than the whole; for if she did not do these things, she would strive toward the things within herself. Again, it will not be that such things are not separate. For that which has received them happened to take something of the "Great" <note>Referring to the Platonic "Great and Small," the principles of extension.</note> so as to be much more than itself, even though it thought it would appear to itself; it will receive it. And this is even more so: and the thing after this is many things in many places and the whole is a part everywhere. And as I was saying, it is not separated, just as it is not a shadow, so that the "Equal" is opposite to the "Equal," having hoped in being to reach the "Great," but it did not strive for the permanence toward that. It approached as much as was possible for it, and having placed before itself what was in front of it—for not being able to grasp that, it received the things that come after it—it nevertheless preserves its own nature through the magnitude of that thing itself. If, for instance, it fled from being clothed, as it were, by the "Beautiful" and from the one who established it, it would not hold the things that came before it. But if it were to take off its clothing, then as it [the form] flees back into the <term>darkness</term><note>original: "skotos." Plotinus often describes Matter as "darkness" because it lacks the "light" of Form and Intellect.</note>, as much as was present of them would no longer happen to be among the things that truly exist. For while she is there, having no form itself, she nevertheless holds these things and is not dragged away, each one being itself. For these are the things that are <term>sensible</term><note>original: "aisthēta." Things perceivable by the senses, as opposed to the "intelligible" things known by the mind.</note>.

Just as stars might appear opposite and be looked upon by the eyes, if one does not stand upon it, it will receive them; but rather by the imposition of the darkness. And so it is with <unclear>base quality</unclear>. And it is not in the magnitudes, or by encompassing the same thing by that which belongs to it, but in those things where it is not, it placed a <term>recollection</term><note>original: "anamnēsin." A Platonic term for the soul's memory of higher truths.</note> of them. But the multitude of them, as if proceeding and poured out and flowing from nothing, will be something else. For the <term>Reason-Principle</term><note>original: "logos." The formative power that emanates from the Soul to shape Matter.</note>, as if moved in an <term>image of imagination</term><note>original: "phantasia eikoni." Here, the way the rational principle reflects into the mirror-like nature of Matter.</note>, exists and not according to witness, striking what is in it, nor was it moved; but while nothing else exists, it is able to be moved together, as it were, while standing in itself, in which it also wrote. But it [Matter] received all beings not all at once, so as to receive them in a <term>divided</term><note>original: "diēirēmena." Cut up or separated into individual parts.</note> way; it proceeds, all things of her having come to it. And it is able to be <unclear>marked</unclear> by all of them and toward all of them, wherever it is not distended according to itself.

This method is for those who wish to examine these things more accurately, even while setting aside contradictory views. Perhaps it is not only possible for those who exist beforehand to be beautified; time falls into "otherness." I say this also in the demonstration: by necessity, the discourse of wisdom <note>original: "sophia"; wisdom personified or the philosophical logos</note> will clarify things that have not arrived here in this way, if indeed the things of the Mind concerning those matters are similar.

<meta>This page transitions from the previous discussion on Matter and Magnitude into a profound investigation of the nature of Eternity (Aion). While the previous page dealt with how physical size relates to underlying substance, the text now elevates the inquiry to the Intelligible World—the realm of pure thought and being—to define what "Eternity" truly is, distinguishing it from the "Time" we experience in the physical world.</meta>

<page-num>22</page-num>

<warning>Staining and darkening in the upper left margin; some text slightly faded near the bottom.</warning>

<margin>What is eternity?</margin>
Therefore, it [the Intelligible World] exists in this way and holds itself together. Again, since the All consists of the solitary, the "Same," and the "Other," and all these things are distinguished in such a way that the All contains itself within itself; for indeed, appearing as one thing within another, the living beings <note>original: "ta zōa"; in this context, Plotinus refers to the "Living Being" or the Divine Forms/Ideas that populate the spiritual realm</note> exist there without spatial separation. Having seen all things, being **Eternity**, that which comes to be is also entirely in the "Same," always possessing the entirety of the present, but not as if it were a later "afterwards." Rather, all things exist together simultaneously. It is not that these things exist now and those things later; instead, there is a **partless life**, where all things exist as one, yet all things proceed in their own expansion. But it always exists in the same way, and not as one thing after another, but as *this* very thing: a whole always in the present, because nothing of it has passed away, nor will anything yet be. Rather, that which it is, it is always. Thus, one should understand **Eternity** <note>original: "aiōn"; specifically the "Eternal Now" or the timeless state of divine reality</note> as being in this state: the being within it, the underlying subject as a sort of foundation. And so it is, and furthermore, regarding its being a whole and all things belonging to it:

<margin>What is eternity?</margin>
These things were so then: that absolutely nothing is missing. For what could later happen to it that does not already exist now? Nor, again, will it be something later which it is not now, or which it never was. It does not come from a state of not-being, nor will it ever again not be, nor will it again become what it currently possesses. Nor is it now something that will never be, or something that has already passed away. Therefore, the whole which *was* is itself also that which has passed, and yet there is no "present" versus a "future." Instead, there is this: the "To Be" <note>original: "to einai"; the essence of existence</note> which is always, which is not *going* to be, but is *now*. This is the state of being where the whole is **unchangeable** in its existence. And again, it must be considered as unchanging within the same state.

<margin>
How the Intelligible World truly exists; in what way it is a whole; and concerning the things here: what they are and from where they come.
</margin>
Therefore, the life surrounding Being in its existence is altogether simultaneous and full, entirely without spatial extension. This is what we are seeking: **Eternity**. It does not possess this as something accidental <note>original: "symbatikon"; a property that can be gained or lost</note>, but from its very nature. It is that, and that, and joined with that, alongside which all other things stand. For all these things, we say, exist always; and whatever things we see as existing, we say they all exist by nature. Let these things be established: just as they are themselves the primary things, and they would hold to the primary things by existing within them and from them. And the truth within them is that all these things exist in them, and that the Cause <note>original: "aitia"; the source or reason for existence</note> contains the things of one another as a whole, a collection of parts, but with the parts standing together as one.

Among these things, the first parts are as if turned back toward themselves, as something that is and is yet to be; if it should happen to project itself again, it would be found. Where then is the "ungraspable" <note>This refers to the difficulty of defining the eternal, which escapes human categories of time</note> for those who posit it? It would instead be a lack. Since nature is good and they act by its power—this very nature, as we ourselves have said—it exists and never fails, so that it is both similar and **eternal** <term>eternal: "aionios", typically referring to that which belongs to the timeless Intelligible realm</term>. Although we speak of many **eternities**, we might use the terms "eternity" and "eternal" in this way: as it was said, that which does not incline toward another nature in any respect is **eternity** <note>original: "aiōn"</note>, already possessing the whole of life, as though never receiving anything from what remains [the future]. We said that "to be eternity" is to be in this state. But "eternal" describes that which exists in that higher realm, being a state of something that comes from itself and exists within itself; we see that the term "eternal" is used for such a state.

All things and the things within God shall be eternal; and it is not that the things in God are merely according to **eternity**, but this very eternity is God appearing and revealing Himself, as something **everlasting** <term>everlasting: "aidios", often used to describe that which exists through all time without beginning or end</term>, as if from the "now" and the "same." And thus, that which "certainly is" does not at all pass away, even if there are many such things. For each thing, being many, does not exhaust itself. We have resolved that "the other" is **infinite** <term>infinite: "apeiron", meaning without boundary or limit</term>. And the infinite is also that which does not stretch out [in time]; and this is fundamentally true because none of these things is consumed. Because of this, eternity is said to be itself, and because it is all things and no single thing, it is **eternal** itself by virtue of the fact that nothing has passed away and nothing [new] is yet to be. 

For how indeed shall it be moved? If this is said, it is because it was possible for it to be all things. And one must understand that "not failing" is the same as being "from the now," since that is its very nature. In this way, the term "eternal" concerns that which has been made manifest. And if they are eternal, even if the same things are not posited, they would not appear as the kind of things that live in a restrictive way. And life exists, and the "still." It has been said that these things live, [possessing] the power that supports all things. This does not belong to an eternity that is merely living, but to the nature of eternity itself, so that it is not only itself that is composed of them, but it also concerns the nature of such lives. And this is what it attempts to show: for this is **eternal** and in this way eternal, and again, it is the only thing which is still a life remaining and present toward that [divine] one, revealing that "being" nowhere possesses their existence in any other way.

It distinguishes between the "eternal" state of divine beings and the "everlasting" nature of God, emphasizing that eternity lacks nothing and does not "stretch out" like time.</summary>
