For it is not from reason or from those who perceive things that are not good, so that (as many possess) it is a ruler in part; a **vision** <note>original: "doxa," which can mean both "glory" and "opinion," but in this philosophical context suggests a conceptual vision or doctrine</note> directed toward the things above. And if it is not of sensible things,

How great is the opinion of the ancients concerning [the state] before time.
</margin>

it is quite manifest. Having heard how it calls us, being contained as if nothing within bodies and **blessed men** <note>A traditional term for sages or those who have achieved a state of divine contemplation</note>, they used the subsequent things graciously. He speaks of all those things concerning the **Father** <note>In this context, the "Father" refers to the Platonic Demiurge or the Primal Source</note> applying them in the mind instead of to created things. Formlessly, he takes the things of the **lover of mankind** <term>lover of mankind: "philanthropos," a common epithet for the Divine in late antiquity</term> here first. For those things deemed worthy to come as such, the present discourse explains them harmoniously, distinguished by its manner of speaking; things entangled at first and then made straight. Nor is "being in time" said causally in the case of bodies. For having scattered the incoherent as if it were nothing, it [scatters] all of us everywhere, our very bodies, even when it is not of itself. Regarding the logic of objections, some said that they are, for others said that being is born within this, speaking of all kinds of lights. Others say they are not at all in a state of rest, nor do they oppose each other, while others follow it entirely. And in all things, even in those that remain, those ones are not possible; nor is it possible to take them all together, as if they do not belong to each individual. Regarding those who possess the members, there are certain movements and actions. But if someone remains in time, they would much more belong to that which has come to be, as movements of a living thing follow it. But this is both itself and this; and otherwise, they might speak of it as being contrary to nature. And for those who would not cease, because of this, time is no longer for all.

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the relationship between time and eternity. Having previously discussed Aristotle’s definition of time as a numerical measurement of motion, the text now pivots toward a Neoplatonic view (likely Plotinus), defining time as the "life of the Soul" as it moves from one state to another.</meta>

<margin>
All time imitates eternity according to its similarity.
</margin>

Time is no longer merely the forms of the past and the future; rather, it is the very **life of the Soul** <term>Soul: "psyche," the cosmic life-force that mediates between the eternal realm of Intellect and the physical world</term>, which consists in the transition from one state of life to another. It does not remain in the same state, but is always active, moving toward something else. 

And yet, one would not say this is located "here" in the physical world. Instead, we say that time is an **image of eternity** <note>original: "eikona tou aionos," a famous Platonic and Neoplatonic concept where the moving world reflects a static, divine original</note>. Just as eternity possesses the whole of reality, time offers a different kind of life that shares the same name, produced by the power of the Soul. 

We can see the contrast between the two realms:
* Instead of the motion found in the eternal realm, we have the Soul’s specific portion of motion.
* Instead of self-sameness and remaining constant, we have that which does not stay the same, but moves from one **activity** <term>activity: "energeia," the active expression of a thing's nature</term> to another.
* Instead of that which is indivisible and one, we have an image of the One found in **continuity** <note>referring to how time flows without gaps, unlike the "all-at-once" nature of eternity</note> and in a sequence of "one thing after another."
* Instead of "always being," we have "always about to be." 
* Instead of the whole existing all at once, time exists part by part, truly divided.

Will it then imitate the whole? Because eternity is infinite, time attempts to mimic this by being infinite in its own way—through the constant addition of parts. One must not think of the Soul as taking time from the outside, just as eternity is not outside of **True Being** <note>original: "tou ontos," the realm of perfect, unchanging reality</note>. Rather, time must follow the Soul from within, unfolding like a scroll <note>original: "periexelikta," suggesting a winding or unrolling motion</note>.

If the Soul remained still and held everything within itself at once, eternity would remain and never depart. Time does not depend on a standing state. Rather, the entire "out-throw" of such a life, proceeding smoothly and through similar, indivisible movements, creates what we find to be time. 

Looking at this more broadly, for the Soul, its **essence** <term>essence: "ousia," the fundamental nature or "being" of a thing</term> is its activity. If we were to imagine this essence standing still and indivisible, and if we supposed the Soul ceased this activity—so that this part of the Soul no longer "wrote" itself through its flow—then we might say we see eternity and that essence as one. But the movement of the Soul creates the "before" and "after." Or rather, the movement toward what is "outside" of the present is what makes time exist. I would say that "before" exists even before we reach the physical sphere of the world, for "before" is a property of time itself.

<summary>This page explores the Neoplatonic definition of time as the "life of the Soul," contrasting it with eternity. It explains how time acts as a moving, divided image of the static, unified whole of eternal being.</summary>
<keywords>Time, Eternity, Soul, Activity, Image of Eternity, Plotinus, Essence, Continuity, Sequence</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the technical critique of Aristotle’s definition of time as "the measure of motion." The previous page established time as the "life of the Soul," and here the author (Plotinus) argues that time is more than just a measurement we apply to moving things; it is an internal reality of the cosmos itself.</meta>

...just as an **accidental property** <term>accidental property: "symbebekos," a characteristic that a thing happens to have (like being tall) but which does not define its essential nature</term>. In this way, that which is "always" would be the thing being measured, and it would not be said to exist *within* the measure, because its essence would be entirely fading and passing away. 

And it is nothing if one defines motion itself by means of a certain part, having taken it superficially and by chance. For in relation to the **past "now"** <term>"now": "nyn," the instantaneous moment that divides the past from the future</term>, there would be as many things within it as there are in the **restoration** <note>original: "apokatastasei," referring to the completion of a celestial cycle or a return to a starting point</note> of time—something different, and not time itself. Nor is it simply the relation to what follows, but rather knowing the very thing upon which other things move and exist. This is most visible through the **division and duration** of what is ordered, appearing clearly to our understanding. 

However, if one sought to understand these things from the perspective of the "measured," it appears clearly as a concept; for things are said to "become" rather than simply "to be" when they are in the measure of what is happening. Indeed, it is better to say that things move within the "measured" by the power of the motion of time, like a **revelation** <note>original: "phasis," an appearance or a showing-forth</note>. In a more recognizable way, we move to understand how much has happened; how many things one knows as "about to be," while those that existed before they happened, one knows after the motion. 

Furthermore, we must add the idea of "being in a measure." What happens by **coincidence** <note>original: "kata symbebekos," occurring by chance or as an attribute rather than essence</note> is a source of stumbling. These things seem to hold the truth within them; for if they were not in the measure, or the measure itself were not what we call the measurement of the heavens, or what is revealed there, how would you know them? We must try to look toward the heavens, because it is said that "being in the measure" is something greater, and they reveal it through their "writing" <note>This refers to the ancient idea that the movements of the stars are like letters that we can read to understand the nature of time and destiny</note>. Nor is there any other "writing" elsewhere. For the heavens have no error, nor could their essence be made by someone within a measure we might possess. 

But what must be said about the **revolutions** <term>revolutions: "periphoran," the circular orbits of the stars and planets</term>? One must remove the idea of being carried along by the smallest part of itself so that one can know from that point—just as the world is based on motion—

<margin>
† and He made the world thus
</margin>

—wishing to show, from its own nature, that it is bounded by the **nows** and the motion of its own **eternity** <term>eternity: "aion," the realm of timeless, perfect being</term>. He made the world move because it was meant to receive the divided parts. Its **celestial motion** <note>original: "ouranios kinesis"</note> runs along with it, because he himself makes the world his own. He does not have it eternally; for in the one case, a thing will be "one and clearly itself," both **together and all at once** <note>original: "homou kai panta," a technical term for the eternal state where everything exists simultaneously without sequence</note>. But for all things in time, they are not the same. And thus, life does not have this sameness; or rather, it seems that there is something more than life. In motion, one perceives the **before** and the **after** not...

All these things, to the extent that it is possible for them according to their natural state, seek this end, though they attain and contemplate it in different ways. Some do so truly, while others receive only **imitations** of it. 

Would anyone tolerate such a paradox, especially if we applied it to ourselves? There is a danger of laughter in our present circumstances; yet even we, when we are **playing** <note>original: "paizontes," a word meaning both acting in a game and the non-serious outward movement of the soul</note> in the present moment, are contemplating—or rather, both we and all who play do so for this purpose. Indeed, one might say that even when people act with serious intent, they are striving for contemplation; one might say that without "play," they could not act with such seriousness. They act with serious intent for the sake of contemplation alone. For there is no one who acts toward an end that is not, for them, a step toward contemplation. Whether the actions are necessary or not, the drive toward contemplation remains, even if it is sought through external actions. Whether one acts willingly or unwillingly, they are ultimately striving for the goal of contemplation, as will be seen later. 

But first, let us speak about **Nature** <term>nature: "physis," here personified as the lowest level of the world-soul that shapes the physical world</term> herself, and how it is that everything produced and born within her is referred back to her contemplation. Let us consider whether the "unconscious" pregnancy of nature is analogous to contemplation. And since she acts for the sake of contemplation, and has herself come into being through it, how does she speak? You might say she speaks here like children. For the Earth does not perceive in a physical sense, nor is it a material thing that acts upon nature. And one must not say that nature works as if pulling levers from a physical toolkit; for what kind of levers or varied colors and such shapes could produce these results? Rather, she acts more easily than those who work by hand. The craftsmen who mold or mix materials do so by looking at the creations of nature, but nature does not need such colors; rather, it is as if the colors are reported to her. Indeed, nature accomplishes her work through a kind of "play" of her own, and yet through this use of materials, she provides for herself and remains as she is, preserving her power. For in her...

For it comes from contemplation, and not out of a contemplation that has performed an action, but by the very fact of becoming a contemplation. And if someone were to ask Nature why it creates, and if it were willing to listen to the questioner and speak, it would say: 

-> "You ought not to ask, but to understand in silence, just as I am silent and not accustomed to speak." <-

What then is there to understand? That what is brought into being is my **silent spectacle**, a **vision** <term>vision: "theorema"</term> brought about by nature. Because I am born of a contemplation of this kind, it is my nature to love seeing. And that which I contemplate creates the visions for me, just as **geometers** <note>Plotinus often compares the creation of the physical world to a mathematician drawing shapes in their mind</note> draw while they are contemplating. But I do not draw; rather, as I contemplate, the lines of physical bodies come into existence as if they were falling out from my vision. And I possess the experience of my mother and those who gave me life. For they too exist as a result of contemplation, and my birth resulted from their act of contemplation—those who, by their very lives, were joined together. A child-like nature might come to be, or something that is not held in that same way.

How then do these things exist? And is there **sense-perception** <term>sense-perception: "aisthesis"</term>? That which has become these things is those very things. For even **motion** completes a "vision" for others, separately. And who wishes to know how each of them appears?

<margin>
How nature possesses **understanding** and **sense-perception**.
</margin>

It would seem that the "understanding" of these things—the soulless or the merely sensing things—is not like that of those who study them; rather, it is like **understanding in sleep**. For it falls upon those who are awake. While Nature contemplates its own vision, it [?] its own head and its **silent contemplation**. We shall see that vision and contemplation itself are something else that has come from it, more distinct. And indeed, wishing to see this very thing and its work, those who move toward the **outside** <note>i.e., those who look at the physical world rather than the mind</note> produce a contemplation that again creates a vision. For it was necessary for it, as much as it wished to look inward, to produce a **shadow of contemplation** and of **reason** <term>reason: "logos"</term> in action. For those who are not sufficient for the act of contemplation—due to the **weakness of their meditation**—cannot grasp the vision sufficiently through both ways, and because of this, they arrive at **action** <note>Plotinus argues that "doing" things is a sign that one isn't strong enough to just "think" or "see" them</note>.

<meta>Continuing from the previous page, Plotinus has established that Nature creates through a "silent vision." He now expands this argument to human behavior, suggesting that even our most frantic actions and the creative "arts" (like painting or building) are actually just indirect ways of trying to achieve that same inner contemplation.</meta>

# { The one contemplation reaches everywhere, and is in all arts }

<margin>The part in the soul is of a like manner to a horse. <note>original: "ἰσότροπος τῷ ἵππῳ ἡ ἐν ψυχῇ," likely a reference to the "spirited" part of the soul or the chariot allegory in Plato's Phaedrus</note></margin>
For it is for the sake of **contemplation** <term>contemplation: "theoria," the act of intellectual vision or direct understanding</term> that beings both act and seek their fortune. Indeed, this type of contemplation is the cause for those who do not possess the goal within themselves to seek it through external means. To look toward oneself and to be defined by that look is what creates contemplation; for contemplation does not consist in **action** <term>action: "praxis," physical doing or practical work</term>, nor is it a subordinate mental state. And for this reason, it [the action] ceases; for the goal is found wherever one happens upon the thing itself. For the things being discussed are not limited as if each thing did not exist [in the mind]; rather, it is as if one finds the whole in every part equally. Therefore, some people act as if they are not acting, in the things they have done—such as those who are **boasters**, or those who might wear the things they have seen as a display. Or, in general, if something is seen but not through the action itself; for they do not even perform the necessary actions for their own sake. But if—

<margin>All action is for the sake of contemplation</margin>
<margin>That happiness consists in contemplating, not in acting</margin>
—the body and that contemplation are united, then that action is a result of the purest contemplation, even for those who act and are defined by it. It is as if they receive from a cause rather than being the cause themselves. This is where they fall short; for it is not that they do not wish for it, but they desired to create with **knowledge**. Yet, if they are unable to see the vision currently present in the soul, and not by any lack in the higher part, they perform the action and find joy in it. This arises from their weakness. They do not act in order to learn, but in order to possess the good that comes from the action. This is the point: that they wish to have, through the "theories" or visions found in action, what they hope to obtain by chance, following along with their own existence. And indeed, the body is a work in which the soul also resides; and the first part is divine. **Contemplation** belongs to all things, or rather, it is set within the order of all things. And the clearer the creation is, the more the worlds—

<margin>The knower is already at the furthest reaches of the thing known</margin>
—and the movement are found rather in the body. And the knower, in so far as they have knowledge, holds the object of their pursuit within the act of knowing and possessing. Both the beginning and the increase of this state happen at once, like an image. The things that exist alongside the act of knowing are equal; they are beings, and just as they are "within" the person, they act even more powerfully. Therefore, at first, the person does not calculate; the thing exists of itself without the person even agreeing to it, each thing as it were—

<margin>Art, while learning, seeks from the outside; for within itself are the reasons for all things <note>original: "logoi," meaning the rational blueprints or principles of existence</note></margin>

The first is primary, the second kind of thinking is second, and the "last life" is the "last thinking." All life comes from that Intellect above, and it possesses the truth of its own differences. Some people only call the clear versions "thinkings," and they do not call the others thinkings at all, because they do not see the intellectual activity happening within the living being.

Yet this argument will appear even more clearly where the mystery of contemplation is hidden. One kind of vision is the truest contemplation, and it holds these very things within the object being contemplated. The truest thinking, the contemplation, and the object of contemplation are thus: living and living, and both are one together. It is not that the intellectual object lacks a body to contemplate, nor does it perform its contemplations through movement. Rather, it is a "touching," like light. This truest part thinks and becomes like an **eye**, sometimes silent, wishing to possess all things within itself and never to release them—for it holds the other as a sort of **center** <term>center: "kentron," the point of origin or unity in a circle</term.

<margin>
How the soul is divided and yet remains indivisible
</margin>

It is clear, then, that the body relates to the soul as if one part has one need and another has another. But it <note>The soul</note> is present in all parts of the body; it is **indivisible** because it is whole in all parts and in every single part of it. It is not a case of "this" being here and "that" there, with one part of the soul in one place and another elsewhere; rather, the soul maintains its common power throughout. That which is within us of the soul will be like something divine <note>original: "θεὸν" — Plotinus and his followers often viewed the highest part of the human soul as essentially divine and connected to the higher realm of Intellect</note>.

This learning concerning a nature that is wonderful and beyond material things—possessing nothing physical—is possible for everyone to learn. Yet there is a danger that, since it does not exist in a physical way, it might not be grasped by the whole body as it will be. 

<margin>
That the soul is incorporeal
That the soul is whole in every part
</margin>

And indeed, the soul is not divided—or rather, we should say it is not divided in itself. For it has not become a "part" made of other parts. Nor are its parts whole entities in themselves. Instead, the soul encompasses the body. It may appear divided, but bodies are the sorts of things made of parts that receive things in place of one another. Since the "affections" <note>original: "πάθημα" — here meaning physical properties or the capacity to be acted upon</note> of bodies do not apply to that which has no parts, such division does not belong to the soul's nature; for the soul must possess a swift and subtle nature. 

It is universally agreed that the soul is not only indivisible, nor only divisible, but both at once. As for its having parts, this is an appearance that comes from other things <note>i.e., from the physical extension of the body it inhabits</note>. For if the soul became like a body, one would not immediately say that the soul is present wherever a part is; but the matter stands as if the soul were taken up by the whole. 

But even if it is of the same kind—for as when craftsmen hollow out wood in such a way that the stamp makes an impression—there are not many wholes, just as the acts of justice performed by each individual belong to a single principle. 

Indeed, the whole is similar, but through "outflows" <note>original: "ἀπορροίαις" — emanations or streams of power flowing from a single source</note> from one another. For continuity, if it does not reach completion, is in vain. Philosophers do not say that the soul passes into bodies in the same way that forms <term>Forms: the ideal, non-physical blueprints of things</term> enter into our sensations. A paradigm of such things: we know what is said regarding the bee <note>The bee is a common ancient metaphor for the soul, often representing its industrious nature or its ability to return to its hive (the divine source)</note>, which is spoken of in a special way. 

For some thinkers divide the soul. One part is considered more of an "outflow," but the part itself is not different, just as the flows of two streams are not fundamentally different from their source. The difference regarding the "veins" and not the body remains with the farmer <note>The "farmer" here likely refers to the soul as the cultivator or animator of the physical body</note>, and other things will be divided. And agriculture <note>The skill or essence of farming</note> remained a single thing, even if a person were to master its various parts in the place it guarded. 

The same will apply to the parts of the soul. Even if one part experiences a chance perception <term>perception: "aisthesis," the soul's ability to process sensory information</term>, it prepares the way, or again the whole experience of the partial things—entirely within the perceptions of each of them—will command their parts according to a certain belief. And honors for the rest no longer exist. For it is in vain, and the soul will be perceptive. And this shall be. And it is not only all of them together, but we do not wait for perception to come from you.

Consider nothing more than the soul.
</margin>

And regarding those things about which men have been at a loss <note>original: "ἀπορήσαντες" — from 'aporia', a state of philosophical confusion or a dead-end</note>, let them be restored to a state of clarity <note>original: "εὐπορίαν" — the opposite of 'aporia', meaning a clear path or resourcefulness</note>; or let these very difficulties lead to the many opinions held on the matter. If it is necessary first to inquire about her, one should undertake these studies; for about what else could one speak more than about the soul? To those who consider it, these pursuits are worth our labor. Whatever knowledge we may claim to have comes through these very means. And it would be a worthy good if we should set ourselves to follow their encouragement. Following that encouragement, let us make our examination of this subject. For while we desire other things, we do not seek through ourselves the primary things, and thus we do not easily attain the heights of contemplation. In order that the **intelligible** <note>original: "νοητὸν" — things that can be grasped by the mind rather than the senses</note> might be found even in this, we must conduct our search among pure things—but where can such be found?

<margin>
Whether the soul’s **substance** <note>original: "ὑπόστασις" — the underlying reality or fundamental nature of a thing</note> comes from the **World Soul**, or whether all other souls are parts of one single soul.
</margin>

One should consider the superiority of the gods in this way; but when one has leisure from all else and becomes part of the intelligible realm, we may best define ourselves by turning toward the nature of souls. And let these matters be as follows: for perhaps it is not worth considering whether our own souls reach the same level as those of the gods, or whether we are merely a part. In another sense, her "parts" are in a different place. For she exists equally according to the parts of the whole; <unclear>under-</unclear> lying this, they will seem to be of the same kind whenever one says they are part of her, just as a body is a part, but not of the whole. That which exists after "being" is our own. And so it is with such things. There is a difference between individual bodies, and that which is said and <unclear>actually</unclear> <unclear>exists</unclear>. And the fates of those whose natures have been established <unclear>will be</unclear>. From this, one must calculate the nature of each of us. From our own soul, one takes up the world itself as being part of the **Reason-Principle** <note>original: "λόγος" — the organizing principle that gives form to the world</note>, and those who share in the soul are part of the fact that all souls belong to the universe.

It questions whether individual human souls are distinct entities or merely parts of a single "World Soul."</summary>

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the nature of the soul, specifically addressing the central Neoplatonic paradox: how the soul can be a single, indivisible unity while simultaneously appearing divided among many individual physical bodies. It builds on the previous page's discussion of the soul's presence in the body.</meta>

<margin>
What is the single principle?
</margin>

Especially for those who consider things of the same kind to be so by mere chance. For if there is a line, it is a part in that it is a line; but it differs simply by **magnitude** <note>original: "μέγεθος" — spatial extent or size</note> even here. But the difference of the soul is that its **essence** <note>original: "τὸ τί ἦν εἶναι" — literally 'the what it was to be', a standard Aristotelian term for the essential nature of a thing</note> and its "whole" are not the same thing. The body is also of such a nature; taking on difference insofar as it is always extended, not being a true **subsistence** <note>original: "ὑπόστασιν" — an underlying reality or primary substance</note>. For souls do not appear to be like spatial magnitudes; they are not divided up in that way, nor do they learn according to every part; for that would exhaust the whole, and it would be a name only. If the "whole" is in "every part," as was said of the point in a line long ago, then each part contains both, being a part itself. We might say the "whole" is derived from these. But the fact is that the soul remains a whole.

This signifies that while the souls themselves remain in the **Universal Soul** <note>the 'All-Soul' which animates the entire cosmos</note>, the particular expressions and **activities** <note>original: "ἐνεργείας" — the actual functioning or manifestation of a power</note> belong to each individual. Furthermore, they are all the same, for each part remains in the "There" <note>a common Plotinian shorthand for the Intelligible Realm, the higher world of forms</note> where the "Whole" remains. It is not as if the soul is split among many; but if it is in the whole, then the whole is in the place of the parts, and they could not be parts of it, but rather it would be a single nature. Nor is this true for these alone, but for all, and for the soul itself: all souls are of the One, being of the same kind. But they have departed from that world to this **cosmos** <note>the physical universe</note> and the things within it. 

But are they "parts" in the way our senses are? There would be a certain sequence here, being parts in the living universe, where the "whole" is revealed. But the soul's "part" becomes the "whole" of the body; it is not in the body, but in the "living" cosmos. The entire soul looks upon this; and through **Intellect** <note>original: "νῷ" — the higher divine mind</note>, all things are held according to her nature. For in the parts, all things are not present <unclear>in part</unclear>, and thus parts would be destroyed and could not provide for each individual. 

You must accept that **activity** <note>original: "ἐνέργειαν"</note> is one and the same in all its "tendrils." It is not according to a starting point; rather, she provides that each thing be a unity. This is especially true for those things whose same **power** <note>original: "δυνάμει"</note> is—

<margin>
From one part of the soul in one part and another part of the body:
<image-desc>A large curly brace connects the first two lines of this marginal note to the subsequent three lines, pointing toward the main text body.</image-desc>
All the **powers** of the soul are in all the organs, but in **activity** they are in all, yet one is in one organ, and another in another.
</margin>

—in all of them, though in some it is different. That [power] remains indestructible and corresponds to all things; they will also give back from within themselves, being simple and not truly [divided]. It is the same thing, just as the power of sight is in each of the two eyes. If the whole power is in both, yet the **organs** <note>original: "ὄργανα" — the physical tools or instruments of the body</note> are different, then the results produced here differ. All of them, however, exist within **Being**. But she wishes to frequent the things of the senses and the necessities of life because of the **imagination** <note>original: "φαντασίαν" — the faculty that translates sense data into mental images</note> of living beings.

<summary>Plotinus explains that while the soul appears divided among different bodies or organs, it remains an indivisible unity. He uses the analogy of sight in two eyes to show how one power can operate through different physical instruments without being split into pieces.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the technical investigation into Neoplatonic psychology, specifically exploring how individual souls relate to the Universal Soul and the Divine Mind (Nous). It transitions from the general definition of the soul's unity to the specific reasons why individual souls appear different from one another despite their common origin.</meta>

<margin>
What and from where is the difference between souls?
</margin>

If the partial things are indeed the parts, and if they are not the same, then those that are partial must attend to being **There** <note>original: "ἐκεῖ" — a term used by Plotinus to refer to the higher Intelligible Realm of Forms</note>. But before reaching that "There," the partial things are the primary ones; they provide the basis for **contemplation** <note>original: "θεωρίας" — the act of intellectual seeing or spiritual vision</note> and causation. Even when standing over the body, they remain something else; those things placed around the body and the body itself act as a **substrate** <note>original: "ἐξ ὑποκειμένου" — the underlying material or subject</note>, yet the soul is not the "whole" of that substrate, nor does it possess a different numerical identity. For the soul tends toward the same reality. Even if we categorize a thing as being "through that" or "from that," in the higher realm, it remains directed toward itself. When it is in a body and acts upon the body's motion, souls set aside their higher state when motion occurs in the body; the **affections** <note>original: "παθήσεις" — the passive experiences or sufferings of the soul</note> surrounding it are not what the souls would call "driving forces" themselves, for the partial parts are not themselves bodily.

<margin>
Diseases of souls in knowledge <unclear>from</unclear> and souls dependent on that one Mind of all souls concerning the Ideas of souls
</margin>

**There**, however, some are separated in a different rank, as if by their own doing, and some are like those who have "mounted" <note>an allusion to the chariot of the soul in Plato's *Phaedrus*</note> each of the things upon which they depend. They might be understood as being a part of that higher reality; for example, as if a body were to emerge from each part of a single **Sun**. While being a part, each individual soul refers back to those higher things as it chooses, and though it is a "part" as if from a part, it does not abandon the **Whole**. Each soul is distinct, and yet all are one. For the core of the argument is that from one and the same source, many things become the same as those from which they were divided, and yet they are not truly divided. The **Reason-principle** <term>Logos: the formative, organizing principle that flows from the Mind into the Soul</term> of the **Mind** <note>original: "νοῦς" — the Divine Intellect</note> remains; and from it, the soul acts as a cause, as if by arranging things within the All. Soul and the **World** <note>original: "κόσμον" — the ordered universe</note> are linked.

<margin>
What and from where is the difference between souls?
</margin>

This signifies the World, and then each soul possesses everything within itself. In this way:

<margin>
World <gloss>itself</gloss> soul has made the World <unclear>with a solution</unclear>
</margin>

For the administration by which it moves the Whole is its task. Other things follow after these. And just as all things are drawn from a source, the Whole is one thing and the partial is another. Some things are known to each soul individually; but in that which is unique, it is not clear why it has made the World. These "parts" are the parts of the World's **Justice** <note>original: "δικαιοσύνης"</note>. It is a marvelous thing in the All that each soul possesses the Whole; some have more and some have less, as if they will always be receiving. Yet it is a Unity. But if the soul does not hold itself back, the difference becomes greater; insofar as one does not act differently,

<margin>
Plotinus, [Ennead IV], Book 3, Chapter 4, on the essence of the soul.
</margin>

it remains whole, but only by **stripping off** <note>original: "ἐκδύσατε" — a metaphor for shedding the body like a garment to return to a pure spiritual state</note> the body from around itself. Others, like sister souls, have shared their allotted portions by fitting together. It is as if they have drawn this destiny to themselves as their own. Some see things by their own power, while others suffer more in relation to their bodies; every soul makes something clear about itself. For it is not the private property of any, but belongs to all.

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the unity of the soul, moving from the theoretical proof of unity into the practical question of how individual souls can be distinct while sharing a single source. It bridges the gap between the "One" soul and the "Many" souls that inhabit human and animal bodies.</meta>

<margin>
He takes this together into all (2 1 30) and it must be written through the Ideas.
</margin>

<margin>
All souls are from one soul; all are one and many, and because of this, they are all in sympathy with one another.
</margin>

<margin>
What are the differences between souls and from what source do they arise?
</margin>

...but regarding the many souls, all are therefore one. They exist both from her <note>original: "παρ’ αὐτῆς" — referring to the Universal Soul</note> and within her. Even when the soul is separated, it does not suffer, but all things are situated elsewhere, both apart from the whole and with the whole, just as it will be granted to you in your own case. We may grant this much: we say that some things are different. Thus, I say that all things in bodies are especially able to possess **rational principles** <note>original: "λόγους" (*logoi*) — the formative, active forces that give shape and meaning to physical matter</note>. And this is an accidental occurrence, for the whole of that higher soul does not yet belong to each individual part; however, because they all come from one and the same whole, they are in **sympathy** <note>original: "συμπαθεῖς" — a technical term in Greek philosophy describing the "co-feeling" or organic interconnection between all parts of the universe</note> even with us. This has been stated because the soul is both one and many, and because of the difference between the part and the whole.

It is a significant task to speak generally about the difference of the soul and the parts it is with, and to show that it differs even from the bodies that are about to come into being. Within the very centers of our faculty of **intellect** <note>original: "διανοίας" (*dianoias*) — discursive reasoning or the mind’s processing power</note>, there is a certain subsistence. From our previous lives <note>original: "προτεθειμένων βίων" — a reference to the Neoplatonic belief in the pre-existence of the soul and reincarnation</note> and the ways we have naturally lived, choices persist in the souls. Perhaps nature distinguishes them, and in these lives, the differences are said to be infinite. Many souls exist in themselves, and they are not equal in their being. As they remain in each of these bodies, it is beneficial for some to be here and others to be nearby; some look outward and, as it were, gaze upon another. Just as they are seen and intellectually grasped, so too are the things full of life, as they exist within the **rational principles**. And so it is with the rest.

The collective arrangement belonging to those souls will never fail them. For if there is a need for all to be varied and complex—just as some think souls have many forms—but if there are many and they belong to the body, these things will not be the same at all, but will belong to others. It is not even clear by such a mind, not even when they are within the bodies. 

And concerning **number** <note>original: "ἀριθμῷ" — Plotinus discusses whether the number of souls is finite or infinite</note>, so that it might always be one, or that the same souls always exist, being the same today as the ancient ones were. For each thing exists in number; for that is how we identify "this particular thing." Regarding the nature of individual bodies, this point should not be contested, since **matter** <note>original: "ὕλης" (*hylēs*) — the underlying "stuff" of the physical world</note> requires it. But for the forms that come from the number of beings, it shall not be determined by the bodies themselves. It is necessary that there is a sufficient number of those things which existed from the beginning, so that the things being born are nevertheless not unequal. But this is not the case for other things which were themselves made from a single matter. If this is so, it must be taken from itself—not like a grain of wheat as previously proposed—but rather as a soul will produce the better things from its own essence. It would often be...

<margin>
Every simple thing is immortal.
</margin>

...undamaged and not consumed by any other thing. And that which is to come in the future, if it is indeed perfect and undamaged, then in such a state **every living thing is immortal** <note>original: "πᾶν ζῶον ἀθάνατον" — a concluding affirmation that because the soul is "simple" (not made of parts), it cannot be broken down or destroyed</note>.

## The descent of souls into bodies: why and how

<margin>
The **World Soul** <note>original: "ψυχὴ Κόϲμου" (*psyche kosmou*)</note>: why she created the body of the Cosmos, from what source, how she descended, and how she relates to the Body of the Cosmos.
</margin>
For those things which happen to arise from it, they do not belong to those <unclear>prior</unclear> things; rather, for the rest, it is like a soul in a body, through her own creative act. Nor is it by a <unclear>departure</unclear> or withdrawal, but they exist together in thought. These things are separated from one another in our minds. For the rest, she is like an invisible fire from a hearth, and the <unclear>smooth</unclear> body near it is made calm by it; for as long as the body has quantity, that which it <unclear>received</unclear> was not the whole of that source, but everything exists within the light. In truth, the whole has not yet moved into it, so that there is hope for the whole body to <unclear>subsist</unclear> as far as her power reaches, like a strong <unclear>muscle</unclear>, or like a great radiance shining toward the furthest edge

<margin>
The origin of **matter** <note>original: "ὕλη" (*hyle*) — the underlying "stuff" of the universe that lacks form</note>: how and from where, and its shaping into form.
</margin>
of the fire. But darkness <unclear>arose</unclear> around the matter, according to which she <unclear>brought fire</unclear> to that very thing which, seen under the intense gaze of Hermes, was found to be without a share in the light, receiving only a dim shadow. Upon this faint darkness she constructed the body, making each part beautiful and varied. As she sent forth its form, she who is the source of all things did not fail to adorn it. For she is worthy of all things, <unclear>honored</unclear> and great, giving the body its benefit and mastery; and as much as it is able to receive, she disciplines its disorder and defines it by its form. Such an arrangement is a living being, though it does not demand to master its master. There are rulers, but I cannot say they exist anywhere except within the soul. Nor is she <unclear>divided into parts</unclear> from herself, but is present at every single point.

<margin>
The body is within the soul like a **net in the water**.
</margin>
The soul is not together with the world in a way that she is made by it; rather, the body is <unclear>suspended</unclear> within the soul, like a **net in the sea** <note>This is a famous Neoplatonic metaphor: just as a net is submerged in the ocean and the water flows through every mesh but remains vast and free beyond it, the soul permeates the body without being confined by it.</note>, stretched out through it. For while the body is composed of various parts from different places, the soul is not neglected; the soul is as vast as the cosmos, so that she occupies it equally, and wherever the net may be, there she is. And this continues until she puts off the body.

<margin>
How the soul is joined to the body of the Cosmos; the origin of quantity in matter; and why the Cosmos is of such a size.
</margin>
For her very magnitude is what shall hold it together, and it exists to the extent that it <unclear>follows</unclear> her. It is defined by the limit to which her power might <unclear>proceed</unclear>. And the shadow is as large as the **Reason-Principle** <note>original: "λόγοϲ" (*logos*) — the formative, organizing principle that translates divine ideas into physical reality</note> that comes from her. This Reason-Principle was such that it could produce a magnitude as great as its form desired. Hearing it thus, one uses the imagination within oneself to grasp all these things together: the air, the light, the soul <unclear>drawing</unclear> the light. ### On the Punishment of Souls

Every divine law punishes souls in **Hades** <note>original: "ᾅδου" (*Haidou*) — the Greek underworld, here referring generally to the state of the soul after death</note>.

---

That perhaps there is another body besides the earthly one, possibly a **spirit** <term>original: "πνεῦμα" (*pneuma*) — in this context, a "subtle" or "astral" body composed of air and fire that the soul inhabits after leaving the physical body</term> made of fire and air. This is what the soul possesses before death in another body.

---

That souls are punished **along with a body**; but those that have been released from them <note>likely meaning those souls that have completely purified themselves from material attachments</note> are in turn unpunished and solitary.

Others [claim it is] possible [to exist] without any body <unclear>partly</unclear> <unclear>optimal</unclear> <unclear>thing</unclear> <note>Translated from the Latin: "Alius poße sine omi..."</note>
For there is a body before life, and [we must ask] in what manner it comes to be.
</insert>

---

Whether the soul, having departed outside the body, **remembers** anything.

---

To remember the occurrences of the whole <note>meaning the universal experiences or the higher truths of the cosmos</note>.

<column-break/>

The difference is material; and even if it is in an arrangement among the same things, for they are rotted by nature, which is what they possess. Again, it falls into strife; having pulled away the **alien body** <note>the physical body, viewed as foreign to the soul's true nature</note>, it finds its place among bodies of like-mind. That which is judged and carried along... the one who suffers is without knowledge, once for all having been formed by nature and necessity. 

For the souls that are suspended or returning, dying like captives from that place and wherever their health exists, they are carried voluntarily. On the contrary, their suffering is investigated; if the things of bodies and the nature of things are gathered together from that punishment... and for the one appearing from those places, holding them down by the power of **harmony**.

While the soul has the body, it perceives these things and the bodily punishments that serve as **purifications** <term>original: "καθάρσεις" (*katharseis*) — ritual or philosophical cleansing of the soul's impurities</term> for these souls; and after punishment, they are carried away from the body. For they exist outside and not in a bodily way, as they would not if they were not a body, nor again an essence and the whole, and the whole is like the divine. It is not about the things of places, and I did not stand by any guard... if at the eyes... in the body and punishment again.

If perhaps these souls, having departed, might **remember**; for in this way, some things [are remembered] and others are not. And some things are from human and visible causes, and from the causes of the chance of the departure. And the like is worthy of contempt, and finally, it is right to make judgments about these things as they truly are. 

To remember is to have remains from a **monument** <note>a play on the Greek *mnēmeion* (monument/tomb) and *mnēmoneuein* (to remember)</note>; but if for all it is unthinkable, being naturally established. For one thing is a monument, and another is different; and it is often rumored. To remember, for those naturally able, would be most accurately judged—whether we suffer unjustly from a lesson or a passion. Nor is there a need for the whole for them... it would become destructive, and to remember... about new divine periods, for there is nothing for them, nor time... the period and when there is another of these. Nor is there fear, but something held in the same arrangement. And how could it be in a form, for not even another body is worthy.

### The Temperaments of the Body and the Soul

The **temperaments** <term>original: "κράσεις" (*kraseis*) — the specific mixture of bodily fluids or "humors" that ancient doctors believed determined health and personality</term> of bodies; and the faculties of **memory**; and the parts of **vision**, or the way **blood** <note>Plotinus often views "thick" blood or a heavy physical constitution as a weight that "clogs" the soul’s higher perception</note> can act as a hindrance; or how these things are shaping factors; because of which the body comes to be. Regarding the things of the soul, one part might be moved by it [the body] in the same way as life in bodies, and how the **common part** <note>the *koinon* or the composite of soul and body together</note> corresponds to it. 

If some living being—both the body and the soul—existed in this way as being in the same place. For it is no less a case of one thing, yet perhaps a body did not come along with that living being; for it would not change both of them, of which the one is the whole of the living being. But if it 

<margin>14</margin>
rules over them. As if these things were feeble in the living being, it would be there in it, and thus it would be in the whole; but this [the soul] would not be as if it were contained, so that nothing rules within it. 

It is scattered. And this again would not be; even if it were a part. Why then is it not possible for it to be? By being **pure**; but simply to place the whole [of memory] out of sight of life because of the **connection with sensible things** <term>original: "αἰσθητῶν σύνεσιν" (*aisthetōn synesin*) — the soul's preoccupation with things perceived by the senses (touch, sight, etc.) rather than intellect</term>, and because of the kind of things which were previously neglected in the body. And it should not just "flow past" but accurately remain within. Not divided 

<column-break/>

as if by parts or by a **seal** <note>a common metaphor in ancient philosophy where memory is compared to a wax tablet being stamped by a signet ring</note>; for it is not like an impression. Because the part must not simply have a body; but not the kind that is like a disease. And if, among **incorporeal things** <term>original: "ἀσωμάτων" (*asōmatōn*) — things without physical bodies, like thoughts, souls, or mathematical truths</term>, some were to escape the difficulties of thoughts; or if the motion of the body belongs to the incorporeal things according to an error of its own movements, but they might think that it [the soul] alone is **recollection**. 

And if it had not enjoyed; there will be no **pain**; for the body is the subject of **passions** <term>original: "παθῶν" (*pathōn*) — not just "passion" in the modern sense, but any "suffering" or "affection" where the soul is acted upon by the body</term>; for it is first in the body, about which there is no pain. But if, again, that which comes from the body has been isolated from the body, which he says does not know the body at all; but it must be 

<margin>25</margin>
taken into the soul. From where, however many passions occur through the body, they belong to the soul; but if the soul is in it, it also holds a certain nature of its own; it would also need it, he says. 

And indeed, the **diviner** <note>original: "μάντις" (*mantis*) — a prophet or seer; Plotinus uses this to discuss intuitive or supernatural knowledge</note> of desire, but also in the desire of the other; and even this itself and its nature; for it does not exist in another way, that which is not... nor do they follow as if they were certain hypotheses and movements. For not having everything in its nature, these things are **common** from the body just as they are **private**. For some of those who think it is the cause—for who would not... and if she brings gifts and the fruitfulness... and by the movements. 

And it has the body which it **ensouls**; so that a living being is added in it, but if it is taken away and brought down, it often arrives, and memory-faculties are not prepared, by which they pour out a natural part of the body itself.

Not even there, by leading the bodies, and especially the **ascent from Hades** <note>original: "ᾅδου ἄνοδος" — Plotinus often uses the "ascent from the underworld" as a metaphor for the soul leaving the physical body</note> being the place; and as if a naked touch; for indeed, the **labors of Heracles** <note>The twelve tasks of the hero Heracles</note> are perhaps like those in **impressions** <term>original: "τύποις" (*typois*) — stamps, molds, or mental imprints</term>.

The soul in the **intelligible world** <term>original: "νοητῷ" (*noētō*) — the realm of pure thought and Forms</term> remembers nothing, or contemplates nothing of the things here <note>the physical world</note>.
</margin>

Such things are also some of the recollections; or rather in that which happens to those there. Therefore it is from there, to contemplate there and about the things there. But some say that we are in the later things; so that the things happening "above nature" are a task for you. And why, not being these things, is it at random? For the same thing belongs to them so that it is toward the **better order**. But because he might act, that too might happen to be contemplated. And in some cases, life is not staying in a worldly way as what has been born, but as if one of them... this too while changing, that which is hidden in the **living being** <term>original: "ζῴῳ" (*zōō*)</term> would not be remembered of the things here; just as those who have remembered them even in the case of the **unjust**. All **knowledge** is **eternity** <term>original: "αἰών" (*aiōn*)</term>; but when such people use things there, they would always have memory, not because they are in the "here" but also entirely such a person; otherwise...

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s investigation into the nature of memory as the soul transitions between the physical world and the higher realm of the Intellect. It builds on the previous discussion of how the soul's "experiences" or "affections" are retained or discarded during its ascent.</meta>

<margin>
This [soul] experiences one thing and another relative to herself and the things beneath her; the purification exists while within the **intelligible** <term>original: "νοητῷ" (*noētō*) — the realm of pure, non-physical thought and being</term>.
</margin>

<margin>
How certain things are in the intelligible, and here in the Intellect.
</margin>

We must say, then, that we here might touch upon them perhaps as much as we happen to; having come to be what is situated. To be in the intelligible is like being in a dwelling; for if anything is around the center here, from where one might go safely to the parts, it should not be thought of in the same way; but casting it down, one must say it proceeds from the same things to the same things. And when it partakes of other things from itself, it is both itself and in the intelligible; but when again it turns toward the better things and itself—for its own self is there, and its being in the intelligible is just as it is there. Just as it places itself in the beginning, so here it is turned from that which is after the **depth** <term>original: "βυθός" (*bythos*) — a term for the unfathomable source of all existence</term>. From a foreseeing movement and cause, its goodness does not perish, but it is both [states], holding even in a certain opinion and changing; yet it holds itself unchangeably and at the peak, possessing its own essence; just as these appear together with those—

<margin>
How the **soul** <term>original: "ψυχή" (*psychē*)</term> having gone out from the intelligible, and how memory also went out from there.
</margin>

Having come from there and being filled with memory, first she has a **perception** <term>original: "αἴσθησιν" (*aisthēsin*)</term> of herself and then a second participation; and as if looking out, becoming anxious for herself, she takes on a **worldly disposition** <term>original: "φρονημα" (*phronēma*) — a sense of pride or individual mind-set</term>. Whatever part of the things there and the things in part from which the sensory world consists—those she carries, but she who is in the intelligible is also there in stability. And here, perhaps, she takes on that **memory** <term>original: "μνήμην" (*mnēmēn*)</term> as a sort of **imagination** <term>original: "φαντασίαν" (*phantasian*)</term>; and it is imagination itself, yet it is not so, but rather like when she looks back again at the lights of the sensory things. Whatever amount of them she looks away from, in this depth—not that there is a limit within herself—and thus an end comes to everything. And bordering and reaching what she was allotted, she **oscillates between two sides** <term>original: "ἐπαμφοτερίζειν" (*epamphoterizein*) — to belong to both worlds at once</term>—

<margin>
The soul is a **borderland** <term>original: "μεθόριον" (*methorion*)</term> between the intelligible and the sensible, and it oscillates between them.
</margin>

It happens regarding the same things in visions; hence they are no longer like the things there, so that neither the things from there nor the things in the body are between them, as if of each. For indeed the body formerly attached itself here before the first things; and from herself, in care and truth, she removes the memories; and in imagination where she wishes. Nor does she remember when she is among the best things; for she no longer has the need to receive memories—it is something similar to thinking one perceives that they have remembered; but even when they are disposed according to—

<margin>
**Double memory** <term>original: "διπλῆ μνήμη" (*diplē mnēmē*)</term>
</margin>

...the present experiences even there. For they might receive foreign memories because she possesses them, unless something from herself is stronger. For even in form, she seeks a memory of those things once and for all, but not a search for their movements.

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the nature of memory, shifting focus from the individual human soul to the souls of the celestial bodies (the stars and planets). It explores whether these divine beings require memory or discursive reasoning in their eternal state.</meta>

<margin>
Whether the souls of the stars <gloss>to be</gloss> [possess] memory and a discursive <term>original: "διέξοδον" (*diexodon*) — a step-by-step or "running through" process of thought</term> path of thought.

<margin>
For there are certain reasonings and syllogisms in their activity and thoughts, but not concerning human affairs.
</margin>

Knowledge of the whole is not necessary. Regarding the causes and the fortunes associated with them, one might say that they also remember; for of those things that have happened and passed away, they themselves, by their own superiority, [perceive] some of the new things. However, there are those among you who testify to the disorder of others and our own **sensible** <term>original: "αἰσθητὸν" (*aisthēton*) — that which can be perceived by the five senses</term> world; yet before these [events], their memories are directed toward what is brilliant. Being in the same state, all of them perhaps move with the same movements, always going toward the same point in the same way. Their thoughts and everything else look toward that higher realm. Things here are not held in high esteem, but they look toward heaven; they do not learn of any human thing, nor do they have knowledge of them, except for those things that are eternal and part of the **cosmos** <term>original: "κόσμου" (*kosmou*) — the universe seen as an ordered, beautiful whole</term>. From these things they hear of our affairs, and in that realm, they know other things in a certain way through which we perceive them, or through which they remember the whole. Or one might wonder if they see through these things, though not having seen them through me. For the body, being under the senses, has nothing in them [the stars]; being a neighbor, it was necessary that the things there were not [like things here]. Nor do they live toward things that are separate, though perhaps they often do these things always. Furthermore, the circuits and the movement would be a cause, just as memories rooted in many things are like the impulses in bodies. There are other necessities as well; many signs and the different occurrences here are called many examples. And [memory] would fade, because nights also intervene; but since for us it is thus by day, the same applies to them. The presence and the distance from them [affects this]; and that which was before their memories would not have passed away, but exists rather in **eternity** <term>original: "αἰωνίῳ" (*aiōniō*) — timeless existence, as opposed to time measured by change</term>. If there is a movement of beings, does it not also involve the changes around them? And because [it comes] from others into this, and because other things are present concerning the things laid down. They would not be there, nor would they be placed there to be contemplated; thus the whole is according to accidental qualities.

<margin>
The perception of heavenly souls, which produces in them memory and **imagination** <term>original: "φαντασίαν" (*phantasian*) — the faculty of forming mental images</term>, is clear from what is evident among us regarding births <unclear>alone</unclear>.
</margin>

An accompanying imagination comes to be, and the knowledge of these things is clearer. Then, if it were to occur through the senses, would their knowledge of particular things not be clearer? Moreover, there is a certain representative economy in them where the part produces knowledge of the whole, which is what we claim to say of each thing here. <meta>This page continues the discussion on the nature of celestial beings, moving from their memory to the nature of their motion and the governing intellect of the universe, often personified as Zeus. It explores how a divine mind manages the infinite details of time and creation.</meta>

<margin>
Motion <term>original: "Κίνησις" (*kinesis*) — in Greek philosophy, this refers to any kind of change or activity, not just moving from place to place</term>, how it is perfect through itself and holds an aspiration toward the end <note>or "goal"</note>.
</margin>
<margin>
The harmony of the blessed celestial motions.
</margin>

All movements, whether they are perfect and essential like those of the divine causes, always participate in their own essence. If they are perfect and exist through one another, these will not be encompassed by time; for they are not a whole <note>in the sense of a finite, completed thing</note>, and thus there is no aspiration coming from time itself. Therefore, they are not moved by disease, neither chronologically nor locally; thus, not even for ten thousand <unclear>years</unclear>, since life for them is so vast. From their own souls and through them, all things exist. The <unclear>nature</unclear> of celestial things comes from <unclear>his</unclear> and through them in the universe <unclear>itself</unclear> <unclear>as</unclear> <unclear>according to</unclear>, as it encompasses all the motions within it, and with an unshakeable <unclear>breath</unclear> <unclear>thought</unclear>. These motions exist as things that are undivided and were <unclear>appearing</unclear> prior to them, and especially toward that very point, they release and provide essence to essence in a <unclear>complete</unclear> way within it. This divinity and life is similar to the purification of the whole.

<margin>
Who is Zeus, having a royal soul and a royal intellect? <note>This refers to a famous passage in Plato's *Philebus* (30d) regarding the governing power of the universe.</note>
</margin>

One must say that those things are eternal, and the things of the predecessors, and why they are established to be both a royal soul and a royal intellect and providence <term>original: "πρόνοια" (*pronoia*) — literally 'forethought,' the divine care for the universe</term> existing for us, and how the act of thinking is established and governs by order. He <unclear>releases</unclear> cycles and <unclear>all</unclear> generations; in these matters, the <unclear>astronomical</unclear> details <unclear>would no longer</unclear> <unclear>become stable</unclear>. <margin>
How the Demiurge <term>original: "δημιουργὸς" (*demiourgos*) — the divine 'Craftsman' or Creator of the physical world</term> knows an infinite number of things and times.
</margin>

Just as the things from him are eternal, <unclear>whatever</unclear> number belongs to him reaches even to the ends of the world. The number of things and times is not as great as all his own world and the infinite things; for he holds all things and the mind, but by the act of thinking, he holds all that is infinite and the whole according to the total, no longer in an <note>untested or infinite</note> way. For his own infinity contains the units <note>monads</note>; thus, his thinking will be established, having the things from his own world <unclear>remaining</unclear> because of their intellect.

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the mental life of divine beings. While the previous page discussed the royal intellect of Zeus and the motion of the heavens, this section contrasts the discursive reasoning of humans with the immediate, eternal wisdom of the gods. It specifically examines whether "reasoning" — a process of moving from problem to solution — has any place in a perfect being.</meta>

<margin>What reasoning is</margin>
These things do not happen in the same way; rather, they are natural cycles of life that occur over time, such as the ripening of fruits or the growth of the body—maturities and old age—while other things are congenital to that which is eternally established. Those things which come about differently are shown by the fact that in the growth of women, there is a consistent and organizing <term>original: "λόγος" (*logos*) — here meaning a formative principle or ratio</term>. And indeed, how could these things not be characterized by <term>original: "φρόνησις" (*phronesis*) — practical wisdom or prudence</term>, if they are measured out in this way? These things must be universal, like a fellowship between political and domestic wisdom, and they will surely fulfill those other things, so that many things are not just parts, but at that time and all at once, they are everything.

<margin>That gods do not use reasoning</margin>
All of their affairs come after and alongside this prudence. <insert>And knowledge</insert> is theirs. Some things belong to nature, while others belong to prudence. Is a "personal calculation" <note>original: "λογισμὸς" (*logismos*) — the step-by-step process of thinking through a problem</note> necessary in the whole of the universe, which "someone," as the saying goes, created? Or should we posit that "thinking" <note>original: "φρονεῖν" (*phronein*)</note> is of such a kind, and that this thinking is entirely derived from a Thinking that has already come to be? For to "reason" about other things would be a denial of the very Idea of prudence, even if it happens to hit upon the same result as the Creator; for reasoning is a process of being carried along and, if it belongs to one thing or another, of being changed. Generally, it belongs to that which exists according to something else.

<margin>The reason for having used [it]</margin>
The reasoning "held together the divine chariot" <note>A reference to Plato's *Phaedrus* (246e), where Zeus leads the heavenly host in a winged chariot</note>, which one might say is not absurd if thinking bears witness to the whole. And yet, this reasoning is unnoticed. For when everything is not "reasoning" and "rest," if thinking is applied according to the present moment of purification, then what was said about the "plans" of the whole is unexpected and full of puzzles. And memories are present alongside—

<margin>How gods know future things</margin>
<margin>They say these [the gods] do not deliberate according to a certain private prudence</margin>
—things that have passed, alongside things that are present, and the one is a motion. But if this [prudence] is also swift for everything, we must consider its thinking to be a "concord" <note>original: "ὁμονόησιν" (*homonoiesin*) — a literal "sameness of mind" or internal harmony</note> of itself. That which is according to the <term>original: "νοῦς" (*nous*) — the divine Mind or Intellect</term> is especially so, for it would be absurd to say they no longer possess it. Because of this, they did not see the things here. But if they know them, and how they will be, it is a matter of trust in reasoning. And as for the fact that past things coincide with present things, this is consistent with common faith; and the same for future things, if indeed it is granted to him to be present in this way. These concepts are present to some, namely to the virtuous themselves, since they are most trustworthy. And this is so for the messengers <note>original: "ἀγγέλοις" (*aggelois*) — in this Neoplatonic context, these are "angels" or intermediary spirits that bridge the gap between gods and the physical world</note> who are everywhere; they are not in doubt nor are they uncertain. Therefore, it is not at all necessary for every part to wait for prudence to be present in that particular thing, and to be that thing itself. For the rest, this would seem to be worthy of consideration.

<summary>This page explores why divine beings do not need discursive reasoning (logismos), arguing that their "prudence" is a form of immediate, harmonious knowledge rather than a step-by-step deliberation. It concludes by suggesting that gods and intermediary spirits (angels) possess a "concord" of mind that transcends time, knowing the past and future as a unified present.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the exploration of the hierarchy of being. While the previous page discussed the distinction between the gods' immediate wisdom and human reasoning, this page moves down the scale to examine how "Reason-principles" (*Logoi*) operate in the Intellect, the Soul, and finally in Nature and Matter. It also introduces the relationship between these levels and the concepts of Time and Eternity.</meta>

# **Reason-principles in the Intellect are all things; in the Soul, they are secondary; in Nature, they are the lowest.**
# **In Matter, they are either non-beings or clearly imitations; and matter itself is already an imitation.**

---

<margin>Nature and the reason-principles within it were the furthest reaches of the Intellect; after these, I say, are imitations of the intelligibles, or things that are already intelligible.</margin>
Having received an image from that higher realm, <term>Nature</term> <note>original: "φύσις" (*physis*)</note> begins to exist; these are the beings, and all things, and these are the lowest parts of the <term>Intellect</term> <note>original: "νοῦς" (*nous*)</note>. For the things that come before it are the primary, unmoved beings. But Nature here, being passive, has been affected by that higher source; it is not independent, yet while it acts upon all things, it also undergoes experience. Those things within are subsequent and occur as soon as it acts. 

Bodies, however, are produced by Nature from that which does not come into being; bodies do not possess these parts in themselves. But animals and plants possess Nature as something adjacent to them, as if it were an escape from the body. In the case of man, Nature is separated, yet even while being separated, it is like a moved world of fire and of heating—

<margin>Whether Nature is an image of the Soul, or if it exists alongside the body, like light or like fire.</margin>
—without the heat departing, however, but coming to rest in that thing. Whether we should place it around the bodies of what has been heated in part, by the form in another place, or in the whole body alongside Nature itself. Then again in another, this is brought along after this and Nature itself. In these and in the differences of Nature. These things are truly present in the parts, but it is difficult for them to be in this; these memories of mental images <note>original: "φαντασμῶν" (*phantasmōn*) — appearances or mental impressions</note> do not possess reality regarding Nature itself. 

Time is involved in these things, for it has a phantom-like quality because those higher things still exist; regarding souls, they are divided. And some souls undergo these things while that which is above is divided; and possessing what has passed away, they are divided here as well, and the soul turns herself toward the past. They act, and do not imitate only in part. For some are in the realm of the <term>eternities</term> <note>original: "αἰώνων" (*aiōnōn*) — the realm of timeless being</note>, while all these things happen by chance, some being placed earlier. And they are called eternal—

<margin>How the Earth in the cosmos, or as a mother, possesses motion and a differing sense of time.</margin>
—time, they say that souls exist but that their movement <note>original: "μεταβαίνειν" (*metabainein*) — the process of passing from one state to another</note> is not bodily in the cosmos, receiving changes around the souls; these are different and of the lesser sort, such as those that exist in time by nature. But the <term>Soul of the All</term> <note>original: "τοῦ ὅλου ψυχὴν" — the World Soul that animates the entire universe</note> makes use of these, but would not be in time; rather, bodies are placed in time, while she generates time for the cosmos, and simultaneously <term>Eternity</term> <note>original: "αἰῶνα" (*aiōna*)</note>. 

And again, we encompass the cosmos together, yet it is in time, while souls are in time. But these same souls are unswerving <note>original: "ἀπλανεῖς" (*aplaneis*) — a term often applied to the "fixed stars" that do not wander</note>, and their works are those things remaining as causes, and those that follow; and it possessed no less of time. Arriving at this, we hold that what is present in place and in number is its own plunder.
