<meta>This page continues the investigation into the relationship between the higher principles and the physical world. While the previous page focused on how Reason-principles (Logoi) descend from the Intellect into Nature, this page shifts focus to the internal state of the human being—specifically, how the Soul interacts with the Body, the origin of internal conflict, and the different ways a soul can "govern" itself, using political metaphors drawn from Plato’s Republic.</meta>

<margin>
How and from where does the battle between the soul's motions arise?
</margin>
<margin>
Why do different people at different times hold different opinions, and why do they desire different things at different times?
</margin>
<margin>
How do passions bring destruction to reason; and why do they sometimes rule, and other times find themselves ruled?
</margin>
<margin>
How many types of constitutions are there in our soul?

**Constitutions**
*   **Kingship** <note>original: "βασιλεία" (*basileia*); the rule of the highest reason.</note>
*   **Aristocracy** <note>original: "ἀριστοκρατία" (*aristokratia*); the rule of the best elements.</note>
*   **Democracy** <note>original: "δημοκρατία" (*demokratia*); the rule of the many/desires.</note>
*   **Oligarchy** <note>original: "ὀλιγαρχία" (*oligarchia*); the rule of the few/wealthy interests.</note>
*   **Tyranny** <note>original: "τυραννίς" (*tyrannis*); the rule of a single consuming passion.</note>
</margin>

And yet, is it not the case that whenever the body is moved in some way, immediately a certain <term>imagination</term> <note>original: "φαντασία" (*phantasia*)</note> and <term>perception</term> <note>original: "αἴσθησις" (*aisthesis*)</note> will accompany it? Memory of the <term>passion</term> <note>original: "πάθος" (*pathos*); here meaning an external effect or suffering upon the body</note> would occur in this way; yet it does not reside within the perceiving faculty itself. For if one, being among these experiences—passions, pains, and anger—calls upon them all at once, he will stir the same motions again. The need of the body will cause the body to form other opinions. One might say that these sufferings occur in the body, yet they are also something else to the soul: they are simultaneously a perception and a state of doubt or dispute. For how can this be right or not right? It is because the soul is weak in that it is not whole, nor does it always master that "other nature" <note>likely referring to the material or animal nature</note> in its desires. It perceives things as they are, yet does not see their true form. This is because the soul is not without turmoil; even if it exists according to itself, it is nonetheless caught in the noise of the things pressing upon it. It is as if the soul is in the company of base men; from all sides, these men <unclear>pluck at</unclear> <note>original: "τιλᾶσιν" (*tilasin*); perhaps meaning "to pull at" or "harass"</note> the soul when it is in a poor state, just as in a city. They employ "aristocratic" constitutions not in name only, but even more so, the aristocratic way belongs to all—or else such a thing exists poorly without it. And yet, if aristocratic qualities were in the body, in the flesh, then perceptions would arise from that source, just as if there were a city within the body that is being disturbed—

<margin>
Just as the quickening of the soul is one thing, the animal [quickening] is another... it is also an image of the quickening...
<note>original Latin: "Sicut vivificatio animae aliud est animalis... imago etiam est vivificatio..." This note explores the "bestowal of life" (vivificatio) and how the animal life is a mere image of the soul's true life.</note>
</margin>
<margin>
Is there something between the soul and the body, or is it about the soul, or is body bound to body?
</margin>

—being ordered, and no longer is there such a base thing. These things are communal or social in every other way. And it has now been said: these things are so <insert>concerning the soul by itself in relation to the body</insert>. For you could not say that some souls possess these things in themselves, for they are not "natures" in that sense; rather, this is the failing of bodies, and the body was being renewed. But within its own nature, these things exist in some, such as perception, which is not like a limb of light; rather, it is like a heating element or something corporeal. One might say this regarding the "chasms" <note>likely a metaphor for the gaps between the material and the spiritual</note> and that the pleasures of the body come to the body in such a way. It is not because of this that the soul perceives or shares in the opinions again. It leads toward sensory knowledge and—

<margin>
Regarding what in us are the passions?
</margin>

—especially everything of this sort. Since this is not alien to the body that suffers or grieves, we should not say the soul "shares" in it as if it were entirely affected; the soul does not have this experience purely, but is dragged along, as if by certain unjudged impulses.

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s investigation into how the soul relates to the physical universe. # The Universal Animal and Cosmic Sympathy

...into poverty and lack of resources. Then, [consider] these things in their individual parts. But even these parts will seek what they need; both the rich and the poor, and those who are primary among them. Since everyone chooses what is their own, one could say ten thousand things that are physically dreaded and all that exists within the living being—whether these are the bodies of the living being itself or the souls of each individual. 

Nonetheless, these souls would not withdraw themselves from the whole, nor would any portion of the intellect belonging to the universe. In addition to these things, there remains the principle of **sympathy** <note>original: "συμπαθεῖν" (*sympathein*); the Stoic and Neoplatonic concept that the universe is a single organism where every part feels and reacts to the state of every other part.</note> and the way the things within it are healed <note>original: "περιακᾶται"; likely referring to the restorative or "healing" processes of the cosmic order.</note>, just as those parts must contrive for themselves. In this way, the most beautiful thing ought not to be destroyed; for there is a need for walls, just as temple-robbers and bandits exist through human causes. These shameful acts are not from the gods. 

Neither should we blame **divination** <note>original: "μαντείαν" (*manteian*); Plotinus argues that prophecy works not because gods "send" signs, but because the universe is a single interconnected system where one part can signify another.</note>; for if one were to define the things that are enslaved to time and blame them, nothing more would happen here. But if these things are not attributed to physical causes, nor to the choices of those who bring evils upon us from elsewhere, and if they arrive at the whole generally, what other reasonable cause remains? 

First, then, we must accept that the whole is a **living being** <term>Universal Animal</term> <note>original: "πᾶν ζῷον" (*pan zoon*); the Greek concept that the entire cosmos is a single, living, breathing organism with its own soul.</note>. All other living things are included as its parts. Each part, in turn, possesses all its own parts insofar as the soul of each is a part of the whole. And because it is a part of the body, and its use is according to the use of the whole and the universe in respect to the body, these parts—sharing in the same nature—also share in a common experience. A "suffering" or "affection" <note>original: "πάθος" (*pathos*); in philosophy, this refers to any state where a thing is "acted upon" or "affected" by an outside force.</note> given to one part would certainly be felt by the other part in turn. 

If the whole is indeed a whole, then everything established within it belongs to it. In its parts, it is worthy of **sympathy** with the whole because it is a living being. Just as in a single, established body—like a nail, a horn, or a finger—what comes from those nearby is felt. Although the variety of parts means they are distinct from one another, and the intervening spaces might make the appearances seem unclear (like the nails compared to the rest of the body or the hair), the impulse is nonetheless pulled through the whole. It is not that they do not feel; even if it is necessary for an influence to travel far, such as when a living being’s hair is cut by something, it still occurs within the whole. Thus, the whole is one, just as the parts of a single animal are one. In addition to this, even if a body does not have a direct similarity to the whole living being, it is modeled after it from similar principles. In this way, an experience becomes alienated, and it bows down...

πάσχον <note>Catchword: "suffering" or "being acted upon."</note>

<meta>The previous page established that sensory perception is an internal activity mediated by the "pneuma" (spirit) acting as a bridge between the physical organ and the soul. <margin>Where is the origin of desires?</margin>

Let us observe: regarding which part of the body, such as the heart, one might say it resides, it is not far from the body and is therefore clear to all those who contest this view. Is anger located here? Is it not found in the spirited person and such types? These things remain throughout the natural body, and all things belong to the body; some act within it, and it is spoken of as a starting point for sensation. For it is found in the substance of the spleen <gloss>and</gloss> is not absent from sexual matters; rather, it relates to the organs of such ends, for example, the testicles.

<margin>What is anger or wrath and how? Is it in the body or in the soul?</margin>

Desire is clearly a natural thing, arising primarily from a central hearth <note>original: *hestia*; in ancient physiology, the "hearth" often refers to the source of vital heat or the liver as the seat of desire.</note> from which it starts. It serves the ends of vital functions and provides for the body. Even if a starting point for anger is established more in the soul—both in the soul itself and in relation to the person—perhaps it is located around the heart. Whether this is harmful to the body or to reason is clear, even if you cannot grasp it here, but rather through a correct mental image. First, one must consider what it is: that it does not exist without the body, yet it is not the body alone, but is as if joined to it. Just as there is a stomach among our parts, there are also common eyes and other organs through which the **spirit** <note>original: *pneuma*; the vital breath or subtle substance mediating between soul and body.</note> itself somehow participates in the body. For this reason, in humble people, anger is not found in their doctrines so much as in a sensory humor <term>humor: one of the four bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) believed to determine health and temperament.</term> that commands their attention. When bodily dispositions involve a certain liquid or blood that is warm, they are prone to anger. Those who I believe are naturally chilled are humble. Regarding temperaments <note>original: *kraseis*; the "mixing" of the humors that defines a person's physical and mental character.</note>, it is not the same as in others; it seems easily corrupted through the relationships back to the bodily state. Within the constitution of the living being, one might trace desires back to instances when the same people are ill and become more irritable; the cause is the bodily weakness, so that one sees the origins of desires. The blood, like the spirit, provides the movement. Mental movements, just like sensations, occur in such a body; thus the blood is moved by its own perception, or what one might call imagination. In general, all such things are dispositions of a specific body which lead to the sensory presentation of these states.

# On the Causes of Natural and Artificial Production

### Just as they told you, concerning the three signs through <unclear>signs</unclear>

<margin>
To distinguish between the types of production: those concerning natural things and those concerning technical things.
</margin>

Otherwise, it would not be possible to grant this, and to establish a more philosophical view regarding the opinion on strange phenomena. It is also worth considering the movements that arise from **dreams** <note>original: *enypnion*; these are the "visions" or "residues" of sensory movement that persist during sleep</note>. And we must ask why this occurs in dreams and in other things, as the **cause** <note>original: *aitia*; the "reason why" something happens</note> in these cases is within the things themselves. There are some thinkers, however, who claim that this is the entire cause. Yet, we must suspect that among the arts [crafts], some are arts but are not causes in this specific way. In general, we should take this as a starting point. Therefore, these are the causes of **production** <note>original: *poiesis*; in this context, it refers to the act of making or bringing something into being, whether by nature or by hand</note> in general, both for all living animals and for everything else we say exists by nature.

This applies both to things made by art and those born by nature, where the parts are produced according to their own kind. From these parts—the parts within us—some come to be in part, while others come to be by art. These arts achieve their end by utilizing a certain trust or belief. For just as the parts of natural productions possess natural powers, so too does the whole and the parts that are moved. The parts themselves often produce their own **metaphors** <note>likely meaning "transfers" or "analogies" of movement here</note>. As many things as participate in the parts, they in turn affect each other through alterations, movements, and certain states of rest. This is what is most continuous among them and all other things. This is the method through which each thing **must be examined** <term>original: *exetasteon*; a technical term in philosophy for a systematic investigation or scrutiny</term>.

Indeed, some do not produce in the same way as other craftsmen. There are, for instance, the arts of **ivory-working** <term>original: *elephantourgike*; the specialized craft of carving ivory, often used for luxury statues</term> and carving, and such arts as these follow a downward flow. It seems that some move toward the natural, as if according to nature, such as rhetoric and music, and every form of **mechanics** <term>original: *mechanologia*; the study or application of machines and mechanical principles to solve problems</term>, which is best suited for completing what is necessary. It is likely that the arts are even more numerous. Indeed, they possess power, and there is a necessity for crafted objects to meet a present need. And the reason why nature acts through them—and why destruction follows so quickly—is because of how they are first disposed. They disagree after we have established our own causes elsewhere, each regarding the placement of the parts as their own. In general, they say that those who learn later—like children—concede to these views in most cases as they happen.

It argues that while nature and art follow different rules, they both rely on specific causes and the arrangement of parts to function.</summary>

Yet, these are better than the things that follow the genus. 
The living being, as a living being, is not without a share in the whole; and while it remains in accordance with **nature** <note>original: *physis*</note>, it gives back

they cannot fail to exist. And although they are parts of the whole, they exist for the sake of the universe and are divided—or rather, it would not be a 
danger to say that they themselves are living beings. If there is a concern for the part, it is not entirely

<meta>This page continues the discussion of cosmic animation and the internal logic of the universe. While the previous page touched upon how the parts of the world relate to the whole, this page delves into the specific "natural powers" within objects—like stones or plants—and argues that even seemingly "inanimate" things participate in the life of the Great Whole (the Cosmos) through their inner formative principles.</meta>

### On the Internal Powers of the World

It could not be that a thing lacks the power to act according to its nature; and yet, how could motion arise from mere shape? If it were so, it would be spontaneous. For even in the stem of a plant, beauty consists in its capacity for motion. Why does this part move in one way, and another part in a different way? It is not merely by their beauties and differences, but because inanimate nature produces these forms from within itself. Is it not then the case that even there <note>referring to the intelligible or spiritual realm</note>, shapes are held as formative principles? And generally, the very act of producing—hidden within the works themselves—is capable of possessing the causes. For the act of producing exists in such a way in all things.

<margin>In all underlying subjects, it is granted that natural powers <note>original: "φυσικαὶ δυνάμεις"</note> are received alongside shapes and qualities.</margin>

And this indeed is the universe’s way of producing; so that, as we might say, the underlying subjects possess powers beyond their outward shapes. Even in the things before us, there are many that provide heating or cooling. But one might say that the power of acting arises from the mixture <note>original: "κρᾶμα," the blending of elements</note> and is added to the forms, and the powers of nature follow after these, as is seen in the nature of stones. Regarding those things whose activities are wonderful, one would not say that the Whole <note>the Universe as a living organism</note> acts through these by chance. Rather, they participate in reason <note>original: "λόγος" (Logos), the rational principle that organizes the world</note> and in life. It is like the circles some speak of, or the bloodless quality found in the eyes; and this too: we see that motion does not occur only through hands and feet—for motion exists even there—but in all things within the Whole. And those things which are brought near, falling upon each part, change them; thus the Whole acts even more so, through the "trace" of the things within it directed toward the Whole itself. It is impossible for this not to be the case, for the Whole is great. There are powers even in those things carried within its inhabitants. For it is not merely intellect; beyond this, there is truly "another earth and sea" <note>A reference to the Platonic and Plotinian idea that there is an Intelligible World—a divine blueprint—containing the "true" versions of Earth and Sea.</note>. For since those things possess life, so too do these, such as stones and wood. If this were not so, the world would be something dishonorable, whereas in the world all things are understood by the mind,

<margin>Note: That this Whole is entirely ensouled <note>original: "ἔμψυχον" (empsychon), meaning alive or possessing a soul</note> and it does not seem to us that certain things within it move in a way perceptible to the senses.</margin>

so that the world itself holds all things in its sight; and everything is beautiful. It is not that those higher things exist while these do not; I see that he has life in himself. Therefore, even in these things, individual atoms are understood. And how could inanimate things truly be inanimate? For while common reasoning says so, it is not so in the same way as things here on earth. And as for that which does not move sensibly <note>original: "αἰσθητικῶς" (aisthetikos), through the senses</note>, moving by itself, one should not say it is not alive. For there is a hidden life within the living being as well as a life perceptible to the senses; it binds together the furthest and the sensory parts, which are marvelous and inspire awe. One will not fail to notice if such life is present in these beings.

<margin>All things live in the world; but some in one way, others in another.</margin>

It is worthy to consider that the world moves itself, from its own parts, both in being and in existence. It moves not as a single whole <note>meaning it does not move from place to place like an animal</note>, but because each of the living things within it lives with its own life, even if individual choice is not present. Like children, even if it stands beside them, it happens without prior choice—yet it is not "prior" in time; for this is often clear.

Each thing pursues its own ends; many things are given by the givers according to their own nature. Yet, all things are interwoven and possess a wonderful harmony. Not only this, but all things here are directed toward the betterment of what comes to be. These administrations are perfect; they do not rule through the kind of calculations we use <note>original: "λογισμῶν," referring to human-like deliberation or "figuring things out"</note>, as if the work were external to them. Rather, actions are dispensed within the beings themselves from that higher source, so that the movements of the stars and all that has been said provide a kind of reliability to these manifestations. 

For these things are moved, and all the virtue of the Master <note>referring to the presiding intellect or "World-Soul"</note> is sympathetic to the whole, and thus He performs His own works. He said that those things are what they are because of the Master; in this whole, everything is for the best. And this state of affairs is not accidental; things in the universe do not happen according to seminal principles <note>internal biological codes</note> but according to productive principles <note>original: "λόγους ποιητικούς," the higher creative reasons derived from Providence</note>. These are prior to and higher than the other principles, for they are not merely "seeds" (even if some "paraseminal" opinions suggest it), because nothing that contributes to the Whole is lacking there. 

Rather, these things are consistent—or better, they are necessary. The entire world exists according to Reason <term>Logos</term>, just as a city yields to laws. The citizens act, and they act for a reason, and over all these things the world acts as a legislator. The laws reveal themselves both in the actions of the individuals and in the results of their works. Certain causes and sequences follow automatically from this harmony and serve as signs; it is this that the stars signify to us. 

In such a harmony, "acting" and "seeing" occur because it is likely that one thing can be known from another, and from the same causes. One can know what came before from what follows after, and thus preserve the relationship between them. For a person has agreed to what they have seen. Here, however, difficulties arise through the passages of the stars, and concerning evil things or whatever else happens. Some things are "contrary to nature," yet such things occur by natural necessities. These are parts acting against parts, just as in a whole living being, some parts are taken away for the sake of what is coming to be. And while doing wrong might exist in the part, it would not be "wrong" when viewed within the context of the Whole. At different times, individuals participate in this life more than others.

<summary>Plotinus explains that the universe is a harmonious system governed by "legislative" productive principles rather than mere biological seeds. He argues that the stars act as signs of this cosmic order and that even "evil" or "unnatural" events are simply the result of parts of the Great Living Being interacting within a larger, perfect providence.</summary>

<meta>This page transitions from the general concept of cosmic harmony and natural affinity (oikeiosis) discussed on the previous page to a specific investigation into the mechanics of sense-perception (aisthesis). It specifically addresses whether perception requires a physical medium (metaxy) and how the soul interacts with the body's organs to receive impressions from the outside world.</meta>

<margin>
That perception occurs through the organs. But the soul, having been born within and yet standing apart <note>original: "ἐκσταθεῖσα" (ekstatheisa), suggesting the soul is both present in the body and transcendent of it</note>
</margin>

<margin>
Whether there must be a body as a medium between the eye and the color
</margin>

Concerning the act of <term>aisthesis: sense-perception</term>, the situation is such that it does not occur in one way alone; rather, it happens because our sensory powers become, in a sense, connate <note>sharing a common nature or "grown together"</note> with the objects of perception. This occurs through a certain prior communion with these objects, allowing the soul to produce a form of knowledge that is an "unaffected affection" <note>original: "ἀπαθήματος" (apathematos). This refers to the paradoxical idea that the soul "perceives" a physical change without itself being physically altered</note>. For this reason, knowledge is also achieved through bodily <term>organon: instruments or organs</term>. For through these organs—as if they were things naturally united and familiar to us—the soul's power goes out toward the objects of perception themselves, much like light. It becomes "like-affected" with those things that are in motion.

When these objects are encompassed by something bodily, so that they might be affected without a direct <term>aphe: physical touch</term>, the process is quite <unclear>favorable</unclear>. This is the case because seeing and tasting operate differently; however, it is perhaps worth stopping later to consider what this process actually is. Regarding color, it is possible for it to be positioned accidentally in opposition to the sight. It happens to color in various other things that are seen, so that these bodies would not be exactly like things placed directly upon the eye. This brings us to the <term>metaxy: the medium</term> through which we see. It is as if one were to move the very thing beneath oneself. Even if the medium does not possess these specific qualities, I have just said that these are weakening factors; rather, we must first address what is said concerning the medium.

It is as if one were "limping" <note>likely a metaphor for an imperfect or indirect process</note> under the influence of something; either there will be color, and in the space where we see, the medium would be affected so that if there were nothing there, the perception would never reach us. And even if the sense-organs were affected by the medium, this is to be affected according to nature. The eye is affected. Consequently, we are unable to be affected in our entirety if the medium is not present. We must consider the categories of perception and the specific parts involved; if there were no medium at all, there would be no source from which the middle could be affected.

This point itself might be disputed. For as I said, it is not the thing seen that is said to be the "sufferer" or the thing affected. Rather, because the medium is moved, the entire <term>thorax: the chest or central cavity</term> <note>In ancient physiology, the chest was often seen as the seat of the "common sense" or central processing of sensations</note> is also moved. One should know this: the entire living being is naturally disposed to be affected as a whole, or even if the medium—acting from the proper organs—would not be affected by the object itself. If, therefore, perceiving is no longer a matter of being affected in the way that physical things are prone to be affected, then the medium would no longer be considered part of those physical "affections." <insert>If indeed seeing is like this, where the act is so by nature</insert> then one must perceive according to the nature of the medium. For why does the medium not "suffer" in this hypothesis? The medium would not, then, make the body either more primary or <unclear>more critical</unclear>. What prevents the surface of the object from being oriented toward the act of seeing? Thus, the medium is a necessity, even if it does not exist as a primary nature, for the "suffering" or reception of all these impressions.

# On the Nature of Radiance and the Medium

And this itself, instead of the body, was clothed in the **forms** <note>original: εἴδη (eidē), referring to the visual appearances or "species" of objects</note> within the points of entry. But it is not possible to reach it when it is immediately full; for instance, the "being-present" of the body. When it is no longer present, the greater parts are as if they are giving additional light, or shining all around. But the "more" in this case is only so much, because the **air** has been deceived at the same time. For he says it happens that the air is made dark and not pure; and in this way, when the bodies come together again, it is no more. Then, furthermore, that underlying thing is no more.

Regarding the **light** of the air, it must be said that they relate to one another as things having contrary **affections** <note>original: πάθη (pathē), meaning "passive states" or "ways of being acted upon"</note>. And its darkness has not become "darkness," but rather it is as if it has become "not-idle" <note>Plotinus is arguing that light is an "activity" (energeia) rather than a static quality</note>. For such a thing is indeed possible, though how could it not be? But as for the "purity," that belongs to its bodies or the whole. Thus, it is not even its **color**; rather, it is a body unto itself, possessing its own power. 

And this has been considered so as to be stated thus: whether it is destroyed or simply departs. For good things, having taken from this, lead toward the additional reception of being also from within, so that the participating light—whether in the heavens indeed—those things are also generated from light. But if all **vision** <term>opsis: the faculty of sight or the visual stream</term> is not a "flowing" <note>a critique of the theory that vision consists of physical particles flowing into the eye</note>, it has also bypassed the body’s own internal logic from which those surpassing things do not perish. However, light is not primarily a **subsistence** <note>original: ὑπόστασιν (hypostasin), meaning a distinct underlying reality</note> of that which provides light, even if it is moving.

If it is not so, then it is not as if all the "re-flows" are happening again; rather, it is like a **form** <note>original: εἶδος (eidos)</note> of that body. And by accepting as much as that which is in it, and the remaining things within itself which come from it, there is also a limit to the sun, so that it may reach its peak and light may reach that far without even having any obstacle in between, so that it is not unequal to it. But when—

<margin>
Each good thing is an **eternal activity** and a **double activity**. <note>A core Neoplatonic concept: one activity remains within the source (essence), while the other flows out from it (effect).</note>
</margin>

—so that there is more than what is proper to the body being illuminated; and it is like a leaving behind of **activities** <term>energeiai: the active realization or "work" of a thing's power</term> and a coming together. After the furthest part of the body, there exists the **radiance** <term>selas: a bright gleam, flash, or splendor</term> itself. This indeed does not proceed from us alone, but from those bodies. And it is a **likeness** of it, so that one will see it even when it is lying still. And while it remains, it reaches into the distance, whether more or less. And while some senses are dim, others have stood alongside those dim ones. And it reaches into the distance; and whenever it departs into the distance, it no longer exists, where the radiance is nothing and has no power—even while it is defending itself and shining in the eyes of animals. <meta>This page transitions from the physical mechanics of light and vision discussed on page 5 to the metaphysical principle of "universal sympathy." Plotinus argues that perception is possible only because the universe is a single, unified living organism where all parts—no matter how distant—are interconnected.</meta>

<margin>
Sympathy of the parts of the cosmos.
Perception is directed toward that which is in sympathy.
</margin>

Since the **living being** <note>original: ζῷον (zōon); Plotinus views the entire universe as a single, organic, living entity</note> is one by nature, it is a living being in sympathy with itself. This includes things that are far apart and those that are very near, and the senses function in this way. Our bodies would not be external parts to us, nor external to the living being as a whole. For if we perhaps feel pain in one part, the rest of the body feels it too; the parts that are separated still act as one, just as there is a single **reason-principle** <note>original: λόγος (logos); the organizing principle or "blueprint" of a thing</note> governing the organs and their movements and foundations. One cannot remove the "affections" <note>original: πάθη (pathē); the passive experiences or "feelings" of the body</note> from these foundations. For he says it would be a puzzle if every sensation required a physical striking <note>original: κόπτον (kopton); literally a "beating" or "clashing"</note> or contact, as if the other senses only worked when things were present right against them and did not travel toward them from a distance. But we will say that not everything we perceive is "striking" us in this way; nevertheless, we know and perceive these things. That is to say, even when something is far off, it is still "there" and also "here." And that **sympathy** <note>original: συμπάθεια (sympatheia); the "feeling-together" or resonance between distant parts of the universe</note> exists is clear through the practice of **divination** <note>original: μαντεῖον (manteion); the art of predicting the future or seeing distant events by reading signs</note>. One part is sufficient to reveal another, just as with parts of a whole. But it is not as if things are physically there; rather, there is an **apprehension** <note>original: ἀντίληψις (antilēpsis); a conscious grasping or perception</note> by the living being and a sensation that the part affected participates in the whole. For the organ of sense is similar to the object itself, so that in our perception we see things through similarities to other things. Senses do not perceive through opposites, but rather all things governed by the living being are apprehended through likeness. Since the soul will apprehend things outside, it does so not by chance, but by that which is within itself; it will apprehend them as "likenesses" because the things that produce the sensation are similar to all. If the thing producing the effect and the experience itself are the same, then the things experiencing them are similar. These things are not just experienced by one part, but they possess the experience as if the whole had felt it. For reason-principles and yet more reason-principles do not merely come together; they are similar and dissimilar just as they hold the same qualities. And as many say, these are "hypotheses" for us; for if such a thing is not a "whole," then it cannot be "all." It is necessary for it to be both sentient and perfect. And if it were not perfect, you would have to abandon the hypothesis regarding **apprehension** <note>original: κατάληψιν (katalēpsin); the mental grasp of a truth</note> which follows from the things we have assumed. —

<margin>
a
</margin>

The senses do not know [in isolation]; nor is the "stamping" <note>referring to the theory that perception is like a seal ring stamping wax</note> of a part the same as the whole; whether these are the things that become of all things; and consequently, there follows a mathematical possession.

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the soul's relationship with the physical world. While the previous page focused on the soul as an interpreter of the world (like a reader of a book), this page shifts toward a more technical, hierarchical argument: the "incorporeal" (the non-physical) must logically exist before the "corporeal" (the physical) because matter requires the soul to give it order and life.</meta>

<margin>
That indeed, the **incorporeal** <note>original: ἀσώματον (asōmaton); that which has no physical body or dimensions</note> exists before the bodies.
</margin>

For even the incorporeal things are not "strengthened" <note>in the sense of being made solid or heavy like physical matter</note>; and for this very reason, they are not bodies. In this way, people will say that something "comes to be." Therefore, through this cause, there is also a cause for the bodies so that they may possess a sense of **order**. And again, the **soul** <note>original: ψυχή (psuchē)</note> must be viewed in this same way: for as for those souls that might come to be within bodies, these <gloss>are in a worse state</gloss> <note>This reflects the Neoplatonic idea that the soul's "descent" into a physical body is a step away from its pure, divine origin</note>. And everything that approaches **matter** <note>original: ὕλη (hulē); the raw, formless "stuff" of the universe</note> within a body creates a body. But nowhere else is there anything that does not come <unclear>from</unclear> the soul; and if someone were to speak in this way, they would say that even the entire and most **indivisible** <note>The soul is "indivisible" because, unlike a body, you cannot cut it into halves; it is present as a whole wherever it is</note> soul brings about the process of **becoming** <note>original: γένεσιν (genesin); the state of physical existence and change</note> within matter. And similarly, a thing would not be described merely by its **juxtaposition** <note>the act of placing physical things side-by-side</note>; it does not act through the whole upon the part, nor do these things "feel sympathy" <note>sharing a common experience or physical connection</note> with one another.

Nor does it "become" as if it were inside a body. And if the soul, in turn, <unclear>rearranges</unclear> this—if it is a body within a body—then neither would the body ever be completely and entirely released from the body. For they will <unclear>grow together</unclear> with a child that is not small, since it is matter. From where should bodies flee for refuge, and toward what kind of life? For if the argument leaves it thus, this is truly not the case... but if the soul should make one of them, then the body would no longer receive this, or again, it would dissolve in the same way. And if the bodies also exist, some will say they do not, while others say they do not even live once they have entered into matter. 

One must say to them: for it is not matter itself that the soul **forms** <note>gives a specific shape or essence to</note>, nor is it the soul itself that has "arrived." Or perhaps the "worse" is nothing other than "nothingness" itself. Whether one must posit that matter provides for all bodies—from which also these movements of a bodily nature arise—the result is that the body would not possess anything if the cause were not present. For even its "carriage" <note>its movement or weight</note> is a motion. And all things [move] as quickly as possible, or else one must name "motion" as the entirety of the bodies. But they are certainly not the causes in every respect. For these things would happen to the other bodies; matter is never... or rather, it would never even "become."

There will be a dissolution of all things in matter, lest they be part of that which has been formed by it. Perhaps it is nowhere, or it is something very similar. It will also be established to show, finally, that it is so for all bodies <unclear>to be arranged</unclear> by the **order of the soul**. For reaching as far as names, it is scattered throughout the body; and by its being a "whole," it is not present among those things that are absent. For how could bodies be divided—those things which some so ignorantly call "just"? They do not leave, but are carried out from all things; for what [is made] of elements?

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the soul's relationship with the body. While the previous page established that the "incorporeal" (the soul) must logically precede the physical body to provide order, this page tackles the specific "difficulties" (aporias) of how an indivisible soul can govern a physical body that grows, moves, and changes its parts over time.</meta>

Now many **difficulties** <note>original: ἀπορίας (aporias); philosophical puzzles or dead-ends that require solving</note> arise regarding these assertions. But truly, these concern the movement of every body; for indeed, it is not a matter of **deliberate choice** <note>original: προαιρέσεως (proaireseōs); the capacity for rational will or intent</note>, though these are correctly identified as causes. Yet, choice itself is not a physical thing; rather, it is **Reason** <note>original: ὁ λόγος (ho logos); here meaning the guiding principle or rational structure</note> itself, even while differences exist. Just as this [reason] comes from the body—for the body itself is of such a nature—it would seem to belong to the body itself whether it is **hot or cold**. 

Regarding the **growth** <note>original: αὔξειν (auxein)</note> of living beings: this is not governed merely by measure. The body itself might experience certain conditions as growth is added to it, but the soul itself must be **indivisible** <note>original: ἀμέριστον (ameriston); unlike a physical object, the soul cannot be cut into pieces</note>. To what extent should the soul be understood to serve the potential of all things in their radiance and towards that [higher] end? For this reason, growth occurs; and at the same time as this growth, the addition [of matter] follows a certain **ratio** <note>original: λόγον (logon); used here in the mathematical sense of a proportion that keeps the body's form consistent</note> similar to that of the body. If the added material were not equal to it, it would appear dissimilar, or the body would be incomplete. Where does this added material come from, and how is it added? If one considers the ratio of what is added, and the source from which it comes, it must be of a like mind; thus the added parts will cause the body to grow. 

But it is not as though these parts are simply contained within it; it is necessary that the parts exist within the soul as if concerning another thing, which is perceived by the senses.

<margin>4</margin> 

One part of the body might pass away, and another part will be added; but this does not change the whole. While the body is preserved, how do you recognize it? For it is not immediately the same because of its colors, even though it is a body. The nature of the body is <unclear>something that is led</unclear>. In what way is each of the parts not the same as the whole? This is especially true of **quantity** <note>original: ποσόν (poson)</note>; even if there is a removal of parts, the same form remains as it was before. Even if some parts become worse than they were there, the soul does not become a body <gloss>through this joining</gloss>. 

The things that act upon the body and the things the body suffers will indeed remain the same, being preserved throughout. What, then, will they say to those who claim there is more to this? First, you have not surrounded the parts of the soul as if they were parts in the same body; for every single part of the soul is such that it is also the **whole** <note>A core Neoplatonic concept: the soul is not "spread out" like a physical fluid; rather, the entire soul is present in every part of the body simultaneously</note>. For even the divisions of a part do not contribute an "atomic" or indivisible form to such things. And yet, it was necessary for this to be seen in you as an existing thing. But the **whole** is present in many places, which would be impossible for a physical body to manifest. If some part were to suffer illness, the same principle would apply; for indeed—

<summary>This page explores the metaphysical problem of growth and identity, arguing that while the body's physical matter changes and is added to (growth), the soul remains an indivisible whole that provides the consistent "ratio" or form of the individual.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the soul's indivisibility. Having established that the soul provides the "ratio" for growth, the text now shifts to the mechanism of sensation—specifically how a centralized soul can perceive pain in a localized extremity, like a finger, and the role of the "spirit-vehicle" (pneuma) in carrying these signals.</meta>

For how could it be hindered? For sensation is not carried through bodies; but whenever it exists in the **spirit-vehicle** <note>original: πνεύματι (pneumati); a subtle, airy body that serves as an intermediary between the immaterial soul and the physical flesh</note> alone—in its specific parts—it is through the soul itself that the spirit also receives these impressions. This is just as the senses possess **recognition** <note>original: ἐπίγνωσιν (epignōsin)</note> without a purely material sensation. Regarding the specific mixture of the parts of the soul: do the senses also possess these in the soul's parts, even if there is some physical body in that location?

But here is the **solution to the difficulty** <note>original: λύσις τῆς ἀπορίας (lysis tēs aporias)</note>: for in this way, one will perceive of necessity that my character and nature are being destroyed. One perceives especially that what strikes the body is established for it and directed toward each part of the body. For this reason, the "punisher" <note>an interpretive term for the faculty that reacts to pain or damage</note> addresses the evil occurring there in the body. 

And indeed, since the **sense-organ** <note>original: αἰσθητηρίου (aisthētēriou)</note> is itself a body, no perceptible thing could be carried through it without the organ itself being affected, unless it is not considered in relation to the physical body. Consider the **seal of a ring** <note>original: δακτυλίου σφραγῖδα; a classic metaphor where the form/shape of the seal is transferred to wax without the metal of the ring entering the wax</note>. If sensation receives things in their **form** <note>original: εἴδει (eidei)</note>, it does not receive them along with their material shapes and masses as found in moist bodies; otherwise, those body parts would be confused into the fluid and would cease to truly exist. 

But if sensation exists, each of these parts must signify that form and see it. Consequently, the senses occurring in the spirit-vehicle happen in a different way, while the senses first enjoy the **forms** of the body within the body itself. To perceive in all things occurs otherwise—not purely from "sufferings" <note>passive impressions</note> and actions, as is the case with **spiritual bodies** <note>original: πνευματικῶν σωμάτων; the subtle bodies of light or air discussed in Neoplatonic physics</note>. For the spirit exists both by itself and according to itself while within the physical body.

This is the same case as when, for example, a **finger is cut off** <note>original: δακτύλου... ἀποτετμήται; this refers to the "phantom limb" problem in ancient philosophy: why we feel pain in a part of the body that is no longer there or is being separated</note>. The pain is felt "around the finger," and the act of perceiving stretches out toward that which has been left behind. For just as the spirit is divided and its parts are cut off with these members, it is by this spirit that one perceives what has happened—and not by the soul itself suffering the same wound. 

How could this be understood? They say that while the spirit has suffered around the finger, that which carries the sensation is left behind until the other part arrives at the place in isolation. If, however, it should return again to the same place—among the other senses and the part left behind—it is likely that this also belongs to the **perceptive faculty** <note>original: αἰσθητικοῦ (aisthētikou)</note> through **sympathy** <note>the principle that parts of a living organism "feel together" because they belong to one whole</note>. It would then happen that many things are perceived, and many events occur there. After all these things, one perceives what has happened, and perceives oneself alongside them. 

But the truth is that regarding each of those sensations, one does not perceive the spirit itself, but rather perceives by that part of the soul which is immediately next to the finger. Whenever sensation is in the spirit-vehicle, because it is the same principle for both, it happens to be left in isolation; thus, one does not perceive the pain located *at* the finger, but rather the soul itself <unclear>suffering pain</unclear>.

<summary>This page discusses the "pneuma" (spirit-vehicle) as the medium for sensation, explaining how the soul remains unaffected by physical damage while perceiving pain in extremities like a finger through "sympathy."</summary>

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the soul's relationship with the body. Following the previous page’s discussion on sensation and the "seal" metaphor, the text now transitions into a metaphysical proof of the soul’s immortality, defining it as the self-moving source of all life that ultimately seeks to return to its original divine state.</meta>

<margin>
That [the soul] is not primarily a living creature, but is rather unbegotten and immortal
</margin>

For the **principle of motion** <note>original: ἀρχὴ κινήσεως (archē kinēseōs); a classic Platonic and Aristotelian concept defining the soul as the starting point for all movement in the universe</note>, having supplied motion to all other things, did not derive its own power from anything other than itself. And having bound itself to the **ensouled body** <note>original: ἐμψύχῳ σώματι (empsychō sōmati)</note>, they release it, though it possesses its power from its own nature. It possesses this power from itself even within the "filth" of living creatures, and although they may fall into deception, there is a certain nature that allows a living thing to exist. And it might prevail. And it is demonstrated of necessity to be **immortal** <note>original: ἀθάνατον (athanaton)</note> and to belong to all other essences as well. And this is because of its unique quality: life comes from it primarily, and it is the primary cause of change. It is neither without a share in knowledge, nor could it ever become alienated from itself, nor would it perish. And in truth, it is **more ancient** <note>original: πρεσβυτέραν (presbyteran); implying the soul exists prior to the physical matter it inhabits</note> than all things; it does not exist at one time and not at another, like the body that fell to its lot, nor was its power ever lacking. From where did its power over noble deeds fail? These things are again mostly matters of motion, but there is a need for a single **hypothesis** <note>original: ὑποθέσεως (hypotheseōs); a foundational assumption or underlying principle</note>. 

Since this [principle] is present from itself and is a "primary being," it does not have a cause for its existence—being primary and whole—nor does it have a superfluous center. Instead, it is both life and a life that is pure and good, as much as has been ordered by it. They all sound together throughout time, even when many have been summoned into the unseen. With all these things, it is possible to recover the nature that was lost. And having run back to its **ancient state** <note>original: ἀρχαίαν κατάστασιν (archaian katastasin); the original, pure condition of the soul before its descent into the material world</note>, it attempts to do those things which are natural to its manifestation, making it clear that all things, including their middle point, will be clothed in it and in the principle of motion. For it does not come from itself again at all, but from those things moved by the divine; nevertheless, it has come together into the cause of God and of **True Reality** <note>original: ὄντως ὄντος (ontōs ontos); a technical term in Neoplatonism for the highest level of existence, beyond the physical world</note>, having escaped notice for a time. And being master, it transformed its aim into a sensory one along with a certain indifference. This is like a body mixed with nature—not something moved, but something that has taken on irrational impulses against you. And again, having received all these **sense-organs** <note>original: αἰσθητήρια (aisthētēria)</note> in a greater way, and being established without sharing in the body, its faith/trust is made clear and it applies itself to things that are honorable and most beautiful. And see how they are understood by the soul itself, and how its own things are always cared for, insofar as it resolves the things written beneath it back into itself. All its nature is **unmoved** <note>original: ἀκίνητος (akinētos); here meaning stable and unchanging in essence, even while it causes motion in others</note>, such as is set forth by the gods to exist through the whole of the universe. For its virtue is also divine.

<summary>This page argues that the soul is the self-existent "principle of motion" and "True Reality" that remains immortal and divine despite being bound to a physical body. It describes the soul's journey of recovering its "ancient state" by turning away from irrational sensory impulses toward honorable, divine virtues.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the philosophical investigation of the soul's journey. Having previously discussed the soul as an animating principle that gives life to corruptible matter, the author now shifts to a personal, mystical account of the soul’s "awakening" and its subsequent descent into the physical body, citing the authority of ancient sages like Heraclitus, Empedocles, and Plato.</meta>

<margin>
That the **soul** <note>original: ψυχὴ (psychē)</note>, having come to be in a **body** <note>original: σώματι (sōmati)</note>, <unclear>makes</unclear> an **ascent** <note>original: ἄνοδον (anodon)</note> and a **descent** <note>original: κάθοδον (kathodon)</note>.
</margin>

Many times, awakening into myself out of the body, and becoming external to all other things but internal to myself, I see a beauty of marvelous greatness. I believe then, more than ever, that I belong to the better portion <note>meaning the spiritual or divine realm</note>, having lived the most excellent life and become one with the divine. Being established in that divine state, and having come to that level of activity, I established myself above all other **intelligible things** <note>original: νοητὸν (noēton); things understood by the mind rather than the senses</note>. Yet, after this standing-still within the divine, when I descend from **Intellect** <note>original: νοῦ (nou); the higher, intuitive mind</note> to **reasoning** <note>original: λογισμὸν (logismon); the analytical, step-by-step mind</note>, I am puzzled as to how I am even now descending, and how it is that my soul has come to be inside a body, since she is, in herself, such as she appeared even while residing in a body.

For **Heraclitus** <note>original: Ἡράκλειτος; a philosopher famous for the idea that "all things flow"</note>, who urges us to seek this, posited that there are necessary "exchanges" between opposites; he spoke of a "way up and a way down," and said that "it rests in change" and that "it is weariness to toil at the same tasks and to begin anew." He allowed us to guess at his meaning, neglecting to make his argument clear to us, as if he knew the truth in his own heart. So too **Empedocles** <note>original: Ἐμπεδοκλῆς; a philosopher who taught that the world is moved by Love and Strife</note>, who said that it is a sin for souls to fall here, and who himself became "a fugitive from God and a wanderer." In my judgment, he revealed only as much as **Pythagoras** and his followers did, speaking in riddles about this matter. But in the works of **Plato** <note>original: Πλάτωνι (Platōni)</note>, one might find further clarity, for it is spoken of clearly in his myths, of which he makes frequent and beautiful use. He has spoken in many places about the soul's arrival here, so that one might take from him whatever clear meaning one wishes. What, then, must we say of this philosopher? He seems to say the same thing to all, so that if one wishes to grasp the man's main points—concerning how the ancient world, through the goodwill of a man <unclear>standing from God</unclear>, was <unclear>made to appear</unclear> to the senses—

<margin>
The world is a cave or a grotto. The body is a tomb and a bond for the soul.
</margin>

—yet he quickly disdains it, blaming the soul's communion with the body. He says the soul is "in bonds" and that it is "buried" within the body. He says that the "cave" mentioned in the secret mysteries <note>likely referring to the Orphic or Eleusinian mysteries</note> is the same as the cave in his own writings. For him, this "cave" is the same as the "grotto" in Empedocles and the [resting place] in Heraclitus; where he speaks of a "release from bonds" and an "ascent from the cave" for the soul, for those journeying toward the **Intelligible** <note>the realm of pure thought and reality</note>.

<summary>Plotinus describes his personal experience of mystical union with the divine and struggles to explain why the soul must descend into the physical body, comparing his views with those of Heraclitus, Empedocles, and Plato.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s investigation into the unity of the soul. Having previously discussed the "descent" of the soul into the material realm, the text now pivots to a technical psychological question: if the Soul is ultimately one, why doesn't every living thing feel the same pain or sensation simultaneously? It explores the concept of "sympathy" (cosmic resonance) between parts and the whole.</meta>

### { Whether all souls are one }

Both of those views must be guarded against, but these things must be said especially in response to the difficulties we face regarding each of them: how the parts perceive, and how they perceive differently, and when that [higher soul] is present, how they [the parts] exist. It is just as in the soul itself there is deliberation—for indeed we **feel together** <note>original: ὁμοπαθεῖν (homopathein); to experience a shared state or emotion simultaneously, implying a deep-seated connection.</note> with one another—and just as friends stationed together in armies **feel with** <note>original: συμπάσχειν (sympaskhein); the root of our word "sympathy," describing how one part of a system reacts to what happens to another part.</note> each other, so the parts feel with the whole, and even more so with one another. This occurs throughout the whole and, quite reasonably, even in a plant; yet it is not difficult for it to participate in that [unity] from nothing, for then it ceases to be a single harmony.

For the parts do not always obey; if they did, there would not be "one and another" [soul], and the **composite** <note>original: τὸ συνἀμφότερον (to sunamphoteron); refers to the human being as a joined entity of both body and soul.</note> would be the same as the other composite. For if fortunes were in another, the experiences would not be the same in each of them; for one moves because I move, and another moves because I move. And in whatever thing is moving, it moves because [the soul] moves. Perhaps this contains an understanding, and not in this way is it more true: for the "always" and the "same" belong to the soul and to **me as a human being** together, and every experience <note>original: πάθος (pathos); a term meaning "passion," "affection," or simply "something that happens to one."</note> of these would be the same. 

<margin>
That this is a discourse concerning the **transmission of affections** <note>original: μεταδόσεως πάθων (metadoseōs pathōn); the process by which a sensation in the body is communicated to the conscious mind.</note>
</margin>

Nothing comes from the body, which is the experience of the other part, yet the other part and the whole "will" it. But if, on the other hand, the part recognizes something by judgment, what of both? Together with those things, there is **one soul**; for in this way, it would not be anticipated so that the same thing will perceive in a more-than-manifold way, both the parts and those things becoming present in the same body. Whatever magnitude [comes] from the body, it is as much as concerns itself; and those things from which there is an experience as if concerning the part, the same experience [travels] through some part by means of a movement. No experience comes to the one who will suffer, for it is through the **rational principle** <note>original: λόγου (logou); the formative or organizing principle that connects the physical sensation to the perceiving mind.</note> of how sensation will reach the whole and then cease. 

It is not a necessity that some who have suffered must **feel with** the whole; or rather, do they not say that the **sensitive faculty** <note>original: αἰσθητικὸν (aisthētikon); the part of the soul responsible for processing sensory data.</note> must recognize it or be present? It is in my very self, and even if it is in another, I shall know it as unstable; to be moved in one and then another is the cause. The present reality would not have a single rational principle for each, as if changing according to the multitude—for this is the necessity of nature—but rather one must speak of it as **one and an experience**.

<summary>This page explores how sensations are communicated between the body and the soul, arguing that while the soul is unified, different parts of the body experience sensations uniquely through a shared 'sympathy.' Plotinus addresses the problem of how a single soul can perceive multiple, distinct experiences from different parts of the body or different individuals.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the investigation from the previous section into whether all individual souls are actually manifestations of a single, universal Soul. It addresses the paradox of how something can be "divided" among many bodies without actually losing its unity, building on the previous discussion of "sympathy" or shared sensation.</meta>

<margin>
<note>original: Πλω: (Plo:); abbreviation for Plotinus.</note> Plotinus
</margin>
Shall we then say that the **essence** <note>original: οὐσία (ousia); the fundamental reality or "substance" of a thing.</note> <insert>being divided</insert> <gloss>itself</gloss> among bodies is one? Or again, is it one in all cases, both indivisible and—even when it is divided—not diminished at all? While it produces out of itself many parts that are divided, the whole remains one within our collective [understanding]. After we have summoned this idea, we must consider how these things exist in themselves and are surpassed. And in this same way, these "many" exist as if always in one, just as those that are divided by location become many. But if they were to cease, they would maintain the same endurance. And if it is **of the same kind** <note>original: ὁμοιομερούς (homoiomerous); a technical term for a substance where every part is the same as the whole, like water or gold.</note>, then all would likewise

How does it happen to have a specific Form?
How does the one happen to be in many?
How do many happen to be from the whole?
</margin>

be situated; but if it brings the whole to the same point, how can the part be similar if it is already according to all the underlying locations? What is it they use, or how can they be from one another? But if it is according to the <unclear>particular</unclear> whole, by the gods, it is also the divided thing; it happens to be one and the same in many bodies. And before everything else, regarding the "one in many," it is impossible for there to be only one from which the "one in the many" comes, as if it were an **image** <note>original: εἴδωλον (eidolon); a reflection or phantom, like a face in a mirror.</note> carried in many places. Consider the analogy of a single signet ring making many impressions in wax; the same [shape] remains in the different pieces, but the wax would be a part that has been divided. But if it is taken as one and entirely **incorporeal** <note>original: ἀσώματον (asomaton); existing without a physical body.</note>, its parts are such by nature.

<margin>
That it is one and the same, whole in many
</margin>

Like the **day** <note>Plotinus often uses the metaphor of "daylight" to explain how something can be in many places at once without being split into pieces; the same light hits many people, but they don't each have a "different" sun.</note>, it would be wonderful if a single quality became present in many. Consider whether both are in many and according to the body, or take it as we do: we position it as something incorporeal in itself and already an essence. This is one essence in many; for either the one is indivisible, and there would not be many from the one, or the many come from that one by its dividing; or it is like a single magnitude that gives itself into a multitude and is not able to provide itself to all as a whole. For it can be as a [fragment], and each part would not be taken away from this. Therefore, they are the same as one another. 

One must indeed have **perception** <note>original: αἴσθησιν (aisthesin); referring to the ability to feel and process sensory information.</note>. For indeed it is called perception. And its parts are like parts of the whole. And if the parts of it and the thing suffering are different, the cause is that the parts are naturally disposed to be divided. And each is a whole, and the whole is not diminished; but if these parts are collected together, they were worked through, and you would know the part is not the whole—and the other part [likewise].

<summary>Plotinus explores the paradox of how the Soul can be present in many different bodies while remaining a single, unified essence. He uses metaphors like the light of day and a wax seal to explain how unity can coexist with apparent division.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the metaphysical investigation into the origins of reality. While the previous page established that the Soul is rooted in the Intellect (Nous), this page ascends further to the "One"—the ultimate, simple source of everything. It explains the process of "emanation," or how a single, perfect source can produce the complexity of the universe without losing anything of itself.</meta>

<page-num>ζ</page-num>

<margin>
That everything subsists <note>original: ὑφίσταται (hyphistatai)</note> from the **One**, whether it be a plurality, a **dyad** <note>In Pythagorean and Platonic thought, the "dyad" represents the principle of "twoness" or the beginning of diversity.</note>, or a number.
</margin>

For it is not merely sight, but a vision that encompasses both [the seer and the seen]. Who then is the one who sees, and what is seen? And how did it come into existence? It came from that source [the One] so that it might see; for it is a marvel how the same things come from either side. Regarding what follows: we should not be easily swayed, even by the ancient sages, as to how **Being** <note>original: τὸ ὂν (to on)</note> subsists from something such as the One. The explanation is this: since it was not possible for Being to remain hidden within the One—if each was to exist distinctly—it therefore flowed out from the One. And how did it emerge from the One, which is simple, with nothing diverse or "double" within it? It is precisely because nothing was *in* it that all things come *from* it. In order for Being to exist, that source must not be Being, but rather its generator. And this is the first generation: being perfect because it seeks nothing, possesses nothing, and needs nothing, the One "overflowed," as it were, and its "over-fullness" has produced something else. But that which was generated turned back toward its source and was filled; it came to be by looking toward the One.

<margin>
That the **One** generates **Being**; not through its own movement.
</margin>

This is the **Intellect** <term>Nous: The Divine Mind or second level of reality. It contains the "Forms" or blueprints of all things.</term>. Its state of rest toward the One produced Being, while its vision toward the One produced the Intellect itself. Since it stood toward the One in order to see, it became simultaneously Intellect and Being. And being like the One, it creates similar things, pouring out a great power of activity. This is its **Form** <note>original: εἶδος (eidos)</note>, just as the One preceded it. It is like the surrounding—

<margin>
<note>original Latin: quomodo mens genatur a primo desideriū quod itidem ipsius</note>
How the mind is generated from the **First** [the One]; and the desire likewise of itself.
</margin>

<margin>
How Intellect comes from the One; how it relates to it; and what is contained therein.
</margin>

—brightness surrounding it, running out from the source while the source remains still, always shining out like the brilliant light encircling the sun, which is forever generated from it. All things, as long as they endure, necessarily produce a secondary **subsistence** <term>Hypostasis: An underlying reality or "layer" of existence that stands below the source but remains connected to it.</term> around themselves, directed outward by their own essential power. This is an image of the archetypes from which they sprang. For example, fire gives off heat, and ice does not keep its coldness only within itself. This is especially true of those things which are eternal and truly <unclear>productive</unclear>.

<meta>This page continues the exploration of the metaphysical hierarchy, specifically describing the "procession" or overflowing of reality from the absolute source—the One—down through the Intellect and the Soul, eventually reaching the level of plant life. It explains how each level of reality "turns back" to contemplate its source.</meta>

When the soul, by means of its powers of perception, keeps itself pure, and when those who hear from God look toward what is above—

---

<margin>
.2.
</margin>

<margin>
Metaphorically, they are those who possess the temple within themselves; for this is what "exceptional" <note>original: περιττός (perittos). Meaning extraordinary or surpassing the common measure.</note> signifies.
</margin>
...as if they were all things. Yet [the One] is not even one of these all, but is all things; for that One is all things in the sense that it is their Principle <note>original: ἀρχὴ (archē). The source or first cause of all things.</note>. It is not as if it does not exist, but rather it is all those things in a higher way; for there, everything is stored away. It is enriched while no variety appears within it. For it is not any specific thing; for nothing is in it. But through it, all things have their own existence <note>original: ὑπέστη (hypestē). To stand under or have a foundation; the root of the term "hypostasis."</note>, so that it might possess its own self more fully. And regarding its generation: that too is all things. For whatever we see coming to life, we must remember that all things extend even to the masculine. Its over-fullness <note>Plotinus uses the metaphor of a fountain overflowing to describe how the One creates the next level of reality without losing anything of itself.</note> has made another; and that which poured forth turned back toward it and was filled. It became looking toward it; and this is the **Intellect** <term>Nous (Intellect)<note>In Neoplatonism, the second level of reality, representing pure thought and the realm of the Forms.</note></term>. Its state of "standing" toward that One is **Being**; but its vision directed toward it is **Intellect**. Since, therefore, it stood toward the One in order to see, it becomes simultaneously Intellect and Being.

<margin>
In those new things, the beings derived from them are deemed worthy of sensation and nature.
</margin>

**Soul**
</margin>
This [Intellect], then, being like the One, produces similar things by pouring out a great power. This too is a form of it, just as the Intellect proceeded from what was before it. Proceeding from this essence, the **Soul** <term>Psyche (Soul)<note>The third level of reality, which bridges the divine realm of ideas and the physical world.</note></term> comes into being, while the Intellect remains unchanged; for the Intellect also came to be while that which was before it remained still. For the Intellect did not move, but [the Soul] moved out from it like a radiance—just as the light around the sun runs around it forever, while the sun itself remains still.

<margin>
Movement and the image of the Soul, which possesses sensation and nature.
</margin>
But the Soul did not move while remaining; rather, it moved again, and yet not again. It possesses sensation and nature; for even in plants, the soul is not severed from its first principle, nor is it ever severed from the things of the whole or the lowest degree.

<margin>
How the soul reaches as far as plants.
</margin>
The Soul reaches as far as plants; for in a certain way, the things in plants are similar [to the higher levels]. However, not all of the Soul is in plants; rather, only a certain part of it is in plants in this way: because it proceeds so far downward, it has produced another **subsistence** <term>Hypostasis<note>A distinct level of reality or "individual" existence in the hierarchy of being.</note></term>—advancing forward from that part. From this comes that which is not dependent; for while that which is from it remains, it produces another subsistence as if from the beginning to the end, with each level left in its own proper seat. That which is generated takes a different rank in a lower degree. Yet each becomes the same as that from which it stood, as long as it follows in sequence. But this is not the case when the whole soul is in a plant; rather, it is like a certain part of it is there.

For everything else would require a purification of itself, and for this purpose it granted the "impassibility of opinion" <note>original: τὸ ἀπαθὲς τῆς δόξης (to apathes tēs doxēs). This refers to a state where one's beliefs are no longer swayed by the "passions" or disturbances of the physical body.</note>. But regarding that which is contained within itself: how could it even possess a part of this opinion? Nor does it act by divination, for it has long been aware of what results. For even that which appears to these things according to the law is not to be given as the "natural" part of the Intellect. But for those who imagine that it has knowledge of great things <unclear>it may be</unclear>, but not of itself. Let this be said also regarding signs you might grasp; for while external things and the **sensations** <note>original: αἰσθήσεις (aisthēseis). The Greek term for sense-perception.</note> of them are not left behind, there is also **discursive thought** <term>Dianoia (Discursive Thought)<note>The level of mind that reasons through logic, mathematics, and language, moving from one step to another, unlike the Intellect which sees everything at once.</note></term> and **opinion** <note>original: δόξα (doxa). A judgment or belief that can be true or false, but lacks the absolute certainty of pure knowledge.</note> concerning them.

But as for those things known within these faculties, each beyond its goal, it is the **Intellect** <term>Nous (Intellect)<note>The highest level of the human mind, which shares the nature of the divine. It does not "think through" problems but possesses direct, intuitive grasp of Truth.</note></term> that acts. For it will clearly know all that is within itself, and it will know itself as these things. For the one who knows within themselves that they only know will be convinced they are known; but further, they are known in that they know—yet what they are as they know, or what thing they are, is discovered only if they know their own contents and their own self.

And what the manner of this is, and to what extent, must be considered. First, let us establish something regarding the **Soul** <note>original: ψυχή (psychē). In this philosophy, the Soul is the bridge between the eternal world of ideas and the physical world of change.</note>, whether there is any knowledge of itself within it. And who is the one who knows within it, and how? We would say that the "sensory" part of the soul belongs only to the outside world. For even when the soul returns to its vital state alongside the sensations that came before, the sensations still lie outside of themselves as perceptions. For when the sufferings <note>original: παθημάτων (pathēmatōn). Often translated as "affections" or "impacts"; the way the physical body is "acted upon" by the world.</note> occur in the external body, the soul calculates the experiences within itself as if coming from itself, based on some sensation or imagination. 

The soul then makes its judgment, both collecting and dividing; and while all these things exist, it looks toward them as if they were its own. It possesses the same power regarding these things and takes a **memory** of itself. It is like one who knows and fits things to the "types" <note>original: τύποις (typois). The internal blueprints or patterns that the soul uses to recognize things in the world.</note> or parts within itself, making them harmonize. This is why we say that "recognizing" <note>original: ἀναγνῶσαι (anagnōsai). Here implying a form of recollection or "re-knowing" what is already in the soul.</note> is a memory of the soul itself. And indeed, the soul's power reaches as far as the sensory... power. And there it must turn back and know itself, insofar as it does not know this state as something inactive. For we shall say that this belongs to the part of the soul that has been "released" <note>original: λελυμένου (lelymenou). A soul that has freed itself from the distractions of the body.</note> within it. We shall set this out clearly in more detail; let us not give in or become those who walk only in generalities. And again, regarding that same thing, what must be considered once more here is the difference in some animals regarding the ability to "think oneself" <note>original: νοεῖν ἑαυτὸν (noein heauton). Self-intellection; the act of the mind being its own object of study.</note>, which is what needs consideration—whether it is an interpretation or because of <unclear>unmixed</unclear>...

It is under the influence of those higher things, not knowing them partially but knowing them completely. And it is not by its own side but by itself alone that it reaches our final goal, which extends through all things.
