It takes the lead, yet there are opposites that descend from it. But since it is understood that this arises from a certain "therefore," it follows that being exists within the act of knowing. <margin>
In itself
</margin>

But know that there is a loss of reason and things in which they did not rejoice; it knows no conflict. All things are like letters from a painter or the impression of seals. These things have been distilled within it unto the things that truly exist. We, however, are suspended by another power; we might know its intellect and how it is seen and contemplate those higher things. If it is transcendently beautiful, then so are we. And the vision of that higher reality knows even itself and is raised up and unified with it. If we are strengthened by it, what is it that knows itself according to that higher principle? I want someone to say: that by knowing other things before itself, it also sees this. It sees itself by itself, and not as if seen in another; I see another thing in its heart, but there it looks down upon itself, for it is everything.

How the intellect sees itself

Others have only a dim image derived from it, just as is the case with similarities found among sensible objects. And of what kind? For example, the form of fire is prevalent in them; but it does not use such bodies as color and shape. For before these physical things exist, those higher forms exist. The **rational principle** <term>Rational Principle (Logos)<note>The divine "reason" or "word" that acts as a formative force in the universe, shaping matter according to the higher Forms.</term> within the seeds that produce these things is not the physical things themselves, as the principles are invisible by nature. Indeed, those higher things possess more reality; they are nature itself. And those things themselves belong to the invisible realm, like the principle in the seed and the things within the **intelligibles** <term>Intelligibles (Noēta)<note>Realities that can be perceived only by the mind, not the senses.</term>.

The principles themselves are not seen, nor are the things residing upon them; yet they are truly there. It is like the principle within a sphere: the truth is not found in the primary physical parts. What is seen of it belongs to it, but it comes from another part of the intelligible realm. Therefore, it does not come from "nothing," nor are the primary things located there. These things are ordered toward those higher realities. The author denies that souls and the Intellect exist only after "that" [the One] exists, even though they possess intellect. There is a true **intellection** <term>Intellection (Noēsis)<note>The act of pure, intuitive thinking by the Intellect.</term> within the intelligibles. It is not that He [the One] sends it out like a mere act of seeing the truth, but it is Vision itself. And the visible object comes from there; even such a thing as this is seen as Vision is. And Vision is like the intelligible visible object which produces intellection. For it is nothing less, and one must not think of it as anything greater. Colors are seen from that source through a kind of "wearing away" <note>Plotinus uses the concept of "overflow" or "diminishment" to explain how the perfect light of the higher realm becomes the physical colors we see.</note>, so that both require a light coming from the outside. For light itself does not lack for light.

This light which comes from it is not merely accidental; it illuminates that which receives it and rouses it. How might one understand this? Certainly not as something material, but as something immaterial and divine. It is agreed that color is a "body" of light, and something similar exists in the soul. If the soul becomes more intellectual and more active, it would become light—and not just any light. Both the realm there and the things belonging to it possess this lightness; they live entirely, as if experiencing the "evening life" of that which is beneficent. On the contrary, every "procession" <note>The Neoplatonic concept of 'Proodos,' where reality flows outward from the One into lower forms of existence.</note> exists as such. I believe this should be examined: it is not [merely a part], but it is the entirety of motion, except for that of the One itself. But he does not assign any cause to it, not even the title of "Cause." For the One is Being itself, and True Being. One cannot even grasp it by the negation of true things—as if the primary things did not belong to others—but rather the opposite: that all things come from it. Its hidden nature is thus preserved. It belongs to Life; for there, true things exist in living and in perception. The Light which is there is with the One and within the One primarily; and around it, there is a brightness, yet it is greater even than that brightness. It is the truly intelligible: both the one who thinks and the thing being thought, and it is itself the Intelligible.

### L L E Ch <note>These characters likely serve as a filing code or a reference to a specific section in a larger commentary.</note>

**Every act of seeing itself is "the other"—it is a multiplicity.**
**For in everything it sees itself and something else.**

<column-break/>

In the same way, this also applies to the parts themselves; for the "Living Being" <note>Referring to the "Intelligible Living Being," the totality of all Forms.</note> has been divided into parts. And even that is not a single part; it must be that there are other lives, not just one, belonging to different things. These lives, flowing alongside one another, would not belong to it if they were not bounded. Nor is the unformed part of itself and of itself, being separate from the whole; nor are its own things more common than they are its own.

Indeed, in the Whole, it must be simply as it is, since it belongs to the first things. Already thinking purely in that same realm, one may receive it from a teacher. Then, from this, comes a reflection and an **image** <term>Image (Eidolon)<note>In Neoplatonism, an "eidolon" is a secondary reflection or "ghostly" copy of a higher reality, much like a reflection in a mirror.</note> of this; in perception it exists within itself, and in the parts themselves. It must also exist in themselves with whatever powers they have, and not only in the lesser things. 

For if someone were descending, even to the point of a gnat being produced by the work of the Whole, how could those things in the upper realms always be as they are if the influence reaches to the very last extremes? But if so, it was more fitting that these first things be themselves. If these are divine, they do not always produce the most "human" things at the end; hence there are things in the body, and the kinds of things that can exist, and both together. But if not, they belong to wholes or others, and their contents do not exist according to themselves—the world not being this world, but the heaven of this world not being in the power of sight. 

This is because of the things in which they exist, and not even in themselves. For the things in itself are not the things of someone else. But we must state again the question under investigation: how does it see itself? Rather, let us persist with the **Intellect** <term>Intellect (Nous)<note>The second "hypostasis" or level of reality; the divine mind that contains all the eternal Forms or "Ideas."</note> rather than with the **Soul** <term>Soul (Psyche)<note>The third level of reality, which translates the eternal Ideas of the Intellect into the changing world of time and space.</note>, regarding its state of being. 

Then, this too: it is by necessity both a "seeing thing" and a "seeing thing of That One" <note>The "One," which is the ultimate source above the Intellect.</note>. There is also a vision of the things within itself. And is there a vision of another at all, when there ought not to be a vision, which is more beautiful? It is necessary, then, for there to be a plurality in the seeing subject. And thus, from certain things, the vision is directed to the object of sight; and because the part is in itself, but is only and uniquely one. Everyone and everything sees another and another; or if not "another," then what and how is that "other" which was present? 

Therefore, that which is directed toward such a thing, and which exists around another light belonging to itself, is most truly in itself; from which it will also proceed from another toward itself. But when it is all in all, there is no place where it will not be, provided it is not in nature alone. And from both, let both belong to it: both to be before itself and to be the same. By necessity, it is primarily alone toward the alone, yet they are themselves and different, and by necessity, they are a plurality.

He is before all things, and the principle of these—not as a "ruler," as you might say. For that which is simple does not come from elsewhere; it is not any individual thing, not any individual thing. Rather, all things are in the One. But it is not those things; it is **before all things**. Thus, it is even before the contemplating of all these things; thus, it is even before this **essence** <note>original: "οὐσίαν"</note>, and before this order, and before this which is prior to all things, of which the first essence also partakes. For it belongs to these; and even "to think" <note>original: "τὸ νοεῖν"</note> does not properly belong to Him. For He is not the act of thinking, nor does He exist by the act of thinking. For this was necessary for that which is "before all things"—which this author named "Activity" <note>original: "ἐνέργειαν"</note>—to be of a certain kind. So long as it is a single essence. For the multiplicity belongs to the intelligibles; and His activities, while His activities as essences provide variety... His activities are not all essences within Him; but neither are His activities the multiplicity. His essence is as great as His multiplicity; but the multiplicity, while granted to the intelligibles, is not perceived according to the One itself. The multiplicity in the intelligibles is not in the "First" <note>The One</note>; for it has been shown that the One is that from which the whole comes. For if the One comes from number, how can it be the First? Rather, it is the first of that which is numbered, as they say; for the things that follow are a synthesis. Again, the **Monad** <note>The mathematical or metaphysical unit</note> is before the "All." And if these things are so, how do the many come from the One? It is because the One was, in a sense, all things—except that it was not those things yet. But the things of the "composed" come from elsewhere. If it should happen that he is not this absolute and simple thing, how will he be? For he saw the One; and yet he poses a certain difficulty before the activities. Furthermore, he poses those as remaining still, just as the essences which—it should be noted—give form to all things, which produce a "single-form" <unclear>disturbance</unclear> and will exist. And if it remained only in one way, it would produce nothing. But if it is that from which a multiplicity comes, and in its being every activity is from that—and these activities are certain ones, and these you shall have. And if the multiplicity shall exist, and if these are the primary essences, then the "Other" creates a state of rest. And the essences are defined from that source, and the activities, which reach out, are also something else here. Regarding the activities, he allows the activities to yield—for it is not the One itself, but rather that other thing which speaks of the **One** <unclear>itself</unclear>.

---

Plotinus here cannot name God in any other way, and all things seem to pertain to the simplest, finally, so that it is possible, but not in a strict sense, as more correctly announced in the preceding words. Number is not there where the highest unity is the source of all things... in multiplicities, and whoever imagines things in Him—there is neither essence unless it is in Him, nor quality... as if you call it "first." For what you wish to explain, you cannot. It is similar through the letters <note>original: "p[er] l[ite]ras"</note>, you announce properly those who have held God by reason... that he might be revealed to us in his own way, thus that thing attains itself through the absolute of the worthy, which they attempt to affirm.

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the nature of the Intellect and the One. While the previous page discussed the Intellect as a "one-many" containing the Ideas, this page addresses the concept of self-sufficiency (autarkeia) and the limits of human language in describing the absolute "One," which transcends even the act of thinking.</meta>

<margin>
Self-sufficiency first
Self-sufficiency second
</margin>

<margin>
Concerning that which thinks itself and the nature of the agreement <note>original: "σύμβασις," referring to the union or correspondence between the thinker and the thought</note>; that in which it thinks itself, it exists, but it is not "One" <note>In Neoplatonic thought, "The One" is absolutely simple; if something thinks itself, it creates a duality of subject and object, and is thus no longer the "One."</note>.
</margin>

What then? Is it not even self-sufficient? If indeed it stands before the eternal things that follow it, it does not even <unclear>move</unclear> toward the outside; it is simply the state of not needing another. And in this state, it is not even <unclear>thought</unclear>. Therefore, it is not "self-sufficient" in the sense of needing itself—for that would be the state of thinking.

<margin>
Everything that thinks itself is a multiplicity.
</margin>

And Plotinus says of it <note>Referring to the first principle or the "One"</note>, that being self-sufficient is not quite enough, for self-sufficiency arises from a requirement, creating a "station" or fixed state within it. And if there is <unclear>thought</unclear> <unclear>directed</unclear> toward itself, there is a "shared-consciousness" <term>synaisthesis<gloss>an internal awareness or "feeling-with" oneself</gloss></term>; all of this is a form of perception. And the Intellect <term>Nous<gloss>The divine Mind or second principle in the Neoplatonic hierarchy</gloss></term> also bears witness to this. For those things that are prior, it <unclear>wills</unclear> to turn inward toward itself, long before the <unclear>self-sufficient ones</unclear>, to <unclear>look</unclear> only at this inward reality, as he <note>likely Plotinus</note> says. And for the Mind to <unclear>think</unclear> <unclear>inwardly</unclear> means that every act of thinking is a multiplicity. For that which departs toward another belongs to the tradition of Orpheus <note>original: "ὀρφέως"; a reference to the mystical Orphic hymns or cosmogony</note>; it has reached neither itself nor the things belonging to it. Thinking would not be desired when it is simply itself; but this stands as a witness, for this is what it was granted to be. And again he said, this "thinking the whole" is not "One"; because of this, he says it is as if it <unclear>takes the lead</unclear> <unclear>within</unclear> it. In the act of <unclear>thinking</unclear>, each thing is not established by itself, but is deserted and almost <note>original: "μονονού"</note> desiring a grasp of thought. For this is why it is praised.

<image-desc>A scribal symbol or monogram in the left margin, resembling a cross with stylized characters or flourishes, possibly a 'Nota' mark indicating an important passage.</image-desc>

<margin>
How we know God; how we speak of Him.
</margin>

<margin>
Concerning God, we say what He is not; but what He is, we do not say.
</margin>

<margin>
How the inspired ones <note>original: "ἐνθουσιασταὶ" (enthusiasts)</note> know.
</margin>

And again he says that the knowing of this "One" is not knowledge but an outshining <term>apaugasma<gloss>a radiance or reflection, like light from a sun</gloss></term>; for He does not possess knowledge from the beginning. For to "have" that thing is to be the thing itself; when it exists, it does not belong to itself. Nor do we say of Him what we say [ordinarily], nor does what we say "happen" concerning Him. We are aware that we have neither knowledge nor intellection of Him, even when we speak of Him as if we "have" Him. Nevertheless, we speak of the things of knowledge, though we do not "have" the things concerning Him. In this way, we "have" Him, so as to be overcome by Him rather than speaking of Him. And insofar as we know Him, we realize that we do not say what He is. He is the cause of the things that come after; we must speak of those, but not of what is with Him. And even if we do not speak, we are like the inspired ones <note>the "enthusiasts"</note> who, becoming possessed, know at least this much: that there is something greater within them, even if they do not know what it is that has moved them. And they say that they receive a certain part of the "whole" of that movement, which is different from the Mover itself. And we risk having a relation toward that, whenever we use a pure mind, as he says, whoever is thinking. But the Intellect is essence, and all other things belong to this "rank" <note>original: "τίχου" for "τεῖχος" (wall) or "στοίχου" (row/rank)</note>; but He Himself is such that He is not these things. Rather, He is better than all, not even "thinking," but something more and greater than what we call "Being," because He is both the Cause and the End.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the "One" (the First Principle) and explains why all existence must derive from a single, simple source. It expands on the previous page's theme by arguing that the physical world—and even the realm of pure thought—must trace back to this absolute unity which lacks any division.</meta>

<margin>That there must simply be one before all things, and there cannot be two principles <term>archai<gloss>the fundamental origins or sources of reality</gloss></term>, but only one "One."</margin>

Whatever exists after the First must necessarily come from it. This follows the order of second and third things that come after the intermediate levels. While the second falls short of the First, the First remains toward a state of being completely self-sufficient <note>original: "anendeës," meaning lacking nothing and needing nothing from outside itself</note>. For that which is before all things must be simple <term>haploun<gloss>not made of parts; non-composite</gloss></term>. This applies to all things that exist after it—whether they exist by themselves or as a part of it—as they are derived from it. Some things are close to it, while others must be present to others, being truly without magnitude while existing in another.

When we speak of it as a substance <term>ousia<gloss>the essential "being" or "stuff" of a thing</gloss></term> from which other things are yielded, we are describing the combinations from which all things and compositions arise. In such a state, it would not be simple. Yet, in the First, self-sufficiency existed; and in its being is the being of all. For that which is first in honor is never among the things that follow it.

<margin>Why or how the First is one, yet to other things it is also many.</margin>

But that which comes from it—from those infinite things within it—remains there, so that from that source, it continues.

<margin><image-desc>A marginal annotation consisting of a circled cross mark with the abbreviation "seek" or "note" written above it.</image-desc></margin>

From such a source, it does not only "be"; it is also a form <term>eidos<gloss>the structural idea or pattern of a thing</gloss></term> of such a kind as the others possess. For we do not say that bodies are the source, or that the first body or other things come from a body. A body is something that is generated <note>original: "ginomenon," something that comes into being rather than existing eternally</note>, but it is not a principle. Even if it is called a principle, it is not bodily in nature, but is truly one; for that unity is the First. If there were something else after the First, the First would no longer be simple. If anything draws from it, it is because that thing comes from the First. For that which pulls at bodies would no longer be that First Principle; it is the source of all.

How then does a single thing come from the First? One might call it the First because it is the most perfect of all. It is a power <term>dynamis<gloss>the potential or capacity to act</gloss></term> before all things. We must consider it the most powerful of all beings, and that all other powers imitate it as much as they are able. Whenever we see anything else reach its perfection, it generates; for things that achieve their own state do not simply stay within themselves, but produce something else. This is true not only for things that have the power of choice <term>proairesis<gloss>deliberate moral or intellectual choice</gloss></term>, but also for things that lack choice by nature. Even soulless things share of themselves as much as they can: for example, fire heats, snow cools, and medicines perform their various effects. Everything else acts in a way that imitates the Source according to its own power. Toward the eternal, the things that come from it are most perfect. The First, having taken all things into itself as though looking beyond itself, has produced them everywhere. How then could they come from the source? It is because the source itself produces them.

<summary>Plotinus argues that all reality must stem from a single, simple "One" rather than multiple sources. He explains that everything in existence, from the highest intellects to simple elements like fire and snow, naturally imitates the One by overflowing and producing new things once they reach their own perfection.</summary>
<keywords>The One, First Principle, simplicity, emanation, perfection, nature, causality, Plotinus, Neoplatonism</keywords>

Glory; and that it is so named from the word "to receive" <note>original: "dokhō"</note> and so forth.

There is, again, another kind of <term>glory<gloss>doxa; in Greek, this word signifies both "radiance/glory" and "opinion/appearance"</gloss></term> which, being itself received by sense-perception, is received and altered by that from which it is taken. It possesses a single truth in reality—this being the source—just as a ray is received from the sun. In this way, it is altered from being called entirely "true"; it is not truth itself, but rather "glory" <note>The author is playing on the idea that human opinion or "appearance" is a refracted, diminished version of divine Truth, just as a ray is a secondary manifestation of the sun.</note>. For such glory is already the object of these inquiries, neither being a mere impression from things—nor a rising upward—nor, again, a turning away from truth itself. Instead, it is like the spheres described in the study of optics; it is called a "productive removal" toward the light for those who turn away from it and from this truth. And it is known that each thing has its own place, even if it is altered; and the deviations of this glory, though they possess color, are altered both in their actual color and in what is blended with them, yet they do not possess the truth entirely. For so it is, again, with being in the realm of the senses; for since it desires to enjoy divinity, it also wishes to receive its beauty and to be manifested within it. And yet, this is a new idea; but the entire nature concerning the most blessed things is <term>impassible<gloss>apathes; unaffected by external influence or suffering</gloss></term> and belongs to the whole world. For it is not in this way, nor any other way, like a human being, nor do these things give them a <term>substantial reality<gloss>hypostasis; a distinct, individual existence</gloss></term>. And they let it into themselves; and this is not at all out of place, for it is outside and according to their own power; and never yet has anything from them concerning it revealed what it is or how it is. And entirely ethereal things are not in agreement with us when we speak. And that which comes from them leaves us behind. And the beautiful God is and shall be. He is very near; and the divine essence is perfect, for it is the remedy that achieves wisdom. For even if it is not carried along as he is, it nevertheless holds securely to the divine. And it is so, for they do not have a different position; from which truth they have a single knowledge of themselves and of the Intellect and of all things, and the beauty of divinity is great—or rather, it is that all these things live.

...contained on both sides. In this case, then, these things must be stated; but one must observe the things of that higher realm with a moderate sense of **proportion**. In this world, all things belonging to that One will have their <term>reality<gloss>hypostasis; a technical term for the underlying "stuff" or fundamental reality of a thing</gloss></term> from the One, provided they come from anything at all. <margin>
That substance <note>original: "ousia"</note> is the One being substance.

Nor does one see it by a light coming from something else; rather, one looks into the Source itself, which is light and the very beginning of light. But in our own case, it is as if this light comes from without. This light is not seen, however, until it meets the blood <note>a reference to ancient theories of vision where internal "fire" or "spirits" in the blood produced sight</note> and the light within us, the very thing by which we see and through which lower things are made visible. <margin>
God is everywhere; and what must be done so that we may see Him.
</margin>

And when it has passed, one might say, "It was within, and yet not within," or perhaps "It did not come from anywhere." For the One has no "where." It neither arrives nor departs to any place, but it simply appears and does not appear. Therefore, one must not pursue it, but remain in quietness until it manifests, preparing oneself to be a spectator, just as the eye waits for the rising of the sun. As the poets say, the sun appearing over the horizon from the ocean offers itself to be seen by our eyes—passing over all the things the sun represents, coming from some place beyond. <meta>This page continues the discussion from page 239. It specifically examines "paliggenesia"—the rebirth or recurrence of all things—and how individual differences, such as those between the sexes, are formed by the "Logos" or rational principles.</meta>

<margin>
The rebirth <term>rebirth</term> <note>original: "παλιγγενεσία" (paliggenesia) – literally "beginning again," referring here to the Neoplatonic cycle of cosmic recurrence.</note> of all things, or all things together within the definition.
</margin>

<margin>
What kind of seeds of male and female, and how they have a mixture.
</margin>

<margin>
Through causes.
</margin>

<margin>
That the same identity returns in all things in the rebirth.
</margin>

Everything flows away, and among these differences, it is not possible for these things to be the same, nor even as if they were themselves the models for some of those very differences—those of the causes and the things drawn from them. Yet, there are rightly ten thousand differences. For it is not as if each thing is made simply according to the archetype <term>archetype</term> <note>original: "ἀρχέτυπον" (archetypon) – the original "blueprint" or Form in the divine Mind.</note>, but it is also made of the things that differ, both in its formation and in every cycle. Rebirth is the rational principle <term>Logos</term> <note>original: "λόγος" (logos) – the formative, ordering principle that transmits the Forms into the material world.</note> itself, rising again from within itself, bringing certain rational principles into the history of these things; rather, they are not merely the things alongside it, for they flow together. And as it pertains to being and non-being, some are mixtures of parts and, according to our view, they produce differences. The rational principle of each genus holds sway whenever each parent, as if establishing a foundation, acts not merely according to common differences, but according to the same qualities that belong to it. And if anyone should encounter these differing things, even through their opposites, it is not impossible; rather, as the generation pours forth, the "where" and the "how" of their appearance becomes manifest.

This includes the male and the female, which do not differ by their position alone, but because both participate equally in the power that holds them, even as one gives to the other and is mastered by that power. For if someone were to ask, "From what place does the difference come?" or rather, "How is the difference similarly mastered?", everything is mixed into nearly identical forms. But toward those things that are different, the principle is many-sided, and it happens somehow. But how is it possible for there to be a similarity of the rational principles of generations, both those that are hidden and those that are paths? Let the differences of the wholes emerge, such as the cycle of the body; then, in the difference of these same wholes, they appear in love. 

We have not recognized that what is given to children from the whole is mastered in such a way that the same appearance belongs to a different cycle, yet the same things are given. For the same body gives the same difference again; we shall say this of the rational principles, and even of how other animals give birth. For they too are said to be without variation <note>original: "ἀπαραλλάκτως" (aparallaktōs) – meaning identical or indistinguishable in form.</note>, not only changing, and not only in as many as there are particulars. So also are the rational principles: as many as there are differences in particulars, there is also a difference in them, even in those that follow after and are indistinguishable by rules. Consequently, before anything else, all things that differ are present. For just as a certain art makes even the "indifferent" courses, so the same principle receives a rational difference according to how they change, toward making everything different upon the same foundation; thus, by nature, it becomes our task to make the whole similar once more.

<summary>This page discusses the Neoplatonic concept of "paliggenesia" (rebirth/recurrence), arguing that the Logos or rational principle governs the return of individual forms and biological differences, such as sex, through "seeds" of formative power.</summary>

<meta>This page transitions from the abstract discussion of the cycle of rebirth (paliggenesia) to the specific manifestation of beauty in the physical world. While the previous page examined how the "Logos" or rational principle creates individual differences, this page explores how that same principle bestows "kallos" (beauty) upon both works of art and natural beings. It establishes that beauty is not a result of material bulk, but of the internal Form that the artist or Nature imposes upon matter.</meta>

# That beauty exists according to form in artificial objects
# and in natural things and in rational principles
---

<margin>All arts imitate nature and derive their power from nature.</margin>

Regarding material things, these are less sacred to the degree they are material; but we hold that the beauty which shines forth from within itself is evident to all. There are qualities, such as warmth or "well-temperedness," which, if they exist in a truly living being, constitute its beauty—not a beauty of the surface, but a primary beauty that acts according to its own energy. For it is not a music lacking the Muses <note>original: "ἀκάμουσα μουσικὴ" (amousa mousike) – a play on words suggesting a craft without the inspiration of the Muses.</note> that creates, but Music itself which imparts its musicality. The primary evidence of this in the arts is that art creates by imitating nature. We must recognize that those natures which correspond to these arts do not imitate what is merely seen with the eyes, but rather they reach back up to the rational principles <term>Logos</term> <note>original: "λόγους" (logous) – the underlying blueprints or formative laws of reality.</note> from which Nature itself arises. Furthermore, we must understand that the arts do much on their own and add to nature; for they possess beauty and make up for what is lacking in the physical world. They possess a perfecting power. Consider how Phidias <note>Phidias was the most famous sculptor of Classical Greece, known for the Statue of Zeus at Olympia.</note> created his Zeus: he did not use any model from the world of the senses, but rather he grasped what Zeus would look like if he chose to appear before our eyes. Thus, some arts stand apart, while others create works that are complete in themselves, following the beauty found in nature. We speak of this when we contemplate living animals and everything within them, especially those parts that are perfectly formed, because of the light that shines through them and gives them shape. But what of arts that use voices or touch, or those that find ease in movements—where is the beauty in these? Surely it is not in the blood or the physical components, but in the color and the form <term>morphe</term> <note>original: "μορφή" (morphe) – the outward shape that reveals the inner essence.</note> given to them. It is nothing based on mere opinion or the wealth of those who perish, but it receives the things from within. Beauty does not dwell in conflict; rather, the inner things are seen as they are. Even in the case of Aphrodite herself, everything that is <unclear>beautiful</unclear> and <unclear>good</unclear> in the goddess exists to aid even that which does not yet exist. Life is present in all things seen, and one clearly sees this harmony followed everywhere, as it surrounds both the complete and the incomplete. The arts prepare all things to be beautiful, treating both the complete and the deficient according to beauty. One must see if beauty does not also exist in the creator, just as it does in the work. And if the creator is beautiful in himself, then is it not the case that his work is an adornment only insofar as it dwells within his inner vision? A man possesses all things more fully within himself.

<margin>
1. The reason which is called the highest truth is the same as the greatest beauty in the body.
That the beauty of bodies does not exist in mass or quantity <note>original: "ὄγκῳ ἢ ποσότητι" (onko e posoteti) – Plotinus argues against the Stoic idea that beauty is merely "symmetry" or physical size.</note>.
</margin>

Our faith in this beauty is itself a kind of vision and an image of happiness; that which remains always the same also disposes the things below it. Beauty exists by the power of this principle, just as it dwells within the world at every moment. It exists in the vastness and in the things outside us, just as I believe it lies within our internal disposition; it is present in names and in things that appear unadorned, <unclear>however</unclear> briefly.

<summary>This page argues that beauty is not a physical property like size or mass, but is an internal "Form" or "Rational Principle" that artists and Nature both use to shape the world. It famously cites the sculptor Phidias to show that true art imitates the divine archetypes rather than just copying physical reality.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the exploration of beauty, moving from its manifestation in the physical world (as discussed on the previous page regarding Phidias and the nature of art) to its ultimate source: the Intelligible World. This transition shifts the focus from how material objects participate in beauty to how the divine "Intellect" (Noûs) perceives and contains all things in a state of perfect, transparent unity.</meta>

<margin>
How the heavenly gods are understood both in the perceptible world and outside of the heavens in the intelligible realm.
</margin>

...as if they were being traversed; for the conditions of bodies do not exist there, nor are their beings such as the bodies found here. Rather, their nature is always that of Intellect <term>Noûs</term> <note>original: "νοῦν" (noun) – in Neoplatonism, this refers to the Divine Mind, the second principle of reality where all true Forms exist.</note>. And all of these, and the rest as well, are not idle in their wisdom, but they all shine forth. They say that there, things are like light for everyone—star-like and pure—and they go through all things and know all things without any error. They see their own internal realities and those of others. Some of the gods are joined together...

<margin>
How all works relate to one another in the intelligible world; how the whole is in every part of it; and how all things are transparent.
</margin>

...for as many as are there, they behold all things from a distance, as it were, yet also in that transcendent state where "the head" <note>This likely refers to the highest part of the soul or the summit of the Intellect.</note> governs all. In that world, as much of it as is inhabited is within each individual. It is as if they lived in every path at once; for everything there is "heaven." The earth there is heaven, the sea is heaven, and so too are the animals, the plants, and the humans. Every heavenly thing there is a heaven. 

The gods who dwell within it do not look down upon humans nor anything else that is there; for they traverse every region and find rest in every place. There, life is effortless. Truth is their parent, their nurse, their essence, and their nourishment. They see all things—not those to which "becoming" <note>original: "γένεσις" (genesis) – the realm of change, birth, and decay.</note> is attached, but those to which "essence" <note>original: "οὐσία" (ousia) – true, unchanging Being.</note> belongs. They see themselves in others, for all things there are transparent <note>original: "διαφανῆ" (diaphane) – a key concept in Plotinus; in the divine realm, there are no opaque barriers, and one being does not block the view of another.</note>. Nothing is dark or resistant; instead, every being is manifest to every other, into their very depths. For light is manifest to light. 

Each being contains all things within itself, and again, sees all things in every other. Thus, all things are everywhere, and everything is all things, and each is all. The splendor there is boundless. For even what is "small" there is "great"; the sun there is all the stars, and each star is in turn the sun and all the stars. In each, a different quality stands out, yet all things are manifest in each. 

Their movement is pure; for the movement does not come from something different than itself to disturb it. Stability, too, is not shaken, because it is not mixed with that which is unstable. And the Beautiful is truly beautiful, because it does not reside in what is not beautiful. Justice <note>original: "δίκαιον" (dikaion)</note> does not walk on foreign ground, like an alien land, but is rooted in the very essence of each being. Each thing is that which it is from its own source. It does not exist merely as a reflection of eternity, but is eternity itself. One part is not different from the whole; the underlying reality is Intellect. 

It is not as if one were to look at a temple and see light coming from the outside; rather, that light is within one’s own eyes. The stars beheld there are seen not as parts, but as if each were the whole. Each part is also a whole, and simultaneously something more. It appears this way because there is no darkness there; everything shines toward the Beautiful. One who possesses this vision sees it within themselves, just as they see the external world.

<summary>Plotinus describes the Intelligible World as a realm of perfect transparency where every being contains the whole, and the "heavenly gods" exist as pure Intellect rather than physical bodies. This is the realm of true Being, where knowledge is direct, light is omnipresent, and all things are interconnected without the limitations of space or matter.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s exploration of the Intelligible World. Having previously described the transparency and unity of the Divine Mind (Noûs), he now investigates the nature of Wisdom (Sophia). He argues that true Wisdom is not a collection of logical arguments, but is identical to Being itself. To illustrate this non-discursive, immediate way of knowing, he famously points to Egyptian hieroglyphs as symbols that represent entire concepts at once, rather than building meaning through strings of words.</meta>

...is himself by nature. And they will call this principle "Nature." But where shall we find it? They will say it comes from him. If it comes from him, and we have already conceived of it as being divided into many parts, then it was not some "wisdom" that generated it according to equal laws. They will ask, then, from where does it come? It comes from him, but in a self-immaterial way. If one were to rank him as wisdom itself, then he is truly wisdom—the very Being and that by which Being exists. Thus, Being is wisdom, and Being 
<margin>Wisdom created the things that exist in the Mind. How beings and ideas are in the Mind.</margin> 
comes from wisdom. For this reason, true Being comes from wisdom. Therefore, all those "wisdoms" that do not possess Being—on the grounds that they came into existence through some other wisdom—do not concern themselves with being true Beings. If wisdom is within them, they are not true Beings simply because they exist through wisdom.

<term>Axioms</term> <note>original: "ἀξιώματα" (axiōmata) – here referring to logical propositions or self-evident truths.</note> are what the gods see. And their happiness there is not a dream. Rather, each of the things spoken of there are beautiful **statues** <note>original: "ἀγάλματα" (agalmata) – in Neoplatonism, these are not just physical statues, but "living" divine images or manifestations of the Forms.</note>, such as those a wise man might imagine existing in his soul. They are the "letters" of Zeus—images and things that are likely to be the Ideas themselves. 

It seems to me that the ancients, and those among the Egyptians who were wise—either through exact scientific knowledge or by a natural intuition—wished to demonstrate their wisdom when they 
<margin>Regarding the sacred letters of the Egyptians</margin>
did not use the forms of letters which travel through 
<margin>Why the Egyptians used animals and plants instead of letters</margin>
discourses and propositions, nor did they imitate the sounds and the pronunciation of axioms. Instead, they drew **images**, carving in their temples a single image for each particular thing. 

In this way, they manifested the fact that there is no discursive "running-through" <note>Plotinus uses the word "diexodos" to contrast step-by-step reasoning with the "all-at-once" nature of divine thought.</note> of thought there. Every image is a kind of science and wisdom; it is a whole, simultaneous thing, not a collection of thoughts or a product of research. Only later, starting from this unified wisdom, does a partial image unfold in something else. This unfolded version then speaks in a narrative "running-through," discovering the causes of why things are as they are. When something is so beautifully arranged, we marvel at its creation. And for those who marveled, he said that Wisdom is such a great cause that it contains these Beings, and therefore it was necessary to create them through a living medium.
<margin>57</margin>
According to Wisdom itself, the "well-arranged" is thus. And if someone were to ask why things are so, it would be reasonable to say: because they exist in a state that is just now being removed from a proposition and just now being removed from the reasoning processes that exist here. For example, let us take one case among many—the way the universe is described and how this whole is kept from being overwhelmed by another. In such a case, do we really think its creator <note>Referring to the Demiurge or Divine Craftsman.</note> first conceived of the "earth" in his mind, and then decided to fix it in its place?

<summary>Plotinus discusses the nature of divine Wisdom (Sophia), arguing that it is a unified, non-discursive reality. He uses Egyptian hieroglyphs as a primary metaphor for how the Divine Mind perceives all truths simultaneously as "images" rather than through the step-by-step logic of human language.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of how the Intelligible world—the realm of pure thought—operates differently than our physical world. Having established that "Wisdom" in that higher realm is not a collection of arguments but is identical to Being itself, the text now examines the relationship between logical "conclusions" and the "First Beauty." It concludes with a famous visualization exercise: the Transparent Sphere.</meta>

What, then, is the entire conclusion? It is just as if it were drawn from premises, yet not brought in from the outside nor as a secondary thought, but rather following naturally and being fully contained within them. For this is how all these things are. And such are the proofs and the certainty found there. For how, and from where, does the principle move all these things? The very act of living is the beginning of the cause; it possesses a certain blessedness and establishes such a thing securely among those things that live. Both the beginning and the act of demonstration itself are one and the same; it is beyond the accountability of mere human reason <note>original: "λόγῳ" (logō) — here meaning discursive, step-by-step logic</note> and similar constraints. Nor is the "Whole" located in any one place, but rather the "Whole" is present in every part.

<margin>
x How?
What then does he say?
[Note regarding the] chorus?
</margin>

For indeed, how could they speak of **Beauty**? For surely we do not see it as an external object. Rather, it is not something "held," but something already contained within itself—and that very thing is the beauty of the other. All of their beauty, therefore, already desires to be "Beautiful." But the **First Beauty** <term>First Beauty</term> <note>The ultimate source of all aesthetic and moral value in Plotinus's system, often identified with the Form of the Good.</note> did not merely pass by. It is necessary for this and the "All" to be seen at once. If one wishes for something less than the Intelligible <term>Intelligible</term> <note>original: "νοητοῦ" (noētou) — referring to the realm of pure Ideas or Forms that can only be grasped by the mind, not the senses.</note>, accepting a mere reflection <note>original: "ἐνθύμησιν" (enthymēsin) — a thought-process or internal reflection</note> instead of the clearer realities we discussed before, that would be an absurd beauty, and one would fail to set aside the beauty within. This very Model <term>Paradigm</term> <note>original: "παράδειγμα" (paradeigma) — the perfect divine blueprint of which our world is a copy.</note> is itself beautiful as an Idea, just as it claims to be.

<margin>Question: What is it that is wondered at, etc.?</margin>

Is that which is "wonderful" the thing itself, or is it that which causes the wonder by the way it is situated? It is clear that we, the onlookers, would wonder; and those who have wondered at the First Beauty are unaware that the thing they wonder at is because of "That." Because it is suspended from the Model, it is indeed clear that one must grasp the sequence of the argument. For in this way, Beauty will be even more **transparent** alongside it. It wishes to make the beauty of the Model similar to itself, as if it had stripped away its outer layers. Because of this, those who hold onto beauty appear to be images of the beautiful. We must settle our gaze even on the beauty here... what can be said of this visible beauty? From this point, those who find fault with it may correctly show that it is not "That" [the original]. Therefore, this world is not merely a likeness of the parts, which would be confused and limited. Let us take the "rarefied" and the "all," as if there were another vision of whatever is appearing. While bodily forms follow one after another and are crowded together, let us imagine the other stars...

<margin>
How we are able to be loved, or a representation of Intelligible Beauty.
</margin>

...a representation <term>Phantasia</term> <note>original: "φαντασίαν" (phantasian) — a mental image or visualization used as a meditative tool.</note> where the earth, the sea, and every living creature are seen within a **transparent sphere**. One sees all things at once as a single unity. It is as if one held within a light-filled representation a sphere that contains everything within itself.

<meta>This page continues the exploration of the Intelligible realm (the world of pure intellect). It moves from describing the "Transparent Sphere" as an exercise in visualizing the unity of all things to the actual experience of the soul in the presence of the Divine. The previous discussion on Wisdom and Beauty now transitions into how individual souls experience this vision differently, yet eventually find union with the "All."</meta>

<margin>
How the blessed souls see God in various and different ways from one another.
</margin>

Those who are able to see these things find that He <note>Refers to "The One" or the "First Beauty," the source of all things in Plotinian philosophy.</note> does not appear to them as something invisible. Rather, having dawned from within them, He illuminates the entire world of His own being. Upon Him, a certain world—even this sensible world—has blossomed. Yet, this divine realm is by no means seen through the physical sun; for the heavenly bodies are not seen there in the same way, nor are the things derived from them seen through our physical senses. 

Those who see do not see with bodies, nor do they see an external sight or specific shapes. While everyone is moved by these things and originates from them, they do not merely look at them as separate objects. Instead, each soul carries within itself the vision it has seen, a blessed **radiance** that shines upon them. They adapt their own internal state of being to the nature of the spectacle. 

These souls arrive at this state when they have nothing that hinders or weighs them down. When nothing pushes against them or distracts them from all sides, they are finally led to this end. For those who have already been greatly helped, they are now "blessed gods," partaking in divine things and the Good. Such are the souls that are oriented toward the things "there" <note>original: "ἐκεῖ" (ekei) — a common term in Plotinus for the higher, Intelligible realm as opposed to the physical world "here."</note>; and having been born out of the "All," they are as one.

<margin>
How the soul, seeing God, sees the same things and is in spirit with God.
</margin>

The soul possesses all things there; He is both their beginning and their end. Whatever and however many things they have, they hold in relation to those higher realities. Toward them, they possess that entire "Whole." When they are in that state, even through a part of their own contemplations <term>contemplations</term> <note>original: "θεωριῶν" (theōriōn) — not just thinking, but a direct, spiritual gazing or "seeing" with the mind.</note>, they possess the essence of those things. Then, in addition to these, the very "Place" is seen by all, and it shares in the things there, for it sends forth all things. 

Many are the things there, such as they are and of what kind they are; and they become part of the souls. Whatever spirits they possess and however they are moved to think <note>original: "νοῆσαι" (noēsai) — to perceive with the divine Intellect.</note>—for they possess the **Divine Color**. This belongs to the realm of true knowledge, which comes through the fulfillment of prayer. Having been made like Him, they see Him within themselves, a beauty that is more than just a surface, but rather a total radiance and excellence of form.

<margin>
(That the perceptions of evil things are more jarring than those of good things; therefore they also have disturbances, while the perceptions of lovely things are joyful.)
</margin>

For they do not put on a foreign beauty, but rather they see the greater beauty within themselves. This has been considered a state of remaining or abiding. For those who have seen Him, it is as if they have become one with Him, moving in harmony. Instead of "drinking" the nectar—as if it were something separate—they possess the very thing they would drink. This state is not a fleeting one. 

Seeing is not something entirely external; rather, the act of "seeing" is the same as the "thing seen." The seer was once looking from the outside, but now possesses the thing seen within himself. When he experiences this, he no longer looks at it as a physical object or as something seen from without, because he sees it as the very act of seeing itself. He wishes to hold the "Whole," not just as a spectator looking inward, but by transforming into the very image and form of what he contemplates. He recognizes both that vision and himself, becoming one with the light that shines from Him. Only those who have been "seized" by Him can truly be said to exist in this way.

<summary>This page describes the mystical union of the soul with the Divine, explaining that the "vision" of God is not like looking at an object, but rather an internal transformation where the soul becomes the beauty it beholds.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the exploration of the Intelligible realm (the world of pure Thought and Form) and how the human soul can ascend from the "secondary beauties" of the physical world to the primary Beauty of the Good. It expands on the previous page's contrast between the external view of the world and the internal realization of the divine.</meta>

<margin>
How the Good is the beautiful object of the mind, recognized through the secondary beauties of the world.
</margin>

<margin>
That beneath bodies there must be souls, and beneath souls there must be the Mind <note>original: "νοῦν" (nous) — in Neoplatonism, the "Mind" or "Intellect" is the first emanation from the One, containing all perfect Forms.</note>.
</margin>

<margin>
The body is not beautiful in its entirety <note>original: "Corpus non est se toto pulchrum"</note>. It does not possess beauty of its own accord: unless it follows something else or is equally beautiful. But it is not beautiful in only a small way: if it affects the whole: and for that reason, it is like itself: through another thing rather than the body and more beautiful: in which quite often the form in the body is sufficient. Since the whole is not entirely Mind: these things together show that beauty does not arise from a lack of form: but rather something else brings it all together: otherwise, what is made would perish, as they say.
</margin>

This place is the Good. And how might one arrive at it? One would arrive there in the way the argument describes: by having acquired the right disposition from the very beginning. Thus, by harmonizing oneself with the beauty found in bodies, speaking of beautiful things, and partaking in the truth <note>original: "ἀφηνεῖα" — likely a transcription for ἀλήθεια (truth)</note> of the things there, one moves toward beauty itself and beauty alone. By quieting the senses that lead to mere words, and turning toward the ancient Mind that existed before this, one leaves behind all other senses and finds rest. For a light will shine within him, directed toward his own internal beauty. 

And how will this humble you? It will educate you quickly through this process. For the highest beauty in bodies comes from the forms <note>original: "μορφαὶ" (morphai) — the spiritual blueprints that give shape to matter.</note> within them, by which the underlying matter is transformed. As long as these forms call out, the soul will perceive them. 

After all, the argument says, everything that makes a physical body beautiful possesses that beauty from a different, higher beauty. Those higher things are the true forms and the "form-givers" for anyone who creates temporary beauty. It is not that some people are temperate and beautiful while others are foolish and ugly. Rather, by loosening the bonds of the senses, they might be brought to their senses by what lies before them, and turn their Mind toward the heavenly things—or rather, to the things above. 

The one who descends from his own state hopes for this and for a true salvation, justly feeling a need for beauty. He will present himself to the First Principle <note>original: "ἀρχῆς τε πρώτης" — referring to "The One," the source of all existence.</note> as if coming from a single source, as a single being, laughing as he receives the "good-like" gifts <note>original: "ἀγαθοειδῆ" (agathoeidē) — qualities that share the nature of the Good.</note>, because all things belong to that One more than to anything else. While that One remains constant, the soul perhaps thinks within itself; for the argument proclaims the nature of Being both now and hereafter, establishing its certainty along the way. 

To think that there is such a divine nature might perhaps seem ridiculous to some, yet it is present in these things, even if it is not the whole. Some might say a light shines within these things. Rather, we say that which creates in this way is something separate... and it exists in the heights, concerning which we see existing things spoken of as being composed of all things. And from what things did a body arise when it was originally nothing? Each thing leaps forward, claiming to provide the nature of these things—wood and stone—but from these material things, beauty could never be completed without the abundance of the Idea <note>original: "ἰδέας" (ideas) — the perfect archetype or Form that exists in the Mind of the Divine.</note>.

<summary>This page discusses the hierarchy of existence, moving from the physical beauty of bodies to the spiritual beauty of the Soul and the Mind. It argues that physical beauty is merely a reflection of divine "Forms" and that the soul must turn away from the senses to find the light of the "Good" within itself.</summary>
<keywords>The Good, Mind (Nous), Form (Idea), Beauty, Senses, First Principle, Neoplatonism, Soul’s Ascent</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the technical metaphysical argument from the previous section. Having established that the soul must ascend to the Mind (Nous), the text now investigates the internal mechanics of that Mind: specifically, how it contains the "Forms" or "Ideas" within itself rather than looking at the external world for its knowledge. This is a foundational concept in Neoplatonism: the source of all reality is internal and intellectual, not material.</meta>

<margin>
That the primary Mind <note>original: "νοῦς πρῶτος" (nous prōtos) — in this philosophy, the divine Intellect that contains all potential truths.</note> thinks from its own resources; it thinks itself and the object of thought <note>original: "νοητὸν" (noēton)</note>, and the Mind and its object are one and the same.
</margin>

Every world exists within body and matter, yet nothing truly identical comes from this matter; though things may be beautiful, they are not "the thing itself," nor are they truly perceived by the senses alone. Thus, the primary Mind thinks itself and draws from itself during its own contemplation <note>original: "θεωρίᾳ" (theōria) — a state of focused, divine looking or meditation.</note>. This is because it is joined with its own name, not by external power or by some grasping from the outside. We see it as a Mind from within, not something preceding it (for why else would we call it Mind?). If it does not think itself, what then does it think? If it thinks something else, does that come from itself or from another? If it comes from itself, then it thinks itself, sensing its own nature and bringing itself forth into being. These are not things external to it, but are the Mind itself. It dissolves inward, so to speak. While earthly birth produces things separate from the parent, I do not know of any such "otherness" there. Leave aside those evils found among us. Divine nature likely brings forth its own contents, so that those things are good, even if they appear as "others." In this way, they are truly "objects of thought" <note>original: "νοητὰ" (noēta) — the eternal blueprints or "Forms" of all things.</note> and exist through the Mind. They do not come from another, nor do they exist in isolation; they exist from themselves as their own essence, within the thought and within the Mind's own self. Even in sensible things <note>original: "αἰσθητοῖς" (aisthētois) — things we can touch and see.</note>, their essence is contained. What shall I call each thing, if not a sensible manifestation? For the "form" within them is what receives the matter, yet that form is someone else's property; but in the divine realm, the thing "is" and exists in itself.

<margin>
The primary Mind thinks not by looking at the sensible world, but by looking toward itself (because that is where the Ideas exist).
</margin>

If we must conclude that the Mind and these Ideas <note>original: "ἰδέας" (ideas) — the perfect, eternal archetypes of all things in the physical world.</note> are the same, then the Ideas must be with the Mind for it to truly be itself. Thus, they exist before the world. The Mind knows the "kinds" of things, and these are not the property of others, but are the primary principles themselves. They have the power to be self-sufficient. If the things there are eternal and unchanging, they are truly intellectual, existing prior to any habit or physical nature. We might call the totality of these "beings" the "arts," or say that true reality is found there. For the Mind does not look out at them; it is with them. They are like the primary lawgivers—or rather, they are the very "forms" of being itself. If they were to stop, being itself would cease to exist. This is what the memory of the ancients refers to: the identity between the Mind and the "essence of what it is to be" <note>original: "τὶ ἦν εἶναι" (ti ēn einai) — an Aristotelian term for the core essence or definition of a thing.</note>. For example, while we speak of flesh, the true essence is not "flesh and blood" in the physical sense. They are not external to the living beings themselves. The ancients did not fear that these things would change or suffer corruption. There is no blood there, perhaps, or if there is, it is not the blood that rots. If all things consist in the "use" of beings, they would change according to those uses. Sensible things participate in this reality, but they are "other" than it. In the divine realm, there is no body that receives its shape from the outside, like bronze shaped by a craftsman.

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the relationship between the divine Mind (Intellect) and the objects of its thought. Having established that the Mind is not dependent on external perception, the text now explores the priority of "Being" over the act of "Thinking," arguing that the two are ultimately a unified whole within the Intelligible World.</meta>

ς <note>The Greek numeral for 6, indicating page or section six.</note>

<margin>
It is itself.
</margin>

<margin>
What is the Idea?
</margin>

<margin>
**Beings** <note>original: "ὄντα" (onta) — the fundamental realities or things that truly exist.</note> are in the mind before the act of thinking; it is because it thinks that it is beings. But because it is, for this reason it thinks. For Being <note>original: "ὄν" (on) — the state of existence itself.</note> and beings exist before the mind. The Idea, however, exists with the mind. For the Idea exists along with the act of knowing. There are, therefore, two parts to the Idea: Being serves as the matter, and knowing serves as the form. The whole is the Form <note>original: "εἶδος" (eidos) — the blueprint or essential nature of a thing.</note> or that which has been brought into existence.
</margin>

Both might fall short, and both must be avoided: to think that the whole mind is active, yet to think that all things are not outside it. It causes itself and recognizes itself, not grasping for things as if it did not already possess them; thus it stands firm within the Form. It has been treated well and graced. For the soul, these things exist alongside it, even if the soul herself thinks as if they were not within her, or as if they came from a distance—for she is no longer that [pure mind]. But neither is Being a form of motion; for motion is a sequence and a coming-forth. From wherever everything wishes to come, it stands together as if directed toward Being. Motion must be the Form itself. 

Regarding this act of thinking, I believe Being must exist first, so that Being may be the thing which the mind thinks. For if something is not identical to itself, then beings do not truly exist. The mind, being in a state of true actuality <note>original: "ἐνεργείᾳ" (energeia) — the state of being "at work" or fully realized, as opposed to mere potential.</note>, and the beings it thinks are one and the same. And if they are the beings themselves, then they are both Mind and Essence. They are yoked together so that they do not appear as separate from one another. 

Yet these are also parts. Each Form thinks, and though it is not the whole, it represents the divisions. Each is a part of the whole, not as something severed, but in the way that each Form can exist within the whole. This Mind is the totality of them. For them, there is either a quietude, or you see it in the act of thinking, which surrounds the Mind. Being exists in the Mind first, in actuality before the act of thinking. Beings exist because the Mind thinks, or they are the beings themselves. One might think of the Mind beforehand, and the beings are there; or because the beings are in the Mind, they must make the Mind exist in actuality. For it is not like things where the actor performs an action; rather, thinking appears within Being.

Their activity is their very existence, or rather, both are a single Being. More accurately, the two are only one: Being is natural, because it thinks. Therefore, beings and Being are the same thing, as is a Mind of this kind. Those who exist within the Mind are clear, both as the shape of Being and its activity. For just as the Mind would be a kind of living thing, certain things exist before others. For the Mind is different—undivided and not dividing—possessing all things as if they were one in Being, not divided there as they are for us. For the causes flow as if from a source; therefore, from itself, it places us in the realm of the senses to contemplate the things that exist within Being. Each thing is not the whole, though it contains all things, even if one possesses a specific kind of knowledge from it. It is a clear mind that thinks the part; it is necessary that the things present in the Mind should exist. And the Intelligible World <note>original: "κόσμος νοητὸς" (kosmos noētos) — the spiritual or intellectual realm that serves as the blueprint for the physical world.</note> is that upon which the Mind takes its stand.

<margin>
Induction <note>original: "ἐπαγωγή" (epagōgē) — a logical method of moving from specific instances to a general conclusion.</note>
</margin>

<summary>This page argues that in the divine realm, "Being" and "Thinking" are a single, unified reality. The Mind does not look outside itself for truth; instead, it contains all the Forms (the essential blueprints of reality) as its own internal activity and essence.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the relationship between the Divine Mind (Intellect) and the reality it perceives. While the previous page established that Being and Mind are unified, this page explores how the "Forms" or "Ideas" of earthly arts—like architecture, medicine, and even politics—exist in the higher Intelligible World.</meta>

<page-num>31</page-num>

<margin>
**All things:**
That the **Sensible World** <note>original: "αἰσθητὸς Κόσμος" (aisthetos kosmos) — the physical world we perceive with our five senses.</note> belongs to Reason, but the **Intelligible World** <note>original: "νοητὸς" (noetos) — the higher realm of pure thought and perfect Ideas.</note> belongs to the Good.
</margin>

...the creations possess **harmony** <note>original: "ἁρμονίαν" (harmonian)</note>. Or, in the same way, just as in the intelligible realm they possess rhythm, so do all those things that are productive of sensible objects. For instance, the **productive arts** <note>original: "τέχναι" (technai)</note>, such as architecture and carpentry, insofar as they use symmetries, derive their principles from those higher realities and contemplate the truths found there. For there is a harmony in all things within the sensible world. Yet, the things here are not exactly like the things there; for they do not contemplate "agriculture" among those higher beings in a sensible light, nor do they see "medicine" as the health found here, or the art of physical strength. 

There are also arts of great worth, which correspond to what are power and glory in that higher realm. Just as these arts are themselves and are beautiful, so too are the sensible arts of **rhetoric**, **generalship** <note>original: "στρατηγία" (strategia)</note>, **politics**, and **kingship**. In some of these, beauty is hidden within their actions. Those higher realities are contemplated there; a portion of each is held by each person, though not everyone possesses this awareness as their own. 

Regarding diseases: all that is according to wisdom is furthest from the **substantial** <note>original: "οὐσιώδου" (ousiodou) — that which pertains to the true essence or being of a thing.</note> and possesses a limit. There are also things according to the mind that are of a lesser degree, as well as logical and technical arts. Some arts, being what they are, make use of the "universals" found here. Thus, the world is governed, but not in a way that the higher things belong to everyone equally, nor in the same way as other things. From where does each thing arise along with the others? It is as if while a thing *is* something in essence, a specific individual then becomes it. This difference arises even in that higher realm; just as there is a difference in each case among us and within our physical materials. The primary source of activities is the cause of the differences in colors. 

We must consider those higher **substances** <note>original: "οὐσίας" (ousias)</note> as existing through themselves, along with the qualities of their differences. Finally, it was necessary to look again at the sensible things there, and how they are limited by one another. Some things are but an **image** <note>original: "ἀπεικόνισμα" (apeikonisma)</note> of them; our own mind and the Mind itself exist there. It remains to be said that while one might think illness arises there, one must instead realize that the *principles* of all things exist there. 

Let us speak more precisely so that the genus itself is clear: what exists there and the other common differences are also found here. There is an equal strength here in each of them, belonging to each substance, and there exists there a certain **Justice** and **Temperance** <note>original: "σωφροσύνην" (sophrosyne) — the virtue of self-control, moderation, and mental clarity.</note>. In the sciences and in perceptions, these things exist truly and are not merely images. However, we must attribute the "images" of those things to the sensible world when we talk about all the things here. For those higher realities are not confined to any specific place. Just as the physical body is derived from the things there, the higher realm itself contains no vision that can be perceived by the senses.

<summary>This page explains that human arts—such as architecture, medicine, and politics—are grounded in perfect, "intelligible" versions of themselves in the divine realm. Plotinus argues that while physical things are mere images, their essential principles, including virtues like Justice and Temperance, exist truly and harmoniously in the higher world of the Mind.</summary>

They say that quantity consists of the **discrete** <note>original: "διωρισμένον" (diorismenon) — things that can be counted individually, like a group of people.</note> and the **continuous** <note>original: "συνεχές" (syneches) — things that are connected without gaps, like a line or time.</note>. In other cases, when they belong to the **categories** <note>original: "κατηγορίας" (kategorias) — the basic ways we describe existence, such as "quality" or "place."</note> of numbers, they were not "so many lines." Thus the category and the objects of thought are "so much." Therefore, the things belonging to quantity are called quantities in themselves when they are set side-by-side. For example, let there be three lines. Or perhaps only **number** <note>original: "ἀριθμός"</note> is truly called quantity, but it remains in the numbers themselves. For the **Forms** <note>original: "εἴδη" (eide)</note> and the things that are already underlying in themselves are said to participate in the numbers by which we count: **units** <note>original: "μονάδας" (monadas)</note>, one, two, three, four, ten, and so on.

First, this is shown by the fact that if they are thought of, it is not merely that these things are "near," but those who measure the underlying subjects find that quantity exists alongside them. Through other things, like **rulers** <note>original: "κανόνες" (kanones)</note> and measures, they measure the surface by which they are taken with a measure. It is not that quantity is in the underlying subjects as if the subjects themselves lacked it; rather, they measure quantity. Why are these measures themselves called quantities and parts of quantity? Since they also fit other things, these are called quantities; for even the **unit** <note>original: "μονὰς" (monas)</note> itself produces these, as does the body. And number remains. It is measured and exists either in relation to **color** <note>original: "χρῶμα"</note> being measured, or the surface of a mouth. And because they are **qualities** <note>original: "ποιά" (poia)</note>, they are related to each other, like **whiteness**, **heat**, or **beauty**. But others are quantities in themselves. For whether they participate in it is seen in the things themselves or in those that possess them. Thus it is with three juices...

There is another way to speak of a single thing. After this has been stated and encompassed by him, no <unclear>other</unclear> <unclear>this</unclear> [remains]; rather, it will perceive both motions and, in general, the excellences of the things that came before, as well as the emergence of **states** and **dispositions** <note>original: "ἀνέχεως καὶ διαθέσεως" — "hexis" and "diathesis," referring to permanent habits versus temporary arrangements.</note>. Concerning each of these, the same things are spoken of as reciprocal, such as **slave and master** <note>A classic example of a relation: one cannot be a master without a slave, and vice versa.</note>, the equal, the best, the political, the passive, and the measure or share.

I am also able to perceive the senses and the abundance of each thing alongside them in an example; or perhaps, by adding a certain excellence to the relative things, one finds the goal of the **passive state** <note>original: "πάθους" (pathous) — an experience or emotion acted upon the subject.</note> and the pre-sensory compositions of perception—the four—compared to the ancient way, and one might desire the choices within them. On one hand, the "relative" provides direction. We have seen what it is, and that the **world** <note>original: "κόσμον" (kosmon)</note> is a relative thing within its own **actuality** <note>original: "ἐνεργείᾳ" (energeia) — the state of being active or fully realized.</note>, both existing and being ranked as the same in the "acting" part. 

Yet there are also similar things, both for the world and for the things themselves. For the "same" is a relative thing, in terms of its existence and its relation to opinion. Others rule by measure, comparing the phantoms of the things that exist, and saying that the "common" is the greatest thing and the same quality. And this [relation] has been made for this purpose. It subordinates this, and is established as a **position** <note>original: "στάσις" (stasis)</note>, sitting nearby and forming an ordered arrangement or a "settling" disposition, as it is called. Others signify things according to **accident** <note>original: "συμβεβηκὸς" (symbebekos) — a non-essential property.</note>, or things that act and have a disposition in the same way. Therefore, all the things set before us happen to all, and the comparison of those who are failing is not later; one part participates in the **continuous** <note>original: "συνεχές" (syneches)</note>, while the other, being "so much," involves a release, and the other is different. Even the things placed in comparison within them—the "worthy" in relation to the "virtuous"—and the things before it, and in the stays and the orthodox cautions; the whole power is the One and the representation they have found. For he said that within them, the **prior and the posterior** <note>original: "πρότερον καὶ ὕστερον" (proteron kai hysteron) — a logical or chronological sequence.</note> occur according to time, the prior and posterior happening together with the relation itself; for these things happen to those who exist and those who act, or as my own [properties] compared to others.

<meta>The previous page introduced the category of Quality, specifically discussing shapes, external forms, and the inherent "power" (dynamis) of an individual, such as the skill of a boxer.
