Quality and **form** <note>original: "μορφὴ" (morphē) — the outward shape or appearance of an object.</note> are a kind of universal existence; they are not only the universal itself, but also the <gloss>the</gloss> <insert>under</insert> underlying **species** <note>original: "εἶδος" (eidos) — the specific "type" or "form" that gives a thing its identity.</note> and its "stamp" or "seal." Rationally speaking, all these things are a whole.

And regarding smoothness, rarity, and density: the ancient thinkers <note>likely referring to the Pre-Socratics or early Atomists</note> did not speak correctly regarding these. In these cases, they treated dimensions as being the same as <gloss>but the</gloss> the "more and the less," or the "greater and the smaller," as well as inwardness and thickness. Generally, this applies to the tensions of unevenness and smoothness in each thing, which are either a **power** <term>power <note>original: "δύναμιν" (dynamis) — the capacity to act or be acted upon.</note></term> or an **activity** <term>activity <note>original: "ἐνέργειαν" (energeia) — the actual functioning or manifestation of a power.</note></term>. 

Furthermore, "light" and "heavy" are well-aimed terms for these, and <gloss>but</gloss> they are comprehensive names. For just as we use "more" and "less" in weights, we also speak of the "strong" and the <unclear>weak</unclear> <note>original: "ἀσθενῆ"</note> among those who miss the mark. But that specific aspect of the claim—the "of what sort" <note>original: "τὸ ποῖον" (to poion) — the fundamental question of quality.</note>—is what we must <unclear>distinguish</unclear>. 

Some qualities are not called "affections" <note>original: "παθήματα" (pathēmata) — things that happen to a person or body, often translated as 'passions' or 'sufferings.'</note>; some are said to belong to the body, others to the **soul**. Many factors divide the senses: we speak of some regarding hearing and smell, but also of scent and the sensations of **touch**. These senses belong to the "spirited" <note>original: "θυμοειδοῦς" (thymoeidous) — the part of the soul associated with anger, courage, and emotion.</note> and the "rational" <note>original: "λογιστικοῦ" (logistikou)</note> parts of the soul. There are seven differences or categories that arise according to these parts. These are the generative forces of nature that produce both beneficial and harmful things, leading to **friendships** and **factions** <note>original: "στάσεις" (staseis) — civil strife or discord.</note>. 

These distinctions are made by the judgments of the body regarding what is useful or harmful. For these differences are made relative to the self. Thus, one thing leads to friendship and pleasantness, while another leads to hatred and pain. This order establishes our relationship to other things. 

The "qualified person" <note>original: "ὁ ποῖος"</note> is not defined simply by participating in a quality; for it is not a private matter. Since there is a power within touch itself, how could it not involve both "acting" <term>acting <note>original: "ποιεῖν" (poiein) — to do or produce an effect.</note></term> and "being acted upon" <term>being acted upon <note>original: "πάσχειν" (paschein) — to receive an effect or undergo a change.</note></term>? This sort of quality is such that "to act" and "to be acted upon" are not separate. There are certain affective qualities and <unclear>bodies</unclear> that are <unclear>better</unclear> at being "active" according to their power. Some things are described as "acting" insofar as they possess this power. Such a natural disposition would never fail to differ. 

In terms of their underlying **substance** <note>original: "ὑπόστασιν" (hypostasin)</note>, "acting" and "being acted upon" are generally concerned with grasping what kind of thing it is. In the parts of a thing, "acting" and "being acted upon" might be the same cause, but they are spoken of differently. Action <note>original: "πρᾶξις" (praxis)</note> disposes things, for they are not yet questions or "habits" <note>original: "ἑκτικαὶ" (hektikai) — stable dispositions or states of being.</note> of the things themselves. While other things are "kinetic" <note>moving or causing change</note>, through which a person considers a thing in relation to another or in relation to changing matters, we must consider how the soul is disposed toward itself. We must ask: "of what sort" <note>what quality</note> is it?

<margin>That "being acted upon" is twofold.</margin>
<margin>Being acted upon is twofold.</margin>

We speak of "being acted upon" <note>original: "πάσχειν" (paschein) — This term refers to the category of "Passion" or "Suffering," meaning to receive an action from something else.</note> more truly and properly when it concerns wretched things, specifically when a thing departs from its natural state. In such a case, we do not say the thing is simply "moving," but that it is "being acted upon." For that which contains does not belong to the thing being acted upon; nor are the powers such that the movement through them is a disordered **accident** <note>original: "συμβεβηκός" (symbebekos) — a property that is not essential to a thing’s nature, like a person happens to be sitting.</note>. In this way, bodies like bronze might cast off their hardness to become **soft**. However, being moved does not prevent shape or the giving of form, nor is that truly "being acted upon." Therefore, becoming worse is what is properly called "being acted upon." For it becomes a "suffering" when the thing itself becomes worse, and the **alteration** <note>original: "ἀλλοίωσιν" (alloiosin) — a change in quality rather than quantity or location.</note> is toward the worse. In both cases, "reacting" <note>original: "ἀντιπάσχειν" (antipaschein) — being acted upon in return.</note> is also mentioned, just as one might decline movement or alteration.

Regarding changes that occur all at once from the thing itself: nevertheless, it is not the thing that has been changed; yet movements exist. There are differences, and flowing things, and ideas, and "being acted upon." However, insofar as a thing is good, it is <unclear>deprived</unclear>. "Being acted upon" does not consist in movement caused by another, or of another, but in the essence of the thing being acted upon, nor in its being "active" <note>original: "πρακτικόν" (praktikon).</note>. As each thing alters the thing being acted upon, the act of "doing" is defined by the **essence** <note>original: "οὐσίᾳ" (ousia).</note> 
<margin>† folio 122</margin>
of such a kind. Perhaps the same applies to "acting." Just as with "being acted upon," it is understood by being observed. Everything is both a movement and a comparison to being acted upon. This is the truth: that movement is always established from something toward something, which constitutes "acting." "Being acted upon" stands in this same relation to all other things. For "being acted upon" itself, when both are observed, is not considered in itself, but as the **subject** <note>original: "ὑποκείμενον" (hypokeimenon) — the underlying material or person that experiences a change.</note> is, so too is the thing being acted upon.
These are the things that move; and there is a certain subject; and the **predication** <note>original: "κατηγορεῖσθαι" (kategoreisthai) — how we describe or categorize a subject.</note> is different; and thus it is deceptive.

But regarding that which moved the thing, it is understood as "completing"; both through what, by what, and toward what. Generally, regarding what color might be, that too is thought of as a movement; and it is itself movement. It is either the movement itself or it is within the thing being acted upon. So, while it is indeed in the thing being acted upon, it is also in the thing "acting," as if in 
<margin>Note these things</margin>
an abundance of what is present. One acts, or perhaps happens upon something by means of similar things. But "being acted upon" comes from and concerns other things. For some things arise from being "the other," which belongs to the category of "the other." Others arise from "being acted upon," and the act of "acting" itself acts. For "acting" is not itself a part, but stems from its **actuality** <note>original: "ἐνεργείας" (energeias).</note>. Nor is it entirely its own; nor indeed does every movement "act" more, or "act" at all. By **accident**, however, it is a movement: one was weary 
from **walking**; one **produced footprints**. To act in a slippery or tenuous way is to be moved; but it is for the sake of the thing being itself. To act is by accident. And the actuality is by accident, whenever it concerns this thing being itself; and for the rest, we also say "to act," such as to say one is **boasting**.

If **substrates** <note>original: "ὑποκείμενα" (hypokeimena) — literally "that which lies under." By doing so, they leave no room for **differences** <note>original: "διαφοράς" (diaphoras) — the specific characteristics that distinguish one species from another within a genus.</note>. 

How then can these things endure, and how can there be something common to both? For by ranking the "substrates" as primary, and placing **matter** <note>original: "ὕλη" (hyle) — the raw material of the universe.</note> here, they designate these as the first principles. If "being" is to encompass both the prior and the posterior, it must be because "being" is found in things under the same **genus** <note>original: "γένος" (genos) — a broad class or category.</note>. In such a case, each thing must necessarily partake of that genus. If a genus is to be that which is predicated of other things, as they themselves say, then the "being" of other things resides in **matter**. ### Later, it seems we must also consider **coming-to-be**, **acting**, and the **movement of the cosmos**.

<margin>
How beings and ideas exist in the **Intelligible realm**—how there are **genera** and **atoms** <note>original: "ἄτομα" (atoma) — in this context, Plotinus refers not to physical particles, but to "indivisible species," the most specific level of a category that cannot be divided any further.</note>.

Now that we have established these points, we say: if there are certain numbers and **genera** <note>original: "γένη" (genē) — the primary classes or categories of existence, such as Being, Motion, and Rest.</note> of beings, how do we perceive the **principles** <note>original: "ἀρχὰς" (archas) — the starting points or fundamental origins of reality.</note> of these beings? We speak of all things, including those that act upon them. For many things possess a share of "being," insofar as they exist within things that are not. Therefore, if they were to exist by way of "coming-to-be" [becoming], and if these very things—through which many such things exist—are **genera** [categories] under a single unity, then all things that "become" are included. For these genera are nothing other than the things themselves, containing both the genera beneath them and the things themselves. But it is not possible for these to be principles and for all things, including nature, to be completed under them. All things are **intelligibles** <note>original: "νοητὰ" (noēta) — things belonging to the higher realm of pure thought, rather than the physical world of the senses.</note> and belong to that realm; they are not merely within the "genera" of beings. There must be a **constitution** <note>original: "σύστασιν" (systasin) — the underlying structure or composition of a thing.</note> of this, for it would mean that these are both the principles and the impulses of "being" existing together. It is not possible, then, for these to be anything other than what belongs to each thing, along with the things that accompany them and the "atoms" [indivisibles]. But how could there be an existence consisting of many things, or an existence arising out of many? Whether for all things or for each individual thing, and for the things that are composed, what sort of thing would they produce? The words suggest that these things are indeed the principles of what might come to be. For it is not possible for the things that move and the things that act to be anything other than these, and such things are the principles. That which begins would come to be as a **genus**.

Therefore, those things might also be said to be both the same things and the principles. But how is it that each thing is the same as the things accompanying them, while being together with one another? For we complete the whole in this way. And we create a **mixture** <note>original: "σύγκρασιν" (synkrasin) — a blending or tempering together of different elements.</note> from them; yet each will belong to each, and each one will not be "pure" in itself. Instead, they will be "atoms" [indivisibles] again, appearing as individual things mixed within themselves. Those things, too, exist by themselves and as wholes, and the things that are mixed would also come to be. And how can they exist from as much as they say? For we have conceded both their coming-to-be and their "turnings," and as many as the principles are. For principles also arise from other things and for things that must be composed. We must speak regarding the "atoms" [indivisible species] and the **genera**, and how they are divided from one another, and how things would come to be—for instance, in relation to the things that result from the parts and the purpose for which they are made.

And yet, it is far more strange if all things are established within these. There is a release for these atoms. And nothing is created from the outside in an unequal way, just as the position or the removal of these same things would be. For it is because of the other things; yet there will not be many things under a single unity at all, but rather alongside the parts—if they exist, and they are not "outside"—being from the genus of the "One." For how else could it be, unless they are removed, so that nothing flows away? Similarly, regarding the other things, for it would not be...

<meta>This page continues the exploration of the Intelligible realm, specifically investigating how the Intellect and Soul relate to the physical world. It shifts focus toward the problem of "the One and the Many"—how a single, indivisible principle like the Soul or Intellect can be present in a multitude of physical bodies without being divided itself.</meta>

<margin>
Every body
~~Many~~
Many in one
Soul in many
Intellect in many
</margin>

And we know what is spoken of by thought alone, as one might say; for we do not seek the nature of bodies for its own sake—such as that which exists in true **Being** or in the nature of the **All**—nor do we seek to understand the **Intellect** <note>original: "νοῦν" (noun) — the divine Mind or second hypostasis in Neoplatonic thought, containing the perfect Forms.</note> and its very **principle** <note>original: "ἀρχήν" (archēn) — the fundamental starting point or origin.</note> merely as a part of something else. We should not view it as if the specific nature of its **non-extended** <note>original: "ἀδιαστάτου" (adiastatou) — lacking physical dimensions or spatial extension; a purely spiritual quality.</note> essence were just a matter of size. For the nature of a body is, in a sense, material. And in every other body that exists, it is entirely unlike the nature of these higher bodies. 

The **Whole** is all things together, while each of the parts is its own specific thing. And the world is not simply a result of an "illumination" from it; rather, its entire state is innate. We might speak of the movements of bodies and how they do not flow into it. Indeed, the body seems to be contained within it; and in its nature, the remaining **intelligibles** <note>original: "νοητά" (noēta) — things belonging to the realm of thought rather than the senses.</note> exist with it in a state of abundance. For others, it is necessary to hold these principles as **indivisible** <note>original: "ἀμερινούς" (amerinous) — not capable of being partitioned into parts.</note>, having stripped away the movements found in bodies. By setting aside sensory perception, one will come to understand those things that follow.

For it is in this way that we understand the **Soul** <note>original: "ψυχήν" (psuchēn)</note>, the **Intellect**, and those other things which we say constitute the **hypostasis** <note>original: "ὑπόστασιν" (hypostasin) — a fundamental reality or underlying substance.</note> of all things. And truly, the "wonder" is even more present within us: that we are both many and one. This happens because people have conceded to the great multitude of bodies. It is necessary to lead this same concept back toward clarity; the written word exists for this purpose. If we pull ourselves away and separate ourselves from the body, we may simultaneously become entirely **non-extended** <note>original: "ἀδίαστατον" (adiastaton)</note>, in such a way that we first receive the likeness of that same essence. 

Then, every part becomes the whole again, and the whole returns to itself, ending in this realization. For the soul rules the body as a living thing, yet the body is **intricate and composite** <note>original: "πολύπλεκτον καί σύνθετον" (polyplekton kai syntheton) — made of many parts woven together, unlike the simple unity of the soul.</note>. The variety of souls is such that one must approach the principles with haste to find a simpler state. Therefore, it is as if the soul <unclear>no longer</unclear> spoke through oracles among the gods. 

The body is taken from the realm of the sensible, but the Intellect is taken as something else—for it is "many." And how are the many also one? It is not a composite made of many parts, but rather a **single nature**; yet it possesses many distinct qualities. For we are caught by this and call it a "part." We say that the truth of beings found within us is **unifying**. We must consider this <insert>primarily</insert>: just as in the bodies of animals and plants, each of them is "many" in terms of colors, shapes, sizes, and extensions—with different parts in different places—yet they all proceed from a single state of being. For if every point were the whole, or rather a part of the whole, or even its own self, then the soul would be all the more...

<vocab>soul, intellect, body, reality/substance, intelligibles, multitude, nature</vocab>

<summary>This page explores how the indivisible Intellect and Soul can be present in the "many" parts of the physical world without losing their unity. It argues that while bodies are complex composites, the higher principles are simple and non-extended, acting as the unifying source for the diversity seen in living things.</summary>

<margin>
**The five kinds of beings.**
**Essence** <note>original: "οὐσία" (ousia) — substance or true being.</note> · **Motion** · **Rest**
**Difference** · **Sameness**

How each might be divided

<margin>
This is the passage where he discusses these things, proceeding first regarding essence and <unclear>substance</unclear> <unclear>...</unclear> <note>original: "locus hic q̄ de his d. pmo de essentia z substa..." — Latin marginalia identifying the thematic focus on substance.</note>

...recapitulations and the **Intellect** <note>original: "νοῦν" (noun) — the divine Mind.</note> and those things of which the common element is a certain kind of knowledge. Thoughts are essences, and they say this is especially true of those things that are primarily living. For we shall become such, since our mind knows the **Forms** <note>original: "εἴδη" (eidē) — the perfect, eternal archetypes of all things.</note> by separating the things within us. Indeed, it would not be able to separate them otherwise. Look clearly at how there is more **motion** in other things, yet not when they are separated—even if they do not exist in some other way. Rather, they say the Forms are like a "shadow" and are named homonymously <note>original: "ὁμωνύμως" (homonymōs) — sharing a name but having different definitions, like a "real" man and a "painting" of a man.</note>. Just as in the "spear" of the mind there are certain things—and truly not only living things—so too in the world of the senses, **Being** is a shadow from which one might participate in existence most fully. This is because that which comes from "the other" is also "otherwise," belonging to that higher source. Both the things that are separated from themselves and the things existing within them—such as "the straight" and these shapes—these are not, in a sense, the Forms themselves. Nor are they the things that are not causes <margin>under</margin> and the things of non-being. 

But it was found in the thing itself, not as if in a substrate; it is constituted with it. And again, his **thought** <note>original: "διάνοια" (dianoia) — discursive reasoning or the process of thinking.</note> is not different from his very essence. And again, **intellection** <note>original: "νόησις" (noēsis) — the act of the mind perceiving truth.</note> is not different; for it is not likely they are the same, nor is life. We shall separate the Forms in these things, and they say those things that do not involve motions, and again those that are the motions of the heavens—each of these can exist without the other. Nevertheless, the thought, having been distinguished, can also pass through such things as motion in the objects of thought. 

Bodies are not among these things, but are taken as the "extremes" within them. Thus, such things belong to nature and are truly an **essence of essence**. They say it holds in these same things, but some do and some do not; and by bringing them together and separating them as if from a different relationship, they address both the thoughts and the intellections. 

How then do the **Five Kinds** <note>The "Five Great Kinds" or *megista genē* from Plato’s *Sophist*: Being, Motion, Rest, Sameness, and Difference.</note> share in one another? For that which is according to these things and in the same way, and which possesses a single definition for each of the Forms—whether one gives it a different name and relationship—clearly exists in the Forms themselves. They say it is not as if one thing fights against many Forms. And because if it were the same as **Being**, **Motion** would not be called "motion" but "being." For motion is one of the things that are the same as being, yet it would have been left behind. But the motion of those very things which exist is life; it is both in the things that are and in the things of essence, and of simply **Being** itself. They are separated from the motions in them, being both "the same" and "not the same" in the same way. And if this were removed by the mind, it would be removed from that other in the same way. And how, they ask, is there a separation of it? And again, a separation to such an extent, having separated it by the mind, insofar as it is foreign—according to which they clash. Let it be as something that appears there; how could it relate to the **Idea** if not even a single thing were present?

<meta>This page continues the technical ontological investigation from page 230, shifting from the "Five Great Kinds" of the Platonic tradition to a critique of "the One" and "Being" as universal categories (genera). <margin>
And another good is this and that.
</margin>
<margin>
It is not so properly said of essence <note>original: "essencia"</note> that it itself is primarily some being <note>original: "ens"</note>.
</margin>
Furthermore, if the genus <note>A "genus" is a broad category or family of things, like "animal."</note> is nothing apart from its species <note>A "species" is a specific type within a genus, like "human."</note>, it would follow that it belongs immediately to those things within the species. For "the One" and "Being," if they are not themselves genera, then they would not even be part of the species, nor of essences <note>original: "οὐσιῶν" (ousiōn) — the core substances or "whatness" of things.</note> at all. Generally speaking, such terms are said of all things that exist. But things that do not possess "Being" could not even be said "not to possess" it, if they are spoken of in this way. Nor could their opposites exist, nor could anything exist prior to "Being." Rather, because these are the primary attributes for all things, he would confirm that they apply to those things just as they do to others—that the same things apply to all.

<margin>
That "the One" is a genus of some things.
</margin>
In this case, how could anyone trust that things are "the same" in this way? Furthermore, if "the One" and "Being" are a genus, then to know "the One" is also to know all other things; for all other things are also "one." For by their differences <note>original: "διαφοραῖς" (diaphorais) — the specific traits that distinguish one species from another within the same genus.</note>, each thing is one. Firstly, the species belong only to species, but these [the One and Being] also belong to the genus. If it seems necessary for something to be added to some of the species—for example, whatever it might be where the differences are the same—then all things in the genus are species of that genus. But if "the One" and "Being" are divided by differences again, so that they become "the One" itself, then the species of "the One" would themselves be many.

<margin>
Another <note>original Latin: "alius"</note>
</margin>
The same reasoning would apply to "Being," so that "Being" would be just like "the One" and the species; just as there is an essence of being. For the genera and the differences would not exist if they were not among the things from which each thing arises. If the difference is not "one," then "the One" is not like those things added to a unit <note>original: "μονάδι" (monadi) — a mathematical or metaphysical "one."</note>; for "the One" is that which does not disappear. But if some of the perceptible things <note>Things we can see and touch.</note> are among the species of "the One," then they must also be among the exceptional things.

<margin>
That which is being <note>original Latin: "id quod ens"</note>
</margin>
Furthermore, after this, there would also be "the One." For some people, in speaking of "the One" itself and "Being" itself, say that these are not a "difference" but are a genus—the genus itself. They say this is common to all things.

<margin>
That which is one <note>original Latin: "id quod unū"</note>

But while one thing might be "primary" in this way, and another thing might be "Being" and "the One" in another way, they would not speak of "the One" as a genus of itself, but rather that other things are genera prior to "the One." For the number of "Being" is contained within the species, as one might name them.

<margin>

Because of this, it is necessary for those things to be the things of which these are said. For both "Being" and the things in the genera and in the species are "one." Therefore, "Being" itself and the genus would not be the primary things. By now, the primary thing itself, as a genus, is that which is separated; this he treats as a "difference," using it through "Being" as if for the sake of the "Beautiful" which we might posit of it, or even that which is subsequent to...

<meta>This page continues the investigation into "the One" and "Being." <margin>
How the One is shared in different ways by all existing things.
</margin>
It is not shared by any of them at all in a simple way; for it is not like the number "one" is to other numbers, nor as a point is to lines. It is not divided by number nor by eternity <note>original: "aiōn" — refers to timeless existence</note>. And yet, it is said to be "somewhere"; for it must use its own specific movements, both those that fall short and those that exceed. Consider the qualities and the differences: it is understood that even these, when falling short, are unable to receive it. And these qualities themselves belong to "Being." And they were called by a name; and his name is sufficient; <unclear>and upon</unclear> his name.

Why then is the One not these things? And how is the Word <note>original: "logos" — can mean reason, proportion, or the divine Word</note> not a part of it? And how does the Good <note>original: "agathon"</note> come to each thing in an opposite way? For it does not stand in all things as if it were in a single, identical state. Therefore, we speak correctly and according to the laws of reason when we say that those self-moving things <note>original: "autokineta" — things that have the principle of motion within themselves</note> exist as if from themselves. It is the same: for those things in sequence are not the same as the things that depend directly upon it. Some things are not even "the whole," nor are they a composition of these parts. Similarly, the body will not be granted the same status as its own concise and harmonious parts, which are so ready to speak in accord with the harmonies proceeding from the source. Some things are more or less "more beautiful." Why is this? Why is this "one" known more than that "one"? Even when we speak of things that sink downward by their weight, we are collecting them into a group. And as it is held in this way according to its form <note>original: "eidos"</note> and its natural character, these are not the causes by which it stands. Everything reaches its ultimate limit. But the choirs that follow behind <note>The author uses "choirs" as a metaphor for the ranks of angels or levels of reality following God</note> follow after; for example, the—

How all things in the state of becoming are said to be in a state of desire for the Good within each thing.

—light-rays. It is preserved to the extent that it saves itself. For where each thing does not hold together but is destroyed, it falls away from the Good. Because of this, some things are carried toward it as best they can.

<margin>
That each thing is something suitable beyond just "being," or not just one thing beyond "being"; for to be, insofar as it is simply in itself, is something to be yearned for.
</margin>

And some things are external; for this is how sensory things <note>Things perceived by the five senses</note> are, and how those things are which, being of whatever sort they are, would not possess the highest practical power, though they may seem impressive to nature. This is also how it is in the arts: it deprives each thing of this as much as it can, and in the way it can there. And so also with "what is necessary" <note>original: "to deon" — duty or that which is right</note>, for this especially happens. But the most upright things are the others...

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the nature of "Being" and its structure. While the previous page discussed how the "One" and the "Good" participate in reality without being diminished, this page moves into a technical classification of the "Genera" (the fundamental kinds) of Being. Specifically, it examines how "Number" and "Quantity" relate to "Essence," and how "Quality" can be either an essential part of a thing or merely an external attribute.</meta>

<margin>
of itself <note>original: "autou"</note>
</margin>

<margin>
Number and composition: how they relate to the kinds of beings. <note>original: "arithmos kai systasis pōs echon pros genei ontōn"</note>
</margin>

If, alongside number, a thing possesses its own color or depth, the <term>quantity (poson)<note>The category of "how much" or "how many."</note></term> is twofold; it is not merely the quantity itself. And just as with other things that come later, those elements from which a <term>genus (genos)<note>A primary class or "family" of things in philosophy.</term> is formed are not themselves the quantity. At any rate, the "whole" which is made of many parts—and the genus within this—would be posterior to the genus found in the primary things; it would not be the primary itself, since the primary exists there as well. If, therefore, the "whole" is not among the primary things, then it is neither the quantity nor the nature. Indeed, while the <term>essence (ousia)<note>The fundamental "what-it-is" of a thing; its core being.</note></term> is less than these [parts] individually, the "system" is the quantity, while that which is composed of both is a **world** or a **world-order**. Thus, number is primary, while magnitude is posterior; yet in relation to the whole, it is all number. But if it consists of the unmoved and of <term>rest (stasis)<note>One of the "Great Kinds" in Platonic thought, representing stability.</note></term>, then magnitude and motion also consist of <term>motion (kinēsis)<note>The opposite of rest; the principle of change or activity.</note></term>. Some things arise from motion proceeding from the infinite, while others arise from rest; those things that proceed, in turn, complete the essential realities, while those arising from the rest of number and magnitude are posterior. One might also observe this in another way: the light of number exists among the primary genera, whereas magnitude appears later in "composition" and "division," from which magnitude the world is formed. But these things will become clearer later.

<margin>
Every quality relates to the kinds of beings.
->composition<-
</margin>

**I**f it is necessary to assign this definition to the primary things—namely, that the things within them exist according to essence—it is not because essence follows these things, but because the primary essence is composed of them. This is especially true of their essences. Unless the "being" is filled up through these, one would not claim that they are the same as the things that complete the nature of bodies. And yet, there are many things in which numbers are present (and they are there themselves), but in those cases, they would be qualities and <term>categories (kategorias)<note>The basic ways in which we can describe any object (e.g., its size, its color, its location).</note></term>. If, on the other hand, the things observed in each of the primary beings have division, the "whole" must also be made a composite. But just as in that case we did not blame "rest" for completing the essence, nor did we blame the "motion" of the body being formed for the fact that a certain essence is completed, so too some would not feel this way about qualities. Rather, essence is placed within these; they exist within the whole. Furthermore, those qualities that complete the essence are called "qualities" <term>homonymously<note>Greek: "homōnymōs" — when two things share the same name but have different definitions, like a "bank" for money and a "bank" of a river.</note></term>. Those things that exist after the essence are "qualified" things; some are activities of the essence, while others—the things that come after these—are called "affections" <note>original: "pathē" — things that happen to an object or passive properties.</note>. Nevertheless, these also seem to complete some sort of essence. For the addition of a <term>difference (diaphoran)<note>A specific characteristic that distinguishes one species from another within a genus.</note></term> to a being in the same state does not create a new essence, but is rather an essence viewed in another way; just as one might say later regarding the "rational" <note>The author is likely referring to the "rational" as the "specific difference" that makes a human distinct from other animals.</note>.

<summary>This page analyzes how abstract concepts like number, rest, and motion combine to form the "essence" of things. It distinguishes between "essential qualities" that make a thing what it is and "accidental qualities" (affections) that merely happen to a thing.</summary>

<keywords>essence, quantity, quality, motion, rest, world-order, category, primary genera, composition, specific difference</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the technical investigation into the hierarchy of reality. While the previous page categorized the "Genera" of being—specifically how Number and Quantity relate to Essence—this page shifts focus toward the relationship between the "Good," the "Beautiful," and the "Intellect." It examines how these primary principles manifest within the realm of "Being."</meta>

<margin>First</margin>
There is also this common point: the **Good** will be "common" in the same way as the first principle; not simply by <unclear>being</unclear>, but as something we attribute to all other things. However, existence seems to be a common trait for the **Beautiful** in relation to those things, and it is a <term>genus (genos)<note>A primary category or "kind" of reality.</note></term> of the things that follow within true Being. It also seems to define the <term>essences (ousiai)<note>The fundamental "what-it-is" of a thing.</note></term> of each thing—not just in the primary realm, but also in the things found here, such as in character and in actions.

<margin>Posterior</margin>
For indeed, these actions are parts, though not of all things; rather, the "common" exists in both a primary and a secondary sense.

<margin>
What the Good is among beings
</margin>
Furthermore, in comparing the "Other," you must set aside mere existence so that the **One** remains. All things come from that source, but each thing is "good" in a way that always accords with its own nature. Each thing desires to be placed in relation to the One, for the essences themselves are posterior to it. Things are "good" because of themselves. This principle rejects the idea of what kind of "offspring of the beautiful" <note>original: "tokon kalōn"; likely an allusion to Plato's *Republic* regarding the "offspring of the Good."</note> essence could be; rather, things are good in and of themselves, being good as their own entities and not merely "beautiful." They have not exchanged their nature for something foreign, but they possess their own nature and maintain a state of permanence. And indeed, if the many <term>Ideas (ideai)<note>The eternal, perfect archetypes of all things.</note></term> constitute the Good, then the Good within Being is like the permanence of the Ideas within the <term>Intellect (nous)<note>The divine Mind or realm of true knowledge.</note></term> itself. It creates the "according to nature" state of that Being, so that it may render back from that source. There, this Good will strive toward the ultimate Good; and this striving is its life, and this is its Intellect.

Both life and intellect are among those things <margin>Note</margin> <insert>concerning the Beautiful,</insert> if indeed the Beautiful is something unknown.

<margin>The Beautiful: that which is beyond the intellect.</margin>
The Beautiful would be the same as the Good if one were to know them together with the fact that the Good is there. And this Idea would suggest that while they are the same, the **Beautiful** is posterior to the **Good**. Furthermore, the Beautiful exists within Essence itself—an essence that clearly holds us, the observers, and creates a <term>state of feeling (pathos)<note>An experience, emotion, or internal affection triggered by an external object.</note></term> through that which dwells within it. What kind of activity is within it? Each thing there is an activity, a motion. Or one might say, as we have said regarding... likewise, they are in activity with one another. Consequently, they themselves are a kind of "form" in activity. They possess their <term>reality (hypostasis)<note>Substantial existence or "standing under."</note></term> from that source from the beginning, such that the thinking subject no longer comes after the Beautiful, but contemplates them together if the Ideas are to exist. That which is in activity is "all eyes." And all these things are beautiful.

<margin>
What will exist in the primary Intellect
</margin>
These things, being capable of being taken as a certain genus, have within them the "elements" of justice, temperance, and the whole of **Virtue**. The Intellect recognizes certain things from all the Ideas that have appeared, both surpassing them and gathering together all that has arrived from that place. It purifies each thing there, just as you might see the source from which all things strive—all things, even now, having come from that place which is outside the Beautiful.

<summary>This page explores the metaphysical relationship between the Good, the Beautiful, and Being, arguing that while they are related, the Good remains the primary source while the Beautiful and Intellect are posterior to it. It describes the "Ideas" (like Virtue and Justice) as active, living forces within the Divine Mind.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the exploration of how the primary principles—the Good and the One—interact with the realm of Being. While the previous page established that all things derive their "goodness" from their relation to the One, this section investigates the "Intellect" (the Divine Mind) and how it can contain the immense variety of the world while remaining a single, unified entity.</meta>

<margin>
How the Intellect is both "one" and "many."
How individual traits exist for all things on earth.
</margin>

Just as that [Intellect] is one, and within that one all things that appear are present by its <term>power (dynamis)<note>original: "dynamei"; in this context, it refers to the inherent capacity or potentiality of the Divine Mind to bring forth reality.</note></term>. It is not that all things are simply lumped together; rather, each thing must remain distinct within it through its own individual powers. Yet, the whole exists as a single potential. To what extent this reaches is not yet fully stated. If it were not understood as a whole, even if that source were "one," it would effectively be nothing in terms of its power. Instead, it divides the <term>forms (morphas)<note>The ideal blueprints or shapes of all things.</note></term> of its own distinct qualities. We should not say that the Intellect is those things; <unclear>but rather</unclear> that they are its own beings. Or perhaps it is not that the Intellect is the primary thing, but it is the "activity" (<term>energeia</term>) of things that are not merely individuals. 

Instead, they are like "eyes." Within the Intellect, there are the activities that proceed from it, or perhaps the parts within the whole are the activities themselves. Or does this apply to all things? How do the parts of each thing exist within the whole, coming from those four <note>Likely referring to the "Four Genera" or primary categories often discussed in Neoplatonism: Being, Motion, Rest, Sameness, and Difference.</note>, in such a way that they are both universal and indivisible? They have not merely come together by chance, but are ordered from one another in this specific way. They are not merely "parts" in the traditional sense. Or, if that is the case, how can "all be in all"? Or again, do those individual powers exist in these heavens and in the things here? 

And these are wonderful powers, each corresponding to one another: parts of itself, like <term>seals (sphragidas)<note>An image used to describe how an ideal form "stamps" its likeness onto matter.</note></term> and sensory powers. It is like a **chorus leader** singing the different parts, the stars, and the components of the whole. Such are the things within the universe, and the universe itself is of the nature of <term>Essence (ousia)<note>True, fundamental reality.</note></term>. Because all things are within it as a "cause," and they are in the light as if in an eye—when you look, you see the creative power. <gloss>And following these things, there is no sense-perception</gloss>, nor indeed are these things merely "appearances." Much of this nature is not <unclear>precise</unclear> or exact when viewed as two or three separate things. There is a third way of being, which relates to the whole, to the gathered collection, and to the **Divine**. It concerns the nature of the "body" of the world and whether you see the traits of the "Other" in all things. 

It involves the act of dividing, and equality, and the differences of shapes, and these various qualities and the nature of place which preserves them, an equality found in education <note>or "disciplined arrangement."</note>. Or perhaps there are "othernesses" between both in the whole. I see other <term>Forms (eide)<note>The eternal, unchanging templates of things.</note></term>, such as the circle and squares, and the succession of shapes with numbers both similar and dissimilar; and roughly speaking, number itself. These things do not possess a life that is external to themselves, nor a part that is incomplete, nor are they found among things that have been left behind. Rather, such powers were all within the One, as if the One possessed them within its own indivisible nature and thought, so that they might come to be. It is understood that this power is not shut up inside itself; rather, in the "sickness" <note>This may be a transcription error in the original Greek for "taxei" (order) or "panti" (the whole).</note> of the whole, there are rational principles (<term>logoi</term>) which are equally distributed. The <term>Reason-Principle (logos)<note>The formative power that translates the silent thoughts of the Intellect into the organized structure of the physical world.</note></term> follows the end. All things are present as if "in the root"; and the activities of these things concern each individual part.

It uses the metaphor of a chorus leader and a root to explain how variety and order emerge from a single divine cause.</summary>

For even if the underlying subject is fragmented into small pieces, perhaps there are principles within them. For in this way—just as with those <term>forms (eides)<note>The "Forms" are the eternal, perfect patterns of things in the Divine Mind.</note></term> in matter which are divisible—the underlying forms are observed, or rather, among the celestial beings, the more divine aspects of the gods are seen. But if one were to separate from them everything carried out from them and according to them, not possessing the teachings as if they belonged to the heavens, then both the products of craft and the celestial things would proceed from the infinite and from the principles; and yet, no such part exists after the final extremes, even if it comes from him and not directly from the divine things there.

Democritus, on the other hand, says that these things manifest in another way through their own <term>effluence (aporrhoe)<note>original: "aporrhoen"; Democritus, an early "atomist" philosopher, believed objects gave off thin films of atoms—effluences—that travel to our eyes to create sight.</note></term> being put into action. He believes that the forms are drawn in after their indwelling in the bodies themselves; but some are as if inside the bodies, and some are participated in by the bodies, while others are participated in by those things in which they exist. Indeed, these same powers manifest the forms according to the same character. And things of this sort are not within the thing itself; rather, from what is left behind, it sends out an <term>image (eidolon)<note>An "eidolon" is a reflection, phantom, or lower-level imitation of a true Reality.</note></term> from itself, just as happens in <term>mirrors (katoptrois)</term>. 

Therefore, just as the <term>paradigms (paradeigmata)<note>The original models or blueprints for reality.</note></term> from matter are first the "outside," and the things from this present material world are reflections from their neighbors—as they say in theological works—"little living things" (<term>zoidia</term>) arise within them like a line, a breath, or a phantom (<term>phantasma</term>). That is to say, as if in water, these things follow the writings, being bodies in a sense, but the result is a shaped form that is presented as if it held likenesses within an image, such as in paintings. However, they make the surrounding area living, and what remains he called "living" and "productive," along with other light-like things.

***

Concerning existence, then, it seems that there is an agreement regarding these opinions and how they appear; and concerning things of another nature that are unobserved—the limit of divine things here—the divine things and the main points fill up the other worlds. Some are as they are "there" (in the divine realm), while others are divided, all receiving their names by analogy and <term>homonymy (homonymia)<note>When two things share the same name but have different definitions or levels of reality.</note></term>. These things, they say, belong to the "knowledgeable" (<term>gnostikon</term>) understanding of the principles from which all things exist, including the sense-perceptible things that give form.

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the structure of reality. # On the Kinds of Being

Where then shall we begin? Let us start from "syllables and elements" <note>Plotinus uses the metaphor of letters and syllables to describe the basic building blocks of reality.</note>; even if not following the division of the ancients, such as <term>sensible substances (aisthetai ousiai)<note>Things we can see, touch, and feel.</note></term> and <term>intelligible substances (noetai ousiai)<note>Things that exist only in the realm of thought or spirit.</note></term>.

<margin>According to nature <note>original: "kata ten physin"</note></margin>

How could someone say that these substances are the same, and how could they relate to the same things? How do things outside of matter exist within them as if in a <term>subsistence (hypostasis)<note>The underlying reality or "standing under" of a thing.</note></term>, and are they the same or different—substances and the <term>accidents (symbebekota)<note>Non-essential qualities, like the color of a shirt versus the shirt itself.</note></term> found in both bodies and the bodiless?

<margin>
Matter, form, and the composite made of things close to one another
</margin>

Rather, let us look first at this: is it as if someone said, "It is thus"? Should we say these things are the same or together with each other, or not? And one moves these things from here to there; and one looks at these in movements and bodies. Many things, as one might say, possess other characteristics.

<margin>The same <note>original: "tauton"</note></margin>

In relation to the same thing, or the same thing there. And the same is different. I do not know how.

<margin>
Quality and the many different things
</margin>

And these things are different along with the things that exist; and in relation to itself; and the things that are different. Not equally different, perhaps, from the things here compared to those there; the same and different 

<margin>Division of bodily natures</margin>

in their forms. It is not necessary for each thing to be with the whole, some being in their own divided natures. <insert>But first we say, is it, or is it first?</insert>

<margin>In the... <note>original: "to" — a fragmentary grammatical marker</note></margin>

...it is said to be in matter. This must be in relation to the mixture of both. Some things are in these, and some are about the same things. Some are predicated, and others are even accidents; of the accidents, some are in the things themselves, and others are the things themselves in those others; their accidents; and the others; and those that follow after. On one hand, matter is something common even in all substances. Similarly, one should not use any distinction unless it is the differences themselves. In terms of "what" it is, and according to the shapes of the air. Who, then, is sufficient to be present with the common? 

<margin>
Plotinus here well divides the ten Categories <note>The scribe is praising Plotinus's analysis of Aristotle's ten categories of being.</note>
</margin>

It is possible to be, even as a whole relates to its parts; otherwise, it is a <term>genus (genos)<note>A broad class or category.</note></term> itself and an element. This thing is able to be both an element and a genus, or sometimes a <term>species (eidos)<note>A specific type within a genus.</note></term>, added to encompass matter within matter, of both these and others, even separately. Yet not everything is included, as many as are essential substances; making substances there, and being called "essential" according to being, nor could we call every substance [that]. How is it that both come from both, because that alone is substance? Indeed, from substance. Or let us say this as well, that which is common to the ten [categories], they are predicated only by association, like a single name for "relative things."

<meta>This page transitions from the physical classification of organic bodies seen on the previous page to a logical and metaphysical investigation of "relatives" and "quantity." It explores how qualities like beauty, size, and temperature are not absolute but depend on comparison.</meta>

<margin>On the **relative** <term>pros ti<note>A category of being that exists only in relation to something else, such as "double" or "larger."</note></term></margin>
It is used instead of the smaller. And while the centers, for the reasons we have mentioned, are not large, yet even in color, being large in **quantity**, these things are all in total agreement. This occurs according to nature, following the proportion of means. We say that opposites, such as the **beautiful** and the **ugly**, are simultaneously **relative**; even a mouse is something in itself, yet we say the most beautiful thing is **relative** (and we call a thing beautiful, or we say it is ugly compared to something else, or **good** or **evil** compared to God <note>This reflects a common philosophical idea, famously associated with Heraclitus, that human excellence is nothing compared to the divine.</note>). Therefore, everything that has a natural length is called ugly more in relation to another thing; but in itself it is beautiful, while in relation to another it is either **more beautiful** or **uglier**. For all these things, in themselves, involve reaching a certain greatness, **but relative to another, it is not such**. <gloss>here</gloss> It is shown, then, that the beautiful and the ugly are not absolute, nor are they compared to nothing else; rather, one of them is greater than others, and it is more a matter of being **relative** to something, even if it is more so.

<margin>chapter 7</margin>
One should not leave this behind, for everything that exists has a relation to the whole. For we speak of these things by name through a comparison of proportions; and when we make a **small** thing, we do so according to the mental images themselves. Just as when we often speak of **similar things**. One must speak about the **few** and the **many**; for these are not inherent properties, but are used instead of "more." And this is in relation to something else. And in the 

<margin>lesser</margin>
one should apply it, instead of the **fewer**. And these things will seem to be so, for they are a portion of what contains them. **Many** <note>original: "plēthos"</note> belongs to the category of **relatives**; and these things in this way are an intensification of number. Regarding the portion... it might be granted with a sense of time. To such a degree, it remains far off in relation to others, whenever the "in relation to something" is also the "greater." But even if there is a **greatest**, there is also another. Shall you grant that the "few" and the "small" do not cease quickly as they proceed? And what of the "many" and the "great"? And what of the **beautiful**? Or the **hot**? For even there, we find the "hotter." But while we say something is "hotter" **relative to something**, "hot" is said simply of everything of that kind; just as something is truly "beautiful" or "great." Just as the truth is not yet like the beauty of the **beautiful**. It is shown, therefore, in this way concerning **quantity** <term>poson<note>One of Aristotle's categories, referring to the extension or magnitude of a thing.</note></term>. For regarding this, it is no longer the case that everything falls under <unclear>quantity</unclear>. And as for quantity, whichever it may be, "up" is not the opposite of "down"; for "down" does not belong to the whole; we do not speak of "up" and "down" in terms of the parts.

<meta>This page continues the logical investigation of the Categories, transitioning from the discussion of "relatives" to the specific properties of "quantity" and "quality." <margin><unclear>...</unclear></margin>
Through this, it has also been demonstrated independently, and it is the cause of the line, as participating in a **differentia** <term>diaphora<note>In logic, a "differentia" is the specific characteristic that distinguishes one species from another within the same genus.</note></term>. <meta>This page continues the technical commentary on Aristotle’s *Categories*, shifting focus from the nature of "Difference" and "Quality" to the category of **Motion** (*kinesis*). The catchword from the previous page, *êsei*, likely completes a verb related to motion or process, leading directly into this discussion on how things change and stay still.</meta>

<margin>Concerning</margin>
For others, the result <note>original: *telos*</note> and the goal are the same, and the primary path is the same. For among these thinkers, things are always a certain way—for nothing in physical bodies is always rare for all things—nor do some things exist only in potential <note>original: *dynamei*</note> because of the way they appear to us. And it is similar because things exist in relation to one another; for everything that **moves** <term>kinesis<note>The Greek term *kinesis* refers not just to physical movement from place to place, but to any kind of change or process.</note></term> does so within time, just as parts move within colors. But it is impossible for a person not to learn from everything; however, we have interpreted how and by what means one thing is moved by another. These things must first be established in order to <insert>be permitted</insert> to see how things move.

<margin>
**Motion**
concerning motion
</margin>
For some things, it is not only their nature to "be," but motion exists above being itself; others say that everything is in a state of flux <note>A reference to the Heraclitean idea that "all things flow."</note> and this allows them to function sufficiently. Each body has its own source of motion within itself and through itself, while **rest** <term>stasis<note>The opposite of motion; a state of standing still or stability.</note></term> is something else entirely. For one should not consider that a thing can simply set itself aside; first, we must observe the causes of present things as necessary. Furthermore, motion is found more in the "doing" of things and in the "seeing" of them, taking its starting points from the many.

<margin>living beings</margin>
Neither the present things nor the acting things are their own origins, but rather we more often give the name "action" to the state of **rest**. For often, even when there is total leisure, there is still a kind of motion in each thing. Because of this, it appears that we call certain movements "actions" because they are somehow encompassed by the thing. Therefore, it is not as if one thing is different from another simply because of the things that act upon them. In the same way for all other things, every name must be rooted in that which moves. Just as "quality" belongs to a certain kind of thing, it is more reliable to say a thing does not move rather than following a different rule of motion. But some appear to grasp motion and coming-to-be at the same time; it is not unreasonable for moving things to generate their own shape, for a thing is similarly situated in relation to another.

<margin>appearance</margin>
For example, **rest** exists in each individual case. But colors also coincide, and many things move because everything that comes into being does so in relation to

<margin>painful thing</margin>
something else being established. These things are meant to be perceived by the senses <term>aisthesis<note>The faculty of perception or feeling.</note></term> and by the whole (it is not necessary to say otherwise). Secondly, so that these things do not belong to others, motion acts as a primary force.

<margin>by nature</margin>
And these things—such as those found in a weaving—lead toward knowledge, and physical **bodies** <note>original: *sômata*</note> exist primarily from motion. If one were to speak of the same things, the superior part of each thing is different. Beyond what has been said, we say that not only have things moved, but that motion is placed there by thought; for I am speaking of the construction of individual things. Thus, motion did not fail because of the many. For if the <unclear>ancestor</unclear> exists in a certain kind of motion, it is not superfluous, but it reveals the whole that is moved.

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of Aristotelian physics, specifically focusing on the relationship between "aggregation" and "segregation" and how they relate to "alteration" and "local motion." The previous page introduced the concept of alteration as a change in quality; here, the author investigates whether combining or separating parts constitutes a motion in itself.</meta>

That is to say, **aggregation** <term>synkrisis<note>The process of things coming together or combining.</note></term> is the approach of one thing toward another, and conversely, **segregation** <term>diakrisis<note>The process of things breaking apart or separating.</note></term> is a withdrawal of this kind; these too would be motions, speaking of them in relation to the things being moved. And those things moving away from one another <unclear>receive</unclear> and receive a mixture <note>original: *krasin*</note>. And through all those things, the occurrence of local change <note>original: *kata topon*; literally "according to place," referring to movement through space</note> occurs, not according to coexistence.

Second, these things—let us bring them all to rest (for from both come the local motions). But everything that becomes is something else. So too with **alteration** <term>alloiosis<note>Qualitative change, like a leaf turning from green to brown.</note></term>, although motion rules over everything, for this is the motion of the thing being moved. In this way, we must also seek the local motion among these motions.

It will certainly not be unclear that these are neither aggregations nor, on the other hand, segregations, but rather a resulting entanglement with the individual parts, aggregated in a confused manner <note>original: *synkechymenos*</note> into the One. Many things are separated and appear again as being separated <margin>Concerning motion</margin> elsewhere, perhaps through being persuaded to change, and again being separated. But this is not according to the motion of the thing moved. It is not that these things are joined together by existence and composition, but rather they follow local motion. 

For while defining this alteration, one must refrain from these other definitions, for "dense" <note>original: *pyknon*</note> and "rare" <note>original: *araion*</note> are terms often used, and it is necessary to distinguish this from segregations and define what it is; just as this other thing is a matter of segregating and unifying, as when water is formed, but both of these occurred. This, however, belongs to the specific excesses of the others.

(A main point <note>original: *kephalaion*</note> to be stated here: that aggregations and segregations belong to alterations; yet they are distinct from aggregations and segregations. For neither are the other alterations of such a kind, nor is alteration simply motion). 

Aggregation and segregation result from what happens; for if it were to admit the void <note>original: *kenon*; a space containing nothing, a major topic of debate in Greek physics</note>... and if someone were to dispute this, for colors and <unclear>lasta</unclear>... removing the motions—or rather all of them. For if we call every alteration a change <note>original: *metabolen*</note>, then to speak of aggregation and segregation as "that which becomes" is nothing; in what kind of change of motion... and these things are separated and are clearly judged by all.

<meta>This page continues the technical investigation into the nature of motion and its primary causes. The previous page discussed the processes of aggregation and segregation as types of local motion; here, the text shifts to the "unmoved" source of motion and the relationship between the soul and the physical universe (the All).</meta>

...of motion. And of that [first principle] is the cause, so to speak, of all motions; because every motion is in the things being moved, but not in those [first causes]. And even the act of moving naturally, insofar as it consists in moving something, it also consists in **being affected** <note>original: *pathein*; to undergo change or be the "patient" in a process, as opposed to the "agent."</note>. For if something moves a thing that is a "motion in potentiality," it is itself **unmoved** <term>akineton<note>A central concept in Aristotelian physics: the "Unmoved Mover" which initiates all change without changing itself.</note></term>. Therefore, it is moved by the motion from that place; when these things must be moved by a motion. But it is impossible there [in the first cause] for it to be from another, but rather it is of the first motion. For to cause the motion itself and to be moved is that which is unmoved.

For that first thing either moves first, or it will cease from this **rest** <term>eremia<note>A state of stillness or absence of motion.</note></term>, or it will not be a cause. And in being affected, it would not fail to be affected; which seemed unhealthy [as an argument]. Indeed, not everything would be at a standstill; but if someone says that the All consists in moving and being moved, the All and the "total" will never exist, so he says; which is absurd. But if it does exist, there would be no "affections" <note>changes or properties</note> in the state of rest. This [motion] is prior to rest, not by ceasing, but that which is prior to the chance thing being a state of **rest** <term>stasis<note>Another term for rest, often implying a stable position or standing.</term> (since the motion is spoken of as being by the "agent" and the "patient," and some motions come from it and others toward it), but one does not think about the objections concerning the other things; which is the same as what will happen concerning the other. It exists but not separately. Motion occurs by entering and departing. And the "relative to what" it will be, it is not possible to make these things as they are becoming; for it will be because they are also powers. For it is not out of "non-motion" that motion comes, but "non-motion" [itself]. (There is also motion). And as for certain affections, they are made as if concerning the same **ancient motions**; and some are measures, and some are excesses and diminutions, while others are entirely separated by similarities or differences. And concerning these matters, let these things suffice.

<margin>How the soul as a whole is everywhere in the All</margin>

Concerning **motion everywhere**, they say the **All** <term>to pan<note>The Greek term for the universe or the totality of existence.</note></term> exists, because it would not, in being the All, create the conditions concerning bodies that exist according to nature (for it would seem so even if all things move toward it). It is not as if it is contained by another body, but it belongs to a body; just like a kind of **ether** <term>aither<note>The "fifth element" or quintessence, thought by ancient Greeks to fill the upper atmosphere and the heavens.</note></term>. Being everywhere prior to it, as if placing it again, he would not find its "non-being" existing around the body itself. And the whole of the All is like a certain body and perhaps a chance body, or because it is in certain things in this way, or to move your own position in a body, and to be present through states of rest; again, this is not especially possible. And if someone were to say that it is not in every body, since the same things would come from its becoming, how could it be said only to move? But when it is "everywhere," it no longer receives all things when it does not possess them. And one might say that the All moves in a body, and being a body, at least as I said,

<meta>This page continues the exploration of how the Intelligible Realm—the world of pure thought and ideal forms—interacts with the physical universe. While the previous page focused on the "Unmoved Mover" and the nature of motion, this section addresses the paradox of how a non-physical entity can be "present" everywhere without being physically divided into pieces.</meta>

<margin>
How the Intelligible World <term>Kosmos Noētos<note>The realm of pure intellect and the Platonic Forms, existing beyond physical space.</note></term> is present to every nature
</margin>

In the realm of the Intelligible, nothing exists within a "place"; for the Intelligible did not come to rest in a location, but rather proceeds from a state of standing still. Furthermore, rather than saying it is "in" something, one must understand it as the True Realities and Essences <term>ousiai<note>The fundamental 'being' or 'substance' of a thing, what it truly is at its core.</note></term> are present among us. For example, while some things are derived from others within Being, they are also within the Intelligible itself; for the things belonging to it are contained within it. Those beings are, as it were, composed along with it, and the concept of a "part" is not used in opposition to the whole there. For if it were a part, it would not be truly present with the source, but would somehow flow out from that which is great and vast, and Nature would be stretched out thin. But this Whole possesses no such physical divisions. "Indivisible" <term>amerei<note>Literally 'without parts'; a key Neoplatonic concept describing how a divine or intellectual thing can be everywhere at once without being split up.</note></term> is the name for that realm, which is not contained within the "All" <note>the physical universe</note> as a whole. Rather, the "All" reaches toward it—or more accurately, the Intelligible is present there in all the parts of the universe. For instance, its roots are everywhere, but they are not "in" the universe as if extending from a single physical point into an infinite distance. It is a dignity of Being, not something governed by physical persuasion; but because it willed it, it is so. It fashioned the Soul—for the physical "All" did not yet exist—but the Soul holds its place through Order <term>taxin<note>The structural arrangement or hierarchy of the universe.</note></term>. It is not a body, though it is present within the body. It exists from itself and contains all things within itself. However, things derived from it, such as this physical body, do not possess what is within them in a way that allows them to be divided. In the case of the Intelligible, the whole runs through the same point. It belongs to the whole and not according to parts, just as the perception of it is a single grasp. Those things are one; for how could everything be there if it did not already encompass the things that come from it? And just as those things there are its own, it desires to touch another; and even the things furthest away are reached. Thus, even that which is furthest from the source turns back again to be directed toward it. And so it is for each thing, like the things that exist before the "furthest" point; so that from wherever they come, for this reason, it is possible for a thing to receive itself as that very thing which comes after all things. Even though it has magnitude, the powers of all things are not extended or stretched out; <unclear>perhaps</unclear> it is itself quickly woven together. For in this way, they say that honors are like divine things, as if they were established within themselves. Some things are fixed, while others remain as the summaries of an indivisible generation—at least this much is in it, belonging to all natural things. It is there, even if the things here are not present to it in an indivisible way. Indeed, it is never said that it fails to provide itself entirely; and even then, it is not cut off from the source while remaining there, so that it might give to another. Rather, having received so much from that from which it took, because the source holds all things: all the powers are present, its light is present, without being subject to the law of the recipient which is divided by its end and stands apart. But as for the things that exist, this is what they are everywhere. And again, they are present "corporeally" <note>in a bodily way</note> and to another "partially" for this reason; and yet again, they are not able to be whatever they wish, though they can receive something. For it is not a "part" of the world; rather, that [Intelligible] is the world.

<summary>This page discusses the Neoplatonic doctrine of how the Intelligible Realm remains whole and indivisible while being present to all parts of the physical universe. Plotinus uses the metaphor of light and roots to explain that the divine does not "stretch" or "split" to inhabit the body, but rather the body participates in the divine order.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the nature of the Soul's omnipresence. Having established that the Soul is not "split" among various bodies, the author now uses the analogy of light and the sun to explain how an immaterial essence can be fully present throughout a physical medium without being divided by it.</meta>

<margin>
The whole soul is in the whole body
</margin>

Let us speak of a certain hypothesis: suppose there is something bounded by its power, yet delimited by the space occupied by the bodies within the universe. Thus it is with both the parts and the whole body. And if one takes each of the individual bodies, one after another, it is necessary that it is not "mastered" by that power; nor could one define as many parts of that power as there are parts of the body. If, then, there is something of this sort in a body, what would be left if it were separated? In the case of bodies, their recovery and the parts themselves existed previously in that which contains them. From this, the same <term>perceptible essence<note>original: αἰσθητὴ οὐσία (aisthētē ousia); the physical substance we can perceive with our senses.</note></term> is in the whole likewise. 

It is like the light from the sun in the air: that which holds the parts together is in that transparent body within the sphere, so that the light of the sun appears in all the air, yet it does not belong to the physical body on the outside. From this, the light is in the body under the sun’s radiance; but even so, the darkness is covered in all the air and the light is seen. For it is not "small," as some say; according to its presence in the whole, the light is not removed from the body or from that part. For the light is in the body—or rather, so to speak, the body is in the light—wherever the <term>essence<note>original: οὐσία (ousia)</note></term> 

<margin>

</margin>

exists. We say that something belongs to the bodies; but no part of the light as a whole is truly "in" that place, just as it is not limited by extension. It is no longer even from the <term>ether<note>original: αἰθερίῳ (aitheriō); the "fifth element" or the substance of the upper heavens.</note></term>; for where it lies in another, it is simply present to the whole by its own nature. But even in bodies—not just in spherical bodies—this light is sought and found. And the light that appears is held by the sun; all the air shines from the body of the sun. The same thing is seen as

Light as a whole in the body
</margin>

For the physical body cannot, nor does it have the power, and the physical powers fail where the diameter of the body separates them. But when light is present, it is no longer merely in the appearance; thus, the light would not be in the whole if it were contained as if in a vessel.

<margin>
How he says the soul comes to be in a body.

Having grasped this from its very essence <note>original: οὐσία (ousia); the fundamental nature or "being" of a thing.</note>, it would not wish to be outside of the "All." It possesses everything within itself according to reason <note>original: λόγος (logos); here meaning the rational structuring principle of the universe.</note> and participates in those rational principles; it is arranged among them and comes to be in the body naturally. And while living things and **Universals** <note>original: καθόλου (katholou); general concepts or types that apply to many individuals.</note> are born in this way or not—but in some such manner—its communions are like light and a whole. The body comes to be as if in light. Thus, the soul is said to "come to be in the body," not because it is literally inside it, nor situated in a physical place. When we say "in the body," we mean that the whole body belongs to the soul, which is a kind of communion. This is nothing else; it is not to be in some specific part of the body. Nor is it said to be in the body in that way because it is near, or in a shorter distance, but because its nature is such that it is not divided into pieces.
