# The Eternity and Divinity of the Heavens

The whole of heaven and the cosmos <note>original: κόσμον (kosmon); the ordered universe.</note> cannot be understood as having been generated, nor can it be destroyed. It never was [at a beginning]; it is not [merely a temporary state]; nor is it in any way [limited]. Instead, it exists having neither an end nor a beginning, stretching into the infinite, or rather, existing within that infinite time itself. It is itself all things, and it is reasonable that it should be considered divine among all divine things. This is the manner in which it is appropriate to hold these concepts in the mind, and the way one should grasp them in accordance with the truth. 

For this reason, he also says concerning immortality that the ancient and ancestral beliefs <note>original: ἀρχαίας καὶ πατρίους δόξας (archaias kai patrious doxas); Aristotle often cited traditional religion to support his view that the stars are divine.</note> are true. For it follows that for the gods, everything is infinite and encompasses all things. However, these points are not only agreed upon in the belief concerning the divine beings themselves; for it is not as if the "All" was defined and utilized by justice. Rather, it concerns the binding forces and all power within it <unclear>everywhere</unclear>, these <unclear>things</unclear> as well as the very last of those things that follow here. Many such things will be thus; this very thing. 

And one should further observe this: just as that which necessarily <insert>possesses the heaven</insert> is this, so it is somehow in the world and is its very self. And this might happen to us by the nature of the day. It is necessarily so, as all things are common to it. But it is divided from it; neither eternity <note>original: αἰῶνα (aiona); meaning the "life-span" or "total duration" of the universe.</note> itself, nor is it either of those things for it <insert>for indeed they must be necessary</insert>. And he says these things are entirely so: <unclear>to be</unclear> unaffected by suffering <note>original: ἀπαθὴς (apathes); meaning "impassible" or unable to be changed by outside forces.</note> even above, <insert>if indeed it is even necessary to be</insert>, <unclear>in another</unclear> <insert>from the outside and from those things standing apart, and no longer even changing further</insert> by foundations. 

It is even itself; and furthermore, it is itself. All these things will be worthy of the poles <note>original: πόλοις (polois); likely referring to the celestial poles around which the heavens rotate.</note>, and we say that this is without itself from itself, lest it ever be part of those things participating here. It is possible for it to be present, in so far as it is living. The <unclear>every</unclear> whole, then, having these hypotheses and the negations—the removals—would be to say that such a nature exists or is the ultimate limit. And by necessity, being of such a nature, it receives the ultimate limit. These things are so in number, but not according to reason <note>original: λόγον (logon); meaning rational proportion or account.</note>. For all things are with it, nor ever as many as are in opinion; but to say this is not to destroy it, so that these things might not be attributed to the cause of them all, and they dissolve it into nothing. All things participate in common in an incorporeal way <note>Incorporeal things lack physical bodies; they are pure spirit or intellect.</note>; this relationship is used as if in a **concentric circle**. The lines do not come from another source, but from themselves they stretch toward the center. And there, all things are together; being in that place, all things are in turn attached to the lines. When those things in the circle are cut off, each is no longer directed solely toward the center. Yet, each remains directed toward the center, being itself the same as all the lines; their ends are the same. As much as it touches, so much only does it appear. But those things that remain—if each thing is demonstrated by itself—all things are all things, provided they are not carried away into another, but remain in what is common.

Many letters appear. In this way, when the lines themselves are in the center, all the lines are present to the center, each according to what is present. And it is as if it were no longer by nature alone; many and many things appear from the **one**. For many things, though they are not [separate], are perceived. Thus, even in itself, every other nature is many and many, **one** even in the many, and all things together. And separately, so as not to belong to the whole, it moves toward the part again along with the whole. Why then has it not acted upon the part first as a part, with the whole following? From some image, so that in turn there might be a starting point for what might come to be. Not from an unequal whole, which through all things produces a deficiency. Many things he made the same as himself. And he is in himself in many things in this way, however great he is. For example, because the "all" appearing in many things would be each thing there and the whole "all," not in such a way that it would be many, but many of the same things. Rather, it is because all the same things are many and everywhere. And because the nature of each would be in every part of the body, and in this way it will suffice; for it would be everywhere, both below and very much so. 

If we do not also ascend toward that, and the first things moving from it are no longer their whole selves, then neither would the first be what it is; but along with all of them being what they are, we would truly participate in that place together. Not slipping away from there, they would be as if we saw both that and the things of the others. For those things are not non-existent; they are from everywhere there. Nevertheless, since it exists with all things, we belong to them.

If indeed all things in the Intelligible <note>The "Intelligible" refers to the Platonic realm of pure concepts and Forms, which Neoplatonists believed was more real than the physical world.</note> existed Sensibly <note>As things perceived by the physical senses.</note>, they would be separated one from another. The overall shape of the encompassing sphere, which runs around them, seems very much to belong to this. For its nature is to exist in many ways and by laws, yet remaining the same; it is not the case that "the expressible things" <note>original: λεκτά (lekta); a term for things that can be spoken of or conceptually defined.</note> are there in it. It is undistributed, yet not existing merely as a single thing within another. 

Here, again, the goal is to give form to everything contained within it, as if here too this nature is thin and sparse. But the form itself will not scatter. It is not for you to decide. If each thing were to become many, it would be possible for it to carry many ideas of itself. For if each instance of fire were shaped differently, then the Ideas <note>The eternal "blueprints" for things in the physical world.</note> would be infinite in number. But if those things that come into being are taken up together, they are bound as one because their source is one. And even if an addition were made, this would be graspable without making the source itself varied. 

In every other case, one must say that the Idea is entirely the same. The same things exist for each part within the whole, and the things that come into being from the whole exist **potentially** <gloss>the capacity to exist or act</gloss>; and the name refers to that which draws them together into a spherical shape. They appear like a sphere, or rather as if they were partitioned toward their own dwellings. The causes of this stability are the **Reason** <term>Logos: the rational principle or blueprint of the universe</term> and the whole of the heaven. 

Yet this could not be so otherwise, for the remaining things would exist all together. To refer to such a thing as "partless" is better—or rather, in that realm, things would appear to be all-encompassing. When it recedes from the spherical shape, creating a sort of halo—for a sphere does not come from the consumption of its parts—the soul is delighted by the divinity of the sphere itself, and thus the whole is a sphere. All these things into one whole. 

Perhaps the physical body moves as a whole; but it is not because it is a specific number that it remains itself. He himself breathes into those who have imagined it in this way, as if from the source of the cause. And the cause is not the mere fullness of things, where even the higher realms are a "world." It would not be right to say it fails to draw its own parts; rather, this is what the "whole" means to him. It could be said to increase in depth. Not as if it is mastered by the physical body, but because the things arising from the whole create a union, lifting up the <unclear>elements</unclear>. It is not like the things in between. For the nature of the other is different. The fire is in the middle. And after this is said, one must be bold: what is truly seen is not made of many parts, and so that it might appear... what of it? The enjoyment of the whole is found in those things where it must not be taken as separate, but in every part at once.

For it has become necessary for new things to be brought to each—simple and unmixed. And it is possible to add "according to the whole," if one definitely knows it is fitting; otherwise, one must not add "of the whole." For not even the act of addition [is simple], but having added "not all" he spoke according to what is truly more; they say it is "simply," to stand apart from the parts of their whole and only incidentally. For the whole, they say, [is] with them; things common of old, through error, but belonging to the one that is in all things. But the truth does not meet [it], for they say it is not the "whole" simply, but "to all"; these very ancient things were written. For in this way even the unmixed things, when they are filled, appear not only as those things which can be common to them, but also as the things of their own proper order, saying—just as they speak of rocks—even if not everything, one must apply it to all. The "to all" and the "absolutely" and the "without it" are no longer opposed to all of them, since this very thing and the forms will seem to have, up to this point, both dissimilar powers and a unique nature compared to those of the stars. —

The path of departure from **multitude** <term>multitude (plēthos): the state of being many, divided, or fragmented, which the soul must transcend to reach the Unity of the divine.</term> is to release all parts to all things. For since it is not possible for it to be in all, and remaining and not throughout every body, and because of the name of multitude, for each thing is a whole. But whenever it is impossible for it alone, and those things not according to what is in the shadow <note>original: ἐν τῷ σκιάσματι; referring to the physical world as a mere shadow of the true reality.</note> are judged, the parts being measured together, the multitudes of the one come to be in that; not in the same things alone, but it is necessary for it to be shown in the form. For just as the future is following, in simple things this is necessary; and from there, whatever comes into being from itself will also appear in another way, whenever the whole comes to be for all, but simply for itself, and it would not appear before. It is rather a necessity for each, not when the whole comes to be, but when it gives itself to itself; one is accustomed to speak of these things generally.

<summary>This page provides a metaphysical analysis of "the Whole" versus "the Many," arguing that true wholeness belongs to the unmixed, intelligible realm, while the physical world consists of "multitudes" that are mere shadows. It emphasizes that the soul must depart from this state of division to return to its own simple, unified essence.</summary>

Just as things are lesser through addition and order, so too are the defined essences of those things that fall under each genus. The being of each thing is not identical; the being of a specific Zeus is one thing, and the being of the common Zeus <note>The "Common Zeus" refers to the universal principle of the Demiurge or Cosmic Mind, as opposed to a specific manifestation.</note> is another. Existing things are similar in terms of their being: some will be henads <note>original: enades; from "hen" (one), these are the supreme unities or divine souls that sit just below the Absolute One.</note>, while others are dyads <note>pairs</note> and triads <note>groups of three</note>. The universal essence of the wholes is not a single whole itself, but belongs to each of the... Next, it provides the substance <note>original: hypostasis; the underlying reality or "standing under" of a thing.</note> for each of them. For it is not the case that Justice exists in the essence of all things. Let there be Justice; but one would not say that it is a "mixture" in some way, or a substance like those things among us that bear the name. For the name does not come from such things; rather, Justice itself is the essence of each thing that participates in it. It exists prior to our knowledge of it, which is why it would not be found in essence alone; and furthermore, the act of thinking what a thing "is" refers to this. These things are the primary forms of Justice; without these, Justice would not even exist. It is according to a certain definition of it; for Justice is either the whole or a mixture—having received its due from them. Such are these things that are substantiated.

Furthermore, the complete living being—in which the thought of all resides, or rather, which contains within itself all living beings—is also such as to be as great as all things combined. <meta>Continuing from the previous discussion on mathematical substances—specifically the nature of the Monad and Number—this page transitions into the classic Plotinian investigation into the nature of Eternity and Time. Having established the fixed reality of the intelligible realm, the author now interrogates common definitions of Time to see if they hold up against the truth of Being.</meta>

Having now reached a point where we consider further opinions regarding this matter, it might be reasonable even to critique their errors for the sake of discovering the truth. And first, if someone should say that <term>Time</term> <note>original: "chronos"</note> is the motion of the universe; and if they mean the celestial revolution, they must think that the parts of the extension of the universe are many, for the things that extend are both bodies and substrates and motions. Nor do they say this only in relation to the fact that other things are thought to be in motion. For the person who says that <term>Time</term> <note>original: "chronos"</note> itself is the motion of the universe also identifies it with <term>Eternity</term> <note>original: "aion"</note>. And it would seem impossible to demonstrate that things outside of this have any relation to the <term>Substantial Reality</term> <note>original: "hypostasis"; the actual existence or essence of a thing.</note> of motion. Rather, it is in the case of Eternity, as we said, that the same things exist, and in this is the <term>Substrate</term> <note>original: "hypokeimenon"; the underlying foundation.</note>. Nevertheless, after this, the same things are in the "other" which is beyond, but such things will not exist; as if to say that nothing exists by substantial reality. Because each of these is separated not long after; but this is not entirely the cause. So that regarding Eternity, the distinctions concerning each thing [must be considered] first upon 

<margin>for</margin> they ask. <insert>And indeed</insert> it is itself a certain intellection of the work of the underlying <term>Essences</term> <note>original: "ousion"</note> of those things, and thus also for the things perceived in the senses. And the <term>Now</term> <note>original: "nyn"; the dimensionless point of the present moment.</note> itself is similar to this and is a cause. For when Eternity appears, it is chosen, for it is the same as the "Now." For there would be no motion, but rather things proceeding from being in it; and indeed, since all things are contained successively by Time, such things would not be motion. But one must define the things demarcated in the "Now." Thus, the things here would still be so, even if they are not the affections of motion. And there is no need for the body; for it is not only in nothing else; for indeed the things in the "Now" also exist in it. Then come the other things, and everything else follows after. For the desires are neither the principles of their own powers, nor are the <term>Accidents</term> <note>original: "symbebekota"; non-essential properties</note> themselves concerning these. Just as the "but it is not" is not that about which it is spoken. But it claims to be about itself before the whole exists. And since it could not again receive motion concerning itself. And it is even now, since nevertheless I wish for many things. By a contraction in the destruction. Upon burning, a loss. <meta>Continuing the investigation from the previous page regarding the nature of Time and Eternity, the author now shifts toward the metaphysical principles of the One (the Monad) and the many (the Dyad). This section examines how these primary principles act as causes for both virtues like courage and physical realities like health or disease, drawing heavily on Aristotelian and Platonic frameworks of participation.</meta>

Since the <term>Rational Principle</term> <note>original: "logos"</note> exists by standing alongside the <term>Substrate</term> <note>original: "hypokeimenon"; the underlying foundation of a thing</note>; its inclination having already arrived, whence the one doing this demonstrates what results. How, then, shall there not be the power of the impossible wherever we might wish it to be moved, just as in the <term>Metaphysics</term> <note>original: "meta ta physika"; referring to Aristotle's foundational treatise on the nature of existence.</note> when the inconsistent appears? Thus even by night, for some, an <term>Accident</term> <note>original: "symbebekos"; a property that happens to belong to a thing but is not part of its essential definition.</note> will exist in itself, for not all things affected are within their own power. And accident is toward accident, but it is not possible for it to be reshaped or added to. For those things having seen their own [parts] to which they are added, neither is the thing being added [independent]; but the categorization in the *Metaphysics* is at least according to parts.

<margin>of parts</margin>

But being separated into parts, those things brought together for the kindred are according to each individual portion. For instance, that the <term>Dyad</term> <note>original: "duas"; the principle of "two-ness" or plurality, often associated with division and matter.</note> is the cause, according to the meeting and binding together, of being; for it produces the same things—or rather those things produced by relation—some of which are even from vice, and it is seen again in opposites. Since the Dyad holds a certain relation to something, it happens in such a way that the cause of <term>Temperance</term> <note>original: "sophrosyne"</note> and <term>Courage</term> <note>original: "andreia"</note> is generally the end and directed toward the first principles. For when it has a certain relation toward something, I write the same thing as possible by the removal of it—as this being the <term>Marginal Correction</term> <note>original: "paragramma"</note>. For how is it in the case of the primary causes spoken of? For this is by the presence of the <term>Monad</term> <note>original: "monados"; the principle of Oneness or Unity</note>, just as in the case of evil things there is evil, and the just is just, and these are not the same; to be the cause of a relation, even in these things, is a cause insofar as it is just.

Because of this, these things are of a certain relation; and one person [says] that being thus disposed, they have no desire for the same things as the substrate—as if for certain of our dispositions. Nor does the <term>Beautiful</term> <note>original: "to kalon"</note> follow those who perceive it; for we say perhaps now that all are mistaken, just as are the evils in the world. For in the One, concerning it as far as possible, with a certain <term>Participation</term> <note>original: "methexis"; the way physical things "share" in the reality of higher Forms</note>, it is the cause of sweet and bitter and other such things. Because not from that "out of which" shall every increase come, but it is not in the things that are, nor toward evil generally in any way. But that which remains in part shall not be, and the measure for existing things as it happens for the rest; for just as when a body is present, so too is disease. And for the Dyad—and their good things consist in how they partake in the <term>Passions</term> <note>original: "pathe"; the experiences or affections</note> of the gods, or rather one must say not of partaking but [not partaking] in the sovereign part, but it is observed in each thing from others as well, nor in bodies [are there] other such compositions from powers, causes, and being...

And let them not just stand there. For even regarding these things, those powers living beside that higher realm are themselves certain **powers** <note>original: "dynameis"; in this context, the active capacities or spiritual forces that bring the higher forms into reality.</note> there, and they come together with those things as if they were of this world; but those things there are that higher Reality. But we give the name **sensation** <note>original: "aisthesis"</note> to the act of attending to it, never departing from it, and never ceasing the perception found there—it is like a "touching" of certain bodies. <margin>That the **Ideas** <note>original: "ideai"; the eternal blueprints or Forms of all things.</note> either look toward the things here, or they have come from the earth so that these things might exist.</margin>
How, then, would these things here wish to look toward those things there? If there is a living being here, let it be so; but if there are irrational animals, will that higher Intellect not also generate them? And why would they wish to be there, as if to exist in those higher states? For if they were to come into being, they would come from that source where they exist and never cease to be. They "cease" only in the sense that they exist there as **sensible things** <note>things perceived by the senses</note> which are actually **intelligible things** <note>things understood by the mind</note>. And both exist within themselves, especially in their newness. Before this, these very things were part of the first generation. And it is not as if they are different things again. It is as if one, looking at them, held within themselves their essence—but in making an **Idea**, one possesses them just as they are there, yet without motion. These things follow what exists even down to the earth; for they themselves are not just any small part.

But that Reality itself is being—an august and venerable multitude. How then is it that this multitude is not an "infinite" one while still being a Unity? Clearly, it is not just these specific things. One might say that one thing is that Reality, and another is equal to it—derived from it. For this is the definition of the "Equal": if that Reality exists, a multitude is born. If the "How" prevents it from being two things, then it must belong to those things.

<margin>Why indeed there is a multitude and how it is an "infinite" multitude.</margin>

From the study of **nature** <note>original: "physikes"</note> there emerges a principle within it; while it is the first mover of these things, it also encompasses every movement, the arts, and subsequently **choice** <note>original: "proairesis"; the capacity for deliberate purpose or will.</note>. Furthermore, it possesses its own peculiar novelty, just as in a living being—and even more so in the cosmos. It exists as a perfect life. Because of this, it is necessary that there be a difference from other things, so that it is not the most paltry of all living beings; its **end** <note>original: "telos"; the goal or ultimate purpose.</note> is great. Some of these are called living beings insofar as each participates more fully in the community of life, while others are said <unclear>to be</unclear> those in which the fact of living is merely hidden. In these same things, there is an equality among the disturbances in the living being compared to its own pure **fire** <note>In Neoplatonic thought, "fire" often represents the most refined, active element of the physical world, closest to the divine.</note> and all other things. And thus, each thing is such as are the **shapes** and **forms**. For these are the forms that we call the forms of **plants**. And among all things, both the better and those in relation to one another—like an eye or a finger—are the work of the <unclear>cosmos</unclear>; some are altered for the better. And the **Reason-principle** <note>original: "Logos"; the formative, rational blueprint that gives shape to matter.</note> is also a living being. Not only are these things living beings, but also, simply put, the child and the honorable; and the beautiful Reason-principle of the indifferent and common does not give the same things. Even the dark things appear to you as not without value compared to the nature of all other things. As for the whole, it is itself fire.

<margin>**Ideas** and **shapes** of plants</margin>

For they possess these things in the same state. How great they are in their entirety, and what kind of **opinion** <note>original: "doxasmon"; a lower form of knowledge or a "seeming."</note> they nourish, they hold in abundance. All these plants are related to those [higher forms], as are the things concerning the <unclear>seeds</unclear>; for if it is in the cosmos, it will also be in the whole branch. And again, each of these is in every way a plant. It has been harmonized with the **Reason-principle** in a brilliant way. And someone might say that a plant here is a gaping mouth for the **form-giving** <note>original: "eidopoiias"</note> Reason-principle of the plant; for indeed, the plant is also <unclear>and</unclear> remains a kind of living child. And this Reason-principle either comes from the plants themselves, <unclear>for</unclear> its first rest is the plant, from which this also comes—for that higher realm saw all things through care and the necessity of abundance, things more peculiar than even <unclear>roots</unclear>.

<margin>That even **seaweed** <note>original: "phychia"</note> possesses these characteristics</margin>

This very thing is what it means to be a plant: from that source come these things, as well as stars and hair. It is also possible to <unclear>perceive</unclear> a trace of images in them, and that they are fire. And for those things in the <unclear>water</unclear>, someone might find them more predatory. This is what it means for these things to be fire: they exist through a certain **form** and a Reason-principle within them. Nothing lives apart from the plant and its own Reason-principle; from which we also received the things of the earth, the most specific of their kind.

<margin>Further regarding the **growth of stones** and **mountains springing up**</margin>

...great things and those that once belonged to the earth, which we would have mentioned even here—the <unclear>breath</unclear>. We have seen, therefore, the **growths** and the stability of stones, and of mountains springing up...

<summary>Plotinus argues that everything in the physical world, from plants and seaweed to stones and mountains, is shaped by a divine "Reason-principle" (Logos) and possesses a degree of life. He suggests that even seemingly inanimate objects like stones participate in the cosmic order and grow according to higher blueprints.</summary>

<margin>The soul</margin>
<margin>According to</margin>

The light there is itself alone, and it is only there that it truly passes through. In this same way, **fire** exists there—as it was said, it is a "circling" fire and not located within you <note>Plotinus is likely referencing a Platonic or Orphic description of divine fire as a self-contained, perfect element rather than the destructive fire of our world.</note>; and so it is with all other things. But again, it must be stated this way: if we must start from these things as examples to describe what must be said of those divine realities, we say that everything was once there, or exists there in its true form. Everything there is complete and identical to those archetypes; all things exist there as a sort of **All-Living Being** <note>original: "pan zoon"; the Platonic concept from the *Timaeus* of a single living creature that encompasses all other living species within it.</note>, and not merely as a part of the things that come to be here. Because the entire heaven and everything within it exists in that realm, they exist not merely in number, but in a much higher sense than anything here. For the "Living Being itself" is all things—including all that are land-dwelling, those in the air, those in the marshes, those in other regions, and those of the sea. All are there. Even the things in the waters are preserved there, though they are not [physical] animals as such, nor are those in the air; rather, they exist there by their very **nature**. Every part is a whole, and the lives within it are analogous to the total life. For the things within it—even those that appear inanimate or heavenly here—how could they not be **souls** there? Even the "evils" as individuals <unclear>exist there</unclear>; for while things exist in parts here by necessity, they do not grow here as they do in themselves. However it may be, they exist there in the same way they are there: for there, every living thing is truly all things and does not pass into non-existence. Nor do those things ever lose their total life. (From where does this come? Or from where does the "will" come? This comes from that very art and life which is "all life" and not just a single life.) And **Intellect** <note>original: "Nous"; the divine mind or second principle of Neoplatonism.</note> is also such that it is not just one life, but receptive of many—or rather, it is a single **Idea** <note>original: "Idea/Eidos"; the eternal form or blueprint of a thing.</note> that is nevertheless all lives

filled and defined by the lives within them, as if they were not to become just one. It is like a certain breath, or a single heat that is poured out, which is one but contains all qualities within itself and preserves them. There is **sweetness** <note>Plotinus uses sensory metaphors—taste, sound, color—to explain how the Intellect holds diversity within unity.</note> according to the senses, yet all are together and not mixed as if in a cup; nothing is weakened,

<meta>This page continues the discussion from Ennead VI.7, where Plotinus describes the Divine Intellect (Nous). The previous page established the archetypes of all animals; this page delves deeper into the internal structure of these archetypes—how the "Many" exist within the "One" without breaking the unity of the Divine, and how "Reason-principles" (Logoi) relate to physical bodies.</meta>

Because of this, they do not have a passage out of themselves, as they are not without parts. Others exist within other things, and according to these, the **virtues** <term>aretē: excellence or moral power</term> are purely concerned with the bodies of things perceived by the senses and similar matters for all; this is the manifest truth. And necessity is, in a way, nowhere; and he is all other things. So, for them, all is as one. And having turned toward them, all is unified. But if he himself were not necessary, then it would be necessary for them. And these things are also there in **potentiality** <note>original: "dynamei"; the capacity for a thing to exist or act, even if it is not currently doing so in the physical world.</note>, because they do not fall short of the Whole in any of their own parts, even if a cause—coming from another—flows through the whole. 

But in another way, the whole is to have its own **essence** <term>ousia: true being or substance</term> diminished, as if remaining within itself; he says this even of the proceeding **powers** <note>Plotinus refers to "emanations" or powers that flow out from the One into the Intellect.</note>. But it is not even possible to always hear of a **Unity** <term>monas: the Monad or the state of being a single, indivisible unit</term> as something that belongs to another, but rather as something that actually exists. For he wishes to speak by taking it as a **paradigm** <term>paradeigma: the perfect celestial model upon which physical things are patterned</term>. Either they were there first and did not exist [here], or they were there for the rest; as in the remainder of what has become the **material** part of the cosmos—though not all things in the cosmos are material. Until this point, all **wisdom** <note>original: "sophia"</note> is present, or rather, the things that belong to it, yet they do not belong to it in the way things are fitting for [physical] bodies; never are they so. But being both **eyes** and **fire**, they are also each other. 

The "other," in turn, must be divided; if indeed the things there are both the primary realities and those that exist in the truest sense. 

<margin>How then is the boundless a division?</margin> 

And the First, again, is in this state: that the All is as "many," not as that [physical] one is one, but as a **manifold Reason-principle** <term>logos: the formative blueprint or "formula" of a thing</term> within a Unity. It is not like a magnitude that has a boundary or outlines. He himself is in the configurations. There are powers and there is disease. And one must not consider the **division** <note>original: "diairesis"; the process of logical or ontological "splitting" of a genus into species.</note> to be like that found in things perceived by the senses—such as the natures of living beings contained within the **Universal Living Being**. And again, at the same time, there are the smaller living things and the lesser powers, so that there might not be a division into the **infinite** <note>original: "apeiron"; Plotinus is arguing that the Divine Intellect has a finite "manyness" of specific archetypes rather than being a chaotic, endless soup of fragments.</note>, as he says. It is not granted according to... <unclear>fragmented text</unclear>. For it is not otherwise, except that this madness is even among us, not as it is in the Whole. Let these things not be a mere display for that realm; if there is another [division], it is for the sake of being and never being separated. 

He says that things are distinguished within the whole of their own kind; by the "many" and by all the primary and diverse **Ideas** <note>original: "ideas"; the eternal Forms in the mind of God.</note>, they are no longer merely "themselves." Each is all things, but they are... <unclear>ink stain</unclear>... for others are dark and below; both small and dim. Yet these [the archetypes] are both **pure** <note>original: "katharai"</note> and they dwell among the pure. And if you are there, you no longer see only the pure ones, nor do you see all of them...

# [ Generation, for the later things of beings. ]

<margin>
Just as the sun’s light relates to the body and visible things, so the One relates to the Intellect and all beings.
</margin>

Having been filled with what that [the One] holds—the things surrounding it—it was filled; it no longer merely moves, but also **thinks** <term>noei: to perceive with the mind or engage in intellectual intuition</term> until satisfied, and having been overfilled, it becomes all things. And this is within itself; and all things are in turn within it. It will remain, and this [Intellect], having been filled, will remain. 

<insert>127</insert> It conceives while looking at these things by means of light, receiving an **image** <term>eikōn: a likeness or reflection</term> from Being, and it will create a world. Because of this, as all essences are always coming into being, he is the cause of its seeing, just as a covering is the cause of it being unseen by things perceived by the senses. He is the cause of its coming-into-being, not from above for all, nor as things shared by all; thus he says of the **Good** <note>original: "agathou"; for Plotinus, the Good is synonymous with the One, the ultimate source of all existence.</note> that those things present participate at the right time. And the analogy for the things seen is neither the beings nor the intellect; there is a glory of the same light, providing a certain fullness. Thus, having been filled with light, it was completed, and he is the beginning for them, filling that beginning of **unity** <term>henotētos: the state of being one or unified</term> as if from outside. This light, like a vapor, fills it...

<margin>
The One exists before the life of Being, but beings become a multitude. And what is life as a possession?
</margin>

...the wonders of its formation. Since they are not beings, they remain in that which filled them, for when it remains it is filled; it did not possess what it might hold, but how it might give. This is what it has given. On one hand, it remains, and that exists. On the other, it is in no way less than the giver. For such is the **generation** <term>genesis: the process of coming into being or origin</term> of such things. For the first is the **activity** <term>energeia: actualization or the "work" of a thing's nature</term> so that the later things exist, just as the first things belong to them and the first things are the cause of their being. For it is better to say that the prior is the activity. Since that activity surrounds them like images. Because of this, nothing of that is changed. It is more beautiful and more honorable than life. It possessed life, then, and did not [just] have its forms, by means of life; a certain **trace** <note>original: "ichnos"; a footprint or vestige of a higher reality found in a lower one.</note> of that, but not that itself.

<margin>
Concerning chaos.
</margin>

Turning then and looking, it is **indefinite** <term>aoristei: lacking limit, boundary, or definition</term> in itself, but it was defined by that which has no limit. For looking toward that, it is defined and circumscribed and receives **form** <term>eidos: the intelligible shape or essence of a thing</term>. And the things appearing to me in each part to be formed were formless, just as that [the One] is not a magnitude in itself. But in all the visions of that life, there are many reflections of an infinite essence, as if the nature itself were shining. Life there was not defined, but was like an individual defined among others. Thus, having been defined, it is something of a great...

<meta>This page continues the investigation into how the One (the Good) relates to the multiplicity of the world. While the previous page focused on the Intellect (Nous) receiving its form from the One, this section explores how individual beings participate in "goodness" through their specific essences, life, and internal order.</meta>

# [ On the Good and the Nature of Beings ]

But it is not the Good-itself, but rather a good belonging to themselves; yet those things are also released from that source, for they live from it with a life that is truly real. And nothing is simply good in isolation; rather, it is in their total agreement that they exist. In a general sense, we find that the "goods" are true in all cases by a principle of analogy, just as beings are in relation to Him. They are not "the goods" merely because they come from Him, but because they relate to what is specific to each individual good. And just as there, all things that have been affected are without need, so too is that [the Good] the standard; just as one thing exists primarily, another exists through its **desire** <note>original: "ephesiō"; referring to the natural pull or inclination everything feels toward the Good.</note>. And in general, the primary things of those that have received [goodness] are each unique; just as in **essence** <term>ousia: the fundamental substance or "being-ness" of a thing</term> itself, its good and its being are the same. These primary goods are not simply good in an abstract way, but because there is no gap between what is true and what is adjacent to it. And again, one might say that the difference within them is easy to see; for when that which stands in their place is held fast, nothing further remains in that which is essential, for this is what is present. Yet, the Good in turn gives way; as it is with Him, so it is with each. The primary [good] exists in another, and those things perceptible to sight are derived from secondary things, while the primary things are not. And if both are primary, then the remainder is also good.

<margin>
That too is clear, and it is recorded what concerns another in relation to...
</margin>

But if the Good is that in which their essence exists, and is not, in turn, the Good itself, then what of the things within the Good? How then, and in what part? Are they a part of a certain kind? In the same way, being exists in one way, and the other in another; for even there, the Good is upright. And this whole and defined thing is a good; and the body is both. Even the part that becomes a portion of it is the same; the world comes from Him. But to say that the body is both things provides no real explanation. It is as when a voice sounds toward itself and its foundation; every perfected excellence here exists because there is **order** <term>taxis: the structured arrangement of parts within a whole</term> and **rhythm** <term>rhuthmos: the proportion and flow of existence</term>. From this excellence, as it is here, a whole exists; and as if from the outside, there are differences in the orders surrounding them. And why are these things themselves also "goods"? It is not simply because these things come to all from the One. **Wisdom** <term>phronēsis: practical intelligence or the soul's insight</term> is indeed a great thing, conceding that these things exist from that source. Or what else could it be? But grasping it entirely through a method, he says that from the Good come both its strength and its success. Before reaching moderation, and through the experience of this state, all this is directed toward what we shall call "good." This is because of its relation to the world; and even the instruments regarding this matter do not care for any part of the world. The Good is that toward which we shall move. And many things from those "over there" <note>Plotinus uses "there" (ekei) to refer to the higher intelligible realm, and "here" (entaūtha) to refer to the physical world.</note> do not appear to us. First, it is because the Good is found within **life** <term>zōē: the vital, living principle that animates the universe</term>; then, because there are different things that are desired, some by one, some by another. While all things desired are judged to be better, perhaps nothing is as apparent as the fact that "good" is good—such as these things—and that the goods are good. Rather, they are so according to the **virtue** <term>aretē: the excellence or functional perfection</term> of each.

<summary>Plotinus discusses how the Good is not an abstract label but is realized through the specific essence, order, and life of every being. He emphasizes that "goodness" in the physical world is a reflection of the "order and rhythm" derived from the higher intelligible realm.</summary>
<keywords>The Good, Essence (Ousia), Life (Zoe), Order (Taxis), Rhythm (Rhuthmos), Virtue (Arete), Wisdom (Phronesis), Analogy</keywords>

<margin>

...along with other things. And it is pursued by that which comes from there [the Good]; and reaching toward those things which are its own, it arrives with difficulty. Thus one must reason also regarding the beauty from there. For when each thing is upon its foundation, it is light; or rather, His **grace** <term>charis: a divine radiance or "bloom" that makes beauty "alive" and lovable, rather than just a static arrangement of parts</term> poured over them, making them lovely, just as it is in the arts.

<margin>
How he introduces the soul toward motion
</margin>
It brings forth **loves** <note>original: "erōtas"; refers to the intense, driving desire for the Good</note>. And the Intellect, seeing nothing in itself, nor being moved by mere outflows, becomes frenzied with divine inspiration <note>original: "anabakcheuetai"; literally to be caught up in a Bacchic frenzy or holy madness</note>. As if stung and goaded, it is moved as never before. And being whirled around by Him, first there is the light; and it stretches upward toward it, not as a good for us, but toward those things coming from itself. For it belongs to the Intellect—it has recognized it. Nor can it stay there; just as it is shaken by a sudden heat, it is strengthened and awakened and even grows wings. And it is what lies near and close by. And it is centered around something of Him, like a sweetness, and more full of friendship, as with the beloved. It is raised up, breathing and being lifted. Under this, as if they were different things, it moves toward the highest things, written above the Good. For one is most especially drawn toward those things, and yet it is not [the Good itself], but things dedicated to it that it beholds. Nor could it imitate it; it is beyond all.

<margin>
What beauty is
</margin>
For as if overflowing His own nature, we call it [beauty]. Thus there is also a kind of void in whatever is present. There is a **grace** <note>original: "charis"</note> running over these beauties. When even here beauty appears in **symmetry** <term>symmetria: the mathematical proportion of parts, which Plotinus argues is a necessary but insufficient condition for true beauty</term>, it is the radiance itself that manifests. And this is the lovable thing. For why is there more beauty in a smiling face than in one that is not, even if it is not found in the symmetry? For the Soul, formed by clear and symmetrical parts, is moved...

...of himself; nor should he be cautious, lest there be anything wicked in the fact that the Good belongs to him. For whatever anyone might say, it is fitting for him to be the ultimate and to belong to the ultimate. But not these things; for regarding him, what would it be? And the Good belongs to them, especially the "goodnesses" <note>The author uses the plural "goodnesses" to describe the various ways the ultimate Good is reflected in individual things</note> within them. Since they also belong to "that," and the order of succession and that which is superior to it and its own being, he says that which is such as it is for him—because the Good itself is of them, and as it is over all things, it is not necessary for everything to be made entirely like it; rather, it is something else and a portion of it. 

Therefore, there is all the more a "belonging" <term>oikeiōsis: a Stoic and Neoplatonic term for the process of making something one's own or feeling at home in the world</term> toward it for those things that are nearer. And for those things that are more good, just as being itself comes from the Good, it is itself good. And just as he says fire <note>A common metaphor in Neoplatonism; fire naturally moves upward, just as the soul naturally seeks the Good</note> desires its own nature, so too the "goodnesses" within things are what remain for it. This must be considered: for if this were not to stand at all, then it would fail in relation to itself, and the Good is within it. 

This might happen if, after it, there is also the ascent toward the Good—whether we use that name or whether, as he says, he "makes" the Good. But what if we were to say it is "not-good"? And if someone among existing things, whatever he was beside himself, were not to be whatever he is, [it would be] a choice between the Good and himself. What then should we expect? To be as though one were not, and because that which exists entirely beside it is a "form of the good." And this also regarding that Good: whether they would wish for things to belong to it, or if it should happen, it would not be. 

But these are not [matters of] perception <term>aisthēsis: sensory perception</term>; rather, it would be the Good itself being present. Matter, then, is a mixture <note>Plotinus often describes matter (hylē) as a "mixture" or a "shadow," representing the furthest point from the light of the Good</note>; but evil—this they have. Should we not then designate vice itself as evil, but rather ask how it stands apart from the Good and place matter [as the cause]? But they make it a "hypothesis" and, as it were, something that brings completion—though they are matter. 

These [qualities] of it are not perception, as if they were under the power of the Good, even if feminine things <note>In ancient philosophy, the "feminine" was often associated with the passive principle or matter, while the "masculine" was associated with form and intellect</note> are not in the [right] order. But that evil exists and the remaining vice, if one wished to grasp its being, [it is] that from which its own nature comes. But the Good is concerned with the highest; it is not a chosen evil. Rather, that which is "evilled" <note>An unusual phrasing suggesting a thing affected by evil rather than evil itself</note> has its being in form. And yet this is chosen by the Good. But then they will perceive those very goods and what belongs to the Good. And if someone [belongs] to the Good—for to know it most is not to desire it—we have placed the Good [there], and these things are as they are. But the Good belongs to himself, and as they ascend more, they should more [know it]; for even the Good...

# How pleasure relates to the Good and the End.

<margin>
{ What pleasure is in animals and gods.

Our souls, by the apprehension of their own thoughts, [possess] all things as goods. And so it is for both of these; but the Good itself also desires us to rejoice in its own [nature] and in the One. It is necessary to take up and teach the young intellect <term>nous: the higher mind or divine intellect</term>. And if beings use one another, they do so by contributing to nature; thus, it would not admit that the movement of the body is a hindrance. What is Truth?

—and by the measure of being beside those things, which would not leave the soul the pure and unmixed [quality] found in the body. It is a certain unsparing [bountiful] thing accompanied by pleasure, directed toward purity <note>The OCR "ketaros" is likely a corruption of "katharos" (pure)</note> and toward beautiful things and toward all things. ...which they say is either beautiful or good, since it is from "that" [the Source] and is the element. <meta>This page continues the discussion of the First Principle, shifting from the soul’s ascent to the nature of the "King of All." While the previous page cited Aristotle and Pseudo-Dionysius, this passage focuses on Plotinus’s interpretation of a famous riddle from Plato’s *Second Letter* regarding the relationship between the divine and the created world.</meta>

<margin>
About the King of all, 
all things exist.
<note>This is a foundational quote from Plato’s *Second Letter* (312e), which Neoplatonists like Plotinus used to explain how the entire universe depends on a single divine source.</note>
</margin>

...to have made; he consented to the permanence of it. Of these things, and in this way, he received them in exchange. This—and this is the truth—is a private portion. Each person is all things, and one would not take one thing and another person another for themselves; he says to all these who have set themselves apart from themselves: "Disregard yourselves for as much as you possess." And having learned as much as they might ask for, they know all things. 

It is not even that it exists or ceases because it is what it is—no one is that—and they would recognize and perceive it <unclear>as if</unclear> it were their own. For they do not know each thing individually; rather, they seek to begin and to consume their own ignorance. For they say these things to themselves: their own things are theirs, yet not theirs. This is laughable; for how can there be a <unclear>grasping</unclear> of oneself? One holds nothing, and what one does not hold, it is not likely to be one's own. But if one holds what is one's own, and having yielded all these things, one is with Him. 

And now, each of the things present belongs to the causes; for they belong to those beings. Just as from the one from whom power comes, that power is not even with those for whom the gifts might be superfluous. And at the same time, there is a dispute as to whether the works are likely to be sovereign, and whether <term>being</term><note>The original Greek uses forms of "to be" (*einai*) to distinguish between temporary existence and eternal, true reality.</note> is always such an end. 

They belong neither to themselves, nor to themselves. Because nothing is anything by itself as if present to itself, but to all, everything is, and the whole is all in all, and all things are together. Yet, all things are causes, for even those things would not exist if He were not. And let them neither do their own things alongside him, nor the things prior to those from that place; they are pulled up as others. They are placed around the first. And all things are around Him; for in this way, they possess themselves and Him. And the things that come after are outside of Him. 

Those things concerning God would not exist, which you yourself say. <margin>x</margin> And everything is rightly said to be "all things around the King of all." All things exist for his sake, and all such things, as the same author says. And to belong to Him, for Him and for the things to be causes for themselves; and as it were, they are directed toward Him, that which is in need of all things. 

And He has no need of them, for He is present where you might toil. All things of His are not even in a living being, since He is present to the others that come after Him. He gave also a portion of "having all things." To have a portion, then, and the existence of all beautiful things, is the "Beautiful" for me. That is what seems to be established; but He himself is <term>above the Beautiful</term><note>A key Neoplatonic concept: the source of beauty (the One) must be even greater than beauty itself.</note>; all of these things are other than all.

<margin>

The text seeks to prove that the highest reality does not exist by accident or "luck," but is the sovereign cause of its own existence—what the author describes as a "Will" that is identical to "Being."</meta>

Not by chance, nor...
</margin>

But the Good: is this not also specifically both the Cause and the act of making these things to be as it made them, so that it might be so called? Yet it is indeed as something other than itself, not of its own positioning. But the Cause and Being are to be in such a state, and to belong to such a one—both together. It is clear that it will make these things differently; for some things will be different and otherwise, and especially those things directed toward the best. From this source, these things have already received their power, both in themselves and in relation to that source. Of all those things which have their causes within themselves, everything originates from itself. Nothing of the Cause and the <term>causal essence</term> <note>Greek: "ousias aitiōdous." This refers to the fundamental nature of a thing that serves as the reason for its own existence.</note> is directed toward another. 

But that which transcends all things is without any share in <term>chance</term> <note>Greek: "tychē." In Greek philosophy, "chance" implies an accidental or random occurrence without a purposeful cause. The author argues the Good is too supreme to be accidental.</note>, because everything that comes from it has no communion with chance. Truly, that which is first from itself willed to be, and it is its own <term>will</term> <note>Greek: "boulēma."</note>, so that it is both itself and from itself. And through itself, it is itself; for it is directed toward itself, and it is that which it gave itself. For it is the Cause, and it is the same, and it is Being itself. One must see that principle as absolutely beautiful, and within itself.

For even Being is in it, and the Cause is in it. But the thing is not also the Cause in the sense of being one and the same; yet it was necessary for this to be a single thing. And the manner of being there <note>Referring to the "intelligible realm," the higher plane of reality in Neoplatonic thought.</note> will be found in a great comprehension of <term>hypostasis</term> <note>Greek: "hypostasis." A technical term for a distinct, underlying reality or individual substance.</note>. And like a subject to which one must look, one must reveal and speak of these things: that He is from Himself, and He is Himself exactly what He is. And it is the thing itself, and properly of itself; not as if He later willed to become, but as He wills Himself, so He already is. His will, being directed toward Himself, <gloss>receives itself</gloss>. 

Nor would these things happen to one who wills it. Such a thing would not only be such in itself, but the purest of all things. But in every case, his whole being is dependent on his nature. If we have examples from the images or the purest things among us, it is because it happens by chance. And for these things to exist by chance—whenever He wills not to speak of slavery and necessity—of these things alone it is not possible to say they are of themselves. It would be a light in which it also happens; in the elderly and the purest. It is not that they possess the "beyond-thought"; but if we grant them intellect and judgment, not only that, but leaving all other things aside, whatever it wills for itself comes from that source; and it will be for itself. Collecting together the things of the soul or the mind, one should hold fast to that which is unchangeable and unmoved and stands firm. It will be less by confession unchangeable; and just as other things are partial. And it is sufficient for them to be an <term>essence</term> <note>Greek: "ousia."</note>. But this will not happen there. And this we say. Or it would not be chance; nor would life be for Him, for being is mostly perception.

<summary>This page argues that the First Principle (the Good) is not a product of chance but is self-caused and identical with its own Will. It explores the metaphysical necessity of the Divine being the master of its own essence, existing as a "beyond-thought" reality that anchors all other beings.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the translation of Plotinus’s Ennead VI.8, moving from section 18 into the subsequent arguments. Here, the philosopher deepens the exploration of the "One" (the Divine Principle). He is addressing a difficult paradox: if the One is the source of everything, does it "make" itself? Plotinus argues that God is not a "product" or a "subject" of fate, but is pure Activity (energeia) that exists before the very concept of "Being" or "Essence" (ousia) was even defined.</meta>

<margin>But this [point] is so.</margin>
For even before himself, it is as if there is a commonality in him: whatever he might wish himself to be, that he is—whatever he wills. It is, so to speak, his own, and he is this willingly, if indeed his very "being" was such as it was. He is not simply a <term>subject</term> <note>Greek: "hypokeimenon." In ancient philosophy, this refers to the underlying "stuff" or substrate that has properties. Plotinus argues God is not a "thing" that possesses qualities, but is pure existence itself.</note>, for he is <term>Activity</term> <note>Greek: "energeia." This is a central term for Plotinus; it means a dynamic "doing" or "actuality." The Divine is not a static object but a pure act of being.</note>. All things belonging to him are activities. Just as he made himself—or rather, as it is impossible for some things to be generated and receive their nature from external activities—he remains unmoved toward anything outside himself.

He will say of himself that he is not just as much as he might have willed from "above" in a primary sense, but by being his own, he is so willingly to himself. One might reasonably say these things: that he does not ignore this, just as he possesses his <term>essence</term> <note>Greek: "ousia." Often translated as "substance" or "being," it refers to the core reality of a thing.</note>. But he must also <term>subsist</term> <note>Greek: "hypostēnai," the verb form of "hypostasis." It refers to how the Divine stands in its own reality.</note> for himself and be, as it were, by himself. Having seen that his nature is one—which these other things are not—he is not simply subject to corruption. He is able to fulfill the things that come from him. And now he would hold all things within himself, and those things are there as if seen by an eye. Who then would not see that wherever he loves, he is there? Therefore, they say the Divine is master of himself—especially regarding the things concerning himself which remain, whoever might <insert>see</insert> them.

<margin>How Activity is master of Essence and beyond Essence</margin>
And this is the nature of his essence: he becomes himself. Among those who worship him most deeply, it is not only that he does not "exist" [as a common thing], but that he is neither a people nor an essence; nor is essence his beginning. Rather, he himself is the principle of essence, and he himself is not a <term>substance</term> <note>Greek: "hypostasis." Here used to mean the underlying reality that supports essence. Plotinus argues God is the "source" of reality, not a part of it.</note> for essence. Rather, he is himself by himself, just as it was said: from nothing else could we attribute his being but from himself. Therefore, it is not at all the case that "Being" is something that happens to be in something else, before the act of thinking (intellection) occurs. If, then, he makes himself, he is the essence of himself. But he is the same, as if the <term>subject</term> <note>Greek: "hypokeimenon."</note> exists from himself.

<margin>How God is Activity</margin>
It must be said that he is not many, nor is he merely "making" [himself]. Rather, all these same things release his "making" when he is positioned. It is not so that something else results from him through his making, but because activity is his own—not as a completed result, but as the whole of such a thing. For we should not fear that an activity placed around him creates an essence. Rather, this very thing is greater: to establish God in a <term>substantial reality</term> <note>Greek: "hypostasis."</note> instead of placing him as a mere activity. For every principle is incomplete until it becomes most sovereign. And in another way, the activity which exists in "being" is perfect—not an activity *of* the essence, but the most perfect [state]. Or the first. And the first activity is that which exists in "being" itself. And it is not as if it <unclear>happened by chance</unclear>.

<summary>Plotinus argues that the Divine (the One) is pure Activity (energeia) and is the source of its own existence rather than a product of fate or chance. He clarifies that the Divine is "beyond essence," acting as the very principle that allows essence and being to exist.</summary>
<keywords>Plotinus, Activity, Energeia, Essence, Ousia, Hypostasis, The One, Divine Will, Self-Sufficiency, Neoplatonism</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the exploration of the Divine "One" and its relationship to the created world, following the discussion of God as pure Activity (energeia). Here, the author shifts focus to how this divine influence extends to physical bodies and the hierarchy of "Being," referencing Aristotle to support the ontological argument.</meta>

So too it is with bodies. If one were to contemplate this correctly—how all other things are from God—one sees that each has a certain <term>participation</term> <note>Greek: "metousia." A central concept in Platonic thought where physical things "share in" or "participate" in the qualities of the higher Divine forms.</note> in Him. Even if something is not understood well, He does not withdraw; the administration is neither "worldly" nor "unworldly." Instead, all things, even those below, are always governed by Him as if by an infinite power. By leaning upon Him, all things allow themselves to be carried and beautified by Him alone, without adding or taking anything away. This is not by their own will, but it flows from the One in succession to all. He will receive everything that is capable of contributing to the whole. This is not something received later or named after the fact; it was a name of freedom rather than of slavery, remaining within itself, truly itself. Let this be applied to each of them as is worthy.

<margin>9</margin>
<margin>Each thing is what it is insofar as it is.
<note>original Latin: "Idem exprimitur ab Aristotele libro 1° metaph. et meteorologius. In quibus fidei intentionem et theologiam."</note>
The same is expressed by Aristotle in the 1st book of the *Metaphysics* and the *Meteorology*. In which he [discusses] the intention of faith and theology.</margin>

All these things, which are "non-beings" <note>In Neoplatonism, "non-being" often refers to the physical world, which is less "real" than the eternal world of ideas.</note> insofar as they are compared to the primary Beings, are said to exist for the sake of those Beings, even if they do exist in their own way. Nor are they "out of tune."
<margin>3</margin>
For those things are neither non-existent, nor should they be considered immeasurable. They are "beings," yet they are "non-beings" in the sense that they do not exist by their own nature but according to the needs and requirements of others. They contribute to the whole and to everything just as they are in themselves. But even if they are placed there, they know only as much as they are, yet they miss the mark. Regarding appearances and bodies—as if one were to see a primary likeness—those things imagined are within them. While other things are coming into being, they take on different forms. And if a likeness is made, it is not of the body, but of the doctrines and beauties; when these parts are held "below," they are consumed. There is a virtue sometimes, but when it is a <term>hand-rule</term> <note>Greek/Latin hybrid: "kanōn manualiō." This likely refers to a practical or "manual" standard of measurement used for physical objects rather than spiritual truths.</note> from within, for not all things belong to the image itself. It gives an appearance, deceiving and shaping and arranging, and those who come to it fall into error. Likewise with colors and the shapes themselves; just as other things used by bodies do not belong to the body itself, they give a kind of beauty of form. But these are different from the source. The presence within them does not give of itself, though the body thinks it has been given. And looking toward the "Good," if it creates each thing just as it is toward itself, it creates a lawlessness for itself, yet it has received all these things. Thus, each thing is as it is.

<summary>This page discusses the divine governance of the physical world through "participation," arguing that even lower "non-beings" (physical objects) are beautified by God. It cites Aristotle's Metaphysics to explain how things exist in relation to a primary source of Being.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the nature of the Divine One and its relationship to the "many" things in the world. ...to each part; and while the whole is common to all, it is not the same for all, as one might immediately consider—perhaps contrary to expectation. First, one must realize that the One is not "common" in the sense of being divided among each part, nor is it a sequence of individual things. These matters will be discussed later, for each thing exists externally. For the **soul** <term>Soul</term> <note>Greek: "psyche." It is not simply that because "all things" exist, it must also exist. For it does not exist in that way, nor does it exist within those things. Furthermore, if things come from a source, we must ask "where?"—for "where" does not mean "in what manner." The One is not "all things" in the sense of being their cause in a simple way; for what would it then possess?

<margin>Why it is difficult to know the One.</margin>

But if someone wonders why it is not easy to be that One—which is even less easy than knowing what comes before it—the internal part of it might be moved. If someone were strengthened, beginning in this way within themselves, it would not be possible for any power to fully encompass it; for it is **indefinite** <term>Indefinite</term> <note>Greek: "aoriston." Therefore, in such states, it often retreats from these heights and falls back...

<margin>How one is raised toward the One; and concerning the desire for it.</margin>

...until it reaches the level of **sensation** <note>Greek: "aisthesis." The world of physical sight, sound, and touch.</note>. Having contracted itself as if through a narrow passage, it finds itself among small things, even though it is truly great and stands around the One. The soul desires to see itself and the **Intelligible**, seeing it alone in order to be united with it. There was a time when it was within the One, and did not know the things prior to it. Even if the underlying reality is the Intelligible, we must strive toward a <unclear>conception</unclear> <note>Greek: "ennoia."</note> that belongs to the realm of **philosophy** <term>Philosophize</term> <note>Greek: "philosophein." We perform these tasks and do not allow ourselves to be pushed away toward the "foamy" or superficial things. It is possible to fall from the whole, but one should rather be struck with awe by that which is among the First, turning away from the things of the senses. And yet, what do they say? <meta>This page concludes the transcription of Plotinus’s "Enneads," specifically the final chapter of VI.9, "On the Good or the One." It transitions from the previous page's discussion of the soul’s erotic longing for the divine into the final state of isolation and union with the "Alone." The page concludes with a significant colophon by the famous Byzantine scribe Johannes Scutariotes.</meta>

<margin>
41 <note>This marginal number likely refers to a chapter or section in the scribe's reference text.</note>
</margin>

While every soul is blessed, she shall arrive at the Good, and thus she remains alone, not among the whole but alone for herself; having run the opposite course, she will cease her journey not departing from herself, but entering into herself.
<margin>
<unclear>alkb</unclear> <note>Perhaps a reference code or library shelf mark added later.</note>
</margin>
And so, not being trapped in a material dwelling, she is an indivisible waning <note>original: "phthisin." Here used to describe the "fading away" of the soul's attachment to the physical world.</note> of the lower self. And not only from these things are the contents within read through as pre-voluntary; but the ends and the "burnings" <note>original: "kausias." A metaphorical reference to the intense, refining fire of divine contact.</note> of this contact. From this point, following this very path, matter is made like her. And by the removal of those descending things, she sees the archetype as a rule. The end of **contemplation** <term>contemplation</term> <note>original: "theoria." In this philosophical tradition, it refers to a deep, intellectual "seeing" or direct spiritual intuition of reality.</note> is to understand the soul's whole virtue, to despise the pollutions of vice, and to be lightened from the burden of weaknesses; so that one might appear pure among gods and men. This is the blessed life, having ascended to the things that truly exist here. —— 88. <insert>ee 90.</insert>

The gift is God's, and the labor is Johannes's. —
Written by the hand of Johannes Scutariotes; in the city of Florence, on the 10th of the month of December; at the sixth hour, the 4th day of the week; in the year from the creation of the world 6,960 <note>The Byzantine calendar year 6960 corresponds to 1451/1452 AD.</note>, with the care of Plato <note>original: "meta epimeleias tou Platonos." This likely refers to the scribe's dedication to the Platonic tradition or his work within the circle of the Platonic Academy in Renaissance Florence.</note>.
